question: M is the mother of N. N’s father is O. O’s sister is P. P’s son is Q. Q’s wife is R. R’s brother is S. What is S to M using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: M’s child N and Q are first cousins (children of siblings O and P). R is Q’s wife, so S is R’s brother, i.e., Q’s brother‑in‑law. There is no blood or affinal link that connects S to M within standard English kinship; thus no standard term applies.

question: R is married to S. S's brother is T. T is married to U. U's sister is V. Using standard English kinship terms only (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is V to R?
explanation: R→S (spouse) →T (spouse’s brother, brother‑in‑law) →U (brother‑in‑law’s spouse) →V (spouse’s sibling). This chain exceeds the allowed in‑law scope, so no standard English kin term exists for V relative to R.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: X’s mother has a brother U whose daughter is A. X’s father has a sister V whose son is B. A and B marry and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms, what is C’s relation to X?
explanation: U’s daughter A is X’s maternal first cousin; V’s son B is X’s paternal first cousin. Their child C is one generation below X’s first cousins, making C X’s first cousin once removed. No more specific term exists.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter D. N has a son S, whose son is J. What is the precise standard English kinship term for the relation of J to M?
explanation: M is the sister of N, so M is the aunt/uncle of N’s child S. J is S’s son, making J the grand‑nephew/niece of M. The exact term is great‑aunt (or great‑uncle) for M relative to J, i.e., J is M’s great‑nephew/niece.
choices: D) No standard direct kin term

question: L's mother has a brother R, whose daughter is T. L's father has a sister S, whose son is U. T and U marry and have a child V. What is V's precise relationship to L using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed)?
explanation: T is L's maternal first cousin; U is L's paternal first cousin. V is the child of two of L's first cousins, each from a different parental side, so V shares both sets of L's grandparents. The exact term is double first cousin once removed.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed
B) B) Double first cousin once removed
C) C) Half‑first cousin once removed

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father. M is married to O, who is the child of P. P is the brother of Q, who is the mother of N. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, ignoring in‑law links), what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M’s mother and N’s father are siblings, so M and N are each the child of one of those siblings. That makes them children of siblings, i.e., first cousins. The additional marital ties (O, P, Q) do not affect the blood relationship between M and N.

question: E and F are siblings. G and H are also siblings. E marries H, and F marries G. Their children are X (child of E & H) and Y (child of F & G). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: the parents of E/F and the parents of G/H. Hence they are first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins. No other term captures the dual shared lineage.

question: M is the child of the sister of P’s father, and also the child of the brother of P’s mother. Assuming no intermarriage beyond what is stated, what is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to P?
explanation: The sister of P’s father is P’s paternal aunt, so M is P’s paternal first cousin. The brother of P’s mother is P’s maternal uncle, so M is also P’s maternal first cousin. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes M a double first cousin of P.

question: M and N are brothers. P and Q are sisters. M marries P and they have a son X. N marries Q and they have a daughter Y. No other intermarriages occur. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: M’s parents and P’s parents are also N’s and Q’s parents respectively. Thus they have two common grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the precise term for this doubled ancestry.

question: Person Y’s mother has exactly one sibling, and that sibling is the parent of person X. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: Y’s mother’s sibling is Y’s maternal aunt/uncle. X is the child of that aunt/uncle, making X the child of Y’s maternal aunt/uncle – i.e., Y’s first cousin. No other relations apply.

question: Anna and Beth are half‑sisters who share only their mother. Anna’s son is Carl. Beth marries David, who is the brother of Emma, Carl’s wife. Beth and David have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise blood relation between Carl and Fiona?
explanation: Anna and Beth share only one parent, so they are half‑sisters. Their children Carl and Fiona share only that one grandparent, making them half‑first cousins. David being Emma’s brother adds only an affinal link and does not alter the blood relationship.

question: Let R be a person. R’s mother has exactly one brother, and R’s father has exactly one brother. The child of the maternal uncle and the child of the paternal uncle are the same individual, S. What is S’s precise kinship to R using standard English terms?
explanation: S is the child of a brother of R’s mother (maternal uncle) and also the child of a brother of R’s father (paternal uncle). In either case S is the child of a parent’s sibling, which is the definition of a first cousin.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: L’s mother has a brother M. M’s son N has a daughter O. What is O’s relation to L, using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed)?
explanation: M is L’s maternal uncle, so N is L’s first cousin. O is N’s daughter, making O L’s first cousin once removed.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a daughter X; N and P have a son Y. X and Y marry each other and have children Z (X’s child) and W (Y’s child). What is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between Z and W?
explanation: X and Y are double first cousins, sharing both pairs of grandparents. Their children therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making Z and W double second cousins—the most exact term.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: M and N are siblings. M’s daughter marries N’s son and they have a child X. M’s son marries N’s daughter and they have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X’s parents are first cousins (M’s daughter and N’s son) and Y’s parents are also first cousins (M’s son and N’s daughter). Because the two sibling pairs (M‑N) married each other’s children, X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the exact term for this doubled lineage.

question: In a family with no adoptions, let P be the child of the only brother of R’s mother and also the child of the only brother of R’s father. What is the precise kinship term for P in relation to R?
explanation: Both the mother’s only brother and the father’s only brother are R’s uncles. Their child, P, is the child of two of R’s uncles, i.e., the child of a parent’s sibling on each side. Regardless of which uncle is the father, P is always the child of an uncle, making P R’s first cousin.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M has only one brother N. N is married to O. O has one child, P, from a previous marriage. M has a daughter Q, and Q marries P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption), what is the precise relation of P to M?
explanation: N is M’s brother, so O is M’s sister‑in‑law. P, O’s child from a prior marriage, is N’s step‑child, making P M’s step‑niece. There is no blood link, so ‘niece’ is inaccurate; ‘cousin’ is unrelated; the relation is uniquely ‘step‑niece’.

question: Brothers Kevin and Liam each marry sisters Tara and Zoe, respectively (Kevin + Tara, Liam + Zoe). Kevin and Tara have a daughter Maya; Liam and Zoe have a son Noah. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Maya and Noah?
explanation: Kevin and Liam are brothers; Tara and Zoe are sisters. Each brother married a sister from the other family. Their children therefore share both sets of grandparents, making Maya and Noah double first cousins. No other term captures the doubled ancestry.

question: L and M are full siblings. L’s son is N; M’s daughter is O. N’s daughter is P; O’s son is Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: L and M are siblings, so N and O are first cousins. Their children P and Q are the children of first cousins, which makes them second cousins. No other relationship (e.g., removal) applies.

question: L has one sister and one brother. The only son of L’s sister has a child M, and the only daughter of L’s brother also has a child M (the same person). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s relation to L?
explanation: The sister’s son is L’s nephew; his child is L’s great‑nephew (if male) or great‑niece (if female). The brother’s daughter is L’s niece; her child is likewise L’s great‑nephew/niece. Thus M is L’s great‑nephew or great‑niece, the term depending on M’s gender.
choices: A) A) Great‑nephew or great‑niece (depending on gender)
B) B) First cousin once removed

question: M’s mother has two children, M and N. N is married to O. O’s mother has a son P, who is married to Q. Q’s father is the brother of M’s father. What is the precise kinship term for the relationship between M and P using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: M and Q are first cousins because their fathers are brothers. P is Q’s spouse, making P the spouse of M’s first cousin. The exact term for that relationship is “cousin‑in‑law”.
choices: D) D) No direct kinship term

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, N marries P. M and O have a daughter Q; N and P have a son R. Q and R later marry each other. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the most precise blood relation between Q and R before they marry?
explanation: Q and R are children of two sibling pairs (M–N and O–P). They therefore share both sets of grandparents, giving them the exact relationship of double first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, who has a brother P. N marries Q, who is the sister of P. P and Q each have one child: X (child of P and his spouse) and Y (child of Q and her spouse). Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise kinship term between X and Y?
explanation: M and N are siblings; O and Q are siblings (both children of the same parents). Thus X and Y are children of double first cousins (P and Q are first cousins through O‑Q and also through M‑N). Their children share both sets of great‑grandparents, making X and Y double second cousins, the most specific term.

question: M is the only child of his mother. M’s father has a sister N. N has one child P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of P to M?
explanation: N is the sister of M’s father, i.e., M’s paternal aunt. Her child P is therefore the child of M’s aunt, which makes P M’s first cousin. No half‑blood or step connections exist, so the term is uniquely "first cousin".

question: John and Tom are brothers. Their sister Mary is the mother of Peter. Tom has a daughter, Alice. Peter marries Alice. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between Peter and Alice?
explanation: Mary and Tom are siblings, so their parents are the common grandparents of both Peter (through Mary) and Alice (through Tom). Therefore Peter and Alice are the children of two siblings, i.e., first cousins. No other kin term fits more precisely.

question: Z is simultaneously the child of Y’s maternal uncle and the child of Y’s paternal uncle (no other intermarriages). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise term for Z’s relation to Y?
explanation: Z is the child of both Y’s mother’s brother and Y’s father’s brother, so Z shares both pairs of grandparents with Y. Sharing both grandparent sets makes them double first cousins, the exact term.

question: John’s mother remarried Peter, who is the biological father of John’s half‑sister Mary (they share only their mother). Mary is married to Tom. Tom’s mother, N, is the sister of John’s paternal grandmother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of N to John?
explanation: John’s father’s mother is John’s paternal grandmother. N, being her sister, is a child of the same great‑grandparents, making N John’s great‑aunt (the sister of his grandmother). No other path changes this blood link, so the exact term is great‑aunt.

question: P and Q are brothers. P’s only child is R; Q’s only child is S. R (married to T) has a son A, and S (married to U) has a daughter C. Assuming monogamy (remarriage allowed) and no adoptions, what is the most precise standard English kinship term between A and C?
explanation: R and S are first cousins because their parents (P and Q) are siblings. A and C are the children of those first cousins, so they share the same great‑grandparents, making them second cousins.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary’s son Peter marries Susan, who is the daughter of John’s son Michael. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the most precise description of Peter’s relation to Michael?
explanation: Peter is Mary’s son, making him John’s nephew and Michael’s first cousin. By marrying Susan, Michael’s daughter, Peter also becomes Michael’s son‑in‑law. No single standard term covers both roles, so the precise description is that Peter is both Michael’s first cousin and son‑in‑law.
choices: C) Both first cousin and son‑in‑law (no single term)

question: M and N are siblings. M’s child is A. N’s child is B. M also has a sister whose child is D, and D’s child is C. What is the precise blood relationship between A and C using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: A is M’s child. D is the child of M’s sister, so A and D are first cousins. C is D’s child, making C the first cousin once removed of A. No other listed relation fits.

question: In a family, M and N are siblings. M’s daughter is A; N’s son is B. A marries C, who is the sole child of D. D’s brother is E, whose daughter is F. If B and F are first cousins, what is the most precise kinship term for A to B?
explanation: A is M’s daughter, M is B’s aunt, so A is B’s first cousin. The extra chain through C, D, E, F does not affect A‑B relation, keeping it a single first‑cousin link.

question: Alice and Bob share only their mother (they are half‑brothers). Alice has a daughter Clara. Bob has a son Daniel. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between Clara and Daniel?
explanation: Alice and Bob are half‑siblings, sharing one parent. Their children therefore share only that one grandparent, not a full pair. The exact term for such children is “half‑first cousins.”
choices: D) D) No direct kinship term

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy (but remarriage after death allowed), let X be the child of the only brother of Y's mother, and also the child of the only sister of Y's father. What is the precise kinship term for X in relation to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and simultaneously the child of Y's paternal aunt (father's sister). Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the exact term for cousins related through both parental lines.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let N be a person. N’s father has exactly one sibling (a brother) and N’s mother has exactly one sibling (a sister). The brother of N’s father marries the sister of N’s mother, and they have a single child M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal uncle and also the child of N’s maternal aunt. Because the two siblings married each other, M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making M a double first cousin – the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries P and N marries Q. P and Q are also siblings (no other intermarriages). Their only children are X (child of M + P) and Y (child of N + Q). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their parents are two pairs of siblings. This makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: In a family, M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N marries O's husband’s brother P, and they have a son Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of Q to O?
explanation: O's husband’s brother P is O's brother‑in‑law. N, O's sibling, marries P, making P also O's brother‑in‑law by marriage. Their child Q is therefore the child of O's brother‑in‑law, which makes Q O's nephew‑in‑law. No blood link exists, so the correct term is "nephew‑in‑law".
choices: D) D) No standard kinship term

question: X's mother has a brother A, and X's father has a sister B. A and B are married to each other. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between X and the child of A and B?
explanation: A is X's maternal uncle and B is X's paternal aunt. Their child shares both sets of grandparents with X, making X and that child first cousins on both sides—i.e., double first cousins. No finer term applies.

question: M is married to N. N’s sister O is married to P. P’s brother Q is married to R, who is the daughter of M’s brother S. What is Q’s precise relation to M using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: R is M’s niece (daughter of M’s brother). Q, as R’s husband, is M’s nephew‑in‑law. No blood link exists; the correct term is nephew‑in‑law.

question: M is the mother of J and K. J is married to L. L's brother is P. P's mother is Q, who is also a daughter of M and the sister of K. What is the relation of P to M?
explanation: J and K are siblings, both children of M. Q is also a child of M, making her K’s sister. P is Q’s child, therefore P is the child of M’s daughter – a grandchild of M.

question: Mia's mother has exactly one brother, Alan. Mia's father has exactly one brother, Brian. Alan and Brian are married to each other and have a single child, Zoe. What is Zoe's precise relationship to Mia using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Zoe is the child of Mia’s maternal uncle (her mother’s brother) and also of Mia’s paternal uncle (her father’s brother). Each makes Zoe a first cousin of Mia; because the relationship occurs on both parental sides, the precise term is “double first cousin.”

question: L's mother has a brother N, whose daughter is O. L's father has a sister R, whose son is S. O and S marry and have a child T. What is T's relation to L?
explanation: O is L's maternal first cousin; S is L's paternal first cousin. O and S are unrelated to each other, so their child T is the child of L's first cousin on both sides, making T a first cousin once removed. No other listed relation fits.

question: R’s mother’s brother has a daughter S. R’s father’s sister has a son T. S and T marry and have a child C. What is C’s relation to R, using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: S is R’s maternal first cousin; T is R’s paternal first cousin. Their child C is one generation below R and is the child of R’s first cousin on each side, making C R’s first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: Let R be a person. P is the child of the only brother of R’s mother, and Q is the child of the only brother of R’s father. If we select either P or Q and call that person S, what is S to R using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed)?
explanation: Regardless of whether S is P or Q, S is the child of a parent’s brother – a sibling of a parent. That makes S a first cousin of R. The relation is uniquely determined and does not depend on which side the uncle comes from.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M is the mother of N and O. N is married to P. P’s sister Q is married to O’s son R. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Q’s relation to M?
explanation: M→O (child) →R (grandchild) →Q (spouse of that grandchild). This chain goes beyond the immediate in‑law scope; there is no standard direct kin term for such an affinal link, so Q has no standard direct relation to M.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John and Mary are siblings. John marries Alice and Mary marries Bob. Alice and Bob are also siblings. John and Alice’s child is Carl; Mary and Bob’s child is Dana. Using standard English kinship terms (allowing doubled ancestry), what is the most precise relation between Carl and Dana?
explanation: Carl and Dana share both sets of grandparents: John‑Mary’s parents and Alice‑Bob’s parents. Hence they are first cousins through two independent lines, i.e., double first cousins. No other term captures this exact double relationship.

question: Adam and his sister Beth are siblings. Adam marries Clara; Clara's brother is David. Beth marries David. Adam and Clara have a daughter Emma. Beth and David have a son Frank. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Emma and Frank?
explanation: Adam and Beth share the same parents, as do Clara and David. Their children Emma and Frank therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the dual shared ancestry.

question: A’s mother and B’s father are siblings, and A’s father and B’s mother are also siblings. There are no other intermarriages. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both pairs of grandparents: one through their mothers and one through their fathers. Sharing two grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a distinct term from ordinary first cousins or half‑cousins.

question: X's mother has exactly one brother, and X's father has exactly one sister. The brother of X's mother marries the sister of X's father, and they have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is the most precise relation of Y to X?
explanation: Y is the child of X's maternal uncle and paternal aunt, who are themselves siblings of X's parents. Therefore Y shares both sets of grandparents with X, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: N’s father has a sister A, and N’s mother has a brother B. A and B are married and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s precise relationship to N?
explanation: A is N’s paternal aunt and B is N’s maternal uncle. Their child M is simultaneously the child of N’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle, making M a first cousin on both sides – the exact term is double first cousin.

question: N’s father has exactly one sister, and N’s mother has exactly one brother. The sister and the brother marry each other and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M’s parents are N’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle. Therefore M shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making them first cousins on both sides – the exact term is double first cousin.
choices: C) C) No uniquely determinable relation

question: M and N are siblings. P and Q are siblings. M marries P and N marries Q. Their children are X (child of M and P) and Y (child of N and Q). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X’s parents are both siblings of Y’s parents, so X and Y share both sets of grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: Using standard English kinship terms only (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), Person P is the child of the only brother of Q’s mother and also the child of the only sister of Q’s father. What is the precise relation of P to Q?
explanation: P is the child of Q’s maternal uncle and also the child of Q’s paternal aunt, so P shares both sets of grandparents with Q. This makes them double first cousins, the most exact term.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let Y be a person whose mother has a brother M and whose father has a sister N. M’s child is X, and N’s child is also X (the same individual). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: M is Y’s maternal uncle, so X is Y’s first cousin on the mother’s side. N is Y’s paternal aunt, so X is also Y’s first cousin on the father’s side. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes X a double first cousin of Y.

question: Let X be the child of the only brother of A’s mother and also the child of the only brother of A’s father. Assuming no adoption or remarriage, what is X’s precise kinship term to A?
explanation: X is the child of A’s maternal uncle and also the child of A’s paternal uncle. In both cases X is a child of a parent’s sibling, which makes X a first cousin of A. The double‑uncle link does not change the basic cousin relationship.

question: P's father's sister has a child M, and P's mother's brother also has a child M (the same person). Using standard English kinship terms and assuming no adoption, what is the precise relation between M and P?
explanation: M is the child of P's paternal aunt (father's sister) and also the child of P's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Both links make M a first cousin on each side, i.e., a double first cousin of P.

question: Two brothers marry two sisters (no other marriages among them). The older brother and the older sister have a daughter L; the younger brother and the younger sister have a son M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of L to M?
explanation: Each pair of parents are siblings, so L and M share both sets of grandparents. That makes them first cousins on the paternal side and also first cousins on the maternal side, i.e., double first cousins—the only term that captures both shared grandparent pairs.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, N marries P, and O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. Hence they are first cousins on two distinct parental lines, i.e., double first cousins—the most precise term.

question: A's mother has exactly one brother, and A's father has exactly one sister. The child of that brother and the child of that sister are the same person X. What is the precise kinship term for X in relation to A, using standard English blood‑relation terminology (no in‑laws or adoption)?
explanation: X is the offspring of A's maternal uncle and paternal aunt, who are married. X shares both sets of grandparents with A, making X a double first cousin—the most specific term for this doubled ancestry.

question: M has two children, L and R, by different fathers. L marries Tom; R marries Dan. Tom and Dan are half‑brothers (they share the same mother, Sarah, but have different fathers). What is the precise kinship term for the relation between L’s child and R’s child?
explanation: Tom and Dan are half‑brothers, so their children are children of half‑brothers. That makes L’s child and R’s child half‑first cousins. No other blood link alters this relationship.

question: John’s mother is Eleanor. John has a son Alex from an earlier marriage; Mary (John’s wife) has a daughter Beth from an earlier marriage. Alex and Beth marry and have a child Clara. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only), what is Clara’s relation to Eleanor?
explanation: Alex is Eleanor’s grandson (Eleanor → John → Alex). Clara is Alex’s daughter, adding one more generation. Thus Clara is Eleanor’s great‑granddaughter. No other listed term matches.

question: John has one son, Adam, and one brother, Ben, who has one daughter, Clara. Mary has one sister, Eve, whose only daughter is Fiona, and one brother, George, whose only son is Henry. Adam marries Fiona, and Ben’s daughter Clara marries Henry. Their respective children are P (child of Adam & Fiona) and Q (child of Clara & Henry). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: Adam and Fiona are siblings of opposite families, as are Clara and Henry. Thus P’s parents are children of John and Mary, while Q’s parents are also children of John and Mary. Both P and Q share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: Anna’s mother and Ben’s father are siblings, and Anna’s father and Ben’s mother are also siblings. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between Anna and Ben?
explanation: Anna and Ben share both sets of grandparents because each of their parents are siblings with the opposite parent. Hence they are first cousins with a doubled pedigree, i.e., double first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries P; N marries Q, where P and Q are siblings. M and P have a son S. N and Q have a daughter T. T’s daughter is U. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of S to U?
explanation: M and N share both parents, and P and Q share both parents, so S and T share all four grandparents – they are double first cousins. A child of a double first cousin is a double first cousin once removed. Hence S is U’s double first cousin once removed.
choices: A) Double first cousin once removed

question: A has one paternal uncle (the only brother of A’s father) and one maternal aunt (the only sister of A’s mother). Those two relatives marry each other and have a single child, X. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and A?
explanation: X is the child of A’s paternal uncle and maternal aunt, so X shares both of A’s grandparent pairs. This makes X and A double first cousins, the term that reflects the doubled shared ancestry.

question: Emma’s mother has a brother named Carl. Carl’s daughter Fiona is Emma’s first cousin. Fiona has a son named Leo. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of Emma to Leo?
explanation: Emma and Fiona are first cousins (children of siblings). Fiona’s son Leo is one generation below Fiona, so Emma is one generation above Leo’s parent, making Emma Leo’s first cousin once removed.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: A's mother has a brother B, whose only child is C. A's father has a sister D, whose only child is E. C and E marry and have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation between A and F?
explanation: C is A's maternal first cousin (child of mother's brother). E is A's paternal first cousin (child of father's sister). C and E are unrelated, so their child F is the child of A's first cousin on both sides, making F A's first cousin once removed. No doubling occurs because the cousins share no common grandparents.

question: M is the only child of his mother. His mother’s sister (M’s aunt) is married to N. N’s brother’s daughter is P. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses), what is P to M?
explanation: M’s aunt’s husband N is M’s uncle‑in‑law. N’s brother is unrelated to M; his daughter P is the niece of N, not linked by blood or permitted in‑law ties to M. Hence no standard direct kin term exists between P and M.
choices: A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John's father has a brother who is married to John's mother's sister. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation of John to his father's brother's wife?
explanation: The woman is John's maternal aunt by blood (mother's sister) and also his paternal aunt‑in‑law (wife of his father's brother). Standard kinship does not provide a single term that captures both roles, so the precise relation cannot be uniquely specified.

question: Mara’s mother has a brother, Peter. Peter’s daughter, Nina, is married to Omar, who is the son of Mara’s father’s brother, Victor. Ignoring all affinal links and using only standard English blood‑kin terms, what is the precise relation of Nina to Omar?
explanation: Peter is Mara’s maternal uncle, so Nina is Mara’s first cousin. Victor is Mara’s paternal uncle, so Omar is also Mara’s first cousin. Nina and Omar’s parents (Peter and Victor) are unrelated, so Nina and Omar share no common ancestor. Hence there is no blood‑kin term; they are unrelated.

question: Mary and Susan share the same mother but have different fathers. Mary’s son is John. Susan is married to Thomas. What is Thomas’s precise relationship to John using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: Susan is Mary’s sister, so Thomas is Mary’s brother‑in‑law. To John, that makes Thomas his mother’s brother‑in‑law, i.e., his uncle‑in‑law. No blood link exists, and the term “uncle” alone is inaccurate.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: John and Mary are siblings. Mary has a daughter Anna. Anna is married to Tom. John’s wife Sarah is Tom’s sister. John and Sarah have a son Peter. What is Tom’s relation to Peter using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Tom is Sarah’s brother, making him the brother of Peter’s mother. The mother’s brother is the maternal uncle of the child. Hence Tom is Peter’s maternal uncle.

question: L’s mother has exactly one brother, M, and L’s father has exactly one sister, N. M’s only child is X and N’s only child is Y. If X and Y are the same person, what is the precise kinship term for that person to L (using standard English kinship terms, without ignoring doubled ancestry)?
explanation: X is the child of L’s maternal uncle (M) and paternal aunt (N). Therefore X shares both of L’s grandparent pairs, making X a double first cousin of L.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed

question: M and N are brother and sister. M marries O, whose brother is Q. N marries Q. X is the child of M and O; Y is the child of N and Q. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share both parents, and O and Q share both parents. Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents, which defines them as double first cousins—the most exact term.

question: Person P’s mother has a brother Q. Q’s daughter R is therefore P’s first cousin. P also has a brother S, whose son T is P’s nephew. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between R and T?
explanation: R is first cousin to P; T is nephew of P (child of P’s sibling). Thus T is the child of R’s cousin, making R and T first cousins once removed. No closer or different term applies.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother, and R’s father has exactly one brother. The son of R’s mother’s brother marries the daughter of R’s father’s brother, and they have a child S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation of S to R?
explanation: R’s mother’s brother’s son is R’s maternal first cousin; R’s father’s brother’s daughter is R’s paternal first cousin. Their child S is one generation below each cousin, making S a first cousin once removed on both the maternal and paternal sides. Since the relationship occurs through both parents, the precise term is “double first cousin once removed.”
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed
D) D) Double first cousin once removed

question: John is married to Mary. Mary's sister Lisa is married to John's brother Mark. John and Mary have a son Ben; Mark and Lisa have a daughter Anna. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Ben and Anna?
explanation: Ben's father is John, whose brother is Mark, Anna's father. Ben's mother is Mary, whose sister is Lisa, Anna's mother. Thus Ben and Anna share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures both paternal and maternal common ancestry.

question: Two brothers, Alan and Brian, each marry a sister, Clara and Diana respectively. Alan and Clara have a child, X; Brian and Diana have a child, Y. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: Alan and Brian share both parents, and Clara and Diana share both parents. Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term for this doubled lineage.

question: M and N are siblings. M has children A and D with different spouses; N has children B and E with different spouses. A marries B and they have a child C. D marries E and they have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between C and F?
explanation: A and B are first cousins (children of siblings M and N). D and E are also first cousins. C (child of A&B) and F (child of D&E) each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of M’s spouse and N’s spouse. Sharing all four grandparents makes C and F double first cousins.

question: J's father has exactly one sister and no other siblings; J's mother has exactly one brother and no other siblings. The sister of J's father marries the brother of J's mother, and they have a child M. What is the precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between M and J?
explanation: J's paternal aunt (father’s sister) and maternal uncle (mother’s brother) are spouses. Their child shares both sets of grandparents with J, making them first cousins through both parental lines. The exact term is “double first cousin.”

question: M and N are full siblings. M has a daughter O. N has two children: a son P and a daughter R. R has a daughter Q. What is the precise blood relation between O and Q, using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: O is the child of M, making her a first cousin of N’s children P and R. Since Q is R’s daughter, O is one generation above Q but is a cousin of Q’s mother. That makes O and Q first cousins once removed. No other listed term fits exactly.

question: In a family tree: 1) Alex is the child of Beth. 2) Beth's brother is Carl. 3) Carl's daughter is Dana. 4) Dana's son is Ethan. 5) Ethan marries Fiona, who is the child of Greg. 6) Greg is the sibling of Alex's father, Henry. What is the most precise standard English blood relation between Fiona and Beth?
explanation: Fiona is the child of Greg, who could be either Beth's brother (if Henry and Beth share the same parents) or Beth's brother‑in‑law (if Henry is Beth’s half‑brother). Depending on which parent is shared, Fiona is either Beth’s niece or Beth’s first cousin once removed. The information does not fix which case, so the exact relation cannot be uniquely determined.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: M has two children, A and B, by different fathers (so A and B are half‑siblings). A has a child C, and B has a child D. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between C and D?
explanation: A and B share only one parent, so their children share only one grandparent. The exact term for children of half‑siblings is “half‑first cousins”.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries P and N marries Q, where P and Q are also siblings. M and N each have one child, X and Y respectively. X and Y are unrelated spouses of their own children. What is the most precise standard kinship term between X’s child and Y’s child?
explanation: X and Y are double first cousins, sharing both sets of grandparents. Their children therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the most precise standard term.

question: M is married to W. M’s sister S is married to T. T’s sister U is married to V, who is W’s brother. X is the child of M and W; Y is the child of U and V. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: W and V are full siblings, so X (child of W) and Y (child of V) share both grandparents. Hence they are first cousins.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy, and no other intermarriages, let P be a person. Q is the child of P’s father’s sister, and R is the child of P’s mother’s brother. If Q and R are the same individual, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between P and that individual?
explanation: Q is P’s paternal first cousin (child of a paternal aunt). R is P’s maternal first cousin (child of a maternal uncle). Being the same person makes them both cousins, i.e., a double first cousin, the most specific term.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: Each child’s mother is the sister of the other child’s mother, and each child’s father is the brother of the other child’s father. Thus X and Y share both maternal and paternal grandparents, making them double first cousins.

question: M is the child of the sister of N’s father, and also the child of the brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: M’s mother is N’s paternal aunt and M’s father is N’s maternal uncle, so M shares both sets of grandparents with N. That makes them double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled ancestry.

question: Two brothers, A and B, each marry sisters, C and D, respectively. A and C have a son E; B and D have a daughter F. E and F marry and have a child G. Using standard English kinship terms (excluding modifiers like "double"), what is the precise relationship between G's paternal grandmother and G's maternal grandmother?
explanation: A and B share the same parents. Therefore the mother of A (paternal grandmother of G) is also the mother of B (maternal grandmother of G). The two grandmothers are the same woman, so their relationship is that they are the same individual.

question: R is married to S. S has a sister T, who is married to U. U’s mother is V. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is V’s relation to R?
explanation: S’s sister T is R’s sister‑in‑law. T’s husband U is the brother‑in‑law of S, but not a direct in‑law of R. V is U’s mother, i.e., the mother‑in‑law of T and the mother‑in‑law of R’s sister‑in‑law. No standard term exists for this affinal chain; the relation is not covered by ordinary kinship vocabulary.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, X’s mother has a brother U, and X’s father has a brother V. U and V are married to each other and have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Y’s precise relation to X?
explanation: Y is the child of X’s maternal uncle (U) and paternal uncle (V). Thus Y is X’s first cousin on both the mother’s and the father’s sides, making Y a double first cousin of X – the most specific standard term.

question: John’s mother has exactly one brother, Tom. John’s father has exactly one sister, Lisa. Tom and Lisa are married and have a daughter, Sara. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relationship between John and Sara?
explanation: Tom is John’s maternal uncle, so Sara is John’s first cousin on his mother’s side. Lisa is John’s paternal aunt, so Sara is also John’s first cousin on his father’s side. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the exact term.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother, who has a daughter S. R’s father has exactly one brother, who has a daughter T. If you select either S or T and call that person U, what is U to R?
explanation: Both S and T are children of a parent’s brother (maternal uncle or paternal uncle). In either case the child of an uncle is a first cousin to R, so U is always a first cousin.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, and N marries P. O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents (the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P). This makes them double first cousins, a term that captures the doubled shared ancestry.

question: R’s mother has a brother named M, and M has a daughter A. R’s father has a sister named S, and S has a son B. If we select either A or B and call that person T, what is T’s relation to R using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, in‑law terms limited to spouse and immediate relatives)?
explanation: A is the child of R’s maternal uncle, B is the child of R’s paternal aunt. Both are children of a parent’s sibling, which makes each a first cousin of R. The relation is uniquely first cousin regardless of which child is chosen.

question: Y's mother has exactly one brother and Y's father has exactly one sister. Those two siblings marry each other and have a child X. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is X's precise relation to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and Y's paternal aunt (father's sister). X therefore shares both of Y's maternal grandparents and both of Y's paternal grandparents, making X a double first cousin of Y, the most specific term.

question: M is the mother of N. N’s spouse is O. O’s mother is P. P’s brother is Q. Q’s daughter is R, who is married to S. S’s father is T. T’s sister is U, and U’s son is V. What is V’s relation to M using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no in‑law extensions)?
explanation: All links from M to V pass through marriages: M → N (blood) → O (spouse) → P (mother‑in‑law) → Q (sibling‑in‑law) → R (cousin‑in‑law) → S (spouse) → T (father‑in‑law) → U (sister‑in‑law) → V (nephew‑in‑law). No blood line connects M and V, so they are unrelated by blood.

question: John's mother Mary has a brother Paul. John's father Robert has a sister Linda. Paul and Linda are married and have a son Michael. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Michael's precise relation to John?
explanation: Paul is John’s maternal uncle; Linda is John’s paternal aunt. Their son Michael is therefore the child of John’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt simultaneously. He shares both sets of grandparents with John, making them double first cousins—the most precise term.

question: R is married to S. S’s sister is T, and T’s husband is U. U’s mother is V. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), who is V to R?
explanation: R → S (spouse) → T (sister‑in‑law) → U (brother‑in‑law) → V (U’s mother). This chain passes beyond the immediate in‑law scope; no direct English kin term links V to R. Hence the correct choice is D.
choices: D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M and N are siblings. M marries his first cousin O (child of M's maternal aunt). N marries O's brother P, who is also M's first cousin. M and O have a daughter X. N and P have a son Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share both parents; O and P share both parents. Each couple (M‑O and N‑P) consists of first cousins, so X’s paternal grandparents are M/N’s parents and maternal grandparents are O/P’s parents. Y has the same two sets of grandparents. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes X and Y double first cousins.

question: P is the child of the only brother of Q’s mother, and also the child of the only sister of Q’s father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise kinship term for the relation between P and Q?
explanation: P is the child of Q’s maternal uncle (first‑cousin side) and also the child of Q’s paternal aunt (first‑cousin side). Thus P and Q share both sets of grandparents, giving them the exact term “double first cousins”.
choices: C) C) First cousins once removed

question: Let X be a person. X's mother has exactly one brother, and that brother's son is Y. X's father has exactly one sister, and that sister's son is also Y. Assuming no adoptions or inter‑cousin marriages, what is Y's precise relationship to X?
explanation: Y is the child of X's maternal uncle and also the child of X's paternal aunt. Therefore Y shares both of X's grandparent pairs, making Y a double first cousin of X – the most specific standard term.

question: M is the only child of his father. N is the only child of M's mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of N to M?
explanation: M being his father's sole child means the father has no other offspring. N being the sole child of M's mother means the mother has no other offspring. These facts do not guarantee that M and N share a parent; they could be the same person, half‑siblings, or unrelated. Hence the relation cannot be uniquely determined.

question: X is the child of the only brother of Y's mother and also the child of the only sister of Y's father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for X relative to Y?
explanation: X is child of Y's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and also child of Y's paternal aunt (father's sister). Thus X shares both pairs of grandparents with Y, making them double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: N’s father has one brother, X, and N’s mother has one brother, Y. X and Y are married to each other and have a child M. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between M and N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal uncle (X) and maternal uncle (Y). Because those two uncles are married, M shares both pairs of grandparents with N, making them double first cousins – the exact term for this doubled ancestry.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation

question: M is the mother of N. N’s spouse is O. O’s mother is P, whose brother is Q. Q’s daughter is R, and R is married to S. T is the paternal uncle of M and the parent of S. Using standard English kinship terms, what is S’s relation to N?
explanation: T is M’s paternal uncle, so T’s child S is M’s first cousin. N is M’s child, making S the first cousin of N’s parent, i.e., N’s first cousin once removed. The extra chain through O‑P‑Q‑R only adds marital links and does not affect the blood relation.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoption, let R be a person. R’s mother has a brother (R’s maternal uncle). That uncle has a daughter, and that daughter has a child S. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of S to R?
explanation: The uncle’s daughter is R’s first cousin. Her child is one generation below a first cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed. No other standard term fits this exact generational offset.

question: M is the only child of his mother. M’s father has a sister who has a son N. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption), what is N’s relation to M?
explanation: M’s father’s sister is M’s paternal aunt. Her son is M’s first cousin. No other blood link exists, so the precise term is “first cousin”.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a woman; Adam marries Clara and Brian marries Diana. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring marital connections), what is the precise blood relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents—their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters—so they are double first cousins, the most specific standard term.

question: R’s mother has a brother U, and R’s father has a sister V. U’s daughter is X; V’s son is Y. X and Y marry and have a child Z. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is Z’s relation to R?
explanation: U is R’s maternal uncle, so X is R’s first cousin. V is R’s paternal aunt, so Y is also R’s first cousin. Z is the child of R’s first cousin on both sides, making Z a first cousin once removed of R. The relationship is the same through either parent, with no doubling.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: Using standard English kinship terms only (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), Emily is married to Frank; Frank’s sister is Grace; Grace is married to Henry; Henry’s brother is Ian. Who is Ian to Emily?
explanation: Emily → Frank (spouse) → Grace (spouse’s sister, i.e., sister‑in‑law) → Henry (Grace’s husband) → Ian (Henry’s brother). The chain involves only affinal links and never introduces a blood connection. Standard kinship terms cover only one‑step in‑law relations, so no direct term exists for Ian relative to Emily.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M is married to O. O’s brother is P, who is married to Q. Q’s sister is R, the mother of S. S is married to T, whose sister is U. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is U to M?
explanation: U is the sister of T, who is the spouse of S, child of R, sister of Q, spouse of P, brother of O, spouse of M. This chain involves only affinal links beyond the immediate in‑law scope and no blood connection, so no standard direct kin term exists.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: L has a mother and a father. L’s mother has exactly one brother, and L’s father has exactly one sister. The brother and the sister marry each other and have a child M. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Therefore M is simultaneously a first cousin on L’s mother’s side and on L’s father’s side. The standard term for this is simply “first cousin”. No special term applies.

question: A and B are siblings. A has one child C; B has one child D. C and D marry and have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of E to A?
explanation: E is the child of C, who is A's child, making E A's grandchild. E is also the child of D, who is A's niece/nephew, making E A's grandniece/grandnephew. No single standard term simultaneously expresses both relations, so the precise relation is not uniquely determinable.

question: John's father's sister Mary is married to Tom. John's mother's sister Susan is Tom's sister. Mary and Susan have exactly one child, Lily. What is Lily's precise relation to John using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Mary is John's paternal aunt; Susan is John's maternal aunt. Since Susan is Tom's sister, Mary and Susan are sisters‑in‑law, so Lily shares both John’s paternal and maternal grandparents. The exact term is double first cousin.

question: In a family, Person X’s father is the brother of Person Y’s mother, and Person X’s mother is the sister of Person Y’s father. Assuming no adoptions or remarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father and Y’s mother share one set of parents, and X’s mother and Y’s father share the other set. Thus X and Y share both pairs of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: John’s father has a sister who is the mother of Sam. John’s sister Mary is married to Tom, and Tom’s brother is Sam. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation of Sam to John?
explanation: Sam is the child of John’s paternal aunt, so they share a set of grandparents. That makes Sam John’s first cousin. The brother‑in‑law connections do not create a direct blood term, and no closer term applies.

question: M is married to N. N’s sister O is married to P. P’s mother Q is the sister of R’s father. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of R to M?
explanation: O is M’s sister‑in‑law; her husband P is also M’s sister‑in‑law (co‑sibling‑in‑law). Q, P’s mother, is the paternal aunt of R, making P R’s first cousin. Thus R is connected to M solely through an affinal chain with no blood link, and no standard term exists for that relationship.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: J’s father has a sister (A) and J’s mother has a brother (B). A and B are married and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of M to J?
explanation: A is J’s paternal aunt and B is J’s maternal uncle. Their marriage makes M both the child of J’s paternal aunt and the child of J’s maternal uncle, so M shares both sets of grandparents with J. The exact term for such a relationship is “double first cousin.”

question: A’s mother and B’s father are siblings, and A’s father and B’s mother are also siblings. No other intermarriages occur. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A shares both sets of grandparents with B: one through the mothers’ sibling link and another through the fathers’ sibling link. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than ordinary first cousins.

question: L’s mother has exactly one brother, and L’s father has exactly one sister. The brother and the sister each have a single child, and those two children are the same person M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s maternal uncle (first cousin) and also the child of L’s paternal aunt (first cousin). Because the two parents are unrelated, M shares both sets of grandparents with L, making M a double first cousin – the most specific term.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary’s son Peter marries John’s daughter Lisa. Peter and Lisa have a child Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), which single description most precisely captures Emma’s relation to John?
explanation: Lisa is John’s daughter, so John is Emma’s maternal grandfather. Peter is Mary’s son, making him John’s nephew; therefore John is Emma’s paternal great‑uncle. The only term covering both lines is the combined description “grandfather and great‑uncle.”
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: A’s mother has a brother whose daughter is B. A’s father has a sister whose son is C. B and C marry and have a child D. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is D’s precise relation to A?
explanation: B is A’s maternal first cousin; C is A’s paternal first cousin. Their child D is the child of A’s first cousin on both sides, which makes D A’s first cousin once removed (the “once‑removed” comes from the generational difference). The relation is the same from either side.

question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and also the child of N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus M shares both of N’s sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: Person A's father and Person B's mother are siblings, but it is unknown whether those siblings share both parents (full siblings) or only one parent (half‑siblings). No other intermarriages occur. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the relationship between A and B?
explanation: If the siblings are full, A and B are first cousins; if they are half‑siblings, A and B are half‑first cousins. Because the information does not specify the sibling type, the exact relation cannot be uniquely determined.

question: L is the child of the only brother of M’s mother and also the child of the only sister of N’s father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise blood relationship between M and N?
explanation: L is the offspring of M’s maternal uncle and N’s paternal aunt, who are spouses. M and N therefore share no common ancestor; their connection is only through that marriage, so they are unrelated by blood.

question: In a family tree, B and C are siblings. C has a child D, and D has a child E. B has a child A. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation between A and E?
explanation: B and C are siblings, so B is aunt/uncle of D. B's child A is therefore first cousin of D. Since D is parent of E, A is one generation apart from E, making A and E first cousins once removed. No closer term applies.

question: Anna's mother has a brother Tom, and Anna's father has a sister Sara. Tom and Sara marry each other and have a son Ben. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Ben to Anna?
explanation: Ben is the child of Anna's maternal uncle (Tom) and her paternal aunt (Sara). He therefore shares both of Anna's grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most precise term.

question: L is the daughter of the sister of K’s father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is L’s precise relation to K?
explanation: The sister of K’s father is K’s paternal aunt. L, being her daughter, is the child of K’s aunt, which makes L and K children of siblings. That relationship is a first cousin. No other connections affect the term.

question: John is the son of Mary and Peter. Mary has a sister Susan. Peter has a brother Alan. Susan is married to Alan, and they have a daughter Emma. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Emma's precise relation to John?
explanation: Emma is the child of John’s maternal aunt (Susan) and paternal uncle (Alan). She shares both John’s maternal grandparents (through Susan) and paternal grandparents (through Alan), making them double first cousins.

question: A's mother has a brother B, and A's father has a sister C. B's daughter is D; C's son is E. D and E marry and have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation of F to A?
explanation: B is A's maternal uncle, so D is A's first cousin. C is A's paternal aunt, so E is also A's first cousin. D and E are unrelated to each other, but each is A's first cousin. Their child F is therefore the child of A's first cousin on both sides, making F a double first cousin once removed to A.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed
D) D) Double first cousin once removed

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, Y’s mother has exactly one brother and Y’s father has exactly one sister. X is the child of that brother and also the child of that sister (they are married). What is the most precise standard English kinship term for X’s relation to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle and Y’s paternal aunt, making X simultaneously Y’s first cousin on the mother’s side and on the father’s side. The precise term for such a double link is “double first cousin.”

question: Two brothers marry two sisters (each brother to a different sister). The first couple have child X; the second couple have child Y. X and Y each marry unrelated partners and have children P and Q respectively. Using standard English kinship terms and accounting for the doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: X and Y are double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). Their children P and Q therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins – the most specific standard term.
choices: C) C) First cousins once removed

question: John and Mary are brother and sister. John marries Lisa, and Mary marries Tom, who is Lisa’s brother. John and Lisa have a child X; Mary and Tom have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their parents are two pairs of siblings who married each other’s siblings. Hence they are first cousins on both maternal and paternal sides, i.e., double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Adam marries Clara and Brian marries Diana; Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan, and Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relationship between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Adam and Brian share both parents, and Clara and Diana share both parents. Their children Ethan and Fiona therefore share both sets of grandparents. The exact term for such children is double first cousins, which is more specific than plain first cousins.

question: In a family with monogamy, no adoption or remarriage, Person P’s father is the brother of Person Q’s mother. Q has a daughter R. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of P to R?
explanation: P’s father and Q’s mother are siblings, so P and Q are first cousins. R is Q’s child, one generation below Q. Therefore R is the child of P’s first cousin, making R P’s first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard direct relation

question: M and N share only their mother (they are half‑siblings). M has a daughter X; N has a son Y. No other intermarriages exist. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent (their common maternal grandmother). The correct term is "half‑first cousins"; full first cousins require two shared grandparents, and they are not a generation apart, so other terms do not apply.

question: In a family with monogamy (but remarriage allowed) and no adoption, Alice’s mother is the sister of Bob’s father, and Alice’s father is the brother of Bob’s mother. Assuming no incest, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between Alice and Bob?
explanation: Alice’s mother and Bob’s father share a set of grandparents, and Alice’s father and Bob’s mother share another set. Thus Alice and Bob share both pairs of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: R’s mother’s brother’s daughter is married to R’s father’s sister’s son. What is the precise blood‑relation of the child of that couple to R, using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: R’s mother’s brother’s daughter is R’s maternal first cousin; R’s father’s sister’s son is R’s paternal first cousin. Their child is one generation below each cousin, making the child R’s first cousin once removed on both sides. No closer term exists; “first cousin once removed” is the exact description.

question: Let Y be a person. Y’s father has a sister (Y’s paternal aunt). That aunt has a son, who in turn has a child X. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relationship of X to Y?
explanation: Y’s father’s sister is Y’s aunt. Her son is Y’s first cousin. X is the child of that first cousin, putting X one generation below Y’s cousin, i.e., a first cousin once removed.

question: In a monogamous family, M’s mother is the sister of N’s father. M is married to O, who is unrelated to both M and N. What is M’s blood relation to N?
explanation: M’s mother and N’s father are siblings, sharing the same parents. Their children, M and N, are each the child of one of those siblings, making them first cousins. Marriage to O does not affect the blood relationship.

question: L has one sister S and one brother B. S has exactly one son, and B has exactly one daughter. Those two children marry and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is M's precise relationship to L?
explanation: S’s son is L’s nephew; B’s daughter is L’s niece. They are first cousins, so their child M is the child of L’s nephew/niece, i.e., L’s great‑nephew or great‑niece (also called grand‑nephew/niece). No other blood link exists, making this the most precise term.

question: A and B are siblings. A has a child C. B is married to D. D’s sibling is E, who has a child F. Using standard English kinship terms only (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation between C and F?
explanation: C is A’s child (blood). F is E’s child (blood). The only connection is the affinal chain B → D (spouse) → E (spouse’s sibling) → F. This chain goes beyond the allowed in‑law scope and contains no blood link, so no standard direct kin term exists.
choices: D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a son X. N and P have a daughter Y. X and Y marry each other and have a child Z. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of Z’s relation to M?
explanation: X is M’s son, so Z is M’s grandchild. Y is M’s niece (child of M’s sibling), so Z is also M’s grand‑niece (child of a niece). The only precise label is that Z is both a grandchild and a grand‑niece, i.e., a double relationship.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed
D) D) Both grandchild and grand‑niece (double relation)

question: A and B are full siblings. B is married to C. C’s mother is the sister of A’s father. D is the child of B and C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation of D to A?
explanation: C is A’s first cousin (child of A’s paternal aunt). B is A’s sibling, so D is B’s child – a niece/nephew of A. Although D is also a first cousin once removed of A, the closer lineal relation (niece) is the most precise term.

question: John’s mother Mary has a brother Tom. John’s father Peter has a sister Susan. Tom and Susan are married and have a child Alex. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation of Alex to John?
explanation: Tom is John’s maternal uncle and Susan is John’s paternal aunt. Their child Alex is therefore John’s cousin through both his mother’s side and his father’s side, sharing both sets of grandparents. The exact term for this is “double first cousin.”

question: John has a sister Mary and a brother Tom. Mary's son Peter marries Susan, who is Tom's daughter. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between Peter and Susan?
explanation: Peter is the child of Mary, Susan is the child of Tom. Mary and Tom are siblings, so their children are first cousins. No other blood link exists beyond this generation.

question: M’s mother has a sister (M’s maternal aunt). That aunt has a child C, and C has a child D. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the precise relation of D to M?
explanation: The aunt is the sister of M’s mother, so her child C is M’s first cousin. C’s child D is one generation younger, making D M’s first cousin once removed. No other blood links exist, so this is the exact term.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption or remarriage, let B be a person whose mother has exactly one brother and whose father has exactly one sister. The only child of that brother and the only child of that sister is the same individual, A. What is the precise standard kinship term for A in relation to B?
explanation: A is child of B’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and also child of B’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Thus A shares both of B’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M and N are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). M has one child, A; N has one child, B. Assuming no other intermarriages or adoptions, what is the precise kinship term for A relative to B?
explanation: A and B are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent. The exact term for such a relationship is "half‑first cousins"; full first cousins require both grandparents, and more distant terms do not apply.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a daughter Eva. Brian marries Diana and they have a son Frank. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring the doubled ancestry, what is the precise relation between Eva and Frank before any marriage?
explanation: Eva and Frank share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. That makes them double first cousins, the exact term for cousins who are related through both parental lines.

question: John and Mary are full siblings. John marries Anna, who is the sister of Mary's husband Peter. John and Anna have a son Sam; Mary and Peter have a daughter Lily. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the most precise relation between Sam and Lily?
explanation: John and Mary are full siblings; Anna and Peter are full siblings. Sam’s paternal grandparents are John’s parents (also Mary’s), and his maternal grandparents are Anna’s parents (also Peter’s). Lily’s paternal grandparents are Peter’s parents (also Anna’s), and her maternal grandparents are Mary’s parents (also John’s). Hence Sam and Lily share both grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most precise standard term.

question: In a family with no adoptions, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted, R’s mother has a brother U, whose daughter is V. R’s father has a sister W, whose son is X. V and X marry and have a child Y. What is Y’s precise relation to R using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: V is R’s maternal first cousin; X is R’s paternal first cousin. V and X are unrelated to each other, so their child Y is one generation below each cousin. Hence Y is a first cousin once removed through both lines, i.e., a double first cousin once removed.
choices: A) Double first cousin once removed

question: Brother A marries sister B; A’s brother C marries sister D (B and D are sisters). A and B have a son X; C and D have a son Y. X and Y each have one child, P and Q respectively. Using standard English kinship terms without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins. Their children P and Q therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins – the most specific standard term.

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoption, let Z be the child of the only brother of L’s father and also the child of the only sister of L’s mother. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for Z relative to L?
explanation: Z is the child of L’s paternal uncle (father’s brother) and also the child of L’s maternal aunt (mother’s sister). Each link makes Z a first cousin of L; having both links makes Z a double first cousin, the exact term required.

question: Tom’s mother has a brother Carl, whose daughter is Eva. Tom is married to Sarah. Sarah’s father has a sister Linda, whose son is Mark. What is the precise kinship term for the relationship between Eva and Mark?
explanation: Eva is Tom’s maternal first cousin; Mark is Sarah’s paternal first cousin. Because Tom and Sarah are married, Eva and Mark are linked only through that marriage. Standard kinship terminology does not provide a term for a spouse’s cousin, and they share no blood. Thus they have no standard direct relation.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: Anna is the mother of Ben. Carl is the father of Dana. Ben and Dana are married. Eva is the child of Anna and Carl (they had a child together before Ben and Dana married). Using only standard English kinship terms (no adoption, no step‑relations), what is Eva’s relation to Ben?
explanation: Eva shares the same mother Anna with Ben, but not the same father, making her Ben’s half‑sibling. The fact that Ben’s spouse Dana also shares the same father Carl with Eva does not change Eva’s direct blood relation to Ben.

question: M and N are married and have a child D. M has a sister S; N has a brother B. S and B marry each other and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: C and D share both sets of grandparents because their parents are siblings on both the maternal and paternal sides. This makes them double first cousins, a stricter term than ordinary first cousins.
