question: L's father has exactly one sister, and L's mother has exactly one brother. The child of that sister and that brother is M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relationship of M to L?
explanation: L's paternal aunt (father's sister) and maternal uncle (mother's brother) must be married to have a common child. Their child M shares both of L's paternal grandparents and both of L's maternal grandparents, making M a double first cousin of L—the most specific term.

question: M and N are siblings. M’s child is O; N’s child is P. O marries S and P marries T. S and T are first cousins to each other, and there are no other intermarriages. Q is the child of O + S and R is the child of P + T. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between Q and R?
explanation: O and P are first cousins, so Q and R are second cousins through that line. S and T are also first cousins, giving Q and R a second‑cousin link on the other side. Sharing both pairs of great‑grandparents makes them double second cousins, the most specific term.

question: Eight people A–H sit around a circular table; seat 1 (the marked top) is occupied by A and clockwise direction is considered “right”. G sits immediately to A’s right, B sits immediately to G’s right, and D sits opposite A. H lies strictly on the clockwise arc from B to D (endpoints excluded). C is not adjacent to H. I sits immediately to A’s left. Which statement must be true?
explanation: A at seat1 forces G at seat2 and B at seat3. D opposite A occupies seat5, so the only seat strictly between B (3) and D (5) clockwise is seat4, making H sit there. Hence H is always immediately clockwise of B. All other options can vary with the placement of C, E, and I, so only this statement is invariant.
choices: A) A) C sits immediately clockwise of I.
B) B) H sits immediately clockwise of B.
C) C) E sits opposite G.
D) D) I sits immediately clockwise of D.

question: John and Mark are brothers. Anna and Beth are sisters. John marries Anna and they have a daughter Lily. Mark marries Beth and they have a son Sam. Lily and Sam each marry unrelated partners and have children. What is the most precise standard kinship term for Lily’s child and Sam’s child?
explanation: Lily and Sam are double first cousins because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters, so they share both grandparent pairs. Their children therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the most exact label.

question: Anna’s mother has exactly one brother, whose only child is Ben. Anna’s father has exactly one sister, whose only child is also Ben. Assuming no adoptions or multiple births, what is the most precise standard kinship term for Ben’s relation to Anna?
explanation: Ben is the child of Anna’s maternal uncle and also the child of Anna’s paternal aunt. He therefore shares both sets of grandparents with Anna, making him a double first cousin—the term that reflects the doubled ancestry.

question: Q’s father’s sister (paternal aunt) has a son R. R’s mother is also Q’s mother’s sister (maternal aunt). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Q and R?
explanation: R is the child of Q’s paternal aunt and also the child of Q’s maternal aunt. Thus both of Q’s parents are siblings of R’s parents, giving them two independent lines of first‑cousin relationship – a double first cousin.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, the only child of P. N marries Q, the only child of R. P and R are siblings. M and O have child X; N and Q have child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share both parents, so X and Y are paternal first cousins. O and Q are children of siblings P and R, making O and Q maternal first cousins. Since X and Y share both sets of grandparents, the precise term is double first cousins.

question: John has two children: son Michael and daughter Sarah. John’s brother Peter has two children: daughter Laura and son David. Michael marries Laura and they have a daughter Emma. Sarah marries David and they have a son Noah. Using standard English kinship terms (no extended in‑law), what is the precise relation between Emma and Noah?
explanation: Michael and Sarah are John’s children; Laura and David are Peter’s children. Michael and Laura are first cousins, as are Sarah and David. Their children Emma and Noah each inherit both sets of grandparents (John’s parents and Peter’s parents). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes Emma and Noah double first cousins.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Adam marries Clara; Brian marries Diana, who is Clara’s sister. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan. Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona marry and have a child Greg. Using only standard English blood‑kinship terms (no in‑law designations), what is Greg’s precise relation to Adam?
explanation: Greg is Adam’s grandson through Ethan, and also Adam’s great‑nephew through Fiona (Adam’s brother’s child’s daughter’s child). No single standard term simultaneously expresses both blood lines, so the relation is not uniquely nameable with a single kin term.
choices: D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M is the only child of his mother. M’s mother is the sister of L’s grandfather. All individuals are unrelated otherwise and monogamous marriages are observed. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation of M to L?
explanation: M’s mother and L’s grandfather are siblings, so M is the child of L’s grandfather’s sister. That makes M a first cousin of L’s parent, and consequently M is a first cousin once removed to L.

question: A and B are half‑siblings (they share exactly one parent and have no other common parent). A has a child C; B has a child D. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for the relation between C and D?
explanation: A and B share only one parent, so C and D share only one grandparent. The correct term for cousins who share a single grandparent is half‑first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings who share the same mother. M marries O and has a daughter Q; N marries P and has a son R. Q and R (double first cousins) marry and have a child S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relationship between S and M’s mother?
explanation: M’s mother is the mother of both M and N. Through Q the line is M’s mother → M → Q → S (three generations). Through R the line is M’s mother → N → R → S, also three generations. Thus S is a great‑grandchild of M’s mother (twice), and no closer term exists.
choices: D) D) No standard kin term

question: R’s paternal grandmother has exactly one child, who is R’s father. R’s maternal grandmother also has exactly one child, who is R’s mother. L is the daughter of R’s father, and S is the son of R’s mother. If either L or S is called T, what is T’s precise kinship to R using standard English terms?
explanation: Because each grandmother’s only child is R’s parent, L is the child of R’s father and S is the child of R’s mother. Both L and S are therefore children of R’s parents, i.e., R’s siblings. The gender may differ, but the relationship is uniquely ‘sibling’.

question: In a family tree: Z and W are brothers. Z has one child Y, and Y has one child X. W has one child V. Using standard English kinship terms, what is V’s precise relation to X?
explanation: Z and W are siblings, so their children Y and V are first cousins. X is Y’s child, making X one generation below Y. Therefore V, who is a first cousin of X’s parent, is X’s first cousin once removed. No other listed term fits exactly.

question: M is the child of the sister of P's father, and also the child of the brother of P's mother. Using only standard English kinship terms (ignoring adoption), what is the most precise relation of M to P?
explanation: The sister of P's father is P's paternal aunt; her child is P's first cousin on the father's side. The brother of P's mother is P's maternal uncle; his child is P's first cousin on the mother's side. M occupies both roles, making M a double first cousin of P, a more specific term than plain first cousin.

question: In a family, X’s mother has a brother who has a daughter Y. X’s father has a sister who has a son Z. Y and Z marry and have a child W. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of W to X?
explanation: Y is X’s maternal first cousin; Z is X’s paternal first cousin. Their child W is the child of X’s first cousin on each side, which makes W X’s first cousin once removed (the same degree on both sides, no special term beyond that).
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard direct relation

question: Two brothers, G and H, each marry two sisters, I and J, respectively (G married I, H married J). G and I have a son K; H and J have a daughter L. K and L marry and have a child M. What is the precise kinship term for M’s paternal grandfather to M’s maternal grandmother?
explanation: M’s paternal grandfather is G; M’s maternal grandmother is J. G is the brother of H, who is J’s husband. Thus G is the brother‑in‑law of J. No blood link exists, and the standard term is “brother‑in‑law.”

question: A and B share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). A has a child X and B has a child Y, and there are no other intermarriages. What is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: A and B are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. Their children each inherit the other parent’s lineage, so they share exactly one grandparent, not a full pair. The precise term for such children is half‑first cousins.

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother (M) and R’s father has exactly one sister (S). The only child of M and the only child of S is the same person, X. Using standard English kinship terms (no “double” qualifiers), what is X’s relation to R?
explanation: M is R’s maternal uncle, so his child is R’s first cousin on the mother’s side. S is R’s paternal aunt, so her child is R’s first cousin on the father’s side. Since both children are the same person X, X is still a first cousin of R; no special term beyond “first cousin” is required.
choices: D) D) Relation not uniquely determinable

question: M and N are siblings. M has two children, A (with spouse X) and D (with spouse Y). N has two children, B (with spouse Z) and E (with spouse W). A marries B and they have a child C. D marries E and they have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between C and F?
explanation: C’s parents are A (M’s child) and B (N’s child); F’s parents are D (M’s child) and E (N’s child). Thus C and F share both sets of grandparents (M’s parents and N’s parents). The exact term for such cousins is “double first cousins.”

question: In a family, R’s mother has exactly one brother (her only sibling) and R’s father also has exactly one brother (his only sibling). Let X be the child of R’s maternal uncle and Y be the child of R’s paternal uncle. If either X or Y is selected and called S, what is S’s precise kinship to R using standard English terms?
explanation: Both X and Y are children of R’s uncles, i.e., the brothers of R’s parents. A child of a parent’s sibling is always a first cousin, regardless of whether the uncle is maternal or paternal. Hence S is unambiguously a first cousin of R.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: M and N are full siblings. M marries X and N marries Y, where X and Y are also full siblings (no other intermarriages). M and X have a son A; N and Y have a daughter B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents (the parents of M/N and the parents of X/Y). Hence they are double first cousins – first cousins with doubled ancestry. No other term is more exact.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let Z be the only sibling of L’s mother, and let Z also be the only sibling of L’s father (the same person). Z has one child, M. What is the precise relationship of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, who happen to be the same person. Thus M shares both of L’s grandparent pairs, making M a first cousin of L (the most precise standard term).

question: Alan has a sister Beth. Alan marries Diane, and Diane’s brother Carl marries Beth. Alan and Diane have a son Ethan; Beth and Carl have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are children of a brother‑sister pair (Alan & Beth) who married a sister‑brother pair (Diane & Carl). They share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

question: M and N share the same mother but have different fathers. M has a daughter A. N has a son B, who later has a daughter C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relationship of A to C?
explanation: M and N share only a mother, so they are half‑siblings. Their children A and B are therefore half‑first cousins. C is B’s child, making C a half‑first cousin once removed of A. No other standard term is more precise.
choices: D) D) Half‑first cousin once removed

question: M and N are siblings. M marries X and N marries Y, where X and Y are also siblings. M and X have a child A; N and Y have a child B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between A and B?
explanation: A’s parents are a brother‑sister pair (M and X) and B’s parents are the other brother‑sister pair (N and Y). Thus A and B share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: M and N are siblings. M has two children, A and D, by different spouses. N has one child, B. A marries B (first cousins) and they have a child C. D has a child E with any partner. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between C and E?
explanation: A and D are siblings, so their children C and E are first cousins. The extra link through B (cousin of D) does not create a closer tie, so the most specific term is "first cousin".
choices: C) C) First cousins once removed

question: M is the mother of J. J is married to L. L's father is the brother of M's husband's father. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of L to M?
explanation: L is married to J, so L is M’s child‑in‑law. If L is male, he is son‑in‑law; if female, daughter‑in‑law. Standard kinship does not include a gender‑neutral term, and “cousin‑in‑law” is not a recognized English kin term. Hence the precise relation cannot be uniquely determined.

question: R's mother has exactly one brother, and R's father has exactly one brother. The son of R's maternal uncle marries the daughter of R's paternal uncle, and they have a child S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is S's relation to R?
explanation: R's maternal uncle's son is R's first cousin; his child S is that cousin's child, making S a first cousin once removed. The same holds through the paternal side, so the unique precise term is first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: Twin siblings Tom and Tina each have one child: Tom’s child is Ben and Tina’s child is Amy. Ben and Amy marry and have a child named Lily. What is the most precise standard kinship term for Lily’s relation to Tom?
explanation: Lily is Ben’s daughter, so she is Tom’s grandchild. She is also Amy’s daughter; Amy is Tom’s niece (sister’s child), making Lily Tom’s grand‑niece. Both relations hold, so the most precise description is that Lily is simultaneously Tom’s grandchild and grand‑niece.
choices: C) Both grandchild and grand‑niece (double relation)

question: M and N are full siblings. M marries O and N marries R. O and R are also full siblings (they share both parents). M and O have a child X; N and R have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, ignoring doubled ancestry), what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two couples who are each composed of a pair of full siblings. They share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: M is the child of the only child of L’s sister, and also the child of the only child of L’s brother. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring adoption), what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: L’s sister’s only child is L’s niece/nephew; that child’s child is L’s grandniece/nephew. The same holds for L’s brother’s only child. Both descriptions point to the same person, so M is exactly L’s grandniece (if female) or grandnephew (if male).
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: J’s mother has exactly one brother, and J’s father has exactly one sister. M is the child of that brother and also the child of that sister (i.e., M’s parents are the maternal uncle and paternal aunt of J). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M to J?
explanation: M is the child of J’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and also the child of J’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with J, making them double first cousins – the most precise term.

question: In a monogamous family tree with no adoptions, P’s mother is the only sister of Q’s father. No other marriages link the two sides of the family. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship of P to Q?
explanation: P’s mother and Q’s father are siblings, so P and Q are each the child of a sibling of the other’s parent. That makes them first cousins, the standard term for children of siblings. No other link exists to alter the degree.

question: Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), M is married to N. N’s sister is O. O’s husband is P. P’s sister is Q. What is Q to M?
explanation: M→N (spouse) →O (spouse’s sibling → sister‑in‑law) →P (that sibling’s spouse → brother‑in‑law) →Q (that spouse’s sibling). The chain goes beyond the immediate affinal links; no standard term exists for such a relation.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a family with no adoptions, monogamy, and no remarriages, let P be the child of the only brother of Q’s father, and also the child of the only brother of Q’s mother. What is the most precise standard kinship term for P relative to Q?
explanation: P is the child of Q’s paternal uncle and also of Q’s maternal uncle, so P shares both sets of grandparents with Q. The exact term for such a relationship is double first cousin.

question: Let N be a person. N’s mother has exactly one brother, and N’s father has exactly one brother. The child of the mother’s brother marries the child of the father’s brother, and they have a child M. In standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is M’s precise relation to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s maternal uncle and paternal uncle. Hence M shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making M a double first cousin of N—the most specific term for this doubled ancestry.

question: X’s mother has a brother Y. Y’s daughter is Z. X’s father has a sister V, and V’s son is W. Z marries W. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise blood relation of W to X?
explanation: V is X’s paternal aunt, so V’s son W is X’s first cousin by blood. The marriage to Z (a maternal cousin) does not affect the blood link. No closer or doubled relationship exists, making “first cousin” the exact term.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a daughter Eva; Brian and Diana have a son Frank. Eva and Frank each marry unrelated partners and have children: Eva’s child Grace and Frank’s child Henry. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relationship between Grace and Henry?
explanation: Adam and Brian’s children Eva and Frank are double first cousins because they share both sets of grandparents. Their children Grace and Henry therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the most exact term.

question: M has two children, J and K. J is married to L. L’s brother is N. N is married to P, who is K’s daughter. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is P’s relation to M?
explanation: K is M’s child, so K’s daughter P is M’s grand‑child. The marriage of P to N does not alter the blood link. Hence P is M’s granddaughter (or grandson if male).

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, S’s father has a brother (paternal uncle) who is married to S’s mother’s sister (maternal aunt). Their only child is T. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between T and S?
explanation: T’s parents are S’s paternal uncle and maternal aunt, so T shares both of S’s grandparent couples. This makes T a double first cousin of S – the most specific term for cousins who share both sets of grandparents.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, and N marries Q. O, P, and Q are three siblings (O is sister of both P and Q). M and O have a daughter A; N and Q have a son B. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A’s parents are M (child of grandparents G₁) and O (child of grandparents G₂). B’s parents are N (sibling of M, thus also child of G₁) and Q (sibling of O, thus also child of G₂). Therefore A and B share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: Alice’s mother has only one brother, and Alice’s father has only one brother. Those two brothers marry each other and have a child named Ben. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Ben’s precise relation to Alice?
explanation: Alice’s maternal uncle and paternal uncle are the parents of Ben. Ben therefore shares both sets of grandparents with Alice, making him a double first cousin—the most specific standard term.

question: John has one sister, Mary. Mary’s son Peter marries John’s daughter Lisa. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of Peter to Lisa?
explanation: Peter is the child of John’s sister, making him John’s nephew. Lisa is John’s daughter. A man’s nephew and his daughter are first cousins, sharing the same set of grandparents. No other blood link exists, so the exact term is “first cousin.”

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively (Adam with Clara, Brian with Diana). Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona each marry unrelated partners and have children respectively: Ethan's child Greg and Fiona's child Hannah. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Greg and Hannah?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). Their children Greg and Hannah therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the most precise term.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, N marries P, and O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child A; N and P have a child B. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents: M and N share parents, O and P share parents. Thus A and B have the same paternal and maternal grandparents, making them double first cousins – the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: In a family with no intermarriage, R’s mother has exactly one brother who has a daughter S. R’s father has exactly one sister who has a daughter T. The maternal uncle and the paternal aunt are unrelated to each other. What is the precise standard English blood‑relation term between S and T?
explanation: S is the child of R’s maternal uncle; T is the child of R’s paternal aunt. Since the uncle and aunt are not siblings, S and T share no common ancestor, so they are not blood‑related. No standard kinship term applies.
choices: B) B) No standard blood relation

question: M’s mother has a brother (M’s maternal uncle) who is married to a woman W. W’s sister is M’s father’s sister. What is the most precise standard kinship term for W’s relation to M?
explanation: W is the wife of M’s maternal uncle, making her a maternal aunt by marriage. Since W’s sister is M’s paternal aunt, W shares both parents with that aunt, so W is also a paternal aunt by blood. Thus she is both an aunt by marriage and an aunt by blood – a double aunt.

question: Adam and Ethan are brothers. Adam’s sister Beth marries Carl. Carl’s sister Diana marries Ethan. Adam’s son is Frank and Ethan’s daughter is Grace. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no adoption), what is the precise relation between Frank and Grace?
explanation: Frank and Grace share the same set of grandparents—the parents of Adam and Ethan—because their fathers are brothers. No other blood link changes this. Thus they are first cousins. The marital connections create only in‑law ties, not additional blood ties.
choices: D) No standard term (they are cousins‑in‑law)

question: N’s father has exactly one sister, and N’s mother has exactly one brother. A child M is born to that sister and that brother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: The sister is N’s paternal aunt, so her child is N’s first cousin on the father’s side. The brother is N’s maternal uncle, so his child is N’s first cousin on the mother’s side. Because the two cousins share both sets of grandparents with N, they are double first cousins. No other term is more exact.

question: M has a sister N. N is married to O. O’s sister is P, who is the mother of Q. Q is married to R, and R is the son of S. S is the brother of M. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Q to M?
explanation: S is M’s brother, so R (S’s son) is M’s nephew. Q is R’s spouse, i.e., the wife of M’s nephew. The standard term for a nephew’s wife is niece‑in‑law. No blood term applies.

question: M is married to H and they have a child J. J is married to L. L’s father is the brother of H. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is L’s relation to M?
explanation: J is M’s child, so L, as J’s spouse, is M’s daughter‑in‑law. The fact that L’s father is H’s brother makes L also H’s niece, but that does not affect the direct kin term between L and M.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: R's father has exactly one brother and R's mother has exactly one sister. The brother of R's father marries the sister of R's mother, and they have a child S. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring no ancestry), what is the most precise relation of S to R?
explanation: S is the offspring of R's paternal uncle and maternal aunt, who are married. S shares both of R's grandparents on the father's side and both on the mother's side, thus S and R have the same set of grandparents twice. The most precise term is double first cousin.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Ben, each marry a sister, Emma and Fiona respectively (no other marriages). Adam + Emma have a child Carl; Ben + Fiona have a child Diana. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Carl and Diana?
explanation: Adam and Ben are siblings, Emma and Fiona are siblings. Their children share both paternal and maternal grandparents, i.e., they have the same two grandparent pairs. This makes Carl and Diana double first cousins, a more precise term than ordinary first cousins.

question: In a family with no adoption or remarriage, let X be the child of the only brother of Y’s father. Y has no siblings. Using standard English kinship terms, what is X’s precise relation to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s paternal uncle (the father’s only brother). Children of siblings are first cousins, and no other relation fits.

question: M’s mother has a brother (M’s maternal uncle). That uncle is married to a woman, Aunt X. Aunt X has a sister, Y. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Y’s relation to M?
explanation: Y is the sister of M’s aunt‑by‑marriage. She is connected to M only through an affinal chain (uncle → his spouse → her sister) and has no direct blood or immediate in‑law link. No standard term exists for such a relation, so the correct description is “no standard direct relation (affinal chain only)”.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: Let X be a person. X's mother has a brother (X's maternal uncle) who is married to Y. Y's sister is S. S is the mother of the child of X's father's sister. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the relation of S to X?
explanation: X's father's sister is X's paternal aunt. Her child is X's first cousin, and S is that child's mother, so S must be the paternal aunt herself. Hence S is X's aunt.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a sister, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a child Ethan; Brian and Diana have a child Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Adam and Brian share the same parents, and Clara and Diana share the same parents. Ethan and Fiona therefore share both sets of grandparents, giving them the exact relationship of double first cousins.

question: Two brothers, M and N, each marry two sisters, U and V (M–U and N–V). M and U have a son A; N and V have a daughter B. A and B marry unrelated partners and have children X and Y respectively. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: A and B are double first cousins: their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters, so they share both sets of grandparents. Their children X and Y therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the most specific label.

question: M and N are married. M has a brother, O, who is married to P. N has a sister, Q, who is married to R. O and Q have a child, X. P and R have a child, Y. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father O is M’s brother, and Y’s mother Q is N’s sister, so X and Y share both sets of grandparents (M‑N’s parents and O‑P’s parents). They are therefore double first cousins, a relation more specific than ordinary first cousins.

question: In a family tree, Alex has a sister Beth. Beth’s son is Carl. Alex’s son is David. David marries Carl’s daughter Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is Emma’s precise relation to Alex?
explanation: Beth is Alex’s sister, so Carl is Alex’s nephew. Carl’s daughter Emma is the child of Alex’s nephew, making her Alex’s great‑niece (also called grand‑niece). No other blood link exists, so the exact term is great‑niece.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M is the only child of his mother. His mother's sister (M's maternal aunt) is married to N. N and M's father have a son P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption), what is P's precise relation to M?
explanation: P shares the same father with M but has a different mother (the aunt’s husband N). Therefore they are half‑brothers. Full brothers require both parents in common, cousins share no parent, and uncle would require a generational gap.

question: Person R's father has exactly one sister. That sister's son is S. S has a daughter T. What is T's precise kinship term to R, using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: R's father's sister is R's paternal aunt. Her son S is R's first cousin. S's daughter T is one generation down, making T R's first cousin once removed.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: R’s father has a sister A, and R’s mother has a brother B. A and B marry each other and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, but remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation between R and C?
explanation: C is the child of R’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus C is R’s first cousin on the father's side and also on the mother's side, sharing both pairs of grandparents. The precise term is “double first cousin”.

question: M and N are siblings. M has two children, A and D; N has two children, B and E. A marries B (first cousins) and they have a child C. D marries E (also first cousins) and they have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between C and F?
explanation: C’s father A is sibling of F’s father D, and C’s mother B is sibling of F’s mother E. Thus C and F share both sets of grandparents (M’s parents and N’s parents). The exact term for such a pair is double first cousins.
choices: A) A) First cousins once removed

question: Emma is the only child of her mother. Emma’s mother has a brother Victor, who is married to Nora and they have a daughter Lily. Emma is married to Sam, whose mother is the sister of Victor. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Lily to Sam?
explanation: Victor and his sister (Sam’s mother) are siblings. Lily is Victor’s child; Sam is the child of Victor’s sister. Children of siblings are first cousins, so Lily is Sam’s first cousin.

question: John and Mary are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). John has a son Tom, and Mary has a daughter Lisa. Using standard English kinship terminology (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between Tom and Lisa?
explanation: Tom and Lisa are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent. The correct term for such relatives is “half‑first cousins”. Full first cousins share both grandparents, which is not the case here.

question: M and N are siblings. M has children A and D; N has children B and E. A marries B and they have a child C. D marries E and they have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between C and F?
explanation: A and B (and D and E) are first cousins, so C’s grandparents are M and N. The same grandparents belong to F. Because C and F share both grandparents, the exact term is double first cousins. They are not merely first cousins (only one grandparent pair), nor half‑first cousins (one shared grandparent), nor second cousins (share great‑grandparents).

question:
Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed):
1. M is the only child of his mother.
2. N is M's father's sister.
3. O is N's child.
4. P is O's spouse's mother.
5. Q is P's father's brother.
What is the relation of Q to M?
explanation: N is M's paternal aunt, so O is M's first cousin. O's spouse is unrelated by blood, making P only an in‑law. Q is the brother of P's father, an uncle‑in‑law to O but with no fixed blood link to M. Depending on P's side of the family, Q could be a great‑uncle, a cousin, or have no blood tie, so the precise relation cannot be uniquely determined.

question: M’s mother has a brother U, and M’s father has a sister V. U’s daughter C and V’s son D marry and have a child N. Assuming no adoption or other intermarriages, what is the precise standard English kinship term for the relation between N and M?
explanation: U is M’s maternal uncle, so C is M’s first cousin. V is M’s paternal aunt, so D is also M’s first cousin. N is the child of two of M’s first cousins, making N a first cousin once removed to M (the same relation via either line). No other listed term fits exactly.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard kinship term

question: Let M be a person. X is the child of the only sibling of M’s mother, and also the child of the only sibling of M’s father. Assuming no adoption, monogamy (but remarriage allowed), and no other information about whether the two siblings are the same individual, what is the most precise standard kinship term for X to M?
explanation: If the two siblings are different, X is a first cousin (child of a maternal uncle and a paternal aunt). If they happen to be the same person (e.g., a half‑brother of both parents), X would be a half‑first cousin. Both cases are possible, so the relation cannot be uniquely specified.

question: Let X be a person. X’s paternal grandfather has a brother G. G’s daughter is Y. X also has a maternal aunt A, whose son (who may be a full‑cousin or half‑cousin to X) marries Y. Their child is Z. What is the precise standard English kinship term for Z’s relation to X?
explanation: G is X’s paternal great‑uncle, so Y is X’s first cousin once removed on the father’s side. A’s son could be a full first cousin or a half‑cousin to X, depending on whether A shares both parents with X’s mother. Consequently Z can be a first cousin twice removed, a half‑first cousin twice removed, or a second cousin. The exact term cannot be fixed.
choices: A) A) First cousin twice removed
B) B) Half‑first cousin twice removed

question: Eight people A‑H sit around a round table; the top seat is marked and occupied by A. Clockwise = right. The following conditions hold: B sits immediately to A’s right; C sits immediately to B’s right; D sits immediately to C’s right; E sits directly opposite A; F sits immediately to E’s right; G sits directly opposite D; H sits strictly on the clockwise arc from F to B (endpoints excluded). Which person must sit directly opposite D?
explanation: With A fixed at the top, seats clockwise become: A‑B‑C‑D‑E‑F‑?‑?. Since E is opposite A, it occupies the fifth seat, making F the sixth. G must be opposite D, so G occupies the eighth seat. The only remaining seat (seventh) goes to H, which indeed lies on the arc from F (sixth) to B (second). Thus G is forced opposite D.

question: M is the child of the sister of N’s father and also the child of the brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is the precise blood relation between M and N?
explanation: M’s mother is N’s paternal aunt and M’s father is N’s maternal uncle. Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with N, being first cousins on both the father’s and mother’s sides – the exact term is double first cousins.

question: John has a sister Mary and a brother Tom. Mary’s son Peter marries Tom’s daughter Linda. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between Peter’s child Alex and Linda?
explanation: Peter and Linda are first cousins (children of siblings). Alex, as Peter’s child, is one generation below Peter, so Alex is the child of a first cousin. The correct term for that relation is “first cousin once removed.”
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: Two couples marry as follows: the brother of man A marries the sister of woman B, and the sister of man A marries the brother of woman B. Their respective children, X and Y, are thus the offspring of these two unions. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because each pair of parents are siblings on both paternal and maternal sides. Hence they are double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: In a family, two siblings, Alan (male) and Beth (female), marry another pair of siblings, Carl (male) and Dana (female), respectively: Alan marries Dana, and Beth marries Carl. Their children, X (child of Alan + Dana) and Y (child of Beth + Carl), have no other relatives. Using standard English blood‑kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father Alan is sibling of Y’s mother Beth, and X’s mother Dana is sibling of Y’s father Carl. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, a distinct term from ordinary first cousins.

question: M and N are brother and sister. M marries P and N marries Q, where P and Q are also brother and sister. M and N each have one child, X and Y respectively. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, but remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their parents are two pairs of siblings. This makes them double first cousins—first cousins with doubled ancestry. No other standard term is more specific.

question: Person X’s mother has a brother named Y. Y has a daughter Z. Z has a son W. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of W to X?
explanation: Y is X’s maternal uncle. His daughter Z is X’s first cousin. Z’s son W is one generation below that cousin, making W X’s first cousin once removed.

question: R’s mother has one brother whose daughter is S. R’s father has one sister whose son is T. S and T marry and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, no step‑relations), what is C’s relation to R?
explanation: S is R’s maternal first cousin (child of R’s mother’s brother). T is R’s paternal first cousin (child of R’s father’s sister). Their child C is one generation below each cousin, therefore C is a first cousin once removed from R on both sides; the standard term is simply “first cousin once removed.”

question: R’s father has exactly one brother, and R’s mother has exactly one brother. A person X is the child of one of those two brothers (you are not told which). Using standard English kinship terms, what is X’s relation to R?
explanation: Whether X is the child of R’s paternal uncle or maternal uncle, X is the child of a sibling of one of R’s parents. In either case X is a first cousin of R. No other kin term fits uniquely.

question: Using standard English kinship terms (blood only; in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), consider: John and Mary are siblings. Mary is married to Peter. John marries Peter’s sister Linda. John and Linda have a daughter Emma. What is Emma’s precise relation to Peter?
explanation: Emma is the daughter of Linda, who is Peter’s sister; therefore Emma is Peter’s niece. No other direct kinship term applies.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has two children: a son P and a daughter R. R’s child is Q. What is the precise standard English kinship term for the relation between O and Q?
explanation: O is the child of M, who is N’s sibling, so O is N’s niece. R, N’s daughter, is O’s first cousin. Q is R’s child, making Q one generation below O’s cousin. Hence O and Q are first cousins once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard kinship term

question: Two brothers, A and B, marry two sisters, C and D respectively. A and C have a son E; B and D have a son F. E and F each marry unrelated partners and have children G and H respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between G and H?
explanation: E and F are double first cousins (they share both paternal and maternal grandparents). Consequently their children G and H share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins. No other term expresses the doubling.

question: R’s mother has a brother (maternal uncle) who is married to R’s father’s sister (paternal aunt). They have a single daughter S. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for S’s relationship to R?
explanation: S is the child of R’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, who are themselves spouses. Thus S is R’s cousin on both the mother’s and father’s sides, i.e., a double first cousin—the only term that captures both lines of descent.

question: T’s father has a sister who married T’s mother’s brother, and they have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s precise relation to T?
explanation: M is the child of T’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle, who are married. Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with T, making M T’s double first cousin.

question: P and Q are half‑siblings who share only their mother. P has a child R and Q has a child S. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between R and S?
explanation: P and Q share a single parent, so their children share only that one grandparent. Hence R and S are half‑first cousins, the exact term for cousins who share just one grandparent.

question: Eight people A–H sit around a round table with seat numbers increasing clockwise; A occupies the marked top seat (seat 1). The rules are: B sits immediately clockwise of A; D sits opposite A; E sits immediately clockwise of D; F sits on the clockwise arc from B to D (exclusive); G sits on the clockwise arc from E to A (exclusive); H sits immediately counter‑clockwise of G. Which statement must be true in every arrangement satisfying these conditions?
explanation: A at 1 forces B at 2, D at 5, E at 6. The arc B→D leaves seats 3‑4 for F, so F is 3 or 4. The arc E→A leaves seats 7‑8 for G; H must be counter‑clockwise of G, so G cannot be 7 (H would be 6 occupied), thus G=8, H=7. Hence H is always clockwise of E. All other options can vary.
choices: A) A) C sits immediately clockwise of B.
B) B) F sits immediately clockwise of B.
C) C) H sits immediately clockwise of E.
D) D) G sits opposite C.

question: Two brothers marry two sisters (the brothers each marry a different sister). The first couple has a son X; the second couple has a daughter Y. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because each pair of parents are siblings on both sides. This makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: Let P be a person. Q is the only son of P’s paternal aunt, and R is the only daughter of P’s maternal uncle. If a child S is born to the union of Q and R, what is the precise kinship term for S to P (using standard English kinship, no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed)?
explanation: Q is P’s first cousin (father’s sister’s son). R is also P’s first cousin (mother’s brother’s daughter). Their child S is therefore the child of two first cousins who are not blood‑related to each other (they share no common ancestor). Depending on whether Q and R are themselves related (they could be siblings if P’s parents are siblings, which is prohibited), S could be a first cousin once removed, a second cousin, or a double cousin. The information given does not fix a unique term.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed

question: M has two children, N and O. N is married to P. P’s sister is Q, and Q is married to R, who is O’s son. What is the precise standard kinship term for Q’s relation to N?
explanation: N’s spouse is P; Q is P’s sister, so Q is N’s sister‑in‑law. The fact that Q is also O’s daughter‑in‑law (O being N’s sibling) does not alter the standard term, which remains sister‑in‑law.

question: In a family with no adoptions and monogamous marriages, let S be a person whose mother has exactly one brother. R is the child of that brother. What is R's precise kinship term for S using standard English blood‑relation terminology?
explanation: The brother of S's mother is S's maternal uncle. R, being the uncle's child, is the child of a parent's sibling, which is the definition of a first cousin. No other blood link exists, so the term is uniquely first cousin.

question: M is the child of the sister of J’s father and also the child of the brother of J’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of M to J?
explanation: M is the child of J’s paternal aunt, making M a first cousin on J’s father’s side. M is also the child of J’s maternal uncle, making M a first cousin on J’s mother’s side. Sharing both sets of grandparents, M is a double first cousin of J.

question: Person X's mother has a brother named M. M has a daughter A. X's father has a sister named N. N has a son B. A and B are married. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise blood relation of A to X?
explanation: A is the child of X's maternal uncle (the brother of X's mother). A child of a parent's sibling is a first cousin, regardless of whom A marries.

question: Maya is the only child of her mother. Maya’s maternal uncle is Tom. Tom has two children: Lila and a daughter who is Raj’s mother. Maya marries Raj. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the most precise relation between Maya and Lila?
explanation: Tom’s children are Lila and Raj’s mother, so Lila is the sister of Raj’s mother, i.e., Raj’s aunt. Maya is Raj’s spouse, making her Lila’s aunt‑in‑law. No blood term applies, and “aunt” alone ignores the marital link.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: M and N are siblings. M has children A and D; N has children B and E. A marries B and they have a child C. D marries E and they have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between C and F?
explanation: C’s father (A) is sibling of F’s father (D) and C’s mother (B) is sibling of F’s mother (E). Thus C and F share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

question: R’s mother has a brother U, and R’s father has a sister V. U’s daughter is X; V’s son is Y. X and Y marry and have a child Z. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is Z’s relation to R?
explanation: U is R’s maternal uncle, so X is R’s first cousin on the mother’s side. V is R’s paternal aunt, so Y is R’s first cousin on the father’s side. Z is the child of both X and Y, making Z the child of R’s first cousin (via either side). The child of one’s first cousin is a first cousin once removed, and this holds for both parental lines.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: A is the only child of B; B is the only sibling of C; and C is the parent of D. Using standard English kinship terms, what is A's precise relation to D?
explanation: B, being C's sole sibling, is D's aunt/uncle. A, as B's child, is therefore the child of D's aunt/uncle, which makes A D's first cousin.

question: P's father has a sister who is married to P's mother's brother. Their child is M. What is the precise kinship term for M's relation to P using standard English kinship?
explanation: M is the child of P's paternal aunt and maternal uncle, who are respectively siblings of P's parents. Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with P, making them double first cousins—the most specific standard term.

question: John and Mark are brothers. Anna and Beth are sisters. John marries Anna and has a child X. Mark marries Beth and has a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms and assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. This double sharing makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than merely first cousins.

question: Two brothers, Alan and Ben, marry two sisters, Cara and Dana respectively (Alan‑Cara, Ben‑Dana). Alan and Cara have a son Ethan. Ben and Dana have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona each marry unrelated partners and have one child each (Ethan Jr. and Fiona Jr.). What is the most precise standard kinship term for the relationship between Ethan Jr. and Fiona Jr.?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins because they share both sets of grandparents. Their children therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, which makes them double second cousins—the exact term for this level of doubled ancestry.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter A. N has a son B. B marries C, who is the daughter of D, where D is the brother of A’s husband (and D is unrelated to M and N). Using only standard English blood‑kinship terms (in‑laws limited to the spouse themselves), what is C’s precise relation to M?
explanation: C is the daughter of B’s spouse’s paternal uncle. The only link between C and M runs through B’s marriage; there is no shared ancestor. Since in‑law ties beyond the spouse are excluded, C has no blood relation to M.

question: M has a sister N. M is married to P. P has a brother O, who is married to N. M and P have a child X; N and O have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N are siblings. P and O are siblings. X is child of M‑P; Y is child of N‑O. X’s father M is sibling of Y’s mother N, and X’s mother P is sibling of Y’s father O. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the most precise standard term.
choices: C) C) First cousins once removed

question: In a family, two brothers, Adam and Ben, each marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan. Ben and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona marry each other and have a child Lily. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for Lily’s relation to Adam?
explanation: Ethan is Adam’s son, so Lily, as Ethan’s child, is Adam’s grandchild. Fiona’s lineage does not affect Lily’s direct blood line to Adam; the marriage does not change the vertical relationship.

question: Alice’s mother Fiona has a brother Edward. Edward is married to Dana, who is the sister of Alice’s husband Carl. Alice and Carl have a child Ben. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is Edward’s relation to Ben?
explanation: Edward is Fiona’s brother, making him Alice’s maternal uncle. A parent’s uncle is the child’s great‑uncle (or great‑aunt). The marriage to Dana creates no additional blood link. Therefore Edward is Ben’s great‑uncle.

question: J’s father has a sister (J’s paternal aunt) who is married to J’s mother’s brother (J’s maternal uncle). They have a single child, M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between M and J?
explanation: M is the child of J’s paternal aunt and also the child of J’s maternal uncle. Hence M shares both of J’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the most exact term.

question: M has two sisters, S1 and S2. S1 marries a man whose sister is married to M's brother B. M’s child is C, B’s child is D, and S2’s child is E. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the precise relation between C and E?
explanation: C is the child of M; E is the child of M’s sister S2. They share both of M and S2’s parents as grandparents, so they are first cousins. No other blood link alters this.

question: A is a person whose mother has exactly one brother and whose father has exactly one sister. Let X be the child of that maternal brother and also the child of that paternal sister (i.e., X’s mother is A’s maternal uncle’s wife and X’s father is A’s paternal aunt’s husband). What is X’s precise relationship to A using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: A’s mother’s brother is A’s maternal uncle; his child is A’s first cousin on the mother’s side. A’s father’s sister is A’s paternal aunt; her child is A’s first cousin on the father’s side. Since X is the same individual, X is simultaneously a cousin from both sides – still a first cousin. No more specific standard term applies.

question: R’s mother has a brother M, and R’s father has a sister N. M’s daughter is S and N’s son is T. S and T marry and have a child U. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation of U to R?
explanation: S is R’s maternal first cousin; T is R’s paternal first cousin. U, the child of both S and T, is therefore the child of R’s first cousin on each side – a first cousin once removed, doubled. The exact term is double first cousin once removed.
choices: D) Double first cousin once removed

question: John is married to Mary. Mary’s sister Anna is married to John’s brother Peter. John and Peter each have one child: Sam (John’s child) and Lily (Peter’s child). Before Sam and Lily marry each other, what is the most precise standard kinship term for their relationship?
explanation: Sam and Lily are children of a brother–sister pair (John‑Peter and Mary‑Anna). They share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that reflects the doubled ancestry.

question: A is married to B. A’s brother C is married to B’s sister D, and C and D have a child E. In standard English kinship terms (ignoring in‑law extensions beyond spouse’s siblings), what is the precise relation of E to A?
explanation: E is the child of A’s brother, making E A’s niece or nephew by blood. The same child is also the offspring of B’s sister, which is merely an affinal link that does not change the blood term. The most specific standard term is therefore niece/nephew.

question: M’s paternal grandfather has a brother T. T’s daughter has a son S. M’s maternal grandmother has a sister L. L’s son is also S. What is S’s precise relation to M?
explanation: T is M’s great‑uncle; his daughter is M’s parent’s first cousin, so her son S is M’s second cousin. L is M’s great‑aunt; her son is likewise M’s parent’s first cousin, and his child S is again a second cousin. Both lineages give the same result, so S is uniquely a second cousin of M.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: L is the child of the only brother of K’s mother, and also the child of the only sister of K’s father. Assuming monogamy, no adoption, and no incest, what is L’s precise relation to K?
explanation: The brother of K’s mother is K’s maternal uncle; his child is K’s first cousin. The sister of K’s father is K’s paternal aunt; her child is also K’s first cousin. Both descriptions refer to the same person, so L is uniquely a first cousin of K.

question: Brothers A and B marry sisters C and D respectively; A and C have a child X, while B and D have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the most precise term for the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: A and B are siblings, and C and D are also siblings. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents (the parents of A/B and the parents of C/D). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: John and Mary are siblings. Their other sibling is Peter. Peter has a daughter Anna. John marries Anna and they have a child Sam. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is Sam's precise relation to Peter?
explanation: Peter is Sam's maternal grandfather (Anna’s father) and also Sam's paternal uncle (John’s brother). The only term that captures both lines simultaneously is “both grandson and nephew,” i.e., a double relation.
choices: D) Both grandson and nephew (double relation)

question: Brothers M and N each marry sisters P and Q respectively. M and P have a daughter A; N and Q have a son B. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, and without ignoring doubled ancestry), what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents: M‑P’s parents and N‑Q’s parents. Because they have the same paternal and maternal grandparents, they are double first cousins, a more exact term than simple first cousins.

question: L is the child of the only brother of K's mother, and also the child of the only sister of K's father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for L's relation to K?
explanation: L is the child of K's maternal uncle (first cousin on the mother's side) and also the child of K's paternal aunt (first cousin on the father's side). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes L a double first cousin of K, the most exact term.

question: M is the mother of N and O. O has a son R. N is married to P. P’s sister Q is married to R. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Q’s relation to N?
explanation: N is the aunt of R (sibling of R’s parent O). Q is R’s spouse, so Q is the spouse of N’s niece/nephew. No standard direct kin term exists for this affinal chain; it is not covered by the limited in‑law scope.
choices: D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: R’s mother has a brother U, whose daughter is C. R’s father has a sister A, whose son is D. C and D marry and have a child S. What is the precise kinship term for S’s relation to R (using standard English kinship terms, no adoption, monogamy allowed)?
explanation: C is R’s maternal first cousin (child of R’s maternal uncle). D is R’s paternal first cousin (child of R’s paternal aunt). Their child S is the child of R’s first cousin, which makes S R’s first cousin once removed. The double line does not alter the removal degree.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: M is the mother of J. J is married to L. L's sister is K. K is married to P, who is the son of M's brother. What is the precise relation between P and J using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: M’s brother is J’s maternal uncle; his son P is J’s first cousin. K is L’s sister, and L is J’s spouse, so K is J’s sister‑in‑law. Since P is married to K, P is also J’s brother‑in‑law. Thus P holds two distinct relations to J – first cousin by blood and brother‑in‑law by marriage – and there is no single standard kinship term that combines them.
choices: C) Both first cousin and brother‑in‑law (no single term)

question: John and Mary are siblings. Their other sibling, Peter, has a daughter Anna. John marries Anna, and they have a child Sam. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of Sam to Mary?
explanation: Mary is John’s sister, so she is Sam’s paternal aunt. Mary is also Peter’s sister, making her Anna’s aunt; therefore she is Sam’s maternal aunt as well. Being both paternal and maternal aunt makes Sam a double niece/nephew of Mary, the only term that captures this dual link.

question: N's father has exactly one brother, and N's mother has exactly one sister. M is the child of that brother and also the child of that sister (both parents are unrelated to each other). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is the child of N's paternal uncle and also the child of N's maternal aunt. Thus M shares both of N's grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures both lines of descent.

question: M and N share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). M has a child A; N has a child B. There are no other intermarriages or adoptions. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent. The exact term for such a relationship is "half‑first cousins"; full first cousins require both grandparents, and a more distant term would be inaccurate.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, who is the sister of P. N marries P. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share both parents; O and P share both parents. X and Y therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the exact term for cousins who are related through both parental lines.

question: M is the only child of his mother. M’s father has a sister who is married and has two children: a son N and a daughter P. What is the precise kinship term for P’s relation to M, using standard English blood‑relation terminology?
explanation: M’s father’s sister is M’s paternal aunt. Her son N is M’s first cousin. The aunt’s daughter P is also a child of the same aunt, making P another first cousin of M.

question: L has exactly one sister S and one brother B. S has exactly one child X, and B has exactly one child Y. X and Y marry each other and have a single child M. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring in‑law beyond spouse), what is the most precise term for M's relation to L?
explanation: M is the child of both L’s niece (X, daughter of sister) and L’s nephew (Y, son of brother). Hence M is a grandniece/nephew on each side, i.e., a double grandniece/nephew – the most specific standard label.

question: P's father is the brother of Q's mother, and P's mother is the sister of Q's father. No other intermarriages exist. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between P and Q?
explanation: Each of P's parents is a sibling of one of Q's parents, so P and Q share both sets of grandparents. They are first cousins on the paternal side and also first cousins on the maternal side, giving them the specific term “double first cousins.”

question: Alan and Frank are brothers. Alan's daughter is Mia. Their sister Beth is married to Carl. Carl's mother Diane has a daughter Emma from a previous marriage; Emma is Carl's half‑sister. Emma marries Frank, and they have a daughter Grace. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is Grace's precise relation to Mia?
explanation: Grace is the child of Frank, who is Alan's brother, making Frank Mia's paternal uncle. The child of an uncle is a first cousin. No other blood links affect this relation, so Grace is Mia's first cousin.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: M is the mother of N. N and O are full siblings. O is married to P. R is M’s sibling, and R and P together have a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, but remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of Q to N?
explanation: M and R are siblings, so their children (N and Q) share the same set of grandparents, making them first cousins. The marriage of O to P does not affect blood relation; Q is not a niece/nephew because Q’s parent R is not N’s sibling. Hence the exact term is "first cousin".
choices: C) C) No standard blood relation

question: L has one sister and one brother. The only son of L's sister marries the only daughter of L's brother, and they have a single child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is M's precise relation to L?
explanation: L's sister's son is L's nephew; L's brother's daughter is L's niece. Their child M is the child of L's nephew and niece, which makes M the grandniece or grandnephew of L. No other blood link changes this basic relationship.

question: Let X be a person. X’s mother has a brother (X’s maternal uncle) who has a son Y. X has a daughter Z. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the most precise relation between Y and Z?
explanation: Y is the child of X’s maternal uncle, so Y is X’s first cousin. Z is X’s daughter, one generation below X; therefore Y is a first cousin once removed to Z.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No direct kinship term

question: Two brothers marry two sisters. The elder brother, M, and his wife, N, have a daughter P. The younger brother, Q, and his wife, R, have a son S. P and S marry each other and have a child T. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for T’s relation to M?
explanation: M is P’s father, so T is M’s grandchild. M is also Q’s brother, making S M’s nephew; thus T is M’s great‑niece/nephew. The closest degree of relationship is grandchild (two generations removed), which is the precise term.

question: A and B share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). A has a child C and B has a child D, with no other intermarriages. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between C and D?
explanation: C and D are each the child of a half‑sibling, so they share only one grandparent pair. The exact term for such a relationship is "half‑first cousins"—they are not full first cousins (which require both grandparents) nor second cousins.

question: Brother A marries sister C and brother B marries sister D (C and D are sisters). A and C have a son X; B and D have a son Y. X and Y each marry unrelated spouses and have children M and N respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: X and Y are double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). Their children M and N therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the most specific term.

question: John’s mother has only one brother, whose only child is Emma. John’s father has only one sister, whose only child is Liam. Emma and Liam marry and have a daughter Zoe. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Zoe’s precise relation to John?
explanation: Emma and Liam are John’s first cousins (maternal and paternal respectively). Zoe is one generation below each of them, so she is John’s first cousin once removed. The term is unique and does not involve half‑ or double‑cousin distinctions.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoption, a man says: “My father’s sister’s son is also my mother’s brother’s son.” Using standard English kinship terms (allowing only the affinal link of spouse), what is the most precise term for that son’s relation to the man?
explanation: The father’s sister (paternal aunt) and the mother’s brother (maternal uncle) are married. Their child is the son of both a paternal aunt and a maternal uncle, making him the man’s double first cousin – a first cousin on both parental sides.

question: J’s father has exactly one sister, and J’s mother has exactly one brother. The sister and the brother marry each other and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no incest), what is the most precise relation of M to J?
explanation: M is the child of J’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Those two are siblings of opposite parents who married each other, so M shares both sets of grandparents with J. This makes M and J double first cousins, the precise term.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a son X; N and P have a daughter Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: M and N share parents, and O and P share parents. Hence they are first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins – the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: Brothers A and B each have two children. A’s only child is daughter C. B’s children are son D and daughter E. E marries an unrelated man and has a son G. C marries G. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise blood relation between C and G?
explanation: C is A’s daughter. G is E’s son; E is B’s daughter. A and B are brothers, so C and E are first cousins. G, being E’s child, is one generation below C, making C and G first cousins once removed. No other standard term applies.

question: L has exactly one sister and exactly one brother. The sister’s only son has a child M, and the brother’s only daughter also has a child M (the same person). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s relation to L?
explanation: M is simultaneously the child of L’s nephew (sister’s son) and the child of L’s niece (brother’s daughter). That would make M both a great‑nephew and a great‑niece, which cannot coexist under standard terms; thus no standard direct kinship term applies.
