question: In a lineage, the only son of a man named Frank is Aaron. Frank also has a daughter, Beth, from a different marriage (Aaron and Beth share only Frank as a parent). Aaron marries a woman unrelated to the family and has a child, Clara. Beth also marries an unrelated person and has a child, David. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Clara and David?
explanation: Clara and David are children of half‑siblings (Aaron and Beth share only one parent). Therefore they are half‑first cousins, a distinct term from full first cousins because they share only one grandparent.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: L has a sister and a brother. The sister has exactly one son, and the brother has exactly one daughter. Their only child, M, is the same person. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s nephew (the sister’s son) and also the child of L’s niece (the brother’s daughter). Those two parents are first cousins, so M is the child of L’s niece/nephew, i.e., L’s grand‑niece or grand‑nephew.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, the only child of P. N marries Q, the only child of R. O and Q are first cousins. M and N each have one child: X (child of M) and Y (child of N). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of siblings (M and N) → first cousins. Their other parents O and Q are first cousins, so X and Y are also children of first cousins → second cousins. Since they share both sets of grandparents (paternal A,B and maternal G₁,G₂), the precise term is double first cousins.

question: John is the son of Mary and Peter. Mary’s brother is Tom; Peter’s sister is Linda. Tom and Linda are married and have a child Alex. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for Alex’s relation to John?
explanation: Tom is John’s maternal uncle and Linda is his paternal aunt. Their child Alex shares both sets of grandparents with John, making Alex a double first cousin.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P. O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father (M) and Y’s father (N) are brothers, and X’s mother (O) and Y’s mother (P) are sisters. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: Two brothers, Mark and Luke, each marry a sister, Anne and Beth, respectively. Mark and Anne have a single child Carl; Luke and Beth have a single child Dana. Carl and Dana each have one child: Carl’s child Sam and Dana’s child Tara. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between Sam and Tara?
explanation: Mark‑Luke and Anne‑Beth are two sibling pairs married to each other, so Carl and Dana are double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). Their children Sam and Tara therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins – the most exact term.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona each have one child, respectively named Paul and Quinn. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Paul and Quinn?
explanation: Adam and Brian are brothers; Clara and Diana are sisters. Their children Ethan and Fiona share both paternal and maternal grandparents, making them double first cousins. Consequently, Paul and Quinn share both sets of great‑grandparents, which classifies them as double second cousins – the most specific term.

question: Emma and Fiona are sisters. Alan and Brian are brothers. Emma marries Alan and they have a daughter Clara. Fiona marries Brian and they have a son David. Clara and David each marry unrelated partners and have children Lily and Mark respectively. What is the most precise kinship term between Lily and Mark?
explanation: Emma & Fiona are sisters and Alan & Brian are brothers, so Clara and David share both sets of grandparents—double first cousins. Their children Lily and Mark therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins.

question: M and N share only a mother (they are half‑siblings). M has one child C, and N has one child D. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relationship between C and D?
explanation: C and D are each the child of a half‑sibling of the other. They share exactly one grandparent (the common mother’s parent) but not both, so they are half‑first cousins. Full first cousins would require both grandparents in common.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary’s son Peter marries John’s daughter Anna. Peter and Anna have a child Lily. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only), what is Lily’s relation to John?
explanation: John is Anna’s father, so he is Lily’s maternal grandfather. He is also Mary’s brother, making him Peter’s maternal uncle and thus Lily’s paternal great‑uncle. The closest generational blood link is grandparent, so Lily is John’s granddaughter (grandfather).

question: R’s father has one sister who has a daughter S. R’s mother has one brother who has a son T. S and T marry and have a child U. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation of U to R?
explanation: S is R’s paternal first cousin; T is R’s maternal first cousin. Their child U is the child of two of R’s first cousins, which makes U a first cousin once removed to R (the ‘once removed’ indicates a one‑generation difference). No additional qualifier is needed.

question: M is the mother of N and O. O’s sibling is T (so T is also M’s child). N is married to P. P’s sister is Q, and Q is married to R. What is the precise standard English kinship term for Q’s relation to N?
explanation: N’s spouse is P. Q is P’s sister, making Q the sibling‑in‑law of N. No blood link exists, and no other affinal chain yields a different term. Hence Q is N’s sister‑in‑law.

question: A’s mother has exactly one brother and A’s father has exactly one brother. Each of those brothers has exactly one child. If you are told that a person B is either the child of A’s maternal uncle or the child of A’s paternal uncle (but not which), what is B’s precise relationship to A using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Whether B is the child of the mother’s brother or the father’s brother, B is the child of one of A’s parents’ siblings. That makes B a first cousin to A in either case.

question: Two brothers marry two sisters. The first brother and his wife have a child P; the second brother and his wife have a child Q. P and Q each have one child, R and S respectively. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between R and S?
explanation: P and Q are double first cousins because they share both sets of grandparents. Their children R and S therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins, which is the most precise term.

question: Anna’s mother has a brother Ben. Ben’s daughter Clara marries David, who is the son of Anna’s father’s sister (Anna’s paternal aunt’s son). Anna and David have a child Ethan. What is Ethan’s precise relation to Ben using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Ben is Anna’s maternal uncle. Anna is Ben’s niece. Ethan, being Anna’s child, is the child of Ben’s niece, which makes Ethan Ben’s grandnephew (also called great‑nephew). No other blood link exists.

question: R is married to S. S’s brother is T. T is married to U. U has a sister V. Using standard English kinship terms limited to spouse, parents, siblings, and children of these as in‑laws, what is V’s relation to R?
explanation: S’s brother T is R’s brother‑in‑law. T’s wife U becomes R’s sister‑in‑law. V is U’s sister, which is a sibling of an in‑law, a step beyond the allowed in‑law scope. No standard direct kin term exists for this affinal chain, so the correct description is “no standard direct relation”.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan, and Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relationship between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. This makes them double first cousins, the exact term for cousins who are related through both parental lines.

question: B is the sister of C. A is the son of B. D is the son of C. E is the daughter of D. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the relation of A to E?
explanation: B and C are siblings. A, child of B, and D, child of C, are first cousins. E is D's daughter, making her one generation below A's cousin. Therefore A and E are first cousins once removed.

question: In a family with no adoptions or remarriages, let X be the child of the sister of Y’s mother and also the child of the brother of Y’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: The sister of Y’s mother is Y’s maternal aunt; her child is Y’s first cousin. The brother of Y’s father is Y’s paternal uncle; his child is also Y’s first cousin. X occupies both roles, sharing both sets of grandparents with Y, which is termed a double first cousin—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: Let M be the only brother of L’s mother, and let N be the only sister of K’s father. If P is the child of M and Q is the child of N, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between P and Q?
explanation: M is L’s maternal uncle, so P is L’s first cousin. N is K’s paternal aunt, so Q is K’s first cousin. Since L and K are the same person (the only child of the mother and father), P and Q are both first cousins of that person, making P and Q first cousins to each other. The precise term is “first cousin”.

question: R's mother has a brother T whose daughter is X. R's father has a sister U whose son is Y. X and Y marry and have a child Z. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, but cousin marriage allowed), what is Z's relation to R?
explanation: R and X are first cousins (maternal side); R and Y are first cousins (paternal side). Z is the child of both X and Y, so Z is the child of R's first cousins on each side, making Z R's first cousin once removed. The relationship is the same via either line.

question: In a family with no adoptions and monogamy allowed, M's mother has exactly one brother, A, whose daughter is N. M's father has exactly one sister, B, whose son is P. If we select either N or P and call that person Q, what is Q's relation to M?
explanation: M’s maternal uncle A’s daughter N is the child of M’s mother’s brother – a first cousin. M’s paternal aunt B’s son P is also a first cousin. Whichever of N or P we call Q, Q is always M’s first cousin. No other relationship fits.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries his maternal cousin O (the child of M’s mother’s sister). N marries O’s brother P, who is also M’s maternal cousin. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two sibling pairs (M‑N and O‑P). Since each pair of spouses are also cousins, the children share both sets of grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: R’s father has a sister (paternal aunt) who has a son S. R’s mother has a brother (maternal uncle) who has a daughter T. S and T marry and have a child U. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between R and U?
explanation: S is R’s paternal first cousin; T is R’s maternal first cousin. U is the child of two first cousins who are unrelated to each other. U therefore shares each set of R’s great‑grandparents, making R and U double second cousins – the most exact term.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed
D) D) No standard direct kinship term

question: M and N are married. M has exactly one sibling, a brother B, who is married to a woman C. C has exactly one child, P. N has exactly one sibling, a sister S, who is married to a man D. D also has exactly one child, and that child is the same P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation of P to M?
explanation: P is the child of M's maternal (or paternal) uncle B and also the child of M's paternal (or maternal) aunt S. Thus P shares both of M's grandparents, making P a double first cousin of M – the most specific term.

question: A is the father of B and C, who are half‑siblings (they share only A). B marries D and they have a daughter E. After B’s death, C marries D and they have a son F. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy but remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation between E and F?
explanation: D is the mother of both E and F, so they share a parent, making them half‑siblings. This blood link is more specific than any cousin relationship that also exists, so the precise term is half‑siblings.

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother (M) and R’s father has exactly one sister (N). M’s only child (C1) and N’s only child (C2) marry each other and have a single child S. Using standard English kinship terms, what is S’s precise relation to R?
explanation: M is R’s maternal uncle, so C1 is R’s first cousin. N is R’s paternal aunt, so C2 is also R’s first cousin. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. question: A's mother has a brother B. B's daughter is C. A's father has a sister D, whose son is E. Assuming no intermarriage between B and D's families, what is the precise kinship term for the relation between C and E using standard English blood‑kin terms?
explanation: C is A's maternal first cousin (child of A's maternal uncle B). E is A's paternal first cousin (child of A's paternal aunt D). B and D are unrelated, so C and E share no common ancestor. Thus there is no standard blood‑kin term; they are related only through affinal chains.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M is the mother of J. J is married to L. L's father is the brother of M's husband, and L's mother is the sister of M's father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation of L to M?
explanation: L's father is M's husband's brother, making L M's niece through marriage. L's mother is M's father's sister, also making L M's niece by blood. Both lines give the same blood relation, so L is a double niece of M, regardless of her being J's spouse.

question: A and B are siblings. A marries C and B marries D, where C and D are also siblings. A and C have a son X; B and D have a daughter Y. X and Y (who are double first cousins) marry and have a child Z. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for Z relative to A’s mother?
explanation: A’s mother is the grandmother of X (through A) and also the grandmother of Y (through B). Z is the child of X and Y, so Z is one more generation down from each line, making Z a great‑grandchild of A’s mother via both parental lines. The precise term is therefore great‑grandchild.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries X and N marries Y, where X and Y are also siblings. M and X have a son A; N and Y have a daughter B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents: M‑N’s parents and X‑Y’s parents. Thus they are first cousins through two distinct parent‑pair links, i.e., double first cousins. No other term captures this dual shared ancestry.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John marries Lisa. Mary's only child is Peter. Lisa's brother Kevin marries Peter's sister Anna. Kevin and Anna have a daughter Sophie. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of Sophie to John?
explanation: Anna is John’s niece (daughter of his sister Mary). Sophie is Anna’s daughter, so she is John’s grand‑niece. Although Sophie is also the child of John’s brother‑in‑law Kevin, the blood relationship is more specific. Hence the precise term is grand‑niece.

question: L has a sister and a brother. The only son of L’s sister has a child, and the only daughter of L’s brother also has a child. If those two children are the same person M, what is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to L (using standard English kin terms, without ignoring doubled ancestry)?
explanation: The son of L’s sister is L’s nephew; his child is L’s great‑nephew/niece. Likewise, the daughter of L’s brother is L’s niece; her child is also L’s great‑nephew/niece. Both descriptions refer to the same person, so M is L’s great‑nephew/niece.

question: A is the son of B's sister. C is the daughter of D, where D is B's brother. A and C marry and have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of B to E?
explanation: B's sister's son A is B's nephew; B's brother's daughter C is B's niece. A and C are first cousins, so their child E is B's grand‑niece/nephew, i.e., B is E's grand‑aunt/uncle (great‑aunt/uncle).

question: John is married to Mary. Mary’s brother Tom is married to Susan, who is the daughter of John’s sister Emma. Emma’s son Alex is married to Lisa, who is Tom’s sister. What is the precise kinship term for Alex’s relation to Tom using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: Alex is John’s nephew (child of John’s sister). Tom is John’s brother‑in‑law (husband of John’s wife’s brother). The chain nephew → John → brother‑in‑law yields no recognized blood or immediate in‑law term, so there is no standard direct relation.

question: L’s father has a sister Anna. L’s mother has a brother Ben. Anna and Ben are married and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: Anna is L’s paternal aunt and Ben is L’s maternal uncle. Their child M shares both of L’s grandparent pairs, so M and L are double first cousins—the only term that precisely captures this relationship.

question: M and N are brother and sister. S and R are also brother and sister. M marries S and N marries R. M and S have a child X; N and R have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (and not ignoring doubled ancestry), what is the most precise term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two sibling couples where each parent pair shares both parents. Hence X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the only term that captures the doubled lineage.

question: In a family tree: L is the child of M. M has a brother N. N's child is O. O's child is P. Additionally, L's mother Q is sister of R, who is married to S, and S's son T is a friend of P. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the relation of P to L?
explanation: M’s brother N is L’s uncle. N’s child O is L’s first cousin. O’s child P is one generation down from that cousin, making P L’s first cousin once removed.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has two children: a son P and a daughter R. R is the mother of Q, who is the only child of P. What is the exact kinship term for the relation between O and R?
explanation: O is the child of M, who is N's sibling, so O is N's niece. R is N's daughter. Therefore O and R share the same grandparent pair, making them first cousins. No other qualifier (half, double, etc.) applies.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (without ignoring doubled ancestry), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because each pair of parents are siblings. Hence they are first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins—the most specific label.

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamous marriages, let A be the child of the only brother of B’s mother, and let C be the child of the only brother of B’s father. If one of A or C is selected and called D, what is D’s relation to B?
explanation: Whether D is A or C, D is the child of either B’s maternal uncle or B’s paternal uncle. A child of a parent’s brother is, by definition, a first cousin of the parent’s child. Hence D is always B’s first cousin.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: Person P's mother is the only child of her mother (M1). M1's brother (U) has a daughter C. Person P's father is the only child of his father (F1). F1's sister (V) has a son D. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise blood relation between C and D?
explanation: C is the daughter of P’s maternal great‑uncle (the brother of P’s maternal grandmother). D is the son of P’s paternal great‑aunt (the sister of P’s paternal grandfather). These two ancestors are from different sides of P’s family and share no common ancestors, so C and D have no blood tie. Hence they are not related.

question: M is simultaneously the child of the only sister of N’s father and the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation of M to N?
explanation: The sister of N’s father is N’s paternal aunt; her child is N’s paternal first cousin. The brother of N’s mother is N’s maternal uncle; his child is N’s maternal first cousin. Since both descriptions refer to the same person M, M is both a paternal and a maternal first cousin – a double first cousin of N.

question: M has a brother N. N’s daughter is P. M’s daughter is Q, and Q’s son is R. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of P to R?
explanation: P is M’s niece (child of M’s brother). Q is M’s daughter, so P and Q are first cousins. R is Q’s son, making R the next generation. A first cousin’s child is a first cousin once removed, so P is R’s first cousin once removed.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), R's mother has a brother, and that brother has a daughter S. What is S to R?
explanation: R's mother’s brother is R’s maternal uncle. His daughter is therefore the child of R’s parent’s sibling, which by definition is a first cousin. No other relation applies.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: M is the child of the sister of N’s father, and also the child of the brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: M’s mother is N’s paternal aunt and M’s father is N’s maternal uncle. Both of M’s parents are siblings of N’s parents, so M and N share all four grandparents. The exact term is double first cousins.

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother (M) and R’s father has exactly one brother (P). M’s child (C₁) and P’s child (C₂) marry each other and have a son S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relationship of S to R?
explanation: C₁ and C₂ are each R’s first cousins (maternal and paternal). Their child S is therefore the child of R’s first cousin, which makes S R’s first cousin once removed. The double‑cousin ancestry does not change the generational offset.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: Martha and Carl share only their mother (different fathers). Martha marries Daniel, whose sister is Emma. Emma marries Carl. Martha’s child is Zoe; Carl’s child is Max. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise blood relation between Zoe and Max?
explanation: Martha and Carl are half‑siblings, sharing a single grandparent (their mother’s parents). Their children, Zoe and Max, therefore share only that one grandparent pair, not the full set. The correct term for cousins who share exactly one grandparent is “half‑first cousins.”

question: Adam and Ben are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a child Ethan. Ben marries Diana and they have a child Fiona. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are children of two brothers and two sisters. They share both paternal grandparents (parents of Adam and Ben) and both maternal grandparents (parents of Clara and Diana). Because they share a full set of grandparents on both sides, the exact term is “double first cousins.”

question: In a family with no adoptions, monogamy allowed, and remarriage permitted, let M be the brother of L's mother and N be the sister of L's father. M and N marry each other and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between L and C?
explanation: M is L's maternal uncle and N is L's paternal aunt. Their child C shares both of L's sets of grandparents, i.e., the maternal grandparents (through M) and the paternal grandparents (through N). Therefore L and C are double first cousins, the only term that captures both shared grandparent pairs.

question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father, and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M’s father is N’s maternal uncle (the only brother of N’s mother), and M’s mother is N’s paternal aunt (the only sister of N’s father). Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with N, giving the precise kinship term “double first cousin.”

question: Two brothers, Adam and Ben, each marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Ben and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Ignoring any later marriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for Ethan’s relation to Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents (the parents of Adam/Ben and the parents of Clara/Diana). Hence they are double first cousins, not merely first cousins.

question: Let X and Y be two persons. X is the child of the only brother of Y’s mother, and Y is the child of the only sister of X’s father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for X to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle, making X a first cousin of Y. Simultaneously, Y is the child of X’s paternal aunt, making Y a first cousin of X. Because the two cousin relationships involve both parental lines, they share both pairs of grandparents, giving them the precise relation of double first cousins.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let X be the child of Y's mother's brother, and let Z be the child of Y. What is the precise kinship term between X and Z using standard English relations?
explanation: Y's mother's brother is Y's maternal uncle; his child X is Y's first cousin. Z is Y's child, one generation below Y. Therefore X is one generation apart from Z, making them first cousins once removed.

question: N’s father has exactly one sibling, a man named U, and N’s mother has exactly one sibling, a woman named V. U and V are married to each other and have a child M. Who is M to N, using standard English kinship terms and assuming no incest or adoption?
explanation: U is N’s paternal uncle and V is N’s maternal aunt. Their child M is the child of both N’s paternal uncle and maternal aunt, making M a double first cousin of N. No other standard term fits more precisely.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Adam marries Clara and Brian marries Diana, who are sisters. Adam and Clara have a daughter Eva; Brian and Diana have a son Frank. Before Eva and Frank marry each other, what is the most precise kinship term describing their relationship?
explanation: Eva and Frank share both sets of grandparents: Adam and Brian share the same parents, and Clara and Diana share the same parents. Hence they are first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides, i.e., double first cousins. No other standard term is more precise.

question: John and Mark are brothers. Anna and Beth are sisters. John marries Anna and they have a son Carl. Mark marries Beth and they have a daughter Dana. Carl and Dana each marry unrelated partners and have children Ethan and Fiona respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Carl and Dana share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins. Their children therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making Ethan and Fiona double second cousins. No simpler term captures this double lineage.

question: M is the child of the sibling of N’s father, and also the child of the sibling of N’s mother. Assuming no intermarriage among those siblings, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between M and N?
explanation: M’s father is N’s paternal uncle and M’s mother is N’s maternal aunt; they are unrelated to each other. Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures sharing both grandparent pairs.

question: J’s mother has a sister S, and J’s father has a brother B. S and B marry each other and have a child M. What is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to J, using standard English blood‑relation terminology and without ignoring doubled ancestry?
explanation: M is the child of J’s maternal aunt (mother’s sister) and also the child of J’s paternal uncle (father’s brother). Hence M shares both of J’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: A’s mother has exactly one brother, and A’s father has exactly one brother. Those two brothers are married to each other and have a single child, X. What is the most precise kinship term for X’s relation to A?
explanation: X shares both sets of grandparents with A—maternal and paternal—so X is a first cousin on both sides. The precise term for such a relationship is double first cousin.

question: John has a sister Mary. John’s brother Tom has a daughter Lisa. Mary’s son Peter marries Lisa. Peter and Lisa have a child Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is Emma’s relation to Peter’s mother Mary?
explanation: Mary is Peter’s mother. Emma is Peter’s child, so she is the child of Mary’s son. That makes Emma Mary’s granddaughter, the precise term being "granddaughter".

question: John's mother has exactly one brother, Peter. John's father has exactly one sister, Mary. Peter and Mary are married and have a single child, Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage not allowed), what is Emma's precise relation to John?
explanation: Peter is John’s maternal uncle and Mary is John’s paternal aunt. Their child Emma is simultaneously the child of John’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, making her both a first cousin on the mother’s side and a first cousin on the father’s side. The precise term is “double first cousin.”

question: Maya is the only child of her mother. Maya’s mother has a brother Tom; Tom’s daughter Lily is Maya’s first cousin. Maya’s father has a brother Raj, who marries Lily. Maya has a child Sam; Lily and Raj have a child Nina. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Sam and Nina?
explanation: Lily is Maya’s first cousin (maternal). Raj, Maya’s paternal uncle, is Nina’s father, making Nina Maya’s first cousin (paternal). Sam is Maya’s child, so Sam is one generation below Maya. Therefore Sam is a first cousin once removed to Nina (the child of Maya’s cousin and the cousin of Maya’s child).

question: A's mother is the only sister of B's father, and A's father is married to B's mother. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only, ignoring marriage), what is the precise relation of A to B?
explanation: A's mother is sibling of B's father, so A is the child of B's paternal aunt, making A and B first cousins. The marriage of the other parents does not affect the blood relationship.

question: Alex’s mother has a brother (M) and Alex’s father has a sister (F). M’s child (C1) and F’s child (C2) marry each other and have a child named Sam. What is Sam’s precise relation to Alex, using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: C1 is Alex’s maternal first cousin; C2 is Alex’s paternal first cousin. Sam is the child of each of those cousins, so Sam is one generation below Alex’s first cousins on both sides. That makes Sam a first cousin once removed (the “once removed” indicates the one‑generation gap).
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: Let R be a person. R’s mother has exactly one brother (M) and R’s father has exactly one brother (F). S is the child of either M or F (you do not know which). Using standard English kinship terms, what is S’s precise relation to R?
explanation: Whether S is the child of R’s maternal uncle or paternal uncle, S is the child of a parent’s brother. That makes S a first cousin of R in either case.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: Alice's mother and Bob's father share the same mother but have different fathers (they are half‑siblings). There are no other intermarriages in the family. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Alice and Bob?
explanation: Alice’s mother and Bob’s father are half‑siblings, so Alice and Bob share only one grandparent. Children of half‑siblings are called half‑first cousins. Full first cousins require both grandparents in common, which is not the case here.

question: John is the son of Mary. Mary’s brother Peter is married to Susan. Susan has a daughter Lisa from a previous marriage. Lisa is married to Tom, who is the son of John’s sister Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Lisa’s relation to John?
explanation: Lisa is married to Tom, who is the son of John’s sister Emma; thus Tom is John’s nephew. Lisa, as Tom’s spouse, is John’s niece‑in‑law. No blood link exists via Susan or Peter. Therefore the precise standard term is niece‑in‑law.

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamy (remarriage allowed), L’s mother has a brother U₁ whose daughter is C. L’s father has a brother U₂ whose son is S. C and S marry and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the most precise relation of M to L?
explanation: C is L’s first cousin (maternal) and S is L’s first cousin (paternal). Their child M is the child of L’s first cousin on each side, which makes M a first cousin once removed to L. The double‑cousin fact does not change the standard term; it remains first cousin once removed.

question: L has a sister and a brother. M is the child of the only son of L’s sister, and N is the child of the only daughter of L’s brother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between M and N?
explanation: L’s sister’s son and L’s brother’s daughter are children of two siblings, so they are first cousins. Their children (M and N) are therefore children of first cousins, which makes M and N second cousins. No other common ancestors are involved, so the exact term is second cousins.

question: Alex’s mother has one brother, Martin. Martin’s only son is Ethan. Alex’s sister Beth is married to Carl, whose sister Diana is married to Ethan. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only), what is Ethan to Alex?
explanation: Ethan is the son of Martin, who is Alex’s mother’s brother, i.e., Alex’s maternal uncle. The child of an uncle (or aunt) is a first cousin. No other relationship applies.

question: M is the child of N’s father’s only sister and also the child of N’s mother’s only brother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s precise relation to N?
explanation: M is child of N’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle. Each connection makes M a first cousin of N; the two lines are independent, so M is simply a first cousin (both paternal and maternal). No other distinct kin term applies.
choices: A) First cousin (both paternal and maternal)

question: A and C are brothers; B and D are sisters. A marries B and has a child P. C marries D and has a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no “double” prefixes allowed except when necessary), what is the most precise relationship between P and Q?
explanation: P and Q share both sets of grandparents: the parents of A/C and the parents of B/D. Hence they are first cousins on the paternal side and also first cousins on the maternal side, i.e., double first cousins. No closer term exists in standard kinship.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter X with his wife A. N has a son Y with his wife B. A and B are themselves sisters. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, ignoring step relations), what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of siblings (M and N) and their mothers are sisters, so X and Y share both sets of grandparents. They are therefore double first cousins, a relation more specific than ordinary first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries X and N marries Y, where X and Y are also siblings. M and X have a child A; N and Y have a child B. A and B marry each other and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is the most precise term for the relationship between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents: M‑N’s parents and X‑Y’s parents. Hence they are double first cousins, not merely first cousins or half‑cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has two children, a son P and a daughter R. R has a child Q. What is the precise standard English kinship term for the relation between O and Q?
explanation: M and N are siblings, so O (M’s child) and R (N’s child) are first cousins. Q is R’s child, making Q a first cousin once removed of O. Hence the exact term is first cousin once removed.

question: Let N be a person. N’s mother has exactly one brother, and N’s father has exactly one sister. The child of that maternal uncle marries the child of that paternal aunt, and their only child is M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is M’s precise relationship to N?
explanation: The maternal uncle’s child is N’s first cousin on the mother’s side; the paternal aunt’s child is N’s first cousin on the father’s side. Their child M is therefore the child of two first cousins who share no common grandparents, making M a first cousin once removed to N on both sides, which simplifies to just "first cousin" because the removal cancels when both lines are considered.

question: In a monogamous family, Alex has a sister Beth. Beth’s only child is Carl. Alex’s only child is Dana, who marries Carl. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring remarriage), what is the precise relationship of Carl to Alex?
explanation: Beth is Alex’s sister, so her son Carl is Alex’s nephew. Carl also marries Alex’s daughter Dana, making Carl Alex’s son‑in‑law. Since both blood and affinal links exist, the most exact description is that Carl is both nephew and son‑in‑law to Alex.

question: John has a brother Tom. Tom’s daughter Lisa is therefore John’s niece. Lisa marries Kevin. John and Kevin have no other family connections. Using standard English kinship terms limited to blood relations, what is the precise relation of Kevin to John?
explanation: John and Kevin share no common ancestor; Kevin is only linked to John through his marriage to John’s niece. Hence there is no blood relationship between them.
choices: C) C) No blood relation (affinal only)

question: Two brothers each marry a different sister from the same family, and each couple has exactly one child. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the relationship between the two children?
explanation: The children share both sets of grandparents—their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters—so they are double first cousins, not merely first or half‑first cousins.

question: P's mother M has a brother U, and P's father F has a sister V. U and V marry each other and have a son S. Using standard English kinship terms, what is S's relation to P?
explanation: U is P's maternal uncle, making S P's first cousin on the maternal side. V is P's paternal aunt, making S also P's first cousin on the paternal side. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes S a double first cousin of P.

question: L is the only child of her mother G. G is also the mother of K, who is the only son of his mother K‑m. L’s son is M, and K’s son is N. P is the child of M and Q is the child of N. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: G is the mother of both L and K, so L and K are siblings. M (L’s child) and N (K’s child) are therefore first cousins. Their children P and Q are the children of first cousins, which makes P and Q second cousins. No other relationship fits.
choices: C) C) First cousins once removed

question: M is the child of the only sibling of L’s father and also the child of the only sibling of L’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation between M and L?
explanation: M’s mother is L’s father’s sister and M’s father is L’s mother’s brother. Therefore M shares both sets of grandparents with L, making them double first cousins – the most specific standard term.

question: Emma's father has a brother Tom. Tom's daughter is Lily. Lily's son is Alex. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is Alex's precise relation to Emma?
explanation: Emma and Lily are first cousins (children of siblings). Lily's son Alex is one generation below Lily, making him Emma's first cousin once removed. The term is precise and does not imply any closer or more distant relationship.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard direct relation

question: In a family with no intermarriage, let R be a person. Define P as the child of R’s mother’s sister’s child, and Q as the child of R’s father’s sister’s child. If we select either P or Q and call that person S, what is S’s relation to R using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: R’s mother’s sister is a maternal aunt; her child is a first cousin. The child of that cousin (P) is a first cousin once removed. The same reasoning applies to the paternal aunt’s line (Q). Hence, whichever is chosen, S is a first cousin once removed of R.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has two children: a son P and a daughter R. R has a child Q. Before any marriage, what is the precise blood relation between O and Q?
explanation: M and N are siblings. Therefore M is aunt/uncle of N's children R and P. O, M's daughter, is first cousin of R. Q is R's child, so O is one generation apart from Q, making O Q's first cousin once removed. No other relationship fits.

question: Two brothers, M and O, each marry a sister, N and P respectively. M + N have a son A; O + P have a daughter B. Before A and B marry each other, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. Hence they are first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides, i.e., double first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O; N has a son P. O and P marry and have a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is Q’s precise relation to M’s mother?
explanation: M’s mother is the grandmother of both O and P. Q is the child of those grandchildren, making Q a great‑grandchild through two independent lines. The double descent is captured only by “great‑grandchild (double)”, which is more precise than plain great‑grandchild.

question: John and Mary are married. John's sister Anna marries Mary's brother Ben. Anna and Ben have a child Clara. John and Mary have a child David. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between Clara and David?
explanation: Clara and David share both sets of grandparents: John’s parents are grandparents of both via Anna and John; Mary’s parents are grandparents of both via Ben and Mary. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the exact term.

question: Emma's mother has two children: Emma and her half‑brother Liam (they share only the mother). Liam’s son Noah is married to Emma’s daughter Lily. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for Noah’s relation to Emma?
explanation: Liam is Emma’s half‑brother, so his child Noah is Emma’s half‑nephew. The term “half‑nephew” distinguishes the single‑shared‑parent link from a full nephew. No other answer captures this nuance.

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage possible: X is the child of the woman who is the only sister of Y’s mother, and also the child of the man who is the only brother of Y’s father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for X relative to Y?
explanation: The woman is Y’s maternal aunt, so X is Y’s maternal first cousin. The man is Y’s paternal uncle, so X is also Y’s paternal first cousin. Sharing both a set of grandparents makes X a double first cousin of Y – the most specific standard term.

question: X’s mother has a brother U, and X’s father has a sister V. U and V are married to each other and have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of Y to X?
explanation: Y is the child of X’s maternal uncle (U) – making Y a first cousin on the mother’s side – and also the child of X’s paternal aunt (V) – making Y a first cousin on the father’s side. Sharing both sets of grandparents, Y is a double first cousin of X.

question: M is the mother of J. J is the father of L, whose sister is K. K is married to T. T is the son of S, and S is the brother of M’s husband. What is T’s precise relation to M using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: M’s husband’s brother S is M’s brother‑in‑law. T, being S’s son, is the nephew of M’s husband and therefore M’s nephew‑in‑law. No blood link exists, and the term “nephew‑in‑law” is the most specific standard kinship label.

question: M is the child of the sister of N’s mother, and also the child of the brother of N’s father. Assuming no intermarriage among the relatives, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for M’s relation to N?
explanation: M is a child of N’s maternal aunt (first cousin on the mother’s side) and also a child of N’s paternal uncle (first cousin on the father’s side). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes M a double first cousin of N, the exact term.

question: M is the only child of his father's second wife. The father's first wife had a daughter L. L marries M's paternal uncle (the father's brother). L and the uncle have a son J. What is J's precise relation to M using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: J is the child of M's paternal uncle, making him M's first cousin. The fact that J's mother L is M's half‑sister does not alter the cousin classification, which depends only on the sibling relationship of their parents.

question: A and B are siblings. A has one child C. B has one child D, who in turn has a child E (E is D’s child). What is the precise kinship term for E’s relation to A, using standard English kin terms?
explanation: B is A’s sibling, so D is A’s niece/nephew. E, as D’s child, is A’s great‑niece/nephew, making A E’s great‑aunt/uncle. No other standard term applies.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: Emma’s father Tom has a sister Lisa; Lisa’s son is Mark. Emma’s mother Sarah has a brother Paul; Paul’s daughter is Anna. Mark and Anna marry and have a child Lily. What is Lily’s precise relationship to Emma using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed)?
explanation: Lisa is Emma’s paternal aunt, so Mark is Emma’s first cousin. Paul is Emma’s maternal uncle, so Anna is also Emma’s first cousin. Lily, their child, is the child of two of Emma’s first cousins, making Lily Emma’s first cousin once removed on both sides – a double first cousin once removed.
choices: C) C) Half‑first cousin once removed
D) D) Double first cousin once removed

question: John and Tom are brothers. John’s sister Mary has a son Peter. Tom has a daughter Sarah. Assuming no other marriages or adoptions, what is the precise kinship term between Peter and Sarah?
explanation: Mary is both John’s sister and Tom’s sister. Peter, as Mary’s son, is John’s nephew and also Tom’s nephew. Sarah, as Tom’s daughter, is John’s niece and also Mary’s niece. Thus Peter and Sarah are children of siblings (Mary and Tom), sharing the same set of grandparents, making them first cousins.
choices: D) D) No direct kinship term

question: B has two children: a son A and a daughter (unnamed). B’s sister is C, who is married to D. D and C have a daughter E. E marries F, who is the son of A. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is D to F?
explanation: D is the father of E. E is the spouse of F, so D is F’s father‑in‑law. No other blood or affinal term applies under the given limited in‑law scope.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: X is the child of the sibling of Y’s paternal grandmother and also the child of the sibling of Y’s maternal grandfather. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for X’s relation to Y?
explanation: X is child of the sibling of Y’s paternal grandmother and also child of the sibling of Y’s maternal grandfather. If those two siblings are distinct, X is a first cousin once removed of Y. If they happen to be the same person (the two grandparents are siblings), X becomes a double first cousin once removed. Since the information does not specify, the precise relation cannot be uniquely determined, making D correct.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, Emma is the only child of her parents. Emma’s mother has exactly one brother, Tom. Tom has a daughter, Nina, who in turn has a son, Leo. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of Leo to Emma?
explanation: Tom is Emma’s maternal uncle, making Nina Emma’s first cousin. Nina’s son Leo is one generation below Nina, so he is the child of Emma’s first cousin. That makes Leo Emma’s first cousin once removed, the exact term required.

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoption, let Y be a person. Y’s mother has exactly one sister, and Y’s father has exactly one brother. The sister of Y’s mother marries the brother of Y’s father, and they have a child X. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X’s mother is Y’s maternal aunt and X’s father is Y’s paternal uncle. Thus X is Y’s first cousin on the mother’s side and also on the father’s side, making X a double first cousin of Y. No other relationship applies.

question: J’s paternal grandfather has a daughter who is J’s aunt; that aunt’s child is K. J’s maternal grandmother has a son who is J’s uncle; that uncle’s child is also K. What is K’s precise relation to J?
explanation: K is the child of J's father's sister and also the child of J's mother's brother. Thus K shares both of J's grandparent pairs, which is the definition of a double first cousin. No other option matches this precise relationship.

question: L’s father has exactly one sister, and L’s mother has exactly one brother. M is the child of that sister and also the child of that brother (the two siblings are married to each other). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s relation to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) – a first cousin. M is also the child of L’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) – again a first cousin. Both descriptions give the same relation, so M is L’s first cousin.

question: A and B are brother and sister. C is the son of A. D is the daughter of B. E is the daughter of C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of E to D?
explanation: A and B are siblings, so their children C and D are first cousins. E is C's child, making E a generation below C. Hence E is the child of D's first cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed.

question: R is married to S. S’s sister is T. T is married to U. U’s sister is V. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is V’s relation to R?
explanation: V is the sister of U, who is the spouse of R’s sister‑in‑law (T). This affinal chain goes beyond the scope of recognized in‑law relations and creates no blood link, so no standard direct kinship term applies.
choices: D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a daughter X; N and P have a son Y. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents (their parents are each pair of siblings). Hence they are first cousins on both maternal and paternal sides, i.e., double first cousins.

question: Let Y be a person. Z is the child of the only brother of Y's mother and also the child of the only sister of Y's father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is Z's precise relationship to Y using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Z’s father is Y’s maternal uncle and Z’s mother is Y’s paternal aunt; both are siblings of Y’s parents. Therefore Z is the child of a sibling on each side, making Z Y’s first cousin. No other standard term fits.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: In a family where no intermarriages occur, let N be a person. N’s father has exactly one sibling, a brother F, and N’s mother has exactly one sibling, a sister M. A child X is born to the union of F and M. What is the precise kinship term for X in relation to N?
explanation: X is the child of N’s paternal uncle (F) and maternal aunt (M). Therefore X shares both sets of grandparents with N, making them first cousins on both sides – a double first cousin, the most specific standard term.

question: M is the father of N. M’s sister S is the mother of R. R is married to T, who is the brother of P. P is the mother of Q, and N is married to Q. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of T to M?
explanation: S is M’s sister, so R is M’s niece. T is R’s husband, i.e., the spouse of M’s niece. The spouse of a niece/nephew is called a nephew‑in‑law (or niece‑in‑law). No blood link exists, and other in‑law categories do not apply.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother, whose only child is a daughter D. R’s father has exactly one sister, whose only child is a son S. The child of D and the child of S are the same person X. What is X’s precise relationship to R, using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: S is the son of R’s paternal aunt, making his child a first cousin on the father’s side. D is the daughter of R’s maternal uncle, making her child a first cousin on the mother’s side. Since both cousins are the same individual, X shares both sets of grandparents with R, i.e., X is a double first cousin.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard kinship term

question: L’s mother has exactly one brother, and L’s father has exactly one sister. Those two siblings marry each other and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, so M shares both of L’s grandparent pairs. That makes M and L double first cousins—first cousins on both sides. Only option D states this precisely.

question: Let L be a person. M is the child of (i) the only brother of L’s mother and (ii) the only sister of L’s father’s sister. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is M’s relation to L?
explanation: Clause (i) makes M a first cousin of L (child of L’s maternal uncle). Clause (ii) makes M a first cousin of L (child of L’s paternal aunt’s sister, which could be the same aunt or a different sister). Depending on whether the two parents in (i) and (ii) are the same individual or distinct siblings, M could be a first cousin, a half‑first cousin, or a double first cousin. Hence the precise term is not uniquely determinable.

question: A and B are double first cousins (their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters). C is the child of A, and D is the child of B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins. Their children therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making them second cousins with the same double ancestry. The precise term is “double second cousins.”

question: B's mother has exactly one brother, who has a daughter A. A later has a son C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption), what is the precise relation of C to B?
explanation: B's mother's brother is B's maternal uncle; his daughter A is B's first cousin. A's son C is the child of B's first cousin, which makes C B's first cousin once removed.

question: Brothers A and B each marry sisters C and D, respectively (A with C, B with D). A and C have a son X; B and D have a daughter Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two brothers and two sisters. They share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins—the only term capturing the doubled shared ancestry.

question: In a family, W’s mother has exactly one brother, M, and W’s father has exactly one sister, N. Z is the child of M and also the child of N (i.e., M and N are the parents of Z). What is Z’s precise relationship to W using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Z is the child of W’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) – that makes Z a first cousin. The same Z is also the child of W’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) – again a first cousin. Both lines give the same kin term, so Z is W’s first cousin.

question: Person X has a mother M and a father F. M has exactly one brother U, who is married to Y. Y’s sister W is married to F’s only sister A. W and A together are the parents of Z. What is the precise blood‑relation between X and Z?
explanation: A is F’s sister, so A is X’s paternal aunt. A and W are Z’s parents, making Z the child of X’s paternal aunt. The child of an aunt or uncle is always a first cousin, regardless of any extra affinal links. Hence X and Z are first cousins.

question: In a family with monogamy (remarriage allowed) and no adoptions, X’s father’s sister (paternal aunt) marries X’s mother’s brother (maternal uncle). They have a child Y. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: Y is the child of X’s paternal aunt, making Y a first cousin on the father’s side. Y is also the child of X’s maternal uncle, making Y a first cousin on the mother’s side. Because the two cousin links are independent, Y is a double first cousin of X. No other term is more precise.

question: John’s mother has a brother, Mark. Mark’s daughter, Lisa, is married to Tom. Tom’s mother has a brother, Peter. Peter’s son, Alan, is the only child of his parents. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Alan’s relation to John?
explanation: Lisa is John’s first cousin (maternal uncle’s daughter). Tom is Lisa’s husband, so Tom is John’s cousin‑in‑law. Peter is Tom’s maternal uncle, making Alan Tom’s first cousin by blood. Alan is therefore the cousin of John’s cousin‑in‑law, a relationship that passes beyond the immediate in‑law scope and introduces no blood link. No standard direct kin term exists.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: L and M are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). L has a daughter X. M has a son Y. No other marriages or adoptions occur in the family. Using standard English kinship terminology, what is the most precise term for the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent (their common grandmother). The correct precise term is “half‑first cousins,” which denotes cousins who share only one grandparent pair, unlike full first cousins who share both.

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother (her only sibling) and R’s father has exactly one sister (his only sibling). The brother and the sister are married, and their only child is S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is the precise relation of S to R?
explanation: S is the child of R’s maternal uncle and also the child of R’s paternal aunt. Because those two relatives are married, S shares both sets of grandparents with R, making S a double first cousin of R – the most specific standard term.

question: John and Kevin are brothers. John’s sister Mary is married to Tom. Tom’s sister Lucy is married to Kevin. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Lucy’s precise relation to Mary?
explanation: Lucy is the sister of Mary’s husband (Tom), making her Mary’s sister‑in‑law. She is also the wife of Mary’s brother (Kevin), which is another sister‑in‑law link, but the single standard term covering both is simply sister‑in‑law.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: Anna and Ben are siblings. Anna marries Carl, and Ben marries Diana. Carl and Diana are themselves siblings. Ethan is the child of Anna and Carl, and Fiona is the child of Ben and Diana. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring marriage beyond spouses), what is the precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan is child of Anna (Ben’s sister) and Carl (Diana’s brother). Fiona is child of Ben (Anna’s brother) and Diana (Carl’s sister). They share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins.

question: M is the mother of N. N is married to S. S's father is the brother of M's husband. What is M's relation to S's child?
explanation: M is mother of N, who is a parent of S's child. Hence M is the child's grandparent. The extra information only shows that M's husband and S's father are siblings, which does not affect the direct line of descent. Therefore M is the child's grandmother.

question: Consider the following description (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted): M is married to N. N’s mother has a brother O. O’s daughter P is married to Q. Q’s sister is R, and R is the child of S. S is the sister of M’s father. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is R’s relation to M?
explanation: S is M’s father’s sister, i.e., M’s paternal aunt. Her child R is therefore M’s first cousin. The marriages (M‑N, P‑Q) are affinal and do not alter this blood relationship.

question: M and N are siblings. P and Q are siblings. M marries P and N marries Q. Their children are X (child of M + P) and Y (child of N + Q). Using standard English kinship terms (blood only), what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father (M) and Y’s father (N) are brothers, sharing both paternal grandparents. X’s mother (P) and Y’s mother (Q) are sisters, sharing both maternal grandparents. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – a more specific term than simple first cousins.

question: John and Mary are siblings. Mary is married to Peter. Peter’s sister Linda is married to John’s son Alex. Alex and Linda have a daughter Emma. What is Emma’s relation to Peter?
explanation: Linda is Peter’s sister, so her child Emma is Peter’s niece by blood. The extra marriage to Alex (John’s son) does not alter this direct sibling‑child relationship.

question: Two brothers, Aaron and Ben, each marry a sister: Aaron marries Clara and Ben marries Dana, where Clara and Dana are sisters. Aaron and Clara have a son Ethan, and Ben and Dana have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is the most precise term for the relationship between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are children of two brothers (Aaron and Ben) who married two sisters (Clara and Dana). They share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the most specific standard term.

question: John marries Mary. Mary's brother Tom marries John's sister Anne, and Tom and Anne have a daughter Lily. John and Mary have a son Mark. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Lily and Mark?
explanation: Lily’s mother is Mary’s sister‑in‑law and Lily’s father is John’s brother‑in‑law, so Lily’s grandparents are exactly the two sets of John’s and Mary’s parents. Mark, being John and Mary’s child, has the same two sets of grandparents. Hence Lily and Mark share both grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the only precise term.

question: In a monogamous but remarriage‑permitted lineage, M is the child of L (mother) and K (father). After L’s divorce, she marries N, who is K’s brother. M marries O. O’s mother is P, whose father is Q. Q is also K’s father (M’s paternal grandfather). Using standard English kinship terms and assuming no adoption, what is the precise relation of O to M?
explanation: O could be M’s first cousin (if P is K’s sister) or half‑sibling (if P is L’s daughter from a previous marriage). The information given does not uniquely determine which case holds, so the exact kinship cannot be fixed.

question: John has a son Mark with his first wife. After divorcing, John marries Sarah, who already has a son Kevin from a previous marriage and later a daughter Emma from a new marriage. Mark marries Emma, and they have a child Alice. Using standard English kinship terms (allowing half‑relations), what is the most precise relation between Alice and Kevin?
explanation: Kevin and Emma share only their mother Sarah, so they are half‑siblings. Alice is Emma's daughter, making her the child of Kevin's half‑sister. The correct term for the child of a half‑sibling is half‑niece.

question: M and N are siblings. M has two children, A and D; N has two children, B and E. A marries B and they have a child C. D marries E and they have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between C and F?
explanation: A and B are first cousins, as are D and E. Because M and N are siblings, C and F share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: Let P be the child of the only brother of Q’s mother, and let Q be the child of the only sister of P’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between P and Q?
explanation: P is the child of Q’s maternal uncle (the brother of Q’s mother). Q is the child of P’s paternal aunt (the sister of P’s father). Each is the child of a sibling of the other’s parent, which defines first cousins.

question: M and N are brothers. M marries S1 and N marries S2, where S1 and S2 are sisters. M + S1 have child A; N + S2 have child B. A and B each marry unrelated partners and have children C and D respectively. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins. Their children C and D therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins. First cousins (share one grandparent pair), second cousins (share one great‑grandparent pair), and third cousins (share great‑great‑grandparents) are all less precise.

question: L’s mother and M’s father are first cousins. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between L and M?
explanation: L’s mother and M’s father share a pair of grandparents, making them first cousins. Their children (L and M) are one generation down, thus they share the same great‑grandparents but not the same grandparents. Therefore L and M are exactly second cousins.

question: L's mother has exactly one brother and L's father has exactly one sister. Those two siblings marry each other and have a child named N. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between N and L?
explanation: N is the child of L's maternal uncle and paternal aunt, thus shares both of L's grandparent pairs. This makes N and L double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: A's mother has only one brother B, whose only child is C. A's father has only one sister D, whose only child is E. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only), what is the precise relationship between C and E?
explanation: C is the daughter of A’s maternal uncle, and E is the son of A’s paternal aunt. They share no common ancestors, so they are not blood‑related.

question: In a family, X’s father is the brother of Y’s mother, and X’s mother is the sister of Y’s father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father and Y’s mother are siblings, and X’s mother and Y’s father are siblings. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, being children of two sibling couples. The exact term is double first cousins.

question: R’s mother has a brother (M) and R’s father has a sister (F). M marries F and they have a child S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation of S to R?
explanation: S is the child of R’s maternal uncle (M) and paternal aunt (F). Therefore S shares both of R’s grandparent pairs, giving the exact term “double first cousin.”

question: Person P has a mother whose brother is M. M’s son is N, and N’s child is C₁. P also has a father whose sister is S. S’s daughter is D, and D’s child is C₂. If either C₁ or C₂ is selected and called Q, what is Q’s precise kinship term to P using standard English kinship?
explanation: N is P’s maternal first cousin; his child C₁ is one generation down, so C₁ is P’s first cousin once removed. Likewise, D is P’s paternal first cousin; her child C₂ is also one generation down, making C₂ P’s first cousin once removed. Hence Q is always a first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: P is the only child of Q. Q’s mother has a brother R. R has a daughter S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of S to P?
explanation: Q’s mother’s brother R is P’s great‑uncle. R’s daughter S is the child of that great‑uncle, making S the first cousin of Q (P’s mother). A first cousin of one’s parent is a first cousin once removed to the person. Hence S is P’s first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: A is the only child of his mother. A is married to B. B’s mother has a brother whose only child is C. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is C to A?
explanation: C is B’s first cousin (child of B’s maternal uncle). The permitted in‑law scope does not include a spouse’s cousin, so no standard direct kin term applies; therefore the correct description is “No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)”.
choices: A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a family, M and N are twins. M marries a woman who is the only child of P. N marries a man who is the only child of Q. P and Q are siblings. M and N each have one daughter, X and Y respectively. Ignoring any remarriage, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: M and N are siblings; their spouses are first cousins (children of siblings P and Q). Thus X and Y are children of a sibling pair (M,N) and a first‑cousin pair (their spouses). They share one set of grandparents (through P‑Q) and one set of great‑grandparents (through M‑N), making them double first cousins. The precise term is “double first cousins.”

question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is M’s precise relation to N?
explanation: M’s mother is N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and M’s father is N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus M shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: R's mother has exactly one brother, and R's father has exactly one sister. The brother of R's mother marries the sister of R's father, and they have a child S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation of S to R?
explanation: S is the child of R's maternal uncle and paternal aunt, who are married. Therefore S shares both of R's grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: A and B are full siblings. A’s son is C; B’s daughter is D. C and D each marry unrelated partners and have one child each, named E and F respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between E and F?
explanation: C and D are first cousins because their parents are full siblings. The children of first cousins (E and F) are therefore second cousins. No other common ancestors exist to alter the term.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: L is married to M. M’s brother is N. N’s wife is O. O’s brother is P. Using only the standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is P’s relation to L?
explanation: L→M (spouse) →N (spouse’s brother = brother‑in‑law) →O (brother’s wife = sister‑in‑law) →P (that sister‑in‑law’s brother). The chain passes beyond the allowed affinal scope, and there is no blood link, so no standard direct kin term applies.
choices: A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: R’s mother has a brother A, and R’s father has a sister B. A’s daughter C and B’s son D marry and have a child X. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is X’s precise relation to R?
explanation: C is R’s maternal first cousin; D is R’s paternal first cousin. X is the child of each of those first cousins, so X is a first cousin once removed of R (once removed on both sides). No closer or double term applies.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father (M) and Y’s father (N) are brothers, and X’s mother (O) and Y’s mother (P) are sisters. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: Rita’s mother has two children, Rita and her brother Sam. Sam is married to Lucy. Lucy’s brother Tom has a mother who is the sister of Rita’s father. What is Tom to Rita?
explanation: Tom’s mother is Rita’s paternal aunt (sister of Rita’s father). Therefore Tom, her aunt’s son, is Rita’s first cousin. The marriage links (Sam‑Lucy) do not affect blood relation.

question: M and N are full siblings. P and Q are also full siblings. M marries P, and N marries Q. R is the child of M and P, and S is the child of N and Q. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between R and S?
explanation: R and S each descend from both pairs of grandparents: M/N share one set, P/Q share another. Because their parents are cross‑married siblings, R and S share both grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures this doubled ancestry.

question: John has one sister, Mary. Mary’s only child is Peter. John’s only child is Susan. Susan marries David, who is Peter’s only child. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is David’s relation to John?
explanation: Mary is John’s sister, so her child Peter is John’s nephew. Peter’s child David is therefore the son of John’s nephew, i.e., John’s great‑nephew. No other direct blood link exists.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: In a family, brother N and sister O are siblings. N marries P, O marries Q. N and P have a child X; O and Q have a child Y. Additionally, P and Q are themselves siblings. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two sets of sibling couples. They share both pairs of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: Let N be a person. P is the child of the only brother of N’s mother and also the child of the only sister of N’s father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation of P to N?
explanation: P is the offspring of N’s maternal uncle and also of N’s paternal aunt. Thus P shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, giving them the exact relationship of double first cousins.
