choices: D) D) No direct kinship term

question: P’s mother and Q are half‑sisters (they share only one parent). Q has a daughter R. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of R to P?
explanation: Mother and Q are half‑siblings, so their children (P and R) share exactly one grandparent. That makes them half‑first cousins – the term for children of half‑siblings. Full first cousins require both grandparents in common, which is not the case here.

question: A and B are brothers; C and D are sisters. A marries C and B marries D. A and C have a son X; B and D have a daughter Y. X and Y each have one child, M and N respectively, with unrelated spouses. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between M and N?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. Their children therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, which is precisely a double second‑cousin relationship; no other term is more exact.

question: R’s mother has a brother A, whose daughter is B. R’s father has a sister C, whose son is D. B and D marry and have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is E’s relation to R?
explanation: B is R’s maternal first cousin; D is R’s paternal first cousin. Their child E is the child of two of R’s first cousins, placing E one generation below R’s cousins on both sides. The precise term is first cousin once removed.

question: John and his sister Lisa each marry a sibling: John marries Mary, Lisa marries Mary’s brother Mark. John and Mary have a daughter Alice; Lisa and Mark have a son Bob. Alice and Bob marry and have a child Charlie. What is Charlie’s precise relation to John’s mother?
explanation: John’s mother is mother of John and Lisa, thus grandmother of Alice (John’s child) and of Bob (Lisa’s child). Alice and Bob are double first cousins who marry; their child Charlie therefore has John’s mother as great‑grandmother through both his parents. The standard term is great‑grandmother.
choices: D) No standard direct kin term

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter A. N has a son B. B marries C, who is the only child of D. D is the sibling of E's spouse. Who is E to A?
explanation: If D is the parent of C, then E could be C's sibling-in-law (making E A's aunt‑in‑law). If D is the parent of E, then E is B’s cousin, making E A’s cousin‑in‑law. Both configurations satisfy the statements, yielding different precise relations; thus the relation cannot be uniquely determined.

question: L’s mother has exactly one son, and L’s father has exactly one daughter. The son of L’s mother marries the daughter of L’s father, and they have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring adoption and assuming monogamy), what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: L’s maternal uncle’s child is L’s first cousin; L’s paternal aunt’s child is also L’s first cousin. Because the same person M is both, M is simultaneously a first cousin on the mother’s side and on the father’s side, i.e., a double first cousin. No other term is more precise.

question: John’s mother is the paternal aunt of Mary’s mother. Mary’s father’s father is John’s father’s brother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of John to Mary?
explanation: John’s mother is sister of Mary’s maternal grandfather, so John is first cousin of Mary’s mother. Also, Mary’s father’s father is John’s paternal uncle, making Mary’s father John’s cousin. Both give John as a cousin of Mary’s parent, i.e., John is Mary’s first cousin once removed.

question: A and B are half‑siblings, sharing only their mother. A has a child X and B has a child Y. No other intermarriages exist. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent (their common maternal grandmother). The precise term for such relatives is "half‑first cousins"; full first cousins require both grandparents, and they are not second cousins.

question: Mary and Tom are siblings. Mary’s son is John; Tom’s daughter is Lisa. John’s son is Alex, and Lisa’s son is Ben. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between Alex and Ben?
explanation: John and Lisa are first cousins (they share Mary and Tom’s parents). Alex is John’s son and Ben is Lisa’s son, so Alex and Ben share the same great‑grandparents – the parents of Mary and Tom. Sharing great‑grandparents makes them second cousins, the most specific term.

question: M is married to N. N’s mother is O, whose brother is P. P’s daughter is Q, who is married to R. R’s father is S, the son of T. T is the brother of M’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of Q to M?
explanation: Q is linked to M through two distinct paths: via N’s maternal uncle (making Q a first cousin once removed by marriage) and via M’s paternal uncle (making Q a cousin‑in‑law). Because the two paths involve different sides of the family and one includes a marriage, the exact term varies with gender and marital status, so no single standard relation applies.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter A. A is married to X. X has a brother D. D has a daughter C. What is the precise standard English kinship term for C to M?
explanation: C is the daughter of D, who is the brother of M’s son‑in‑law X. This chain never introduces a blood link to M and exceeds the scope of immediate in‑law terms, so no standard direct kin term exists between them.
choices: B) B) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a family with no adoptions, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted: A and B are full siblings. C is A’s child. D is C’s child. E is B’s child. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between D and E?
explanation: A and B are siblings, so their children C and E are first cousins. D is C’s child, making D one generation removed from that cousin link. Hence D is the first cousin once removed of E, the only precise standard term.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: M is the child of the sister of J’s mother, and also the child of the brother of J’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between M and J?
explanation: M is the child of J’s maternal aunt (mother’s sister) – a first cousin – and also the child of J’s paternal uncle (father’s brother) – another first cousin. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most exact term.

question: Mia’s mother and Noah’s father are siblings. Mia’s father and Noah’s mother are also siblings. No other intermarriages exist. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Mia and Noah?
explanation: Mia’s parents are a sibling pair (her mother’s brother is Noah’s father) and another sibling pair (her father’s sister is Noah’s mother). Thus Mia and Noah share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most exact term.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John marries Anna, whose brother is Ben. Mary marries Ben. John and Anna have a daughter Lily; Mary and Ben have a son Mark. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relationship between Lily and Mark?
explanation: Lily’s father John is sibling of Mark’s mother Mary, and Lily’s mother Anna is sibling of Mark’s father Ben. Thus Lily and Mark share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures both parental sibling links.

question: M is the only child of his mother. N is the mother of M’s spouse. P is the father of N’s sibling. What is the precise kinship term for P’s relation to M, using standard English terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents, siblings, and children’s spouses)?
explanation: N is M’s mother‑in‑law. N’s sibling shares both parents with N, so their father is also N’s father, i.e., M’s spouse’s maternal grandfather. The relation of a spouse’s grandfather to you is “grandfather‑in‑law.”

question: Using only standard English kinship terms (blood only; in‑law terms limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), consider: B has a son A. B’s sister is C. C’s child is D. D is married to E. E’s child is F. What is F to A?
explanation: C is A’s aunt; her child D is A’s first cousin. E is D’s spouse, a cousin‑in‑law, not a blood relative. F, being E’s child, has no blood connection to A, and the affinal chain exceeds the allowed in‑law scope. Hence no standard direct kinship term applies.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John is the only child of his father's second wife. His father's first wife had a son, Mark, who is John’s half‑brother. Mark’s daughter, Lily, marries Tom, who is John’s maternal cousin. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Lily’s relation to John?
explanation: John → Mark (half‑brother) → Lily (niece). Lily’s spouse Tom is John’s maternal cousin, which is a blood link, but Lily herself is linked only through marriage to that cousin. The chain goes beyond the allowed in‑law scope, giving no standard direct kin term.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a family, the mother of X is the sister of the father of Y, and the father of X is the brother of the mother of Y. No other intermarriages exist. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s mother and Y’s father are siblings, giving X and Y a set of shared grandparents. Likewise X’s father and Y’s mother are siblings, providing a second set of shared grandparents. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes X and Y double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled relationship.

question: John and Mary are married. John’s only brother is Paul, and Mary’s only sister is Linda. Paul marries Linda, and they have a daughter Emma. John and Mary have a son Alex. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of Emma to Alex?
explanation: Paul is John’s brother and Linda is Mary’s sister, so their child Emma shares both sets of grandparents with Alex, the child of John and Mary. Hence Emma and Alex are double first cousins, the most precise term.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Ben, each marry a woman who are sisters, Clara and Diana respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Ben and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona each marry unrelated partners and have children: Ethan's child is Grace, Fiona's child is Hannah. What is the most precise kinship term between Grace and Hannah?
explanation: Adam and Ben are brothers and Clara and Diana are sisters, so Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). Their children Grace and Hannah therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins.

question: M is married to N. N's sister O is married to P. P's mother Q is the sister of R, who is the brother of M's father. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Q's relation to M?
explanation: R is M's paternal uncle (father’s brother). R’s sister Q shares the same parents, making her M's father's sister – a paternal aunt. No in‑law steps alter this blood link, so Q is M's aunt.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: L’s father has exactly one brother, and L’s mother has exactly one sister. The brother of L’s father is married to the sister of L’s mother, and they have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s paternal uncle and L’s maternal aunt. Hence M is L’s cousin through the father’s side and also through the mother’s side, sharing both sets of grandparents. The exact term for this is “double first cousin.”

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has a son P. O and P marry and have a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed but not needed), what is the most precise term for the relation of Q to N?
explanation: N is Q's paternal father’s father, making N Q's grandfather. N is also Q's maternal great‑uncle (sibling of Q’s grandmother), but the grandfather relation is more direct and thus the precise term.
choices: D) No standard kin term (double relation)

question: N’s father has exactly one sibling, and N’s mother also has exactly one sibling. The two siblings are married to each other and have a child M. What is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to N (using standard English kinship terms, without ignoring doubled ancestry)?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal uncle/aunt, making M a first cousin on the father’s side. M is also the child of N’s maternal uncle/aunt, making M a first cousin on the mother’s side. Sharing both grandparent pairs yields the precise term “double first cousin.”

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamy (remarriage allowed), X is the child of the only brother of Y’s mother and also the child of the only brother of Y’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle and also of Y’s paternal uncle. Thus X shares both of Y’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most specific term for this doubled ancestry.

question: M is the mother of N. N is married to O. O's sister is P, whose husband is Q. Q's father is R, whose sister is S. S is the mother of T, who is married to U. U is the child of V, and V is the brother of N. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only), what is U's relation to M?
explanation: V is N's brother, so V is also M's child. U is V's child, making U a grandchild of M. The precise term is "grandchild" (grandson or granddaughter).

question: Tom has a brother Sam. Tom’s daughter Lily marries Sam’s son Mark. Lily and Mark have a child Zoe. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Zoe’s relation to Tom?
explanation: Zoe is the child of Tom’s daughter Lily, so she is Tom’s grandchild. She is also the child of Tom’s nephew Mark, which would make her Tom’s great‑niece, but the direct parent‑child line gives the precise term: grandchild.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: M and N are the children of two half‑siblings who share only a mother (no father in common). Assuming no other intermarriages in the family, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between M and N?
explanation: Half‑siblings share one parent, so their children share only one grandparent. That makes M and N children of half‑siblings, i.e., half‑first cousins. Full first cousins require both grandparents in common, which is not the case here.

question: M and N share the same mother but have different fathers. M has a child A; N has a child B. No other marriages or adoptions occur. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B are children of half‑siblings (M and N). They share only one grandparent (their common mother’s parents). Hence they are half‑first cousins, a distinct term from full first cousins.
choices: D) D) No blood relation (affinal only)

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only), what is the most precise relationship between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both paternal grandparents (their fathers are brothers) and both maternal grandparents (their mothers are sisters). Hence they are double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: M is the child of the only brother of L’s mother and also the child of the only sister of L’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: M is both L’s maternal uncle’s child and paternal aunt’s child. For the same person to satisfy both, the uncle and aunt must be married, making M share both sets of grandparents with L. Therefore M is L’s double first cousin.

question: L’s mother has exactly one son, and L’s father has exactly one daughter. The child of that son (L’s maternal uncle) marries the child of that daughter (L’s paternal aunt). Who is that child to L, using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: L’s maternal uncle’s child is L’s first cousin; L’s paternal aunt’s child is also L’s first cousin. Because the two parents are unrelated, the child shares both sets of grandparents with L, making the precise term “double first cousin.”

question: M is the only child of his mother. M’s mother has a sister, whose son is N. N’s daughter is P. M’s father has a brother, whose daughter is Q. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: N is M’s first cousin (maternal side); P is M’s first cousin once removed. Q is M’s first cousin (paternal side). P descends from M’s maternal grandparents, Q from M’s paternal grandparents, sharing no common ancestor, so they have no blood relationship.

question: Mia and Nora share the same mother but have different fathers. Mia's son Ethan and Nora's daughter Lily are each the only child of their mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Lily?
explanation: Mia and Nora are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. Their children are therefore children of half‑siblings, which makes them half‑first cousins. Full first cousins would require both grandparents in common, which they do not have.

question: M’s mother has exactly one brother, T. T has a daughter S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of S to M?
explanation: T is M’s maternal uncle. His daughter S is therefore the child of M’s uncle, which makes S M’s first cousin. No other kinship term fits uniquely.

question: Lena and Maya are half‑sisters: they share the same mother but have different fathers. Lena’s child is Sam, and Maya’s child is Tara. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between Sam and Tara?
explanation: Lena and Maya share one parent, so they are half‑siblings. Their children therefore share exactly one grandparent, not a full pair. The correct term for children of half‑siblings is “half‑first cousins”.

question: A is the biological mother of B. B is married to C. C’s father is the half‑brother of A’s second husband (who is not B’s father). What is the precise kinship term, using standard English kinship, between A and the sister of C’s father (C’s paternal aunt)?
explanation: Because C’s father shares only one parent with A’s second husband, the sister may be A’s aunt‑in‑law (if the shared parent is also A’s spouse’s parent) or a step‑aunt (if the shared parent is unrelated to A). The information does not fix which case holds, so the exact term cannot be determined uniquely.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary marries Tom, who is the brother of John’s wife Anna. John and Anna have a son Peter; Mary and Tom have a daughter Susan. Assuming no other marriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relationship between Peter and Susan?
explanation: John and Mary are siblings; Anna and Tom are siblings. Their two couples each produce a child. Thus Peter and Susan share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins.

question: M is married to N. N’s mother is A. A’s brother is B. B’s daughter is C. C is married to D. D’s father is E. E’s sister is F. Using only standard English kinship terms (blood and immediate in‑law relations), what is F to M?
explanation: M→N (spouse) →A (spouse’s mother) →B (A’s brother) →C (B’s daughter) →D (C’s spouse) →E (D’s father) →F (E’s sister). The link passes through three affinal steps and a cousin link; no direct blood or immediate in‑law term exists between M and F. Hence the relation is not captured by a standard kin term.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John and Mary are half‑siblings (they share the same father but have different mothers). John’s only child is Alice, and Mary’s only child is Bob. No other intermarriages exist. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Alice and Bob?
explanation: Alice and Bob are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent (their common grandfather). The correct term for such relatives is “half‑first cousins.” Full first cousins would share both grandparents, which is not the case here.

question: J’s father has exactly one sister. That sister has exactly one son, and that son has a child named M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of M to J?
explanation: J’s father’s sister is J’s paternal aunt. Her only son is J’s first cousin. The son’s child M is therefore the child of J’s first cousin, making M J’s first cousin once removed. No other blood link exists.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O with his first wife; after divorcing, M marries his niece P (the daughter of N’s sister Q). M and P have a son R. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy per marriage, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation of R to O?
explanation: O is M’s daughter from his first marriage. R is the son of M and his niece P, who is O’s first cousin (daughter of M’s sister’s child). Thus R is O’s half‑sibling (they share father M) and also her first cousin, but the blood link via the father dominates, making the precise term “half‑sibling”.

question: A is the child of the only sibling of B’s paternal grandfather. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is A’s precise relation to B?
explanation: B’s paternal grandfather’s sibling is B’s great‑uncle/aunt. Their child (A) is the cousin of B’s father, making A one generation apart from B. The correct term for a cousin of a parent is “first cousin once removed.”
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: John and Jim are brothers. Anne and Amy are sisters. John marries Anne and they have a child P. Jim marries Amy and they have a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring in‑law extensions), what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: P and Q share both paternal grandparents (John’s parents) and both maternal grandparents (Anne’s parents). Hence they are first cousins with a double link, termed “double first cousins.”

question: L's mother and N's father are siblings. Also, L's father is the brother of N's mother. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between L and N?
explanation: Each of L's parents is a sibling of one of N's parents, so L and N share both sets of grandparents. They are first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled relationship.

question: Anna says: “My mother’s brother’s daughter is my husband’s mother.” Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is Anna’s husband to Anna?
explanation: Anna’s mother’s brother is her maternal uncle; his daughter is Anna’s first cousin. That cousin is Anna’s mother‑in‑law, so Anna’s husband is the child of Anna’s first cousin. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed (downward).

question: In a family with no adoptions and monogamous marriages, let X be the only child of Y. Y has a sibling Z. Z is the parent of W. W is the parent of V. Using standard English kinship terms, what is V's precise relation to X?
explanation: Y is X's parent. Z, being Y's sibling, is X's aunt/uncle. W, child of Z, is X's first cousin. V, child of W, is the next generation down from that cousin, making V X's first cousin once removed. No other term fits precisely.

question: M is the child of the only son of W’s sister, and also the child of the only daughter of W’s brother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is M’s relation to W?
explanation: W’s sister’s only son is W’s nephew; his child is W’s great‑nephew/niece. Likewise, W’s brother’s only daughter is W’s niece; her child is also W’s great‑nephew/niece. Both descriptions refer to the same person M, so the precise term is great‑nephew (if male) or great‑niece (if female).

question: P’s mother and Q’s father are half‑siblings (they share exactly one parent). No other blood relations exist between P and Q. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: Children of half‑siblings share only one grandparent, not a full pair. The correct term is “half‑first cousins”. Full first cousins require both grandparents, second cousins require shared great‑grandparents, and the relation is uniquely determined.

question: A's mother has a brother whose daughter is X. A's father has a sister whose son is Y. X and Y marry and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is C's precise relation to A?
explanation: X is A's maternal first cousin; Y is A's paternal first cousin. The child of any first cousin is a first cousin once removed to the original person, regardless of which side the cousin is on. Hence C is A's first cousin once removed.

question: M and N are siblings. M has two children, A and D; N has two children, B and E. A marries B and they have a child C. D marries E and they have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between C and F?
explanation: C’s parents (A, B) and F’s parents (D, E) are each a pair of first cousins sharing the same two grandparent sets (the parents of M and N). Therefore C and F share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: John and Michael are brothers. John’s sister Mary (their sibling) is married to an unrelated man and they have a son Peter. Michael is married to an unrelated woman and they have a daughter Lisa. Before Peter and Lisa marry each other, what is the precise blood relation between Peter and Lisa using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Peter is the son of Mary, who is John’s sister; Lisa is the daughter of Michael, John’s brother. Mary and Michael are siblings of John, so Peter and Lisa share the same set of grandparents (John’s parents). They are therefore first cousins. No other shared ancestors exist, so the precise term is 'first cousins'.

question: Eight people A–H sit in a left‑to‑right row of seats 1 (leftmost) through 8 (rightmost). H sits in seat 1; A sits immediately to H’s right; D sits in seat 8; F sits in seat 7; the three people B, C, E occupy three consecutive seats in that left‑to‑right order; and G sits somewhere left of D but is not adjacent to A. Which seat could G occupy?
explanation: Seats 1,2,7,8 are fixed (H, A, F, D). The B‑C‑E block must fill three consecutive seats among 3‑6. If it occupies 3‑5, G would be in seat 6, which is not adjacent to A. If it occupies 4‑6, G would be in seat 3, adjacent to A, violating the rule. Hence G can only be in seat 6.

question: Anna and Beth are sisters. Carl and Dave are brothers. Anna marries Carl and they have a son Ethan. Beth marries Dave and they have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan’s parents are Anna (sister of Beth) and Carl (brother of Dave). Fiona’s parents are Beth and Dave. Thus Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures both shared lineages.

question: L has a mother M and a father F. The only brother of M (M's brother) is married to the only sister of F (F's sister). Their child is X. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation between X and L?
explanation: X's father is M's brother (L's maternal uncle) and X's mother is F's sister (L's paternal aunt). Thus X shares both sets of grandparents with L, making them double first cousins.

question: John has a sister Mary. John’s son is Michael, and Mary’s son is Peter. Michael’s daughter is Lisa. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of Peter to Lisa?
explanation: Mary and John are siblings, so Peter is John’s nephew. Michael is John’s son, making Lisa John’s granddaughter. Peter and Michael are first cousins (children of siblings). Hence Peter is one generation above Lisa, giving the relation "first cousin once removed".

question: Two brothers, P and Q, each marry a sister, R and S, respectively (P–R and Q–S). P and R have a son M; Q and S have a daughter N. M and N each have one child: M’s child is A, N’s child is B. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage possible), what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: P and Q are brothers and R and S are sisters, so M and N are double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). Their children A and B therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins – the most specific term.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: L’s mother has exactly one brother, and L’s father has exactly one sister. Both of these siblings have a single child each, and the two children are the same person M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s maternal uncle (first cousin on the mother’s side) and also the child of L’s paternal aunt (first cousin on the father’s side). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes M a double first cousin of L.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, who is the only child of P and Q. N marries R, who is the only child of S and T. O and R are first cousins (their parents P and S are siblings). If X is the child of M and O, and Y is the child of N and R, what is the most precise standard English kinship term between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of first cousins, so they are second cousins. Because O and R share only one set of grandparents (through P‑S), the relation is not doubled; the precise term is simply "second cousins".
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: In a family: (1) Alex is the only child of Beth. (2) Beth and Carl are siblings. (3) Carl is the parent of Dana. (4) Dana is the parent of Eva. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Eva's relation to Alex?
explanation: Beth and Carl are siblings, so Carl is Alex's aunt/uncle. Dana, Carl's child, is Alex's first cousin. Eva, Dana's child, is one generation below, making her Alex's first cousin once removed. No other listed relations fit this precise description.

question: Let R be a person. P is the child of the only brother of R’s mother, and Q is the child of the only brother of R’s father. If we select either P or Q and name that person S, what is S’s precise relation to R using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Both P and Q are the child of a parent’s brother—R’s maternal uncle or paternal uncle. In either case the child is a first cousin of R. The relation is uniquely first cousin.

question: M is the child of the only sibling of N’s father, and also the child of the only sibling of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between M and N?
explanation: M is child of N’s paternal uncle and also child of N’s maternal aunt, so M shares both sets of grandparents with N. That makes them double first cousins—the most precise standard term.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a son Ethan. Brian marries Diana and they have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share the same paternal grandparents (parents of Adam and Brian) and the same maternal grandparents (parents of Clara and Diana). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: L’s mother has exactly one brother, and L’s father has exactly one sister. Both of these siblings have exactly one child, and that child is the same person M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relationship of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s maternal uncle and also the child of L’s paternal aunt. Therefore M shares both of L’s sets of grandparents, making M a double first cousin of L—the only term that captures the dual shared lineage.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted), L’s father is married to a woman named A. A has a sister B, and B has a child C. What is C’s precise relation to L?
explanation: A is L’s mother (the father’s wife). B is A’s sister, i.e., L’s maternal aunt. C, being the child of that aunt, is L’s first cousin. No other standard term applies.

question: John has a sister Mary. John marries Anne. Anne's brother Tom marries Mary. John and Anne have a daughter Lily; Mary and Tom have a son Sam. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Lily and Sam?
explanation: Lily and Sam are children of two sibling pairs: John–Mary and Anne–Tom. They share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, not merely first cousins.

question: M and N are married. M's sister marries N's brother. Their respective children are A (child of M's sister) and B (child of N's brother). Using standard English kinship terms (including doubled ancestry), what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A's mother is M's sister (maternal aunt) and B's father is N's brother (paternal uncle). Thus A and B share both sets of grandparents, giving them the exact term “double first cousins.”

question: Using only the standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses), A is married to B. B’s brother is C. C is married to D. D’s sister is E. E is married to F. What is the relation of F to A?
explanation: A→B (spouse) →C (brother‑in‑law) →D (sister‑in‑law) →E (sibling of D, not blood) →F (spouse). The chain goes beyond the immediate in‑law scope and never introduces a blood link, so no standard direct kin term applies.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M’s mother has a brother whose daughter (M’s first cousin on the maternal side) marries M’s father’s brother. Their child is N. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no extended in‑law), what is N’s relation to M?
explanation: N is the child of M’s paternal uncle, so they share a set of grandparents and are first cousins. Although N is also the child of M’s maternal first cousin (making them first cousins once removed on that side), the closest blood link is the shared grandparents, giving the precise term “first cousin.”

question: L has one sister S and one brother B. S has exactly one son X; B has exactly one daughter Y. The same person M is the child of X and also the child of Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of L to M?
explanation: X is L's nephew (son of sister) and Y is L's niece (daughter of brother). M is the child of both X and Y, so M is the grand‑child of L's siblings. Hence L is M's great‑aunt/uncle. The other options describe different generational distances or cousin relationships, which do not match this lineage.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions or multiple births, Emma’s mother has exactly one brother, and that brother has exactly one child, Lily. What is Lily’s relationship to Emma?
explanation: Emma’s mother’s brother is Emma’s maternal uncle. His child Lily is therefore the child of Emma’s uncle, which makes Lily Emma’s first cousin.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P. O and P are also siblings. M and O have a son X; N and P have a daughter Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s parents are M (brother of N) and O (sister of P). Y’s parents are N and P. Hence X and Y share both sets of grandparents—paternal and maternal—making them double first cousins, the most exact label.

question: Let X and Y be two individuals. X is the child of the only brother of Y’s mother. Y is the child of the only sister of X’s father. Assuming monogamy, no adoption, and that each “only” sibling is distinct, what is the precise kinship term for X to Y using standard English kinship?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle, making X a first cousin of Y. Likewise, Y is the child of X’s paternal aunt, also a first cousin. Both descriptions converge on the same relation, so X is Y’s first cousin.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Ben, each marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam marries Clara and they have a child X. Ben marries Diana and they have a child Y. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. This makes them double first cousins – first cousins with doubled ancestry.

question: John’s sister Mary marries Tom, who is the brother of John’s wife Anna. John and Anna have a daughter Lily; Mary and Tom have a son Sam. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between Lily and Sam?
explanation: Lily’s father John and Sam’s mother Mary are siblings → Sam is Lily’s paternal first cousin. Lily’s mother Anna and Sam’s father Tom are also siblings → Sam is Lily’s maternal first cousin. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Adam marries Clara and Brian marries Diana, who are sisters. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents: Adam and Brian share paternal grandparents, while Clara and Diana share maternal grandparents. Hence they are double first cousins, a more specific term than ordinary first cousins.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Ben, each marry a different sister, Clara and Dana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a child, X; Ben and Dana have a child, Y. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both paternal grandparents (Adam’s parents) and both maternal grandparents (Clara’s parents) because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. Thus they are first cousins through two independent lines, i.e., double first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has a daughter R, and R has a child Q. What is the precise kinship term for the relation between O and Q using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: O is M’s daughter, making her a grandchild of M and N’s parents G. Q is R’s child, also a grandchild of G but one generation lower. Sharing the same grandparents with a one‑generation gap defines a first cousin once removed.

question: John’s mother has a brother Mark; Mark’s daughter Lisa is John’s maternal first cousin. John’s father has a brother Paul; Paul’s son Peter is John’s paternal first cousin. Lisa and Peter marry and each have one child: John’s child is Emma, Peter’s child is Noah. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Emma and Noah?
explanation: John and Peter are first cousins (they share John’s paternal grandparents). Children of first cousins are second cousins. Emma and Noah are both one generation below John and Peter, so they are second cousins, with no additional shared ancestry.

question: M and N share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). M’s only child is A, and N’s only child is B. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for A and B?
explanation: A and B are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent. The exact term is “half‑first cousins,” which denotes first cousins with a single shared grandparent pair, unlike full first cousins who share both.

question: R’s mother has a brother T, and R’s father has a sister U. T’s daughter X and U’s son Y marry and have a child Z. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Z’s relation to R?
explanation: X is R’s maternal first cousin; Y is R’s paternal first cousin. Their child Z is the child of a first cousin on each side, making Z R’s first cousin once removed (the same degree through both lines). No more specific term exists.

question: John has a daughter Mary with his first wife Emma. After divorcing Emma, John marries Linda, who already has a son Peter from a previous marriage. John and Linda have a son Kevin. Mary later marries Peter. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for Kevin's relation to Anna, the child of Mary and Peter?
explanation: Kevin is the half‑brother of Mary (they share John) and the half‑brother of Peter (they share Linda). To Anna, he is a half‑uncle through her mother and also a half‑uncle through her father, making him a double half‑uncle—the most exact description.

question: M and N are full siblings. M marries P, the child of Q and R. N marries S, the child of Q and T. (Thus P and S are half‑siblings sharing father Q.) X is the child of M + P, and Y is the child of N + S. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share both parents, so X and Y share those grandparents. P and S share father Q, so X and Y also share Q’s parents as grandparents. Hence X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. The other options describe only one shared grandparent set.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions, consider the following description: “The person X is the child of the son of my mother’s brother.” Using standard English kinship terms, what is the exact relationship of X to me?
explanation: My mother’s brother is my maternal uncle. His son is my first cousin. The child of that cousin is one generation below my cousin, i.e., a first cousin once removed. No other blood link exists, so the precise term is “first cousin once removed.”
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: John and Mary are siblings. John marries Lisa and they have a daughter Anna. Mary marries Tom. Tom’s sister Susan has a son Carl. What is the precise standard English kinship relation between Anna and Carl?
explanation: Anna is John’s daughter, making her Mary’s niece. Through Mary’s husband Tom, Anna is Tom’s niece‑in‑law. Carl is Susan’s son, so he is Tom’s nephew. Anna and Carl are linked only via Tom, with no blood connection and the affinal chain exceeds immediate in‑law scope; therefore no standard English kin term exists for their relation.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: Emma’s mother has a brother whose daughter is Lily. Emma’s father has a sister whose son is Noah. Assuming no intermarriage among the families, what is the precise blood relationship between Lily and Noah?
explanation: Lily is Emma’s maternal first cousin; Noah is Emma’s paternal first cousin. Their parents are not siblings, so Lily and Noah share no common ancestor. Hence there is no standard blood kinship term between them.

question: M is the mother of N. N's father is O. O has a sister P, who is married to Q. Q's brother is R, who is married to S, who is the paternal aunt of N. What is the precise standard kinship term for the relation between M and R?
explanation: R is married to S, who is O’s sister (N’s paternal aunt). Thus R is the husband of O’s sister, i.e., O’s brother‑in‑law. Because M is O’s spouse, R is also M’s brother‑in‑law. Therefore the precise kin term is brother‑in‑law.

question: In a monogamous, non‑adoptive family, N's father has a sister A and N's mother has a brother B. A and B are married and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terminology, what is the most precise relation between C and N?
explanation: C is the child of N's paternal aunt (A) and maternal uncle (B). Because A and B are married, C shares both of N's grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the most exact term.

question: M has two children: N (a daughter) and O (a son). N is married to P. P has a sister Q, who is married to R, where R is O’s son. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Q’s relation to N?
explanation: Q is married to R, who is N’s nephew (son of N’s brother O). The allowed in‑law scope does not include the spouse of a sibling’s child, so no standard direct kin term applies. Hence Q has no recognized relation to N.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: S's father has a sister (F) and S's mother has a brother (M). F and M are married and have a child R. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of R to S?
explanation: F is S’s paternal aunt and M is S’s maternal uncle. Their child R is the offspring of both a paternal aunt and a maternal uncle, sharing all four of S’s grandparents. Hence R is a double first cousin of S—the most specific term.

question: L is married to K. K’s father’s sister (K’s paternal aunt) is married to J, who is the only son of L’s mother’s brother. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the relation of L to K’s paternal aunt?
explanation: K’s paternal aunt is the spouse of J. J is the child of L’s maternal uncle, making J L’s first cousin. The aunt is related to L only through J’s marriage, which is beyond the allowed in‑law scope. Hence there is no standard direct kin term between L and that aunt.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John has one child, a daughter Anna. John’s sister Mary has one child, a son Ben. Anna and Ben each marry unrelated partners and have exactly one child, X and Y respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: Anna and Ben are first cousins because their parents are siblings. The children of first cousins are second cousins; they share the same great‑grandparents but not the same grandparents. No other qualifying relationship exists, so X and Y are second cousins.
choices: C) C) First cousins once removed

question: P and Q share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). P has a child C1, and Q has a child C2. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between C1 and C2?
explanation: C1 and C2 each have one grandparent in common (the shared parent of P and Q). They therefore share a single grandparent pair, which makes them half‑first cousins. Full first cousins require both grandparents, second cousins need great‑grandparents, and the relation is uniquely determined.

question: Aaron's mother has a sister Beth. Beth's daughter is Clara. Aaron has a son David. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of Clara to David?
explanation: Beth is Aaron's maternal aunt, so Clara is Aaron's first cousin. To Aaron's son David, she is one generation senior, making her his first cousin once removed.

question: Mia’s mother is Laura. Laura’s brother is Kevin. Kevin’s son is Sam. Sam’s daughter is Zoe. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Zoe’s relation to Mia?
explanation: Laura and Kevin are siblings, making Kevin Mia’s maternal uncle. Sam, Kevin’s son, is Mia’s first cousin. Zoe is Sam’s daughter, placing her one generation below Mia’s cousin, i.e., a first cousin once removed. No closer term applies.

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoptions, X is the child of the only brother of Y’s mother. What is X’s relationship to Y?
explanation: The only brother of Y’s mother is Y’s maternal uncle. The child of that uncle is Y’s first cousin. No other kinship term fits this direct blood link.

question: John and Paul are brothers. John marries Mary and Paul marries Nancy, who are sisters. John and Mary have a son Kevin; Paul and Nancy have a daughter Lisa. Before Kevin and Lisa marry each other, what is the most precise standard English kinship term describing their relationship to each other?
explanation: Kevin and Lisa share both sets of grandparents (their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters). This makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: P and R are brothers; Q and S are sisters. P marries Q and they have a child A. R marries S and they have a child B. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents because each pair of parents are siblings of the opposite sex. Thus they are first cousins through both paternal and maternal lines, i.e., double first cousins.

question: Using standard English kinship terms only (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), L is married to M. M’s mother has a brother K, and K’s daughter is S. What is S to L?
explanation: K is M’s maternal uncle; S, his daughter, is M’s first cousin. L is M’s spouse, so S is related to L only through an affinal chain beyond the allowed in‑law scope. No standard term (cousin‑in‑law, etc.) exists under the given restrictions, making the correct description “No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)”.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M is the child of P and Q. P and R are siblings. R is married to S. S’s brother is T, and T has a daughter U. Using standard English kinship terms (allowing only spouse, parents, siblings, children and their spouses), what is the most precise term for the relation between M and U?
explanation: P’s sibling R is M’s aunt/uncle. R’s spouse S is an aunt/uncle‑in‑law. S’s brother T is therefore an uncle‑in‑law to M. T’s daughter U is the child of M’s uncle‑in‑law, which is called a cousin‑in‑law. No blood term applies, and “cousin‑in‑law” is the most specific standard label.

question:
Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted):
1) Alice is the only child of her mother.
2) Alice’s mother’s sister, Beth, is married to Carl.
3) Carl’s brother, Dan, is married to Eva, who is the mother of Alice’s husband, Frank.
4) Frank’s father is George, who is the son of Beth’s brother‑in‑law.
What is the precise relation of George to Alice?
explanation: Beth’s brother‑in‑law could be Carl, Dan, or any spouse of Carl’s siblings. Hence George might be Carl’s son, Dan’s son, or a more distant relative, leading to several possible kin terms (uncle‑in‑law, cousin, etc.). No single standard term uniquely fits all possibilities, so the only accurate answer is that the relation is not uniquely determinable.

question: M is the mother of N. M’s brother is R. N is married to O. O’s sister is P. P and R are the parents of Q. Using standard English kinship terms (including in‑law terms), what is the most precise relationship of Q to N?
explanation: Q is child of R, M’s brother, so Q is N’s first cousin. Q is also child of P, O’s sister; O is N’s spouse, making Q N’s niece‑in‑law. Both relations coexist, so the only correct description is that Q is both a first cousin and a niece‑in‑law.
choices: D) D) Both first cousin and niece‑in‑law

question: M is the child of N’s paternal uncle and also the child of N’s maternal uncle (the two uncles are different men). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s precise relation to N?
explanation: M shares both sets of grandparents with N because each uncle is a sibling of a different parent. This makes M and N double first cousins.

question: In a family with monogamy (remarriage allowed) and no adoption, let F be a man who is (i) the brother of B’s mother and (ii) the husband of B’s father’s sister. A is the only child of F. What is the exact kinship term for A’s relation to B?
explanation: Because F is B’s maternal uncle, A is B’s first cousin on the maternal side. Since F is also married to B’s paternal aunt, A is B’s first cousin on the paternal side as well. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most precise label.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, I say: "My father's sister has exactly one son, and my mother's brother has exactly one daughter; those two cousins are married and have a child X. Who is X to me?"
explanation: My father's sister's son and my mother's brother's daughter are each my first cousin. Their child is the child of my first cousin, making X my first cousin once removed (the same through either parental line). No other relation fits.

question: John and Mary are siblings. Mary’s son Peter marries John’s daughter Susan. Peter and Susan have a child Lily. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring in‑law extensions), what is Lily’s relationship to Mary?
explanation: Peter is Mary’s son, so Mary is Lily’s paternal grandmother. Susan is John’s daughter, i.e., Mary’s niece. Lily, being the child of Mary’s niece, is Mary’s grandniece. No other standard term describes this relation.

question: L and K are siblings. K has a daughter R. L has a son S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no in‑law extensions), what is the precise relation of R to S?
explanation: R is the child of K, who is L's brother. S is the child of L. Children of siblings are first cousins. No other blood link exists, so the exact term is "first cousin".

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy but remarriage allowed, let A and B be half‑siblings sharing only their mother. X is the child of the only son of A’s father, and Y is the child of the only daughter of B’s mother. What is the precise kinship term for Y relative to X?
explanation: A’s father’s only son is A’s full brother; B’s mother’s only daughter is B’s full sister. Depending on whether A and B are related through the mother or father, X and Y can be first cousins, half‑first cousins, or unrelated. The information does not fix a single relation, so it is not uniquely determinable.

question: L has one sister and one brother. The only son of L’s sister has a child, and the only daughter of L’s brother also has a child. Both children are the same person, M. In standard English kinship terms (ignoring gender), what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: L’s sister’s son is L’s nephew; his child is L’s great‑nephew/niece. Likewise, L’s brother’s daughter is L’s niece; her child is also L’s great‑nephew/niece. The only term that covers both is “great‑nephew/niece” (first‑generation removed sibling’s descendant).

question: John and Mark are brothers. Anna and Beth are sisters. John marries Anna and they have a son Carl. Mark marries Beth and they have a daughter Dana. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the precise relation between Carl and Dana?
explanation: Carl and Dana share both sets of grandparents: John‑Mark give the paternal grandparents, Anna‑Beth give the maternal grandparents. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than ordinary first cousins.

question: M is the child of the sibling of P’s mother and also the child of the sibling of P’s father (no intermarriage elsewhere). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s precise relation to P?
explanation: M’s mother’s sibling is P’s maternal aunt/uncle, and M’s father’s sibling is P’s paternal aunt/uncle. Thus M is the child of both a maternal and a paternal aunt/uncle, making M a double first cousin of P.

question: M is the mother of N. N's father's sister is O. O's son is P. P's daughter is Q. Q is married to R, who is the brother of S. S is the child of the only sibling of M. What is S to Q?
explanation: O is N's paternal aunt; P is N's cousin; Q is N's first cousin once removed. R is Q's husband, so S, being R's sibling, is Q's brother‑in‑law (or sister‑in‑law). No blood link exists beyond the marriage tie.

question: M is married to N. N’s sister O is married to P. P’s mother Q is the paternal aunt of R. R’s son S is married to T. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses), what is T to M?
explanation: M→N (spouse) →O (spouse’s sibling) →P (that sibling’s spouse) →Q (spouse’s mother) →R (her brother’s child) →S (R’s son) →T (S’s spouse). The chain passes through three affinal links and ends with a spouse of a non‑blood relative, which has no standard direct kin term.
choices: C) No standard direct kin term (affinal chain only)

question: L’s father has a sister (paternal aunt) whose only son is P. L’s mother has a brother (maternal uncle) whose only daughter is Q. P and Q marry each other and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: P is L’s paternal first cousin; Q is L’s maternal first cousin. Their child M is one generation below each cousin, making M a first cousin once removed on both paternal and maternal sides. The relationship is uniquely “first cousin once removed.”
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed
B) B) Half‑first cousin once removed

question: X is the child of the only brother of Y's mother, and also the child of the only sister of Y's father. Assuming monogamy and no incest, what is X's precise kinship term to Y?
explanation: X is child of Y's maternal uncle and also child of Y's paternal aunt, who are married. Thus X shares both sets of Y's grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: Using only standard English kinship terms (blood only; in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), let T be a person. T’s mother has exactly one brother, and that brother’s daughter is S. T’s father has exactly one sister, and that sister’s son is also S. What is the most precise blood‑relation term for S with respect to T?
explanation: S is the child of T’s maternal uncle and also the child of T’s paternal aunt. Thus S shares both sets of grandparents with T, making S a double first cousin—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: M is the mother of N and O. N is married to P. P's sister Q is married to R, who is the son of O. What is the precise standard English kinship term for Q's relation to N?
explanation: N is married to P. Q is P’s sister, so Q is N’s spouse’s sister, which is the definition of sister‑in‑law. All other connections (through O) are beyond the immediate in‑law scope and have no standard term.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: A and B are brothers. C and D are sisters. A marries C and B marries D. A and C have a son X; B and D have a son Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no “double” shortcuts omitted), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two couples each consisting of a brother and a sister. They share both paternal and maternal grandparents, so they are first cousins on both sides – the exact term is double first cousins.

question: In a family, M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N marries a man P, who is the brother of O's husband Q. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for O to P?
explanation: O is N's niece (sister's daughter). P is N's husband, making him O's uncle‑by‑marriage. However, because P is also Q's brother and Q is O's husband, the only direct blood relation is niece‑uncle. The standard term for this relationship is "uncle" (by marriage) but the precise blood term is "uncle‑in‑law"; however, the puzzle asks for the relation of O to P, which is "niece‑in‑law". The only standard English term that captures both is "niece‑in‑law".
choices: C) C) No direct kinship term

question: M and N are married. M’s sister O is married to P, who is N’s brother. O and P have a child Q. M and N have a child R. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between Q and R?
explanation: Q is the child of M’s sister (M’s niece/nephew) and N’s brother (N’s niece/nephew). R is the child of M and N. Therefore Q shares both sets of grandparents with R: the parents of M and the parents of N. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the exact term for this relationship.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a child X; Brian marries Diana and they have a child Y. No other marriages exist. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because each pair of parents are siblings on both paternal and maternal sides. The exact term for such cousins is double first cousins.

question: R’s mother has a brother who has a son A. R’s father has a brother who has a daughter B, and B has a son C. If we pick either A or C (unknown which) and call that person D, what is D’s precise relation to R using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: A is the child of R’s maternal uncle → first cousin. C is the grand‑child of R’s paternal uncle → first cousin once removed. Since D could be either, the exact kinship cannot be uniquely determined.

question: M and N are siblings who share the same mother (their fathers may differ). M marries O and N marries P. O and P are siblings who share the same father (their mothers may differ). M and O have a son X; N and P have a daughter Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship that can be asserted between X and Y?
explanation: Because we do not know whether M‑N and O‑P are full or half siblings, X and Y could be first cousins, half‑first cousins, or double first cousins. The given facts do not fix the exact type, so the only certain statement is that the precise relation cannot be uniquely determined.

question: A is the son of B. B is the sister of C’s wife. C is the father of D, and D is married to E. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the relation of A to E?
explanation: B and C’s wife are siblings, so A (B’s son) and D (C’s child) are first cousins. E is D’s spouse, making E the cousin‑in‑law of A. No closer blood or affinal term applies.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: R’s mother has a brother U. U’s daughter (R’s maternal first cousin) marries R’s father’s brother V (R’s paternal uncle). Their child is C. Using standard English kinship terms, what is C’s relation to R?
explanation: Through V, C is the child of R’s paternal uncle, making C a first cousin of R. Through U’s daughter, C is the child of R’s maternal first cousin, making C a first cousin once removed of R. No single standard term covers both, so the precise description is that C is both a first cousin and a first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
C) C) No single standard term; C is both a first cousin (paternal) and a first cousin once removed (maternal)

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother, and that brother’s only child is L. R’s father has exactly one sister, and that sister’s only child is also L (the same person). Assuming no adoption or remarriage, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between R and L?
explanation: L is the child of R’s maternal uncle and also the child of R’s paternal aunt, who are married to each other. Thus L shares both sets of grandparents with R, making L a double first cousin of R – the most specific standard term.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: M’s mother has a brother whose daughter married M’s father’s sister. What is the precise kinship term for that daughter’s son in relation to M, using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: Through M’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) the child is M’s first cousin. Through M’s maternal cousin (mother’s brother’s daughter) the child is M’s first cousin once removed. Since the two lines give different standard relations, there is no single precise kin term; both apply.
choices: C) C) No single standard term; the person is both a first cousin and a first cousin once removed

question: L has one child, M. L’s sister N is married to O. O’s brother is P, whose daughter is Q. Q is married to R, who is the son of S. S is the mother of T, and T is the only child of M. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the relation of Q to T?
explanation: M is L’s child; N is M’s aunt. O is aunt‑in‑law, and his brother P is only a sibling of an in‑law, giving no blood link. Q, as P’s daughter, is further removed. No standard term exists for this chain, so the correct answer is that Q has no direct kinship term to T.
choices: B) B) No standard direct kinship (no term)
C) C) Second cousin once removed

question: J’s father has one sister who has exactly one child, and that child has exactly one child named K. J’s mother has one brother who also has exactly one child, and that child has exactly one child named K (the same K). Using standard English kinship terms, what is K’s relation to J?
explanation: Both of J’s parental siblings produce a single first cousin; K is the child of each of those cousins. Thus K is one generation below J’s first cousins, making K J’s first cousin once removed. K is not a first cousin (different generation) nor a second cousin (shared great‑grandparents).

question: For a person R, let S be either (i) the child of R’s father’s only brother, or (ii) the child of R’s mother’s only sister. Without knowing which case holds, what is the precise standard English kinship term for S to R?
explanation: In both cases S is the child of a sibling of one of R’s parents, which by definition makes S R’s first cousin. The paternal or maternal side does not change the term.

question: M is the child of the sister of N’s father and also the child of the brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M’s mother is N’s paternal aunt, and M’s father is N’s maternal uncle. Thus M shares both of N’s sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the dual shared lineage.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries X and N marries Y, where X and Y are also siblings. M + X have a child A; N + Y have a child B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B are children of two couples that are both sibling pairs. Each child’s mother and father are respectively siblings of the other child’s parents, so the children share both paternal and maternal grandparents. Hence they are double first cousins, the most specific standard term.

question: M and N are brother and sister. M marries X and N marries Y, where X and Y are also brother and sister. M and N each have one child (A and B respectively). No other intermarriages occur. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both paternal grandparents (through M and N) and both maternal grandparents (through X and Y). Hence they are first cousins through two independent sibling links, i.e., double first cousins, the most exact term.

question: Adam and Beth are siblings, children of Mr. and Mrs. Smith. Carl and Diana are siblings, children of Mr. and Mrs. Jones. Adam marries Diana and they have a son Ethan. Beth marries Carl and they have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the relationship between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan’s parents are Adam (a Smith) and Diana (a Jones). Fiona’s parents are Beth (a Smith) and Carl (a Jones). Thus Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents – the Smiths and the Joneses – making them double first cousins, the only term that captures this dual lineage.

question: X’s mother has exactly one brother, and X’s father has exactly one sister. The brother of X’s mother (her maternal uncle) marries the sister of X’s father (his paternal aunt) and they have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Y’s precise relation to X?
explanation: Y is the child of X’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, who are themselves married. Y shares both of X’s sets of grandparents, making Y a double first cousin of X – the most specific term for this doubled lineage.

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamy (remarriage allowed), let Y be a person whose mother has exactly one brother. Z is the child of that brother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Z to Y?
explanation: The brother of Y's mother is Y's maternal uncle. His child is therefore the child of a parent's sibling, which is the definition of a first cousin. No other relationship fits the given facts.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, N marries P, and O and P are also siblings. M and O have a daughter X; N and P have a son Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because each pair of parents are siblings on both sides. Hence they are first cousins through the maternal line and also first cousins through the paternal line, i.e., double first cousins – the most specific label.

question: Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), if T is the son of the sister of R's father, what is T's relation to R?
explanation: R's father's sister is R's aunt; her son is R's first cousin.

question: John’s mother Mary has a sister Linda who is married to Paul. Paul’s brother Greg is married to Susan, who is the mother of John’s wife Emma. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Emma’s relation to Paul?
explanation: Emma is Susan’s daughter; Susan is Greg’s wife, making Greg Emma’s step‑father. Greg is Paul’s brother, so Emma is the step‑niece of Paul. No standard English kin term covers a step‑niece relationship; thus the correct answer is that there is no direct standard term.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M and N are siblings. M marries X and N marries Y, where X and Y are also siblings. M and X have child A; N and Y have child B. A and B each marry unrelated partners and have children C and D respectively. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring marriage), what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins. Their children C and D therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins – the exact term for this relationship.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, the following statements are true: (1) Anna’s mother has exactly one brother, Peter; (2) Peter is married to Lisa; (3) Lisa has exactly one brother, Tom; (4) Tom is the only brother of Anna’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Tom’s relation to Anna?
explanation: Statement 4 makes Tom the brother of Anna’s father, i.e., her paternal uncle. The other statements only describe how this uncle is also the brother‑in‑law of a maternal uncle, but they do not alter the blood relation.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John marries Anna and they have a daughter Lily. Mary marries Ben and they have a son Mark. John’s brother Tom marries Carla and they have a daughter Sarah. Mark marries Sarah, and Lily and Mark have a child Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Emma’s relation to Sarah?
explanation: Sarah is first cousin to both Lily and Mark. To Emma, who is the child of Lily and Mark, Sarah is one generation removed, making her Emma’s first cousin once removed. No other listed term fits precisely.

question: L’s father has exactly one brother, and L’s mother has exactly one brother. The two brothers are married to each other and have a single daughter, X. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is X’s precise relation to L?
explanation: X is the child of L’s paternal uncle and also the child of L’s maternal uncle. Both uncles are married, so X shares both sets of grandparents with L, making X L’s first cousin (the double‑cousin case is still called a first cousin in standard terminology).

question: John and Mark are brothers. John marries Anna, and Mark marries Beth. Anna and Beth are sisters. John and Anna have a son Carl; Mark and Beth have a daughter Diana. Carl and Diana each marry unrelated partners and have children Ethan and Fiona respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Carl and Diana are double first cousins, sharing both sets of grandparents. Their children Ethan and Fiona therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the most precise standard term.

question: In a family tree, A is the father of B and also has a sister C. C’s son is D. D marries B’s daughter E, and they have a child F. What is the precise relationship between F and A’s mother?
explanation: A’s mother is also C’s mother. Through C → D → F, F is a great‑grandchild. The alternate line A → B → E → F makes F a great‑great‑grandchild, but the closest valid link is the great‑grandchild line, which defines the precise relation.

question: In a family with monogamy, no adoption or remarriage, let Z be the child of the sister of L’s father and also the child of the brother of L’s mother. What is the precise standard English kinship term for Z to L?
explanation: The sister of L’s father is L’s paternal aunt; her child is L’s first cousin. The brother of L’s mother is L’s maternal uncle; his child is also L’s first cousin. Since the aunt and uncle are married, Z shares both sets of grandparents with L, making Z a double first cousin—a distinct term from a regular first cousin.

question: R’s mother has a brother (maternal uncle) whose daughter is B. R’s father has a sister (paternal aunt) whose son is D. B and D marry and have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only), what is the most precise relation of E to R?
explanation: R is a first cousin to B (maternal side) and also a first cousin to D (paternal side). E is the child of R’s first cousins on both sides, placing E one generation below R in each line. Hence E is R’s first cousin once removed; no more specific term applies.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: A person X has a mother who has exactly one brother, and a father who has exactly one sister. The brother of X's mother has a daughter Y, and the sister of X's father has a son Z. If we pick either Y or Z and call that person P, what is P's precise kinship to X using standard English terms?
explanation: Y is the child of X's maternal uncle; Z is the child of X's paternal aunt. Both are children of a sibling of one of X's parents, which makes each a first cousin to X. The relation is uniquely first cousin regardless of which child is chosen.

question: Person P’s father has exactly one brother and P’s mother has exactly one sister. The father’s brother (P’s paternal uncle) is married to the mother’s sister (P’s maternal aunt). They have a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Q and P?
explanation: Q’s father is P’s paternal uncle, so Q shares P’s paternal grandparents. Q’s mother is P’s maternal aunt, so Q also shares P’s maternal grandparents. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes Q and P double first cousins, the precise term.

question: M and N are full siblings. M’s child is P. N is married to Q. Q’s brother is R, and R is married to S, whose only child is T. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is T to P?
explanation: All links between P and T go through marriages: N–Q, Q–R (siblings), R–S (spouses). No person in T’s line is a blood relative of any person in P’s line, so there is no direct kinship term. Hence the relation is “no standard direct kinship”.
choices: A) A) No standard direct kinship term

question: John and his brother Peter are the only children of their parents. John has two children, Michael (son) and Laura (daughter). Peter has one child, Susan (daughter). Michael marries Susan. Their son is Ethan. What is Ethan’s precise relationship to Laura, using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Laura is Michael’s sister, so Ethan, as Michael’s son, is Laura’s nephew. Although Ethan is also Susan’s son (Laura’s first cousin), the direct line relation (nephew) is the most specific term in standard kinship.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, M is married to N. N's sister is O, who is married to P. P's brother is Q, and Q's daughter is R. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses), what is R's relationship to M?
explanation: M→N (spouse) →O (spouse’s sibling) →P (that sibling’s spouse) →Q (spouse’s sibling’s sibling) →R (that sibling’s daughter). Standard in‑law terms stop at spouse’s sibling’s spouse; beyond that there is no recognized term and no blood link, so R has no standard direct relation to M.
