choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father. N’s mother is the sister of O’s father. O’s mother is the sister of M’s father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise blood relation between M and O?
explanation: M’s father and O’s mother are siblings, so M and O share a pair of grandparents, making them first cousins. The other two statements only create separate cousin links (M‑N and N‑O) and do not add extra shared ancestry between M and O, so the relation remains simple first cousins.

question: Brothers A and B each marry sisters C and D respectively (A with C, B with D). A and C have a child X; B and D have a child Y. X and Y each have one child, P and Q respectively. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only), what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: X and Y are double first cousins because they share both sets of grandparents. Their children P and Q therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, which makes them double second cousins—the most specific label.

question: X’s mother and Y’s father are siblings. Y has a daughter Z. X is married to a person whose mother is the sister of W’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only), what is the precise relation between X and Z?
explanation: X’s mother and Y’s father are siblings → X and Y are first cousins. Z is Y’s daughter, so Z is the child of X’s cousin → X is first cousin once removed of Z. The marriage detail adds no blood link.

question: Using standard English kinship terms only (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses): A and B are siblings. B is married to C. C’s brother is D. D’s daughter is E. A marries E. What is the relation of A’s child F to C?
explanation: B’s spouse C is sister‑in‑law to A. D is C’s brother, so E (D’s daughter) is C’s niece. A (C’s sister‑in‑law) marries E (C’s niece). Their child F is thus the child of C’s sister‑in‑law and C’s niece. No standard direct kin term exists; the link is an affinal chain only.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M is the mother of N. N has a sister who is married to O (so O is N’s brother‑in‑law). O’s sister is P. P’s son is Q. Q is married to R, whose father S is the sibling of M’s husband. What is Q’s relation to M?
explanation: M → N’s sister → O (brother‑in‑law) → P (O’s sister) → Q (P’s son). Q marries R, who is S’s daughter. S is the sibling of M’s husband, so S is M’s brother‑in‑law and R is M’s niece‑in‑law. Q is the spouse of that niece‑in‑law, giving no standard kinship term to M.

question: Two brothers, P and Q, each marry a sister, R and S respectively (P–R and Q–S). P and R have a daughter A; Q and S have a son B. Before A and B marry each other, what is the most precise standard kinship term describing the relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B are children of two brothers and two sisters. They share both sets of grandparents, so they are not merely first cousins (which require only one shared grandparent pair). The exact term is "double first cousins", indicating the doubled ancestry.

question: In a family, Alex has a sister Beth who has exactly one child Charlie. Alex also has a brother Dan who has exactly one child, and that child is also Charlie. Assuming no adoption or remarriage, what is the precise standard kinship term for Charlie to Alex?
explanation: Charlie is the child of Alex's sister (Beth) and also the child of Alex's brother (Dan). In either case Charlie is Alex's niece/nephew. The term does not change because the same person is reached through two sibling lines; the precise label remains "niece/nephew".

question: Two brothers, John and Mark, each marry one of two sisters, Anna and Beth. John marries Anna and they have a son, Carl. Mark marries Beth and they have a daughter, Dana. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Carl and Dana?
explanation: Carl and Dana are children of two brothers who married two sisters. They share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: In a family, let N be a person. M is the child of N’s mother’s brother (i.e., N’s maternal uncle). P is the child of N’s father’s sister (i.e., N’s paternal aunt). Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for the relation between M and P?
explanation: M and P are each the child of a sibling of one of N’s parents. Both are therefore children of N’s parental siblings, making them first cousins to each other. No half‑blood or generational offset exists, so the exact term is “first cousin.”

question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s relation to N?
explanation: M is the offspring of N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Hence M shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making them first cousins on both sides – a double first cousin.

question: Robert had a son Alan with his first wife and a daughter Dana with his second wife. Alan married Eva and they have a son Frank. Dana married Ian and they have a son Jack. Using standard English blood‑relation terms (no in‑law, no adoption), what is the precise relationship between Frank and Jack?
explanation: Alan and Dana are half‑siblings (they share father Robert). Their children Frank and Jack are therefore children of half‑siblings, which makes them half‑first cousins: they share one grandparent (Robert) but not the other. No other standard term fits.

question: John and Mark are brothers. Their mother Mary has a brother Peter. Peter’s daughter Lisa marries Mark. Lisa and Mark have a daughter Emma. What is Emma’s precise kinship term to John, using standard English blood‑relation terminology only?
explanation: Emma is the child of John’s brother, making her his niece. Although she is also the child of his first cousin, the direct blood line through his sibling gives the unique term “niece,” which is more specific than “first cousin once removed.”
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard direct relation

question: E is married to F. F's sister is G. G's husband is H. H's mother is I. I's brother is J. J's son is K. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is K to E?
explanation: E → F (spouse) → G (sister‑in‑law) → H (brother‑in‑law) → I (mother‑in‑law of G) → J (her brother, an uncle‑in‑law) → K (his son, a cousin‑in‑law of H). The chain extends beyond the immediate in‑law scope, yielding no direct kin term for K relative to E.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a family with no adoptions or remarriages, let X be the child of N’s maternal uncle and also the child of N’s paternal aunt (the uncle and aunt are married to each other). Using standard English kinship terms, what is X’s precise relation to N?
explanation: N’s mother’s brother is N’s maternal uncle; N’s father’s sister is N’s paternal aunt. Their marriage makes X simultaneously the child of N’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, so X is a first cousin on both sides – a double first cousin. No other standard term applies.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, N’s father has exactly one sibling, a brother X, and N’s mother has exactly one sibling, a sister Y. X’s child and Y’s child are the same person M. What is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal uncle and also the child of N’s maternal aunt. Hence M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making them double first cousins – the most specific standard term.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, who is the sister of P. N marries Q, who is the brother of O. The child of M and O is X; the child of N and Q is Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share both parents; O and Q are siblings. Thus X’s paternal grandparents (M/N’s parents) are the same as Y’s paternal grandparents, and X’s maternal grandparents (O/Q’s parents) are also the same. X and Y share both grandparent pairs, which is precisely a double first‑cousin relationship.

question: Brother A and brother B are siblings. Sister X and sister Y are siblings. A marries X and B marries Y. A and X have a son M; B and Y have a daughter N. M and N each marry unrelated partners and have children P and Q respectively. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring in‑law relations), what is the most precise relationship between P and Q?
explanation: M and N are double first cousins because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters, sharing both sets of grandparents. Their children P and Q therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the most specific term.

question: John is married to Mary. Mary’s brother is Tom. John and Mary have a son Alan. Alan has a daughter Beth. Beth has a son Carl. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is Tom to Carl?
explanation: Tom is Mary’s brother, i.e., the sibling of Carl’s great‑grandmother (Mary). The sibling of a great‑grandparent is called a great‑uncle (or great‑aunt for females). Thus Tom is Carl’s great‑uncle. The other options refer to closer or different generational relations.

question: Q’s mother has exactly one brother, and Q’s father has exactly one sister. Those two siblings are married to each other and have a single child, P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise term for the relationship between P and Q?
explanation: P is the child of Q’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, so P is both a maternal first cousin and a paternal first cousin of Q. The precise term that captures this dual line is “double first cousin.”

question: John and Mary are siblings. John’s son Peter marries Susan, who is the daughter of Mary’s son Thomas. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation between Peter and Susan?
explanation: Peter is the child of John, Mary’s brother, making Peter Mary’s nephew. Susan is Thomas’s daughter; Thomas is Mary’s son, so Susan is Mary’s granddaughter. Thus Peter (nephew) and Susan (grandniece) are separated by one generation: they are first cousins once removed.

question: P is the child of Q's maternal uncle (the brother of Q's mother) and also the child of Q's paternal aunt (the sister of Q's father). Assuming those two cousins are married to each other, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between P and Q?
explanation: P is the child of Q's maternal uncle, making P a first cousin on the mother's side. P is also the child of Q's paternal aunt, making P a first cousin on the father's side. Because both parental lines are cousins, P and Q share both sets of grandparents, giving them the precise term “double first cousin.”

question: Let X be the child of a man who is the brother of Y's mother, and also the child of a woman who is the sister of Y's father. Using standard English kinship terms without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X's father is the brother of Y's mother, so X is Y's first cousin. X's mother is the sister of Y's father, giving another first‑cousin link. Thus X and Y share both grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most precise term.

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother, whose daughter is S. R’s father has exactly one sister, whose son is T. S and T marry and have a child X. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is X’s relation to R?
explanation: S is R’s maternal first cousin; T is R’s paternal first cousin. X is the child of both of R’s first cousins, placing X one generation below R’s cousins. Hence X is R’s first cousin once removed (the same relation via either side).
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard term (affinal only)

question: Using standard English kinship terms only (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses): R is married to S. S’s sister is T. T’s husband is U. U’s sister is V. What is V to R?
explanation: R’s spouse S’s sister T is R’s sister‑in‑law. The chain then goes to T’s husband U and finally to U’s sister V. Standard kinship does not recognise a sibling’s spouse’s sibling as an in‑law, so V has no direct kin term to R; the relationship is only an affinal chain.
choices: A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M and N are siblings. M has children A and D (with different spouses). N has children B and E (also with different spouses). A marries B and they have a child C. D marries E and they have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between C and F?
explanation: C’s parents are A (child of M) and B (child of N). F’s parents are D (child of M) and E (child of N). A and D are siblings, B and E are siblings, so C and F are children of two pairs of siblings – the definition of double first cousins.

question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to N?
explanation: M is simultaneously the child of N’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle, sharing both grandparent pairs with N. This makes M a double first cousin of N, the most specific standard term.

question: P is the child of the only brother of Q’s mother, and also the child of the only sister of Q’s father. Assuming no adoption and monogamy, what is the most precise kinship term for P’s relation to Q?
explanation: The brother of Q’s mother is Q’s maternal uncle; his child is Q’s maternal first cousin. The sister of Q’s father is Q’s paternal aunt; her child is Q’s paternal first cousin. Since both describe the same person P, P is a first cousin to Q on both sides – a double first cousin.

question: Two brothers marry two sisters. The elder brother and his wife have a son A; the younger brother and his wife have a daughter B. A and B marry each other and have children C and D respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: A and B are double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). Their children therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, which makes C and D double second cousins. No other term captures the doubled ancestry precisely.

question: Mary has an only child Anna from her first marriage. Later she marries John and has a son Ben. Anna’s son Carl and Ben’s daughter Dana meet for the first time. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation between Carl and Dana?
explanation: Carl and Dana are each the child of a half‑sibling (Anna and Ben). They share exactly one grandparent pair (Mary’s parents) and not the other. The correct term for children of half‑siblings is “half‑first cousins”.

question: Let R be a person. X is the child of the only brother of R’s mother. Y is the child of the only sister of R’s father. Assuming no intermarriage among the ancestors, what is the precise blood relation between X and Y?
explanation: X is R’s maternal first cousin (child of R’s maternal uncle). Y is R’s paternal first cousin (child of R’s paternal aunt). The uncle and aunt are unrelated, so X and Y share no common ancestor; they are not blood‑related.

question: My father’s brother has exactly one child. What is the precise kinship term for that child’s child to me, using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: My father’s brother is my paternal uncle. His only child is my first cousin. That cousin’s child is one generation below, making them my first cousin once removed. No other relationship fits.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a son Ethan. Brian marries Diana and they have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona each marry unrelated partners and have children Greg and Helen respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Greg and Helen?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. Their children therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, which is precisely a double second‑cousin relationship.

question: In a family, siblings A and B each marry siblings C and D respectively (A with C, B with D). Their children are E (child of A & C) and F (child of B & D). Using standard English kinship terms and not ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between E and F?
explanation: A and B share both parents, as do C and D. Therefore E and F share both sets of grandparents, giving them the doubled version of first cousins. The exact term is “double first cousins.”

question: In a monogamous family, Y’s mother has a sister M and Y’s father has a brother F. M’s only child is X, and F’s only child is also X (the same person). Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the most precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal aunt (mother’s sister) and also the child of Y’s paternal uncle (father’s brother). Thus X shares both sets of grandparents with Y, making X a double first cousin—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: John’s mother has a sister Mary. Mary’s son Peter marries John’s daughter Lisa. Peter and Lisa have a child Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise blood relation of Emma to John?
explanation: John is Lisa’s father, making him Emma’s maternal grandfather. Although John is also Peter’s cousin (so a first cousin once removed to Emma), the grandparent link is the closest blood tie, giving the precise term “grandfather.”
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed

question: A and B are brothers. C and D are sisters. A marries C and they have a child X. B marries D and they have a child Y. X and Y each have one child (P and Q respectively). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: X and Y are double first cousins (their parents are two sibling pairs). Hence P and Q inherit both sets of great‑grandparents, sharing two grand‑parent lines. That makes them double second cousins, the most precise term.

question: Emma’s father and Lily’s mother are siblings, and Emma’s mother and Lily’s father are also siblings. No other marriages connect these families. Using standard English kinship terms and without assuming whether any of the sibling pairs are full or half‑siblings, what is the most precise term for the relation between Emma and Lily?
explanation: If both sibling pairs are full siblings, Emma and Lily are double first cousins. If either pair are half‑siblings, they are only half‑first cousins. Because the information does not specify full or half sibling status, the exact term cannot be uniquely determined.

question: John has two siblings: a sister Mary and a brother Peter. Mary’s son is Paul, and Peter’s daughter is Susan. Paul and Susan marry each other and have a child Lily. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only), what is Lily’s relation to John?
explanation: John is Mary’s brother, so he is Paul’s maternal uncle. He is also Peter’s brother, so he is Susan’s paternal uncle. Lily is the child of John’s niece (Paul) and nephew (Susan); thus Lily is John’s great‑niece (child of a niece/nephew).

question: Let N be a person. N's father has exactly one sister, and N's mother has exactly one brother. M is the child of that sister and also the child of that brother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is the child of N's paternal aunt (father's sister) and also the child of N's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Thus M is N's first cousin on both sides, i.e., a double first cousin, the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: R is married to S. S’s brother is T. T’s wife is U. U’s brother is V. In standard English kinship (allowing only spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses), what is V’s relation to R?
explanation: R→S (spouse) →T (brother‑in‑law) →U (sister‑in‑law, T’s spouse) →V (U’s brother). The chain never introduces a blood link and exceeds the permitted in‑law scope, so no conventional kin term applies.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M and N are siblings. P and Q are siblings. M marries Q, and N marries P. Their only children are X (from M + Q) and Y (from N + P). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: M and N share parents A and B; P and Q share parents C and D. Thus each child has the same paternal and maternal grandparents, making them double first cousins.

question: Let T be the child of the only brother of M’s mother and also the child of the only sister of M’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, distinct sexes), what is T’s precise relation to M?
explanation: The description forces the maternal uncle (brother of M’s mother) and the paternal aunt (sister of M’s father) to be the same person, which cannot occur under the given assumptions. Hence the relation cannot be uniquely determined.

question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father, and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M’s father is N’s paternal aunt’s son, making M a first cousin on N’s father’s side. Simultaneously, M’s mother is N’s maternal uncle’s daughter, making M a first cousin on N’s mother’s side. Sharing both sets of grandparents, M and N are double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: A is married to B. B’s sister is C. C is married to D. D’s brother is E, and E is the parent of F. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the relation of F to A?
explanation: A → B (spouse) → C (sister‑in‑law) → D (that sister’s spouse) → E (that spouse’s brother) → F (E’s child). The chain stays entirely affinal; no blood link is created and the link exceeds the scope of recognized in‑law terms, so no standard direct kin term applies.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary’s son Peter marries Susan, who is the daughter of John’s son Michael. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of Peter to Susan?
explanation: Peter is John’s nephew (sister’s son). Susan is John’s granddaughter (son’s daughter). A nephew and a granddaughter are first cousins once removed: they share a common ancestor (John) but are one generation apart.
choices: D) D) First cousin once removed

question: A’s mother has a brother B, and A’s father has a sister C. B and C are married and have a child D. What is D’s precise kinship to A using standard English terms?
explanation: B is A’s maternal uncle and C is A’s paternal aunt. Their child D shares both of A’s maternal grandparents (through B) and both paternal grandparents (through C). Thus D is a first cousin on both sides – a double first cousin.

question: Brother A marries sister C; brother B (A’s brother) marries sister D (C’s sister). A and C have child X; B and D have child Y. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two brothers and two sisters. They share both paternal and maternal grandparents, giving them the exact term “double first cousins.”

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively (Adam‑C​lara and Brian‑Diana). Adam and Clara have a child X; Brian and Diana have a child Y. X and Y each marry unrelated partners and have children P and Q. Using standard English kinship terms without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins. Their children P and Q therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them second cousins with doubled ancestry—double second cousins.

question: John and Mary are siblings. Mary’s son Tom marries John’s daughter Susan. Tom and Susan have a child Lily. What is Lily’s precise relationship to Mary?
explanation: Through Tom, Lily is Mary’s granddaughter. Through Susan, Lily is Mary’s great‑niece (Mary is Susan’s aunt). No single standard kin term covers both roles, so the relation cannot be uniquely expressed with one term.

question: M and N are married. M’s brother O marries N’s sister P. O and P have a daughter Q. M and N have a son R. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of Q to R?
explanation: Q is the child of M’s brother (M’s niece/nephew) and N’s sister (N’s niece/nephew). Thus Q and R share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the most specific standard term.

question: M’s mother has a brother A and M’s father has a sister B. A and B are married and have a child N. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is the precise relation between M and N?
explanation: A is M’s maternal uncle (sibling of M’s mother) and B is M’s paternal aunt (sibling of M’s father). Their child N shares both sets of grandparents with M, so M and N are double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: A person X has the following relatives: X’s father has exactly one brother, whose daughter is named B; X’s mother has exactly one sister, whose son is named C. If either B or C is selected and called S, what is S’s precise kinship to X using standard English terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed)?
explanation: Both B and C are children of X’s parental siblings (paternal aunt’s daughter and maternal aunt’s son). In either case S is the child of a parent’s sibling, which is precisely a first cousin. No other relationship fits.

question: B is married to C. C's mother is D, and D has a brother E. A is the child of E. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of A to B?
explanation: B’s spouse C → C’s mother D → D’s brother E; A is E’s child. Thus A is C’s first cousin. Because the link to B is only through B’s spouse, there is no blood tie and it lies beyond the permitted in‑law scope, so no standard direct kinship term exists.
choices: B) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: X’s mother has only one sibling, a brother Y. Y is married to Z. Z is the only child of W. W’s only child is also the mother of X’s father. What is Z’s precise relation to X using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Y is X’s maternal uncle. Z, his wife, is the child of W. W’s only child is X’s paternal grandmother, so Z is the sister of X’s paternal grandmother. The sister of a grandparent is a great‑aunt (or great‑uncle). Hence Z is X’s great‑aunt.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard kinship term

question: Peter is Anna's father. After Anna's mother died, Peter married Laura, who already has a son Mike from a previous marriage. Anna has a sister Emma (same parents as Anna). Later, Mike marries Emma. What is Mike's most precise standard English kinship term to Anna?
explanation: Mike is Anna's stepbrother because his mother married Anna's father, and he is also Anna's brother‑in‑law because he married Anna's sister. No single term covers both, so the precise description is “both stepbrother and brother‑in‑law”.
choices: D) D) Both stepbrother and brother‑in‑law

question: Man X is married to W. W has a brother V. V has a son Z. Who is Z to X, using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law terms limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses)?
explanation: V is X’s brother‑in‑law (W’s brother). Z is V’s son, i.e., the child of X’s brother‑in‑law. The standard term for a spouse’s sibling’s child is nephew/niece‑in‑law. No blood relation exists, so the precise label is nephew‑in‑law (or niece‑in‑law).
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: J’s father has a sister named K. K’s son is L, and L’s daughter is N. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted), what is N’s relation to J?
explanation: K is J’s paternal aunt. Her son L is J’s first cousin. L’s daughter N is one generation below that cousin, making N J’s first cousin once removed. No other listed term fits this precise generational offset.

question: John is the only child of Mary. Mary’s sister Anne is married to Tom. Tom’s brother Sam is married to Linda, who is the mother of John’s wife Eva. Using standard English kinship terms limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses, what is Sam to John?
explanation: Linda is Eva’s mother; Sam, as Linda’s husband, is Eva’s step‑father. Therefore Sam is John’s step‑father‑in‑law, the only precise term fitting the given constraints.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation

question: M is married to N. N’s sister is O, and O is married to P. Using standard English kinship terms limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses, what is P to M?
explanation: N’s sister O is M’s sister‑in‑law. O’s husband P is therefore the spouse of M’s sister‑in‑law, which is defined as a brother‑in‑law. No other listed term fits.

question: L’s mother has a brother named A. L’s father has a sister named B. A and B are married and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of C to L?
explanation: C is the child of L’s maternal uncle (A) and paternal aunt (B). In either case C is L’s first cousin. No other term (e.g., sibling or second cousin) applies, and the relationship is uniquely determined.

question: M and N are double first cousins (their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters). M's child is X and N's child is Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins. Their children X and Y therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making them second cousins with doubled ancestry. The precise term is double second cousins.
choices: A) A) First cousins once removed

question: In a family with no adoptions, monogamy, and no intermarriage between relatives, let S be a person who is either the child of the only brother of J's mother or the child of the only brother of J's father (we are not told which). What is S's relation to J?
explanation: Whether S is the child of J's maternal uncle or paternal uncle, S is always the child of a parent's brother, which by standard kinship terminology makes S a first cousin of J. No other relation fits.

question: In a family with monogamy, no adoption or remarriage, let X be the child of the only brother of Y’s mother and also the child of the only sister of Y’s father. What is X’s precise kinship to Y using standard English terms?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and also of Y’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Thus X shares both sets of grandparents with Y, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: L’s father has exactly one sister and L’s mother has exactly one brother. The sister and the brother are married to each other and have a single child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: L’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle are the parents of M, so M is the child of both a paternal aunt and a maternal uncle. That makes M a first cousin on the father’s side and also a first cousin on the mother’s side – a double first cousin, the most specific term.

question: Two boys, X and Y, are described as follows: X is the son of my father's sister, and Y is the son of my father's brother. Using standard English kinship terminology, what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: My father's sister and brother are siblings, so X and Y are children of two siblings. Children of siblings share the same set of grandparents, making them first cousins. No closer or more distant blood tie applies.

question: In standard English kinship terms (blood only, no adoption, monogamy allowed), let P be the only child of my father's sister, and let Q be the only child of P. What is Q to me?
explanation: My father's sister is my paternal aunt. Her child P is my first cousin. Q, being the child of that cousin, is one generation below me, i.e., my first cousin once removed. No other term fits.

question: Eve and Frank share the same mother but have different fathers. Eve has a son Greg. Frank has a daughter Hannah. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Greg and Hannah?
explanation: Eve and Frank are half‑siblings, sharing one parent. Their children therefore share only one grandparent, not a full pair. The exact term for children of half‑siblings is “half‑first cousins”.

question: Two brothers, Aaron and Ben, each marry two sisters, Clara and Dana, respectively. Aaron and Clara have a son, X. Ben and Dana have a son, Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: Aaron and Ben share both parents; Clara and Dana share both parents. Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific standard term.

question: R’s paternal grandfather has a sister S. S’s grandson is T. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of T to R?
explanation: S is R’s great‑aunt (sibling of his paternal grandparent). S’s child is R’s parent’s first cousin. The child of that cousin – T – is one generation below, making T a first cousin once removed of R.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: R says: “My mother’s brother’s son is my cousin, and my father’s sister’s daughter is also my cousin.” If the two cousins are in fact the same person, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between R and that cousin?
explanation: The cousin could be the child of R’s maternal uncle (full first cousin) or the child of R’s paternal aunt (also a first cousin). If the uncle and aunt are siblings, the cousin is a full first cousin; if they are unrelated, the cousin is a half‑first cousin. Both satisfy the statement, so the exact term cannot be fixed.

question: John's mother has a brother named Tom. Tom has a daughter Lily. Lily has a son Mark. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Mark's precise relation to John?
explanation: Tom is John's maternal uncle, so Lily is John's first cousin. Lily's son Mark is one generation below Lily, making him John's first cousin once removed.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter A. N has a son B. A and B marry and have a child C. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the relation of C to N?
explanation: N is B’s parent, making N C’s grandparent. N is also M’s sibling, and M is A’s parent, so N is A’s great‑aunt/uncle, and therefore also C’s great‑aunt/uncle. Two distinct relations exist and no single standard term covers both, so the relation is not uniquely determinable.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions, let N be a person. N’s father has exactly one sister, and N’s mother has exactly one brother. The sister of N’s father marries the brother of N’s mother, and they have a single child M. What is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to N using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: The sister of N’s father is N’s paternal aunt; the brother of N’s mother is N’s maternal uncle. Their child M is the offspring of both a paternal aunt and a maternal uncle, making M the child of two of N’s parents’ siblings. Hence M is N’s first cousin on both sides, i.e., a first cousin.

question: In a monogamous family, M’s mother has a brother U. M’s father has a sister V. U and V are married to each other. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only, in‑law limited to spouse), what is the most precise term for U in relation to M?
explanation: U is the brother of M’s mother, giving a direct blood link that makes him M’s maternal uncle. Although he is also married to M’s paternal aunt, the blood relationship already defines the precise term. Hence the correct term is simply “uncle”.

question: A’s father (F) dies. Later, A’s mother (M) marries B, who already has a daughter C from a previous marriage. After the wedding, A marries C. Assuming no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted, what is the precise kinship term for B relative to A?
explanation: B is A’s step‑father by marrying A’s mother, and also A’s father‑in‑law because A married B’s daughter. Since the same person fulfills both roles, the exact term cannot be fixed; it is either step‑father or father‑in‑law. Hence the relation is not uniquely determinable.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a son Ethan. Brian marries Diana and they have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms (allowing doubled ancestry), what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Adam and Brian share the same parents, and Clara and Diana share the same parents. Therefore Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most exact term.

question: Alan's mother has exactly one brother, Mark, who has one daughter named Sara. Alan's father has exactly one sister, Nina, who has one son named Tom. It turns out that Sara and Tom are the same person. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of this person to Alan?
explanation: The person is the child of Alan's maternal uncle (Mark) and also the child of Alan's paternal aunt (Nina). In either case the relation is a first cousin; having the same individual fulfill both roles does not change the term.

question: P and Q are half‑siblings who share only their mother. P has a child R; Q has a child S. Before any marriage, what is the precise kinship term for the relation between R and S?
explanation: R and S are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent (their mother's mother). The correct term for such a relationship is half‑first cousins, distinct from full first cousins which require both grandparents in common.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O; N has a son P. N also has another child S, whose child Q is the nephew of P. O marries Q and they have a child R. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of P to R?
explanation: P is sibling of S, making P the aunt/uncle of Q. Since Q is R's father, P is the great‑aunt/uncle of R. This is more specific than "first cousin once removed" and is the standard term for a sibling of a grandparent’s child.

question: M is the child of the only sister of N's father, and also the child of the only brother of N's mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M's precise relation to N?
explanation: M is the child of N's paternal aunt (father's sister) and also the child of N's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Thus M shares both of N's grandparent pairs, which is the definition of a double first cousin. No other relation fits.

question: L’s father has a sister who is married to L’s mother’s brother. They have one child, M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) – that makes M a first cousin. M is also the child of L’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) – again a first cousin. Because the two cousin links involve both of L’s parental lines, M is a double first cousin of L, the most specific standard term.

question: Emily's father's sister married Emily's mother's brother. They have a child, Z. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption), what is Z's precise relation to Emily?
explanation: Emily's paternal aunt (her father's sister) and maternal uncle (her mother's brother) are each a sibling of one of Emily's parents. Their child shares both sets of grandparents with Emily, making Z a double first cousin—the most specific term.

question: M and N are siblings. M has two children, A and D, by different spouses. N has one child, B. A and B (who are first cousins) marry and have a child C. D has a child E with a new partner. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between C and E?
explanation: A and D are siblings, so their children C (through A) and E (through D) are first cousins. The marriage of A to B does not affect the cousin relationship between C and E.

question: Sisters Anna and Bella each marry brothers Carl and Dan respectively (Anna + Carl, Bella + Dan). Anna’s child is Ethan and Bella’s child is Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Anna and Bella are sisters; Carl and Dan are brothers. Their children share both sets of grandparents, giving them two parallel first‑cousin links. The precise term for such children is “double first cousins.”

question: N’s father has exactly one sibling, a brother F. N’s mother has exactly one sibling, a sister G. F and G are married and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is M’s precise relation to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal uncle (F) and maternal aunt (G). Thus M shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most specific term for this relationship.

question: R's mother has exactly one brother, whose daughter is X. R's father has exactly one sister, whose son is Y. If we select either X or Y and call that person S, what is S's relation to R?
explanation: R’s mother’s brother is R’s maternal uncle; his daughter X is R’s first cousin. R’s father’s sister is R’s paternal aunt; her son Y is also R’s first cousin. Whichever child is called S, S is always a first cousin of R.

question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is child of N's paternal aunt (father's sister) and of N's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Those two parents are unrelated, so M shares all four of N's grandparents. Hence M and N are first cousins through both parents, i.e., double first cousins.

question: M and N share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). M has a child X and N has a child Y, and there are no other intermarriages. What is the most precise kinship term for X and Y?
explanation: X and Y each descend from the single shared grandparent of M and N, so they share only one grandparent pair. This makes them half‑first cousins, distinct from full first cousins (who share both grandparents) and from second cousins.

question: M and N are full siblings. M is married to O; N is married to P. O’s brother is Q, and Q’s daughter is R. P’s sister is S, and S’s son is T. Using only standard English kinship terms (blood and immediate in‑law relations), what is the precise relation between R and T?
explanation: R is the daughter of O’s brother, making her O’s niece by blood; O is M’s spouse, so R is M’s niece‑in‑law. T is the son of P’s sister, making him P’s nephew by blood; P is N’s spouse, so T is N’s nephew‑in‑law. The link between R and T passes through two affinal steps beyond immediate in‑law, for which no standard direct kin term exists.
choices: A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a family, the brother of a woman's mother marries the sister of that woman's father. They have a child Z. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Z's relation to the woman?
explanation: Z is the child of the woman's maternal uncle (her mother's brother) and also the child of her paternal aunt (her father's sister). Hence Z is a first cousin on both sides, i.e., a double first cousin, which is the most precise term.

question: Alan and Brian are brothers. Alan has a daughter Clara. Brian has a son David. Clara marries Edward. Edward’s sister Fiona is married to George, who is David’s son. Using standard English kinship terms only (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of George to Clara?
explanation: Clara and David are first cousins (children of brothers). George is David’s son, so he is one generation below Clara’s cousin. That makes Clara and George first cousins once removed. No blood‑line or marriage creates a closer term.

question: M is the mother of N. N's sister is O. O is married to P. P's sister is Q. Q's son is R. What is R's relation to M using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: M is mother of O. O’s husband P is unrelated by blood to M. Q is P’s sister, also unrelated by blood to O. R, Q’s son, is therefore the child of O’s sister‑in‑law. No standard English kin term covers this affinal chain, so there is no direct relation.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M is the child of the sister of P’s father, and also the child of the brother of P’s mother. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of M to P?
explanation: M is a child of P’s paternal aunt and also a child of P’s maternal uncle. If those two spouses are married, M is a double first cousin of P; if they are unrelated, M’s relation cannot be fixed. Hence the relation is not uniquely determinable.

question: A is married to B. B’s mother is C. C’s brother is D. D’s daughter is E. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is E to A?
explanation: B’s mother C is A’s mother‑in‑law. C’s brother D is B’s maternal uncle, but he is not covered by the limited in‑law scope, so D has no standard kin term to A. Consequently D’s daughter E also has no standard direct relation to A; the connection exists only through an affinal chain.
choices: A) A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M and N are half‑siblings because they share only their father. M has a daughter X; N has a son Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the exact relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share one parent, so X and Y share only one grandparent. Children of half‑siblings are therefore half‑first cousins, not full first cousins.

question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Assuming standard monogamy and no adoption, what is the precise kinship term for the relation between M and N?
explanation: M is the offspring of N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Because those two spouses each belong to opposite parental lines, M is simultaneously N’s first cousin on the father’s side and on the mother’s side. The exact term for this dual relationship is double first cousin.

question: In a family with monogamy, no adoption, and no remarriage, let R be a person. The only brother of R’s mother has a child named T. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for T’s relation to R?
explanation: R’s mother’s brother is R’s maternal uncle. The child of an uncle (or aunt) is a first cousin. No other connections are mentioned, so the relation is exactly first cousin.

question: L and M are half‑siblings: they share the same mother but have different fathers. L has one child, P; M has one child, Q. No other marriages or adoptions occur. Using standard English kinship terminology, what is the precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: P and Q are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent (the common mother of L and M). The correct term for such descendants is “half‑first cousins”. Full first cousins require both grandparents in common, which they lack.

question: M is mother of siblings J and K. J is married to L. K has a child R. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation of R to L, using only the allowed in‑law definitions (spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: J and K are siblings, so J is R’s aunt/uncle. L is J’s spouse, therefore L is R’s aunt/uncle by marriage. The only standard term that fits the allowed in‑law scope is “aunt/uncle‑in‑law”.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Adam marries Clara and Brian marries Diana, where Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are children of two brothers (Adam, Brian) and two sisters (Clara, Diana). They share both paternal and maternal grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: John’s mother has a brother named Peter. John’s father has a sister named Mary. Peter is married to Mary. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is Mary’s precise relation to John?
explanation: Peter is John’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Mary is John’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Because Peter and Mary are married, Mary is also John’s aunt‑in‑law through his mother. The standard term covering both is simply “aunt”.

question: J’s father has exactly one sister, and J’s mother has exactly one brother. M is the child of that sister and also the child of that brother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of M to J?
explanation: M is the child of J’s paternal aunt and also the child of J’s maternal uncle. Thus M shares both of J’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: J’s father has a sister and J’s mother has a brother. The sister of J’s father and the brother of J’s mother have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation between M and J?
explanation: M is the child of J’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle, therefore shares both of J’s grandparent pairs. This makes M and J double first cousins, the exact term.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries X, the only child of P. N marries Y, the only child of Q. X and Y are first cousins, and P and Q are siblings. What is the precise kinship term for the children of M and N to each other?
explanation: A and B are children of siblings M and N, so they share one set of grandparents. Their other parents X and Y are first cousins, sharing another set of grandparents. Thus the children share both grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins.

question: Emma is the only child of her mother. Emma’s mother has a brother named Tom. Tom’s daughter Sara has a son Kevin. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Kevin’s relation to Emma?
explanation: Tom is Emma’s maternal uncle. His daughter Sara is Emma’s first cousin. Sara’s son Kevin is one generation down from that cousin, making him Emma’s first cousin once removed.

question: L is the child of the only brother of M's mother, and also the child of the only sister of M's father. Assuming no intermarriage among relatives, what is L's precise relation to M using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: L is the child of M's maternal uncle (brother of M's mother) – making L a first cousin on the maternal side. L is also the child of M's paternal aunt (sister of M's father) – making L a first cousin on the paternal side. Both relations use the same term, so L is simply M's first cousin.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Anna and Beth are sisters. Adam marries Anna and they have a son Carl. Brian marries Beth and they have a daughter Dana. Ignoring the later marriage between Carl and Dana, what is the most precise standard kinship term for Carl and Dana?
explanation: Carl and Dana share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. This makes them double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled relationship.

question: R's mother has exactly one brother, and R's father has exactly one sister. Those two siblings marry each other and have a child S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation of S to R?
explanation: S is the child of R's maternal uncle and paternal aunt, so S shares both of R's grandparent pairs. This makes them first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: L has exactly one sister and exactly one brother. The sister’s only child has a child M, and the brother’s only child also has a child M (the same person). Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s sister’s only child (a niece/nephew) and also the child of L’s brother’s only child (another niece/nephew). Hence M is L’s great‑niece (grandniece) on both sides – a double great‑niece, the only term that captures the doubled lineage.

explanation: If L and K are full siblings, A and B are first cousins; if they are half‑siblings, A and B are half‑first cousins. Because the sibling type is unspecified, the exact relation cannot be uniquely determined.

question: M and N are siblings. M is married to O, and N is married to P. O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X, and N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because each pair of their parents are siblings. Hence they are double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: L’s father has exactly one sister, and L’s mother has exactly one brother. The child of that sister and the child of that brother happen to be the same person, M. What is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to L using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: M is the child of L’s father’s sister (paternal aunt) and also the child of L’s mother’s brother (maternal uncle). In either case M is the child of a parent’s sibling, which is the definition of a first cousin. No other relationship fits.

question: A and C are brothers; B and D are sisters. A marries B and they have a child P. C marries D and they have a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relationship between P and Q?
explanation: P and Q share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. Hence they are double first cousins – the exact term for cousins who are related through both parental lines.

question: L’s father has exactly one brother, and L’s mother has exactly one brother. M is the child of L’s father’s brother and also the child of L’s mother’s brother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s paternal uncle and also of L’s maternal uncle. Each uncle is a sibling of one of L’s parents, so M shares both sets of grandparents with L. The exact term for such a relationship is “double first cousin.”

question: Peter and Susan are siblings. Peter has two children: Mary and her brother Ben. Susan has one child: Kevin. Ben has a son named John. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of John to Kevin?
explanation: Ben and Kevin are first cousins (they share Peter and Susan’s parents). John is Ben’s son, so he is one generation below Kevin’s cousin, making John Kevin’s first cousin once removed.

question: Two brothers each marry two sisters. The first brother and his wife have a child X; the second brother and his wife have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: X and Y are double first cousins because they share both sets of grandparents. Their children, P and Q, therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins. No other listed term captures this doubled ancestry.

question: T's mother and S's father are siblings. T and S each have one child, R and Q respectively. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise relationship between R and Q?
explanation: T and S are first cousins because their parents are siblings. Children of first cousins are second cousins, sharing the same great‑grandparents. Hence R and Q are second cousins, the most specific standard term.

question: Paul and Quentin are brothers. Paul is married to Rachel, and Quentin is married to Sarah, who is Rachel’s sister. Paul and Rachel have a son Tom; Quentin and Sarah have a daughter Lily. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Tom and Lily?
explanation: Tom and Lily share both paternal grandparents (through Paul and Quentin) and both maternal grandparents (through Rachel and Sarah). Therefore they are double first cousins.

question: In a family, my mother has exactly one brother (call him U) and my father has exactly one sister (call her V). I am told that a certain person W is the child of either U or V (but not both). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of W to me?
explanation: Whether W is U’s child (my maternal uncle’s child) or V’s child (my paternal aunt’s child), in both cases W is the child of one of my parents’ siblings, which is the definition of a first cousin. No other relationship fits.

question: M and N are full siblings. M has a daughter O; N has a son P. O and P marry and have a child Q. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for Q’s relation to M’s mother?
explanation: M’s mother is the grandmother of both O (through M) and P (through N). Q is the child of O and P, so Q is one generation below each of them. Hence Q is the great‑grandchild of M’s mother (the relationship is doubled but the term remains great‑grandchild).

question: A's mother has a brother B, whose daughter is C. A's father has a sister D, whose son is E. C and E marry and have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation of F to A?

question: L’s father has exactly one child, and L’s mother also has exactly one child. M is the child of the only child of L’s father, and M is also the grand‑child of the only child of L’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s relation to L?
explanation: The only child of L’s father is L, so M is the child of L’s child – a grand‑child. The only child of L’s mother is also L, and M is her grand‑child, confirming the same relation. Hence M is L’s grand‑child.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P. O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?

explanation: O is M’s daughter; M and N are siblings, so O is first cousin of N’s children P and R. Q is R’s child, making Q the first cousin once removed of O. No closer term applies.

question: John’s mother has a brother Mark. Mark is married to Lisa, who is the sister of John’s father. John has a daughter Emma. Emma marries the son of Mark and Lisa. question: In a monogamous family, X’s father has a sister S. S is married to T. T’s brother is U. U’s wife is V, whose mother is the sister of X’s mother. What is V’s relation to X using standard English kinship terms (limited to blood and immediate in‑law links)?

question: A and B are half‑siblings who share only their mother but have different fathers. A has a child C, and B has a child D. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for the relationship between C and D?
explanation: C and D are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent (their common maternal grandparent). The correct term for such a relation is “half‑first cousins,” distinct from full first cousins who share both grandparents.

question: M and N share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). M has a child X and N has a child Y, with no other intermarriages. What is the precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: Children of half‑siblings share only a single grandparent, not a full pair. The exact term for such a relationship is “half‑first cousins.”

question: John is married to Mary. Mary’s brother Paul is married to Susan, who is John’s sister. Paul and Susan have a child Emma; John and Mary have a child David. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation between Emma and David?

question: A's mother has exactly one brother B. B has one daughter C. C has a son D. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is D's precise relation to A?
explanation: B is A's maternal uncle, so C is A's first cousin. D, being C's child, is one generation below a first cousin, i.e., a first cousin once removed. No other term fits more precisely.

question: John and Peter are brothers. Their sister Mary is also a sibling of both. Mary’s son Tom and Peter’s daughter Lisa meet at a family reunion. Using standard English blood‑kin terms only, what is Tom’s precise relation to Lisa?
explanation: Mary and Peter are siblings. Tom is Mary's child and Lisa is Peter's child. Children of siblings are first cousins, regardless of gender or order.

question: John and Mary are married; James and Linda are married. John is James’s brother, and Mary is Linda’s sister. John and Mary’s only child is Alice; James and Linda’s only child is Bob. explanation: Alice’s father and Bob’s father are brothers, and Alice’s mother and Bob’s mother are sisters. Hence Alice and Bob share both paternal and maternal grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled shared ancestry.

question: John has a sister Mary. John’s wife Lisa has a brother Tom. Mary marries Tom. John and Lisa have a child Emma; Mary and Tom have a child Sam. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Emma and Sam?

question: John is the son of Mary. Mary’s only sibling is Peter, who is married to Linda. Linda’s only sibling is Susan, who is married to Mark. Mark’s only sibling is Tom, who is the father of Alice. What is Alice’s relation to John using standard English kinship terms?

question: M’s father married twice. With his first wife he had two children, M and his sister S. After divorcing, he married a second woman and had a daughter D. question: M is X's mother and has a brother U. F is X's father and has a sister S. U marries S, and they have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is Y's precise relation to X?

question: In a family with monogamy, no adoption, and no remarriage, R is the child of the only brother of S’s mother. What is R’s relation to S?
explanation: The only brother of S’s mother is S’s maternal uncle. R is the child of that uncle, making R the child of S’s aunt/uncle, i.e., S’s first cousin. No other blood link is introduced, so the precise term is "first cousin."

question: X’s mother has exactly one sibling, a brother named Y. X’s father has exactly one sibling, a sister named Z. Y and Z are married and have one child. What is the precise kinship term for that child to X?
explanation: Y is X’s maternal uncle and Z is X’s paternal aunt. Their child shares both of X’s grandparent pairs, making the child X’s double first cousin. No other standard term applies.

question: In a family with monogamy, no adoption, and no twins, X’s mother has a brother whose daughter is Y. X’s father has a sister whose son is Z. Y and Z marry and have a child W. What is the precise kinship term for W’s relation to X?

question: Two brothers, A and B, marry two sisters, C and D, respectively. A and C have a son X; B and D have a daughter Y. question: Mx (X's mother) and Fy (Y's father) are half‑siblings, sharing exactly one parent and no other relatives in common. X and Y are not siblings. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: Mx and Fy share one parent G, making G a grandparent of both X (through Mx) and Y (through Fy). They therefore share only one grandparent, which defines them as half‑first cousins—the exact term, since full first cousins require both grandparents.

question: M and N are half‑siblings who share only their mother X. M has a child A, and N has a child B. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between A and B?

question: Two brothers marry two sisters. The first brother and his wife have a son X; the second brother and his wife have a daughter Y. question: R is married to S. S’s brother is T, and T’s spouse is U (a man). Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is U to R?
explanation: S’s brother T is R’s brother‑in‑law. The spouse of a sibling‑in‑law is also a sibling‑in‑law, so U, being T’s husband, is likewise R’s brother‑in‑law.

question: In a family with no adoption, my mother’s brother (my maternal uncle) is married to my father’s sister (my paternal aunt). They have a child named Z. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Z’s precise relation to me?
explanation: Z is the child of both my maternal uncle and my paternal aunt. Thus Z is my cousin on my mother’s side and also my cousin on my father’s side. When the same person is a first cousin through both parental lines, the exact term is “double first cousin.”

question: Two brothers each marry a different sister from the same sibling pair. The elder brother's child is X and the younger brother's child is Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
