question: X’s mother has a brother U, whose daughter is Y. X’s father has a sister V, whose son is Z. Y and Z marry and have a child W. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the relation of W to X?
explanation: Y is X’s maternal first cousin; Z is X’s paternal first cousin. Their child W is one generation below each cousin, making W X’s first cousin once removed on both sides. The standard term is “first cousin once removed.”
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard direct relation

question: Eight people A–H sit around a round table; seat 0 (top) is occupied by A, and clockwise is considered "right". The following hold: G sits immediately to A’s right; B sits immediately to G’s right; D sits directly opposite A; F sits immediately to A’s left; H sits somewhere on the clockwise arc from B to D (endpoints excluded); C is not adjacent to H. Which statement must be true?
explanation: A at seat0 forces G at seat1, B at seat2, D opposite A at seat4, and F at seat7. The arc B→D exclusive contains only seat3, so H must be seat3, making D the clockwise neighbor of H. All other options can be false depending on where C and E sit.
choices: A) A) The person immediately clockwise of H is G.
B) B) The person immediately clockwise of H is D.
C) C) The person opposite H is B.
D) D) The person opposite H is C.

question: Two brothers, M and P, each marry a sister, N and Q respectively. M + N have a daughter X; P + Q have a son Y. X and Y marry each other and have a child Z. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation of Z to M’s mother?
explanation: M’s mother is the grandmother of both X (her daughter’s child) and Y (her son’s child). Z is therefore the child of two grandchildren of the same woman, making Z her great‑grandchild through both parents—still termed simply a great‑grandchild.

question: John and Mary are married. John’s sister Lisa is married to Mary’s brother Tom. John and Mary have a daughter Anna; Lisa and Tom have a son Ben. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between Anna and Ben?
explanation: Anna and Ben share both sets of grandparents (John’s parents and Mary’s parents) because their parents are sibling pairs. This makes them double first cousins, the precise term for cousins who share two grandparent pairs.

question: L is the first cousin of N (their parents are siblings). M is the child of L. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: L and N share a pair of grandparents, making them first cousins. M is one generation below L, i.e., the child of N's first cousin. This is exactly the definition of a first cousin once removed.

question: P and Q are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). P’s child is R, and Q’s child is S. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between R and S?
explanation: R and S are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent. That makes them half‑first cousins, not full first cousins (which require both shared grandparents).

question: M is the mother of siblings N and O. N is married to P. P’s sister Q is married to O’s son R. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse and spouse’s parents/children), what is Q’s relation to M?
explanation: O is M’s child, so R is M’s grandchild. Q is R’s spouse, i.e., the spouse of M’s grandchild. The precise term is “granddaughter‑in‑law” (or “grandson‑in‑law” if male). No closer blood or in‑law term exists.

question: John and Paul are brothers. John’s daughter is Emma; Paul’s children are Liam and Sarah (Liam and Sarah are siblings). Emma marries Noah, who is unrelated to the brothers. Who is Emma’s child Zoe to Sarah?
explanation: Emma and Sarah are first cousins (their fathers are brothers). Zoe is Emma’s child, one generation below Emma, so Zoe is Sarah’s first cousin once removed.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary and her husband Alan have two children, Peter and Lisa, who are siblings. Lisa marries Kevin and they have a son Tom. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no adoption), what is Tom’s precise relation to John?
explanation: Mary is John’s sister, so Peter and Lisa are John’s nephew and niece. Lisa’s son Tom is one generation below Lisa, making him John’s great‑nephew (also called grandnephew). No other term fits.

question: John and Mary have a daughter Lily. After Mary dies, John marries Anna, who already has a son Mark from a previous marriage. Lily and Mark become step‑siblings. Lily marries Peter and they have a son Sam. Mark marries Susan and they have a daughter Eva. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no adoption), what is the precise relation between Sam and Eva?
explanation: Lily and Mark are step‑siblings, not blood relatives. Their children Sam and Eva share no common ancestor; they are related only through the marriage of their parents, which yields no standard English kin term.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal only)

question: M and N are brothers. M marries X and N marries Y. X and Y are sisters. M‑X have a child A; N‑Y have a child B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between A and B?
explanation: A and B are children of two couples who are both sibling pairs, so they share both sets of grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled ancestry.

question: Let A be the child of B. B’s mother is the sister of C’s father. C is the parent of D. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation between A and D?
explanation: B’s mother and C’s father are siblings, so B and C are first cousins. The children of first cousins (A and D) are second cousins. No other relationship fits uniquely.

question: Let X be a person whose mother has exactly one brother and whose father has exactly one sister. The child of X’s maternal uncle is Y, and the child of X’s paternal aunt is Z. If either Y or Z is called W, what is W to X?
explanation: Both Y and Z are children of a sibling of one of X’s parents, making each a first cousin of X. The relation is identical for either choice.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M and N are half‑siblings (they share exactly one parent). M has a child X; N has a child Y. X and Y each have one child, named P and Q respectively. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between P and Q?
explanation: M and N share one parent, so X and Y are half‑first cousins (they share a single grandparent). Their children P and Q therefore share a single great‑grandparent, making them half‑second cousins. This term is more precise than “second cousins,” which requires two shared great‑grandparents.

question: N’s father has exactly one sister, S, and N’s mother has exactly one brother, B. S and B are married and have a single child, M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal aunt (S) and maternal uncle (B). Hence M is a first cousin of N through the father and also a first cousin through the mother, sharing both sets of grandparents. The exact term is “double first cousin.”

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and they have a child R. O’s brother P marries N’s daughter Q, and they have a child S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between R and S?
explanation: R is child of M (who shares both parents G1,G2 with N) and O (who shares both parents O‑F,O‑M with P). S is child of P (O’s sibling) and Q (N’s daughter). Hence R and S share both grandparent pairs G1,G2 and O‑F,O‑M, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures both lines of descent.

question: Mary has two children, John and Kate. Mary’s brother is Tom. Kate’s daughter is Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse only), what is Tom’s precise relation to Emma?
explanation: Tom is Mary’s brother, so he is Kate’s maternal uncle. Kate’s daughter Emma is Tom’s brother’s niece’s child, i.e., Tom’s great‑niece. Therefore Tom is Emma’s great‑uncle (also called grand‑uncle).

question: Tom’s mother has a brother Carl. Carl has a daughter Nina from his first marriage. Tom’s father has a sister Maya, and Maya later marries Carl. Carl and Maya have a son Sam. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption), what is the most precise relation between Nina and Sam?
explanation: Nina and Sam share the same father, Carl, but have different mothers (Nina’s first‑marriage mother, Sam’s mother Maya). Hence they are half‑siblings. No other blood link exists between them.

question: M and N are siblings. M's daughter is O. N's son is P, and N's daughter is R. R's child is Q. What is the precise kinship term for the relation between O and Q using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: O is child of M; R is child of N, M’s sibling, so O and R are first cousins. Q is R’s child, making Q the child of O’s first cousin, i.e., O’s first cousin once removed.

question: Two brothers, John and Mark, marry two sisters, Emma and Lucy respectively. John and Emma have a son Adam; Mark and Lucy have a daughter Beth. Adam and Beth each marry unrelated partners and have children Carl and Dana respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Carl and Dana?
explanation: Adam and Beth are double first cousins (their parents are two pairs of siblings). Their children Carl and Dana therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, which makes them double second cousins—the most specific term.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has two children: a son P and a daughter R. R has a child Q. O marries Q. Using standard English kinship terms and ignoring the marital link, what is the precise blood relation between O and Q?
explanation: O is the child of M; N is M’s sibling, so O’s first cousins are P and R. Q is R’s child, i.e., the child of O’s first cousin. That makes Q O’s first cousin once removed. No closer term exists.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, who is the sister of P. N marries Q, who is the brother of O. Their children are X (child of M and O) and Y (child of N and Q). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father M is sibling of Y’s mother N; X’s mother O is sibling of Y’s father Q. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the most precise standard term.

question: Brothers Adam and Brian each marry sisters Clara and Diana. Adam + Clara have a son Ethan; Brian + Diana have a son Felix. Ethan and Felix marry unrelated partners and each have a child—Maya and Noah respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the relationship between Maya and Noah?
explanation: Ethan and Felix share both sets of grandparents (their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters), making them double first cousins. Their children, Maya and Noah, therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, which is exactly the definition of double second cousins.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: Two sisters, X and Y, share at least one parent (they may be full sisters or half‑sisters). X has a son S; Y has a daughter D. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the relationship between S and D?
explanation: If X and Y are full sisters, S and D are first cousins. If they are half‑sisters, S and D are half‑first cousins. Because the exact sibling status of X and Y is unspecified, the precise term cannot be fixed; the relation is not uniquely determinable.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries P and N marries Q, where P and Q are also siblings. M and P have a child X; N and Q have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because each pair of their parents are siblings. This makes them double first cousins, the most specific term for their relationship.

question: I say: “M is the child of the only son of my father’s sister, and also the child of the only daughter of my mother’s brother.” Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is M’s relation to me?
explanation: My father’s sister is my aunt; her only son is my paternal cousin. His child is my first cousin once removed. My mother’s brother is my maternal uncle; his only daughter is my maternal cousin. Her child is the same generation down from a cousin, also a first cousin once removed. Both descriptions identify the same relation.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: In a family with monogamy, no adoption or remarriage, let R be a person whose mother has exactly one brother (M) and whose father has exactly one sister (S). M and S are married to each other. What is the most precise standard kinship term for the child of M and S with respect to R?
explanation: M is R's maternal uncle and S is R's paternal aunt. Their child shares both of R's sets of grandparents, making the child a double first cousin of R – the only term that captures the double shared ancestry.

question: Let P be the child of the only brother of Q’s mother, and let Q be the child of the only sister of P’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: P is the child of Q’s maternal uncle, making P Q’s first cousin. Likewise, Q is the child of P’s paternal aunt, making Q P’s first cousin. Both descriptions lead to the same unique kinship: first cousins.

question: M and N are full siblings. M marries X and N marries Y, where X and Y are also full siblings (no other intermarriages). M and X have a child A; N and Y have a child B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of X/Y. Hence they are first cousins through two independent lines, i.e., double first cousins. No other term is more exact.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P. O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both paternal and maternal grandparents because their parents are two pairs of siblings. This makes them double first cousins, the exact term for such a relationship.

question: M and N are siblings. P and Q are siblings. M marries P and N marries Q. Their children X and Y are therefore double first cousins. X has a child R and Y has a child S. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between R and S?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. Their children R and S share both sets of great‑grandparents, which makes R and S double second cousins—the most precise label.
choices: A) A) First cousins once removed

question: M is the child of the sister of L’s father and also the child of the brother of L’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: M is the offspring of L’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and also of L’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with L, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: Consider the following relationships: (1) M is the only child of his mother L. (2) L has a sister S, who is married to N. (3) N has exactly one child, O. (4) O is married to P, who is the only child of Q. (5) Q is the sibling of M's father R. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents, spouse’s siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of O to Q?
explanation: Q is the sibling of M’s father, so Q is M’s paternal aunt/uncle. O is married to P, who is Q’s only child. Therefore O is the spouse of Q’s child, i.e., Q’s son‑in‑law or daughter‑in‑law. No blood term applies.

question: N’s father has exactly one sister, and N’s mother has exactly one brother. The sister of N’s father and the brother of N’s mother have a child M. In standard English kinship terms (ignoring adoption), what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is child of N’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle. Thus M shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most specific standard term.

question: L’s father has exactly one sister and L’s mother has exactly one brother. M is the child of that sister and that brother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relationship between M and L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Each parent is a sibling of one of L’s parents, so M shares both sets of grandparents with L, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, who is the sister of P. N marries Q, who is the brother of O. M and O have a son R; N and Q have a daughter S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation between R and S?
explanation: R’s paternal grandparents are M and N’s parents; S’s paternal grandparents are the same pair, so they share paternal grandparents. R’s maternal grandparents are O’s parents; S’s maternal grandparents are Q’s parents, the same pair, so they share maternal grandparents. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes R and S double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: Consider a person L. L’s mother has exactly one brother; the child of that brother is M. L’s father has exactly one daughter; the child of that daughter is N. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relationship of M to N?
explanation: M is L’s first cousin (child of L’s maternal uncle). N is L’s niece/nephew (child of L’s sister). Since M is first cousin to L’s sister, he is first cousin once removed to her child N. No closer standard term applies.
choices: C) C) First cousins once removed
D) D) No direct kinship term

question: John and Mark are brothers. Alice and Beth are sisters. John marries Alice and they have a son Carl. Mark marries Beth and they have a daughter Dana. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relationship between Carl and Dana?
explanation: Carl’s father and Dana’s father are brothers, and Carl’s mother and Dana’s mother are sisters. Therefore Carl and Dana share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: M is the half‑sister of N’s father. X is the child of M, and Y is the child of N. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N’s father share exactly one parent, so they have only one grandparent in common. X, as M’s child, and Y, as N’s child, therefore share that single grandparent, making them half‑first cousins – they are first cousins but with only one shared grandparent.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, L’s mother has exactly one son and L’s father has exactly one daughter. M is the child of that son and also the child of that daughter. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is M’s relation to L?
explanation: The only son of L’s mother is L’s brother; the only daughter of L’s father is L’s sister. Their child M is the child of L’s sibling, which makes M L’s niece or nephew. No other blood link changes this relationship.

question: M is the only child of L. L has a brother N, who is married to O. O's father P is the brother of Q, and Q is the father of M's mother R. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for O's daughter S with respect to M?
explanation: N is M's maternal uncle, so any child of N—namely S—is M's first cousin. O's own blood ties (her father being a brother of M's maternal grandfather) do not alter the closest kinship, which is the uncle‑niece line giving a first‑cousin relationship.

question: Lara and Omar are half‑brothers (they share the same mother but have different fathers). Lara has a daughter Nina, and Omar has a son Sam. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Nina and Sam?
explanation: Nina and Sam are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent (the mother’s parent). That makes them half‑first cousins, the exact term for cousins who share a single grandparent pair.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries P, and N marries Q. P and Q are also siblings. M and N each have one child, X and Y respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their fathers (or mothers) are siblings and their mothers (or fathers) are also siblings. Sharing all grandparents makes them double first cousins, the exact term.

question: M is the only child of his mother N. N’s mother is O. Q is another daughter of O, and P is the only child of Q. What is the precise kinship term for the relation between M and P using standard English kinship?
explanation: O is the maternal grandmother of both M (through N) and P (through Q). Since Q is O’s daughter other than N, Q is M’s maternal aunt. P, as Q’s child, is therefore M’s first cousin. No half‑blood or further removal occurs.

question: L and N are siblings. L has only one child, M. N has only one child, O. M is married to R. R has a sibling Q, and Q’s child is P. O marries P. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of O to R?
explanation: O is the spouse of P, who is R’s niece/nephew (child of R’s sibling Q). The spouse of a niece/nephew is called a niece‑in‑law (or nephew‑in‑law). Hence O is R’s niece‑in‑law. No other listed term fits.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, who is the sister of P. P marries Q, who is the sister of N. M and O have a child X; P and Q have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share parents; O and P share parents; N and Q share parents. Thus X’s parents (M and O) are each sibling to Y’s parents (N and P) respectively. X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

question: L’s mother has exactly two siblings: a brother and a sister. The brother’s child is X, and the sister’s child is Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: Both X and Y are children of siblings of L’s mother, so they share L’s maternal grandparents. Children of siblings are first cousins, making X and Y first cousins.

question: In a family with no adoptions, let my father's only brother be Uncle U and my mother's only sister be Aunt A. Suppose a person X is the child of both U and A (U and A are married to each other). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of X to me?
explanation: U is my paternal uncle, so his child is my first cousin. A is my maternal aunt, so her child is also my first cousin. Because the same person X is child of both, X is a first cousin on both sides—i.e., a double first cousin.
choices: D) No standard term (affinal relation only)

question: M and N share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). M has a child X, N has a child Y, and there are no other intermarriages. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share only one parent, so X and Y share only one grandparent. That makes them half‑first cousins. Full first cousins require both grandparents, and second cousins require shared great‑grandparents.

question: M is married to N. N’s sister O is married to P. P’s father is Q, whose other son (not P) is R. R’s daughter is S. What is S’s relation to M, using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses)?
explanation: P and R are brothers; S is R’s daughter, thus S is P’s niece. P is O’s husband, and O is N’s sister, making P a brother‑in‑law to N. Consequently S is niece‑in‑law to N, and therefore also niece‑in‑law to M, N’s spouse.
choices: D) D) No standard kinship term

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have two children, Ethan and Hannah. Brian marries Diana and they have two children, Fiona and Ian. Ethan marries Fiona and their son is George. Hannah marries Ian and their daughter is Helen. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between George and Helen?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins (their parents are two pairs of siblings). Hannah and Ian are also double first cousins. George and Helen are each the child of a double first‑cousin pair, so they share both sets of great‑grandparents. The exact term is double second cousins.
choices: A) A) First cousins once removed

question: Anna’s mother has exactly one brother, Ben. Ben is married to Clara, who is the only sister of Anna’s father’s father. What is Clara’s most precise kinship term to Anna, using standard English relations?
explanation: Clara is the sister of Anna’s paternal grandfather, making her Anna’s great‑aunt by blood. She is also Ben’s wife, i.e., Anna’s maternal uncle’s spouse, which makes her an aunt by marriage. The blood link is more specific, so the precise term is “great‑aunt.”

question: A and B are half‑siblings (they share the same mother but have different fathers). A has a child C; B has a child D. No other intermarriages occur. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: C and D are each the child of a half‑sibling. They share only one grandparent (their common maternal grandmother) and not the other. The exact term for such a pair is “half‑first cousins”. Full first cousins require two shared grandparents; second cousins are a generation further.

question: Brothers A and B each marry sisters C and D, respectively. A and C have a son X; B and D have a son Y. X and Y marry unrelated partners and have children P and Q, respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins; their children share both sets of great‑grandparents, which is double second cousins.

question: Let J be a person. P is either the child of the only sister of J’s father or the child of the only brother of J’s mother (the exact parent is unknown). Assuming monogamy, no adoption, and no incest, what is the precise kinship term for P in relation to J?
explanation: Both possibilities make P a child of one of J’s parents’ siblings, i.e., a first cousin. The uncertainty does not change the class of the relationship, so the only correct term is “first cousin.”

question: In a family, M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has a son P, who marries O. O and P have a child Q. Q’s mother’s brother’s daughter is R. What is the precise kinship term for R’s relation to Q, using standard English kinship (no in‑law beyond spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: O is Q’s mother; her brother is M’s brother, i.e., N. N’s daughter is R, making R Q’s first cousin (children of siblings). No further blood link exists, so the exact term is first cousin.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy, and no remarriage, let A have a sister B and a brother F. B’s son is C. F’s child is E. D is the child of E. What is the precise kinship term for D’s relation to A (using standard English terms only)?
explanation: F’s child E is A’s niece/nephew. D, being E’s child, is A’s grandniece (if female) or grandnephew (if male). No other listed terms describe this generation gap, so the correct choice is the grand‑niece/nephew designation.

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted, let X and Y be distinct individuals such that X is the child of the sister of Y’s father, and X is also the child of the brother of Y’s mother. Assuming no other constraints, what is the precise kinship term (standard English) between X and Y?
explanation: If the two siblings (the father's sister and the mother's brother) are the same person, X is Y’s half‑sibling; if they are different but each married Y’s parent, X is a first cousin; if one sibling is also Y’s parent, X could be an aunt/uncle. Because the description allows multiple configurations, the exact relation cannot be uniquely determined.

question: In a family, L’s mother has exactly one brother, and L’s father has exactly one brother. Both of those brothers have a single child each, and those two children are the same person M. What is the precise kinship term for M with respect to L, using standard English kinship without ignoring doubled ancestry?
explanation: L’s mother’s brother is L’s maternal uncle; his child is L’s first cousin on the mother’s side. L’s father’s brother is L’s paternal uncle; his child is L’s first cousin on the father’s side. Since both cousins are the same individual, M shares both sets of grandparents with L, making M L’s double first cousin.

question: In a family, X's father is the brother of Y's mother, and X's mother is the sister of Y's father. No other intermarriages exist. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X's father and Y's mother are siblings, and X's mother and Y's father are siblings. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, giving them the exact term “double first cousins.”

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a woman from the same sister pair, Clara and Diana (Adam‑>Clara, Brian‑>Diana). Adam and Clara have a child, Ethan; Brian and Diana have a child, Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both paternal grandparents (Adam’s parents) and both maternal grandparents (Clara’s parents). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled lineage.

question: A person X is the child of the only son of my father's sister and also the child of the only daughter of my mother's brother. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for X relative to me?
explanation: X's father is the son of my paternal aunt, making him my first cousin. X's mother is the daughter of my maternal uncle, also my first cousin. Since X's parents are first cousins, X shares both sets of grandparents with me, so X is a double first cousin.

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father. N’s mother is the sister of O’s father. O’s mother is the sister of P’s father. Assuming no intermarriage among the three grandparent couples, what is the most precise standard kinship term describing the relation between M and P?
explanation: Each adjacent pair (M‑N, N‑O, O‑P) are first cousins, sharing a different set of grandparents. M and P share no common ancestor, so there is no blood relationship between them. The correct term is “no blood relation.”

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted, let Y be a person. Y’s spouse S has a sibling B. B’s child is X. X is also a grandchild of Y’s mother‑in‑law. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s spouse’s sibling, an affinal link beyond the allowed in‑law scope, and there is no blood connection. Standard kinship provides no direct term for this relationship, so X has no standard direct relation to Y.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law relations limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses): A is married to B; B’s brother is C; C’s wife is D; D’s brother is E. What is E to A?
explanation: A→B (spouse) →C (B’s brother, sibling‑in‑law) →D (C’s wife, sibling‑in‑law) →E (D’s brother, sibling‑in‑law). This chain goes beyond the immediate in‑law scope and never creates a blood link, so no standard direct kin term exists.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a family with no adoption, let Y be a person. Y’s mother has exactly one son, and Y’s father has exactly one daughter. X is the child of that son, and Z is the child of that daughter. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between X and Z?
explanation: The son is Y’s brother; the daughter is Y’s sister. X is the child of Y’s brother, Z is the child of Y’s sister. Children of siblings are first cousins, regardless of whether the siblings are full or half, so X and Z are first cousins.

question: L’s father has exactly one sister, and L’s mother has exactly one brother. The child of that sister (the paternal aunt) is also the child of that brother (the maternal uncle). Who is that child to L?
explanation: The child is the offspring of L’s paternal aunt and L’s maternal uncle, sharing both of L’s grandparent pairs. Hence the child is L’s double first cousin – a first cousin on both sides.

question: P is the child of the only brother of Q’s mother and also the child of the only sister of Q’s father. Assuming monogamy, no adoption, and that the two spouses are unrelated, what is the most precise kinship term for P’s relation to Q?
explanation: Q’s maternal uncle’s child is a first cousin on the mother’s side; Q’s paternal aunt’s child is a first cousin on the father’s side. Because the uncle and aunt are married, P shares both sets of grandparents with Q, making P a double first cousin—the most specific standard term.

question: L has exactly one brother and exactly one sister. The brother has only one daughter, and the sister has only one son. The daughter of the brother and the son of the sister are married to each other and have a single child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is M's relation to L?
explanation: L’s brother’s daughter is L’s niece; her child M is L’s great‑niece/nephew. Likewise, L’s sister’s son is L’s nephew; his child M is also L’s great‑niece/nephew. Both lineage paths give the same precise term.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed

question: Person X’s paternal grandmother has exactly one other child, a daughter A. X’s maternal grandfather has exactly one other child, a son B. A and B marry and have a son C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is C’s precise relation to X?
explanation: A is X’s paternal aunt (sister of X’s father) and B is X’s maternal uncle (brother of X’s mother). Their son C is the child of two siblings of X’s parents who married each other, making C a double first cousin of X – the most specific standard term.

question: Let X be a person. X's mother has a brother Y. Y is married to A. A has a brother Z. Z has a daughter W. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of W to X?
explanation: X → mother → Y (maternal uncle) → A (uncle’s wife, no blood link) → Z (A’s brother, unrelated by blood) → W (Z’s daughter). The chain stays entirely affinal after Y, giving no standard direct kin term between W and X.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: Let Q be a person whose mother has exactly one brother and whose father has exactly one brother. P is the child of the mother’s brother and also the child of the father’s brother (the two brothers are different men). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of P to Q?
explanation: P is the child of Q’s maternal uncle and also the child of Q’s paternal uncle. Thus P and Q share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions, let M be a woman whose mother has a brother named T. T has a daughter S. M also has a brother whose son is R. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between S and R?
explanation: T is M's maternal uncle, so his daughter S is M's first cousin. M's brother is a sibling, and his son R is M's nephew. A first cousin (S) and a nephew (R) are one generation apart, making S and R first cousins once removed. No closer term applies.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: L’s father has exactly one sister and L’s mother has exactly one brother. The child of that sister and the child of that brother happen to be the same person M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: The father’s sister (paternal aunt) and the mother’s brother (maternal uncle) must be married, so their child M shares both sets of grandparents with L. Hence M is L’s double first cousin, the most specific term.

question: John has a sister Mary; Mary's son is Paul. John is married to Lisa, whose brother is Tom; Tom's daughter is Sarah. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only and immediate in‑law), what is the precise relation between Paul and Sarah?
explanation: Paul is John’s nephew (child of John's sister). Sarah is Lisa’s niece (child of Lisa's brother). John and Lisa are spouses, but there is no blood link between Paul and Sarah. English kinship provides terms only for blood relations or direct in‑law links; a spouse’s sibling’s child is not a defined relation to the other spouse’s sibling’s child. Hence no standard direct kin term—option D.
choices: D) No standard direct relation (affinal only)

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, marry two sisters, Clara and Diana respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan. Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona marry each other. What is the most precise standard kinship term for Ethan’s relation to Fiona?
explanation: Adam and Brian are siblings; Clara and Diana are siblings. Their children, Ethan and Fiona, share both sets of grandparents (paternal and maternal). Hence they are double first cousins, the only term that captures the doubled shared ancestry.

question: M is the mother of N’s father’s sister. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: N’s father’s sister is N’s paternal aunt. Her mother is also the mother of N’s father, making her N’s paternal grandmother. Therefore M is N’s grandmother.

question: M and N are siblings. M’s only child is daughter O. N has two children, a son P and a daughter R. R’s only child is Q. O marries Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise blood relation between O and Q before their marriage?
explanation: O is the child of M, who is N’s sibling, so O is N’s niece. R is N’s daughter, making O and R first cousins. Q, as R’s child, is one generation below R, so O and Q are first cousins once removed. This is the most specific term without invoking in‑law relations.
choices: D) No standard blood relation (affinal only)

question: In family 1 there are siblings Adam (male) and Eve (female). In family 2 there are siblings Ben (male) and Dana (female). Adam marries Dana and they have a child X; Eve marries Ben and they have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y each have both sets of grandparents in common, because their parents are two pairs of siblings. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a stricter term than ordinary first cousins.

question: A is married to B. B's mother is C. C's brother is D. D's daughter is E, who is married to F. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses), what is the relation of F to A?
explanation: B is A’s spouse. C is A’s mother‑in‑law. D, C’s brother, is A’s uncle‑in‑law. E, D’s daughter, is A’s cousin‑in‑law. F is the spouse of that cousin‑in‑law, a link beyond the usual in‑law scope, so no standard direct kin term exists.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: X is the child of the only brother of Y’s mother, and also the child of the only sister of Y’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X is child of Y’s maternal uncle, making X a first cousin. X is also child of Y’s paternal aunt, another first‑cousin link. Two independent first‑cousin relations give X the status of a double first cousin of Y.

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father, and M’s father is the brother of N’s mother. Assuming monogamy and no adoptions, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between M and N?
explanation: Each of M’s parents is a sibling of one of N’s parents, so M and N share both sets of grandparents. That makes them double first cousins – the exact term for cousins whose parents are two pairs of siblings.

question: Person X’s mother is the sister of Person Y’s father, and Person Y’s mother is the sister of Person X’s father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term describing the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X’s mother is sister of Y’s father, so they share one set of grandparents. Y’s mother is sister of X’s father, giving a second shared set. Hence X and Y share both paternal and maternal grandparents, making them double first cousins – the most precise term.

question: Person X is the child of the only brother of Y’s mother, and also the child of the only sister of Y’s father. Using standard English kinship terminology, what is the precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X’s mother is the sister of Y’s father and X’s father is the brother of Y’s mother. Therefore X shares both of Y’s grandparents on each side, making them double first cousins—the most exact standard term.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: Let X be a person. X's mother has a brother U who is married to Y. Y's brother B is the father of Z. Additionally, Z is the son of X's father's sister (X's paternal aunt). What is the precise kinship term for Z in relation to X?
explanation: Z's mother is X's father's sister, making Z the child of X's paternal aunt – a first cousin. The paternal aunt's marriage to B (who is Y's brother) does not add any blood link, so the only definitive relationship is that of first cousins.

question: M is married to N. N’s sister is O, and O’s husband is P. P’s mother is Q, whose only son is R. What is the precise kinship term (using standard English kin terms, allowing only spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses as in‑law relations) for R relative to M?
explanation: M → N (spouse) → O (sister‑in‑law) → P (brother‑in‑law) → Q (mother‑in‑law) → R (her son). R is the son of M’s mother‑in‑law, making him M’s nephew‑in‑law, the only standard term for this relationship.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: P is the child of the only brother of Q’s mother and also the child of the only sister of Q’s father. The brother and the sister are married to each other. What is the most precise standard kinship term for P’s relation to Q?
explanation: The brother is Q’s maternal uncle, so his child is Q’s first cousin on the mother’s side. The sister is Q’s paternal aunt, so her child is Q’s first cousin on the father’s side. Because the same person P occupies both roles, P is a double first cousin of Q.

question: Mara and Lena are half‑sisters: they share the same mother but have different fathers. Mara has a son, Carl; Lena has a daughter, Dana. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Carl and Dana?
explanation: Carl and Dana are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent (their common maternal grandmother). The exact term for such a pair is "half‑first cousins"; full first cousins require both grandparents in common.

question: A and B are brothers; C and D are sisters. A marries C and they have a son X. B marries D and they have a daughter Y. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y have the same two sets of grandparents because each pair of siblings married the other pair of siblings. Hence they share both grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, N marries P, and O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terminology, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both pairs of grandparents because each parent pair consists of siblings on both sides. Therefore they are double first cousins, the most specific term that captures the shared ancestry.

question: In a monogamous family tree with no adoptions, let Z be the child of (1) the sister of M’s mother and (2) the brother of M’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of Z to M?
explanation: Z’s mother is M’s maternal aunt, making Z a first cousin on the mother’s side. Z’s father is M’s paternal uncle, making Z a first cousin on the father’s side as well. Sharing both sets of grandparents, Z is a double first cousin of M – the most specific term.

question: L’s father has exactly one sister, and L’s mother has exactly one brother. M is the child of that sister and also the child of that brother. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring remarriage and adoption), what is M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) → first cousin on the father's side, and also the child of L’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) → first cousin on the mother's side. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes M a double first cousin of L, the most precise term.

question: John and Anna are married. John’s sister Lisa marries Tom, who is Anna’s brother. Lisa and Tom have a child Ethan; John and Anna have a child Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Lisa is John’s sister and Tom is Anna’s brother. Ethan is child of Lisa‑Tom, Fiona child of John‑Anna. Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents (John’s parents and Anna’s parents), so they are double first cousins – the most specific standard term.

question: Grandfather G has two children: a son S and a daughter D. It is unknown whether S and D are full siblings (sharing both parents) or half‑siblings (sharing only G). S has a child A; D has a child B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: If S and D are full siblings, A and B are first cousins. If they are half‑siblings, A and B are half‑first cousins. Because the sibling relationship between S and D is unspecified, the exact kinship cannot be uniquely determined.
choices: C) C) First cousins once removed

question: Let Y be a person. Y’s mother has exactly one brother, and Y’s father has exactly one sister. The brother of Y’s mother has a child X, and the sister of Y’s father also has a child X (the same X). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X is simultaneously the child of Y’s maternal uncle and the child of Y’s paternal aunt. Thus X shares both sets of grandparents with Y, making X a double first cousin – a first cousin on both the mother’s and father’s sides.

question: Using only standard English kinship terms (blood relations and immediate in‑law terms: spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), let L be married to M. M’s father has a sister who is married to N. N and his wife have a daughter Q. What is Q to L?
explanation: M’s father’s sister is M’s paternal aunt by blood. Her daughter Q is M’s first cousin (blood). L is M’s spouse, so Q is related to L only through that marriage chain. No standard kin term covers a cousin of one’s spouse, so the relation is not directly named.
choices: A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John's mother has a brother Mark. Mark's daughter Lisa marries Peter, who is the son of John’s father’s brother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Lisa to Peter?
explanation: Lisa is John’s maternal first cousin; Peter is John’s paternal first cousin. Their parents (Mark and John’s paternal uncle) are unrelated, so Lisa and Peter share no common ancestor. Hence there is no blood kinship term between them.
choices: C) No blood relation (no standard kin term)

question: A man's father's sister (his paternal aunt) marries his mother's brother (his maternal uncle). They have a child. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between the man and that child?
explanation: The child is the offspring of the man's paternal aunt, making them first cousins, and also the offspring of his maternal uncle, making them first cousins again. Being first cousins through both parental lines yields the term "double first cousin".
choices: D) D) No blood relation (affinal only)

question: Anna is an only child. Her father's sister (her paternal aunt) has a son Ben. Ben's daughter Clara marries Anna's brother David. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Clara's blood relationship to Anna?
explanation: Anna's paternal aunt's son Ben is Anna's first cousin. Ben's daughter Clara is therefore Anna's first cousin once removed (the child of a first cousin). Marriage to David does not affect the blood link, so Clara remains Anna's first cousin once removed.

question: Emily and Frank are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). Emily has a child Grace; Frank has a child Henry. No other intermarriages exist. Using standard English kinship terminology, what is the precise relation between Grace and Henry?
explanation: Grace and Henry are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent. The correct term for such descendants is “half‑first cousins,” distinct from full first cousins (two shared grandparents) and from second cousins.

question: John and Mary are married. John’s sister Linda is married to Mary’s brother Tom. John and Mary have a son Peter; Linda and Tom have a son Sam. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the most precise relation between Peter and Sam?
explanation: Peter’s father John is sibling of Sam’s mother Linda, and Peter’s mother Mary is sibling of Sam’s father Tom. Thus Peter and Sam share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures this doubled ancestry.

question: M is mother of twin sisters N and O. N marries P, the only child of Q. O marries R, the child of S, where Q and S are siblings. N and P have a daughter X; O and R have a son Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no double‑counting), what is the most precise blood relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y’s mothers N and O are sisters, so the children are first cousins. Their fathers P and R are first cousins, which makes X and Y also second cousins, but the closest degree of relationship is first cousin, the term used in standard kinship.

question: N's father has exactly one sibling, a brother X, and N's mother has exactly one sibling, a sister Y. M is the child of X and also the child of Y (X and Y are married). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship of M to N?
explanation: M is the child of N's paternal uncle (X) and also the child of N's maternal aunt (Y). Thus M shares both of N's grandparent pairs, making M and N double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Ben, each marry one of two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan, and Ben and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Adam and Ben share the same parents, and Clara and Diana share the same parents. Therefore Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents. The exact term for cousins who share both paternal and maternal grandparents is “double first cousins.”

question: Eight people A–H sit around a round table; A occupies the marked top seat and clockwise is considered right. The following conditions hold: (1) B sits immediately clockwise of A; (2) D sits opposite A; (3) E sits immediately clockwise of D; (4) G sits two seats clockwise of B (i.e., exactly one person is between B and G clockwise); (5) H sits immediately counter‑clockwise of G; (6) C lies strictly on the clockwise arc from E to H (endpoints excluded). Under these constraints, who sits immediately clockwise of D?
explanation: B immediately clockwise of A fixes B’s seat. D opposite A fixes D. Condition (3) explicitly places E immediately clockwise of D, so D’s right‑hand neighbor must be E. The remaining constraints only locate G, H and C without affecting D’s neighbor. Hence only choice A) E is forced.

question: L and N are married and have a child M. After divorcing, L has another child P with Q, and N has another child R with S. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise blood relationship between P and R?
explanation: P shares only mother L with M; R shares only father N with M. P and R have no common ancestor, so they are not blood‑related at all. The correct term is ‘no blood relation.’

question: A has one brother on his father's side and one sister on his mother's side, each of whom is the sole sibling of the respective parent. X is the child of that brother and also the child of that sister (no other intermarriages). What is the most precise standard English kinship term for X relative to A?
explanation: X is the child of A's paternal uncle and also the child of A's maternal aunt. Thus X is both a paternal first cousin and a maternal first cousin, i.e., a double first cousin. No other term is more exact.

question: Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), A is married to B. B’s sister C is married to D. D’s mother E is the sister of A’s father F. What is E’s relation to A?
explanation: E and F are siblings, making E the sister of A’s father. Therefore E is A’s paternal aunt. No other standard term applies under the given constraints.
choices: C) C) No direct kinship term

question: L is the child of the only brother of M’s mother. M’s father has no sisters. Who is L to M?
explanation: L is the child of M’s mother’s brother, i.e., a maternal uncle. The child of an uncle (or aunt) is a first cousin. The extra fact about M’s father having no sisters does not change this relationship.

question: M is married to N. M’s brother O is married to P and they have a daughter Q. N’s sister R is married to S and they have a son T. Q and T marry and have a child U. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of U to M?
explanation: Q is M’s niece (child of M’s brother). The child of a niece is a grand‑niece/nephew of the aunt/uncle. The other parent T is a nephew‑in‑law, which does not create a blood link, so the only definitive term is grand‑niece/nephew.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both maternal and paternal grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters, so they are double first cousins – the most specific standard term.

question: John and Mary are siblings. Mary’s brother Michael is also John’s brother (they share the same parents). Michael has a daughter Lisa, and John marries Lisa. John and Lisa have a child Anna. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise term for Anna’s relation to Michael?
explanation: Michael is Lisa’s father, so he is Anna’s maternal grandfather. He is also John’s brother, making him Anna’s paternal uncle. The closest generational link is the grand‑parent level, so the precise kin term is grandfather (with the additional uncle relationship noted).

question: R is married to S. S’s brother is T. T’s wife is U. U’s brother is V. What is V to R using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: R→S (spouse) →T (sibling‑in‑law) →U (that sibling’s spouse) →V (that spouse’s sibling). V is only the sibling of an in‑law; there is no blood or marital link to R, so standard kinship provides no direct term. Hence the correct answer is C.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a standard English kinship system (no adoption, monogamy, ignoring remarriage), let R be a person. Let G be R's paternal grandmother. Let S be G's sister. Let B be S's brother. Let K be B's child. What is the precise relation of K to R?
explanation: G is R's paternal grandmother. G's sister is R's great‑aunt. Her brother is R's great‑uncle, i.e., sibling of a grandparent. The child of a great‑uncle is a first cousin of R's parent, making that child R's first cousin once removed.
choices: D) D) First cousin once removed

question: In a family with no adoptions, monogamy, and using standard English kinship terms, let M be a person. M’s mother’s brother is U. U’s daughter is V. V’s son is W. What is the precise blood relation of W to M?
explanation: U is M’s maternal uncle. V, his daughter, is M’s first cousin. W, V’s son, is one generation below that cousin, making him M’s first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: A and B are half‑brothers (they share only their father). A has a daughter C. B has a son D. C and D marry and have a child E. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for E’s relation to A’s mother?
explanation: A’s mother is the mother of A, so she is the grandmother of A’s daughter C. Consequently she is the great‑grandmother of C’s child E, regardless of B’s side. No closer term applies.
choices: D) D) No direct blood relation

question: E is simultaneously the child of the only brother of F’s mother and the child of the only sister of F’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of E to F?
explanation: The brother of F’s mother is F’s maternal uncle; his child is F’s first cousin. The sister of F’s father is F’s paternal aunt; her child is also F’s first cousin. Since the same person E fulfills both roles, E is a double first cousin of F – a first cousin on both parental sides.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary’s son Peter marries John’s daughter Susan. Peter and Susan have a child Lily. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is Lily’s relation to John?
explanation: Through Susan, Lily is John’s granddaughter. Through Peter, who is John’s nephew, Lily is also John’s grandniece. Because both blood relations hold and no single term captures both simultaneously, the precise relation is not uniquely determinable.

question: A's mother has a brother U, whose daughter is C. A's father has a sister V, whose son is D. C and D marry and have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the relation of A to E?
explanation: C and D are each A's first cousins (maternal and paternal sides). Their child E is the child of A's first cousins, which makes E A's first cousin once removed. The other options describe more distant or incorrect ties.
choices: D) No standard direct kin term

question: Two brothers, Peter and Paul, each have exactly one child: Peter's child is Lily and Paul's child is Mark. Lily has a son Sam. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the precise relation of Mark to Sam?
explanation: Lily and Mark are first cousins. Sam is Lily's son, one generation younger. Hence Mark is Sam's first cousin once removed, the only correct standard term.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a daughter X; N and P have a son Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two couples who are each other's siblings, so they share both paternal and maternal grandparents. This makes them double first cousins.

question: A and B are siblings. X is the child of the only child of A’s brother, and Y is the child of the only child of B’s sister. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: A’s brother is B, so the only child of A’s brother is B’s child. X is that child’s child, i.e., B’s child. Similarly, B’s sister is A, so Y is the child of A’s child. Thus X and Y are children of siblings, making them first cousins. No other relation fits.

question: In a family tree: M has a sister N. N is married to O. O’s mother is P. P’s brother is Q. Q’s daughter is R, who is married to S. S is the son of T, and T is the brother of M’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is S to M?
explanation: M’s father’s brother T is M’s paternal uncle. T’s son S is therefore M’s first cousin. No other blood or affinal link connects them, making “first cousin” the precise term.

question: N has a father and a mother. P is the child of the only brother of N’s father and also the child of the only sister of N’s mother. No other intermarriages exist. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for P relative to N?
explanation: P is the child of N’s paternal uncle and also of N’s maternal aunt. Thus P shares both sets of grandparents with N, making them double first cousins – the most specific label.

question: Emma and Liam are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). Emma marries Tom, Liam marries Sara, who are unrelated. Emma’s child is Alex and Liam’s child is Bella. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Alex and Bella?
explanation: Emma and Liam share only one parent, so their children share only one grandparent, making them half‑first cousins, not full first cousins.

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoption: A and B are siblings. C is the child of A. D is the child of B. C marries E, and D marries F, where E and F are themselves siblings. Using only standard English blood‑kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: C and D are the children of siblings A and B, so they share both grandparents. That makes them full first cousins. The sibling relationship of their spouses does not affect blood kinship, and no half‑ or double‑cousin condition applies.

question: Brothers A and B each marry sisters C and D respectively; A and C have a child X, B and D have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: A and B share both parents, as do C and D. Therefore X and Y share both paternal and maternal grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, the exact term for cousins who share both sets of grandparents.

question: In a monogamous family tree with no adoptions, let R be a person whose paternal grandfather has a sister S. S’s son is T. If T is the father of U, what is the precise kinship term for U in relation to R?
explanation: R’s father’s father’s sister S is R’s great‑aunt. S’s son T is R’s first cousin once removed (child of great‑aunt). T’s child U is therefore R’s second cousin. The standard term is “second cousin”.

question: John's mother Mary has a brother Tom. John's father Paul has a sister Linda. Tom and Linda are married and have a daughter Sarah. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is Sarah's precise relation to John?
explanation: Tom is John's maternal uncle; Linda is John's paternal aunt. Their daughter Sarah is the child of both John's maternal uncle and paternal aunt, making her a double first cousin of John – first cousins through both parents.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: Brother X and Brother Y are siblings. Sister A and Sister B are sisters. X marries A and they have child C; Y marries B and they have child D. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: C’s father (X) and D’s father (Y) are brothers, sharing the same paternal grandparents. C’s mother (A) and D’s mother (B) are sisters, sharing the same maternal grandparents. Thus C and D share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: L’s mother has one sister, and L’s father has one brother. The sister and the brother are married and have a child M. What is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to L using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: M is the child of L’s maternal aunt (mother’s sister) and L’s paternal uncle (father’s brother). Because the aunt and uncle are married, M shares both of L’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the most specific standard term.

question: Anna and Ben are half‑siblings; they share only their mother. Anna has a daughter Clara, and Ben has a son David. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between Clara and David?
explanation: Anna and Ben share one parent, so they have only one common grandparent. Their children, Clara and David, share that single grandparent, making them half‑first cousins. Full first cousins require two shared grandparents; thus the precise term is half‑first cousins.

question: M has a sister N. N is married to O. O’s mother is P. P’s brother is Q. Q’s daughter is R. R is married to S, who is the son of T. T is the brother of M’s father. What is S’s relation to M?
explanation: T is the brother of M’s father, so T’s son S is M’s first cousin. No other blood link changes this; marriage of S to R does not affect their blood relationship.

question: A and B are siblings. C is the child of A. D is the child of B. E is the sibling of B’s spouse. If C marries the child of E, what is the precise kinship term for the relation between C and D?
explanation: A and B share both parents, so their children C and D share the same two grandparents, making them first cousins. The marriage to E’s child does not affect their blood relationship.

question: Let X be a person. X’s mother has a brother Y. Y’s daughter is Z, who is married to W. W’s mother is the sister of X’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between X and W’s mother?
explanation: Y is X’s maternal uncle, so Z is X’s first cousin. W’s mother is the sister of X’s father, i.e., X’s paternal aunt. Hence X is the niece/nephew of W’s mother.

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother, U, and R’s father has exactly one brother, V. A is the child of U and B is the child of V. Assuming no adoptions and monogamous families, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between A and B?
explanation: U and V are siblings of different parents; they share no common ancestors. Therefore their children, A and B, share no blood connection. The only correct description is that they are unrelated by blood.

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage possible: X is the child of the only brother of Y’s mother, and Z is the child of the only sister of Y’s father. If either X or Z is called W, what is W’s relation to Y?
explanation: Both the child of Y’s maternal uncle and the child of Y’s paternal aunt are children of a parent’s sibling, which makes each a first cousin of Y. Hence W is always a first cousin.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: John is married to Mary. Mary’s mother, Linda, has a son Peter from a previous marriage (so Peter is Mary’s half‑brother). Peter is married to Susan. Susan’s father, Robert, has a daughter Emma from another marriage (Emma is Susan’s half‑sister). John’s brother Michael is married to Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is Emma to John?
explanation: Emma is married to Michael, who is John’s brother. The spouse of one’s sibling is the sibling’s wife, i.e., one’s sister‑in‑law. No other blood or affinal link changes this primary relation.

question: M is the only child of his mother. His mother’s sister (M’s maternal aunt) is married to N. N’s mother is the paternal aunt of M’s father. What is the precise blood relation between N’s daughter and M, using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: N’s mother being the paternal aunt of M’s father makes N a first cousin of M’s father. Therefore N’s daughter and M’s father are first cousins once removed, and M and N’s daughter, being of the same generation, share the same great‑grandparents, making them second cousins. No other blood link alters this.

question:
In a family:
1) Alice and Ben are full siblings.
2) Their father is Frank.
3) Frank also has two other children: George and Eve.
4) Ben is married to Clara.
5) Clara's brother David is married to Eve.
6) David's sister Julia is Ian's mother.
7) Ian is married to Hannah, who is George's daughter.
Who is Hannah to Ben?
explanation: George is Ben's brother, so Hannah (George's daughter) is Ben's niece by blood. The marriage links (Ian, Clara, David, Julia) do not change that primary blood relation. Hence Hannah is Ben's niece.

question: M is the child of the only brother of N’s mother and also the child of the only sister of N’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is the offspring of N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and of N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the shared ancestry on both sides.

question: In a family, Alice is the child of the sister of Bob's father, and Bob is the child of the brother of Alice's mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relationship between Alice and Bob?
explanation: Alice is the child of Bob's paternal aunt, making her his first cousin. Bob is the child of Alice's maternal uncle, also making him her first cousin. Since they are first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides, they share both sets of grandparents, which is precisely a "double first cousin."

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P. O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents (maternal and paternal) because their parents are two pairs of siblings. The exact term for such relatives is double first cousins.

question: In a family, Alex’s mother has a brother (Alex’s maternal uncle) who is married to a woman. That woman has a brother whose daughter is Sam. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for Sam with respect to Alex?
explanation: The uncle’s wife may be Alex’s aunt by marriage, but she could also be a blood relative if she is the sister of Alex’s mother (unknown). Consequently Sam could be Alex’s first cousin (if the wife is a blood aunt) or a cousin‑in‑law (if only an affinal aunt). The given data do not fix the relation uniquely.

question: John and Mary are married. Mary has a son Alex from a previous marriage to Peter. John has a daughter Beth from a previous marriage to Linda. Alex and Beth marry and have a child Clara. What is Clara’s precise relation to John’s ex‑wife Linda?
explanation: Linda is Beth’s biological mother; Beth is Clara’s biological mother. Therefore Linda is Clara’s maternal grandmother. No other listed term fits.

question: X’s mother has exactly one brother and X’s father has exactly one brother. The child of X’s maternal uncle is called A; the child of X’s paternal uncle is called B. If either A or B is selected and named C, what is C’s relation to X using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Both A and B are children of a parent’s sibling, i.e., the children of X’s maternal and paternal uncles. In either case the person is X’s first cousin, regardless of which side of the family is considered.

question: M’s mother has a brother (maternal uncle) who is married to N. N’s sister is married to O, and O’s son is P. M’s father has a sister (paternal aunt) who is married to Q. Q’s brother is R, and R’s daughter is S. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, in‑law limited to spouse), what is the precise relation between P and S?
explanation: P descends from the sister of the maternal uncle’s wife; S descends from the brother of the paternal aunt’s husband. Both lines involve only spouses of M’s aunt/uncle, so P and S share no common ancestor. Hence they have no blood kinship.

question: M is the child of the sister of P’s father and also the child of the brother of P’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of M to P?
explanation: M is the offspring of P’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and also of P’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with P, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: M is A's mother; M has a brother U. U's daughter C is A's maternal first cousin. F is A's father; F has a sister S. S's son D is A's paternal first cousin. C and D marry and have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of E to A?
explanation: C is A's maternal first cousin; D is A's paternal first cousin. Their child E is the child of A's first cousin on both sides, making E simultaneously a first cousin once removed through the maternal line and through the paternal line. The most precise single term is “double first cousin once removed.”
choices: A) A) Double first cousin once removed
B) B) Half-first cousin once removed
D) D) No standard term (relationship indeterminate)

question: Each of your parents has exactly one brother, and each brother has exactly one child. You are told to choose either the child of your mother's brother or the child of your father's brother (you do not know which you have chosen). What is the chosen person's relation to you?
explanation: Both the maternal uncle and the paternal uncle are each a brother of one of your parents. Their children are each the child of a parent’s sibling, which by definition is a first cousin. Whether you pick the maternal uncle’s child or the paternal uncle’s child, the relation is the same.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M’s father’s sister (M’s paternal aunt) is married to N’s mother’s brother (N’s maternal uncle). Assuming M and N are not married to each other, what is the precise kinship term between M and N using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: M’s paternal aunt and N’s maternal uncle are spouses, providing only an affinal link. No blood relationship exists between M and N, and standard kinship does not assign a direct term for such a chain. Hence they have no standard direct relation; they are related only through an affinal chain.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: N’s father has exactly one sibling, a brother P; N’s mother has exactly one sibling, a sister Q. M is the child of P and also the child of Q (P and Q are married). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s precise relationship to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal uncle (P) and also the child of N’s maternal aunt (Q). Therefore M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making M a double first cousin of N—the most specific term.

question: P and R are siblings. P has one child M; R has one child Q. M and Q marry and have a child S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise direct kinship term for S’s relation to P?
explanation: M is P’s child, so S (M’s child) is P’s grandchild. Although Q is P’s niece/nephew, making S also a grand‑niece/nephew, the direct line through M gives the precise term “grandchild.”

question: Z’s mother has exactly one brother, and Z’s father has exactly one brother. Each of those brothers has exactly one child, named Y₁ (child of the maternal uncle) and Y₂ (child of the paternal uncle). If we are told that Y is either Y₁ or Y₂ (but we do not know which), what is Y’s precise kinship to Z?
explanation: Both Y₁ and Y₂ are children of Z’s parent’s brothers, i.e., Z’s maternal uncle and paternal uncle. In either case Y is the child of a sibling of one of Z’s parents, which makes Y a first cousin of Z. The relation is uniquely first cousin.

question: R’s mother has a brother A, and R’s father has a sister B. A’s daughter is C; B’s son is D. C and D marry and have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of E to R?
explanation: A is R’s maternal uncle, so C is R’s first cousin. B is R’s paternal aunt, so D is also R’s first cousin. Their child E is the child of R’s first cousin, which makes E R’s first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
