question: A man A and a woman B are siblings. Another man C and a woman D are also siblings. A marries D and C marries B. A and D have a child E; C and B have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no in‑law extensions), what is the most precise relation between E and F?
explanation: E and F each have the same two sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than ordinary first cousins.

question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father, and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between M and N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and also of N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: R’s father has a brother A and R’s mother has a brother B. A and B are married and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is C’s precise relation to R?
explanation: A is R’s paternal uncle, so C shares R’s paternal grandparents. B is R’s maternal uncle, so C also shares R’s maternal grandparents. C therefore shares both grandparent pairs with R, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: M is the child of the only brother of N’s father and also the child of the only sister of N’s mother (the two siblings are unrelated to each other). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal uncle and also the child of N’s maternal aunt, who are distinct individuals. Thus M shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: John and Mark are brothers. John marries Anna, Mark marries Beth. Anna and Beth are first cousins (their mothers are sisters). John and Anna have a child Sam; Mark and Beth have a child Lily. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Sam and Lily?
explanation: Sam and Lily share two distinct grandparent pairs: one set from their fathers (who are brothers) and another set from their mothers (who are first cousins). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more precise term than ordinary first cousins.

question: M’s mother has a brother U, whose daughter is L. M’s father has a sister V, whose son is T. L and T marry and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is C’s precise relation to M?
explanation: L is M’s maternal first cousin; T is M’s paternal first cousin. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Since C is the child of both a maternal and a paternal first cousin, the relation remains first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: John has a sister Mary. John’s wife Anna has a brother Tom. Mary marries Tom. John and Anna have a daughter Lily; Mary and Tom have a son Sam. Lily and Sam marry and have a child Emma. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between Emma and John?
explanation: Emma is John’s biological granddaughter through Lily and simultaneously his great‑niece through Sam (John’s nephew via his sister). No single standard term covers both a direct descendant and a collateral descendant, so the relation cannot be expressed uniquely with one term.

question: M and N are half‑siblings (they share only one parent). M has a child X and N has a child Y. No other intermarriages exist. What is the precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share a single parent, making them half‑siblings. Their children X and Y therefore share only one grandparent, the common parent’s parent. This specific kinship is called half‑first cousins, distinct from full first cousins who share both grandparents.

question: Brothers Adam and Brian each marry sisters Clara and Diana respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan, and Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the relationship between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Adam and Brian share the same parents, and Clara and Diana share the same parents. Ethan and Fiona therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through two independent lines—i.e., double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: In a monogamous, non‑adoptive family, Z is the child of the only brother of Y’s mother. What is Z’s precise kinship term for Y using standard English blood‑relation terminology?
explanation: The only brother of Y’s mother is Y’s maternal uncle. The child of that uncle is Y’s first cousin, sharing both grandparents on the maternal side. No half‑relation or generational offset exists, so the exact term is “first cousin.”

question: Man1 and Woman1 are siblings. Man2 and Woman2 are also siblings. Man1 marries Woman2 and Man2 marries Woman1. Each couple has exactly one child: Child A (of Man1 & Woman2) and Child B (of Man2 & Woman1). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise blood relationship between Child A and Child B?
explanation: Child A and Child B share both sets of grandparents: Man1’s parents are also Woman1’s parents, and Man2’s parents are also Woman2’s parents. Hence they are first cousins on both the paternal and maternal sides, i.e., double first cousins.

question: Q’s mother has exactly one brother, and Q’s father has exactly one sister. The brother of Q’s mother and the sister of Q’s father have the same child, P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation of P to Q?
explanation: P is the child of Q’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and also the child of Q’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Thus P shares both sets of grandparents with Q, making them double first cousins – the only term that captures the two distinct grandparent pairs.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: John’s mother has a brother Mark. Mark’s daughter Lisa marries Tom, who is the son of John’s father’s brother. Lisa and Tom have a child Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is Emma’s relation to John?
explanation: Mark is John’s maternal uncle, so Lisa is John’s first cousin. Tom is the son of John’s paternal uncle, making Tom also John’s first cousin. Emma is the child of John’s first cousin (Lisa) – the child of a cousin is a first cousin once removed. The paternal/maternal side does not change this classification.

question: John is the son of Mary and Peter. Mary’s brother Alan is married to Susan. Susan’s sister Linda is married to Peter’s brother Mark. Emma is the daughter of Alan and Susan, and Kevin is the son of Mark and Linda. What is Emma’s relation to Kevin, using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Emma’s mother Susan and Kevin’s mother Linda are sisters, so they share the same maternal grandparents. Their fathers are unrelated. Therefore Emma and Kevin are children of two sisters, making them full first cousins.

question: M is the only child of his mother. M’s mother’s sister (M’s maternal aunt) is married to a man who is the brother of M’s father (M’s paternal uncle). The couple has a daughter N. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: M’s maternal aunt shares M’s maternal grandparents; the paternal uncle shares M’s paternal grandparents. Their child N therefore shares both grandparent pairs with M, making them double first cousins – the exact term for this doubled ancestry.
choices: C) C) First cousins once removed
D) D) No blood relation (in‑law only)

question: In a family with monogamous marriages and no adoption, let X be the child of the only brother of Y’s mother, and also the child of the only sister of Z’s father. Assuming Y and Z are distinct individuals, which of the following best describes X’s relation to Y?
explanation: X’s mother could be Y’s aunt (brother’s sister) or could be Y’s mother’s sister‑in‑law if the brother is married; likewise the father’s sister could be Z’s aunt or aunt‑by‑marriage. Because the gender and marital status of the siblings are not fixed, X’s precise kinship to Y cannot be uniquely determined.

question: M is the only child of his father. N is the sister of M's mother. P is the child of N. M's paternal aunt (his father's sister) has a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, and only blood links), what is the precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: N is M's maternal aunt, so P is M's first cousin on his mother's side. The paternal aunt is unrelated to N; her child Q is M's first cousin on his father's side. Since the two aunts share no common ancestors, P and Q share none either, giving them no blood relationship.

question: In a family, two brothers, M and N, each marry two sisters, P and Q respectively (M with P, N with Q). M and P have a son S; N and Q have a daughter T. S and T later marry each other. What is the most precise kinship term for S's child R to T's child U, using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry?
explanation: S and T are double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). Their children R and U therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins – the most specific term.

question: Brothers A and B each marry sisters C and D respectively; A and C have a child X, while B and D have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both paternal and maternal grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. This double sharing makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: L's mother has exactly one brother, and L's father has exactly one sister. The child of that brother and the child of that sister are the same person, M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L's maternal uncle and also the child of L's paternal aunt. Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with L, making them double first cousins—the most specific term available.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John has two children: Lily and Tom. Mary has a son Sam. Lily (John’s daughter) marries Sam (Mary’s son), who are first cousins, and they have a daughter Emma. Emma has a son Noah. What is the precise kinship term for Tom in relation to Noah?
explanation: Lily and Sam are first cousins whose child Emma is John’s grandchild. Noah, Emma’s son, is John’s great‑grandchild. Lily’s brother Tom is also John’s child, therefore Tom is one generation above Noah’s parent, making Tom Noah’s great‑uncle (or grand‑uncle). No other listed term fits.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: In a family with no adoptions and monogamy, P’s mother has exactly one brother Q, and P’s father has exactly one sister S. Q and S are married to each other and have a single child R. Using standard English blood‑relation terminology (ignoring in‑law extensions), what is the precise kinship term for R with respect to P?
explanation: R is child of P's maternal uncle and paternal aunt, therefore shares both of P's grandparent pairs. That makes them first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins, the most precise term.

question: Person X is the child of a man whose mother is the sister of X’s paternal grandfather. Person Y is the child of a woman whose father is the brother of Y’s maternal grandmother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: Both X and Y are children of a parent's sibling: X’s father is the son of his aunt, making X the child of a maternal uncle’s son, and Y’s mother is the daughter of her uncle. In either case the parent of X and the parent of Y are siblings, so X and Y are first cousins. No half‑blood or further removal applies.

question: Two brothers, A and B, marry two sisters, C and D, respectively (A with C, B with D). A and C have a child X; B and D have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: A and B share parents, and C and D share parents. Thus they are first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides, i.e., double first cousins – the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: M is the son of the only brother of N’s mother, and N is the daughter of the only sister of M’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between M and N?
explanation: M is child of N’s maternal uncle, making them first cousins. N is also child of M’s paternal aunt, which again gives a first‑cousin link. Both statements point to the same unique relation: first cousins.

question: L’s mother has a sister (M1) and L’s father has a brother (F1). M1 and F1 are married and have a child X. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between X and L?
explanation: M1 is L’s maternal aunt and F1 is L’s paternal uncle. Their child X shares both sets of grandparents with L, because the two families are linked by two sibling marriages. The exact term for such relatives is “double first cousin.”

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary is married to Tom. Tom’s sister Anna is married to John’s son Peter. Using standard English kinship terms (only spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Anna’s relation to Mary?
explanation: Anna is Tom’s sister; Tom is Mary’s husband. Thus Anna is the sister of Mary’s spouse‑in‑law. No standard direct kinship term covers this connection, so the correct choice is that there is no such term.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John’s father has exactly one sister, Mary, and John’s mother has exactly one brother, Peter. Mary marries Peter, and they have a child, Lily. What is Lily’s precise relationship to John under standard English kinship terms, assuming no other intermarriages?
explanation: Mary is John’s paternal aunt; Peter is his maternal uncle. Lily is their child, so she shares John’s paternal grandparents through Mary and his maternal grandparents through Peter. Hence she shares both grandparent pairs with John, making Lily a double first cousin.

question: In a monogamous family without adoption, let N be a person. N’s father has exactly one sibling, a sister F, and N’s mother has exactly one sibling, a brother M. The child of F (with her spouse) and the child of M (with his spouse) happen to be the same individual X. What is the precise kinship term for X’s relation to N, using standard English kinship vocabulary?
explanation: X is the child of N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and also the child of N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus X is N’s first cousin on both parental sides, i.e., a double first cousin. No other term captures the double shared grandparent pair.

question: John is the only child of his mother. Mary's mother is the sister of John's father, and Mary's father is the brother of John's mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation between John and Mary?
explanation: John's paternal aunt is Mary's mother, making them first cousins on John's father's side. Simultaneously, John's maternal uncle is Mary's father, making them first cousins on John's mother's side. Sharing both sets of grandparents, they are double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: John is married to Mary. Mary’s brother Tom is married to Susan. Susan and Linda share the same mother, and Linda is John’s sister (they have a different father). Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Tom’s relation to Linda?
explanation: Susan is Linda’s half‑sister, so Susan is Linda’s sibling. Tom is Susan’s husband, i.e., the spouse of Linda’s sibling. By definition that makes Tom Linda’s brother‑in‑law. No blood link exists, and the term fits the allowed in‑law scope.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation

question: Around a round table with ten seats numbered clockwise from the marked top seat occupied by A (right = clockwise), the following hold: G sits immediately to A’s right; B sits immediately to G’s right; E sits directly opposite A; D sits immediately to E’s left; H lies strictly on the clockwise arc from B to E (endpoints excluded); C is not adjacent to H; and I sits immediately to A’s left. Which person must sit immediately clockwise of H?
explanation: A is at seat 0, so G at 1, B at 2, E opposite at 5, D left of E at 4, I left of A at 9. The arc B→E exclusive contains seats 3 and 4; seat 4 is D, so H must be at 3. The clockwise neighbor of seat 3 is seat 4, occupied by D. Hence D is forced.

question: In Family 1, siblings A (male) and B (female) are born to the same parents. In Family 2, siblings C (male) and D (female) are born to the same parents. A marries C and they have a child X. B marries D and they have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: A and B share one pair, C and D share another. Hence they are double first cousins, a more specific term than ordinary first cousins.

question: X and Y are the only children of two siblings who are themselves first cousins. X marries Y, and they each have exactly one child (A and B, respectively). Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, and ignoring doubled ancestry), what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: X and Y are first cousins, so they share a pair of grandparents. Their children A and B therefore share the same great‑grandparents and no closer common ancestors, making them second cousins. No other term is more precise.
choices: D) D) No blood relation (affinal only)

question: A and B are brothers; they each marry sisters C and D respectively. A and C have a son X; B and D have a son Y. X and Y each have an unrelated spouse and a child, P and Q respectively. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise term for the relationship between P and Q?
explanation: X and Y are double first cousins because they share both sets of grandparents. Their children P and Q therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the most precise label.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a sister, Clara and Dana respectively (Clara and Dana are sisters). Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Dana have a son Felix. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Felix?
explanation: Ethan and Felix share both sets of grandparents: Adam and Brian share the same parents, and Clara and Dana share the same parents. Hence they are first cousins with double lineage, i.e., double first cousins.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, R’s mother has exactly one sister, who has exactly one child X. R’s spouse has exactly one sibling, who is married to X. Who is X’s child Y to R?
explanation: The sister of R’s mother is R’s maternal aunt; her child X is therefore R’s first cousin. Y, being X’s child, is one generation below a first cousin, which is precisely a first cousin once removed. The marriage of X to R’s spouse’s sibling adds no blood link and does not affect the relationship.

question: M has two siblings: brother N and sister O. N’s only child is daughter P; O’s only child is son Q. P and Q marry each other and have a child R. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of M to R?
explanation: P and Q are first cousins (children of siblings N and O). Their child R is the grandchild of both N and O. Since M is the sibling of R’s grandparents, M is R’s great‑uncle (or great‑aunt). No closer term applies.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: John and Mary are siblings. Mary marries Peter. Peter’s sister, Linda, is the daughter of Peter’s mother, Susan. Linda marries Alex, who is John’s son. Alex and Linda have a daughter, Emma. What is Emma’s relation to Susan?
explanation: Susan is the mother of Peter and Linda. Emma is the child of Linda, making her Susan’s granddaughter. No other kinship term applies, so the precise relation is granddaughter.

question: M is the mother of N. N’s father’s sister is O. O’s son is P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is P’s relation to M?
explanation: N’s father is M’s husband. His sister O is M’s sister‑in‑law. O’s son P is the child of M’s sister‑in‑law, making P M’s nephew/niece. No blood link exists, but the affinal term is niece/nephew.

question: Person X is the child of the only sibling of Y's father, and also the child of the only sibling of Y's mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption), what is X to Y?
explanation: If the two siblings are different individuals, X is Y's first cousin (through either side). If they happen to be the same person (possible only if Y's parents are siblings), X would be Y's half‑sibling. Because both situations fit the description, the exact kin term cannot be fixed; it is not uniquely determinable.

question: M and N are brother and sister. M marries P and N marries Q, where P and Q are also brother and sister. M and N each have exactly one child, X and Y respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their parents are two pairs of siblings. This double shared ancestry makes them double first cousins, the exact term for such a relationship.

question: John and Michael are brothers. Their sister Sarah marries Peter, who is the brother of John’s wife Laura. John and Laura have a daughter Anna; Sarah and Peter have a son Ben. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Anna and Ben?
explanation: John and Sarah are siblings; Laura and Peter are siblings. Anna (child of John + Laura) and Ben (child of Sarah + Peter) share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: M is the only child of his mother. N is the sister of M’s father. P is N’s child. Q is the child of M’s mother’s brother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: N is M’s paternal aunt, so P is M’s first cousin on his father’s side. M’s mother’s brother is M’s maternal uncle, so Q is M’s first cousin on his mother’s side. N and the maternal uncle are unrelated, therefore P and Q share no common ancestor and have no consanguineous kinship term.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John marries his first cousin Lisa (they share both grandparents). Mary marries Lisa’s brother Mark. John and Lisa have a child P; Mary and Mark have a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relationship between P and Q?
explanation: P and Q are children of two couples who are both double first cousins: John–Lisa share both grandparents, and Mary–Mark share the same grandparents. Their children therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double first cousins, the exact term.

question: Anna is Mia’s mother. Anna’s brother is Carl. Carl’s son is Ben. Ben’s daughter is Dana. Dana marries Mia’s brother Ethan, and they have a child Fiona. What is Fiona’s relation to Carl?
explanation: Carl → Ben (son) → Dana (granddaughter) → Fiona (great‑granddaughter). The other lines (Mia’s side) do not affect Carl’s blood line. Hence Fiona is Carl’s great‑granddaughter.

question: A and B are siblings. A's child is C. B's child is D. D's child is E. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of C to E?
explanation: C and D are first cousins (children of siblings). E is D's child, so E is one generation below D. Therefore C is a first cousin once removed of E. No other standard term fits more precisely.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: Brother B1 and Sister S1 are siblings. Brother B2 and Sister S2 are another set of siblings. B1 marries S2 and B2 marries S1. B1 and S2 have child C1; B2 and S1 have child C2. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation between C1 and C2?
explanation: C1 and C2 share both pairs of grandparents because each child’s father is a brother of the other child’s mother and vice‑versa. The exact term is "double first cousins".

question: L has a sister and a brother. M is the child of the only son of L’s sister, and N is the child of the only daughter of L’s brother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation between M and N?
explanation: L’s sister’s son and L’s brother’s daughter are children of two different siblings of L, so they are first cousins. Their children M and N are therefore children of first cousins, which makes M and N second cousins. No other term fits.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: Arun’s mother has a brother (Arun’s maternal uncle) who is married to Leela. Leela is the sister of Priya’s mother. Priya is Arun’s wife. Using only standard English kinship terms (blood only, in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of Arun to Priya’s mother?
explanation: Leela, Priya’s mother’s sister, is Arun’s aunt by marriage. Arun’s maternal uncle is Leela’s husband, making him brother‑in‑law to Priya’s mother. No blood link exists between Arun and Priya’s mother, and the affinal chain exceeds the allowed in‑law scope, so there is no standard direct kin term.
choices: B) B) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: R’s father has a sister (paternal aunt) who has a child A, and R’s mother has a brother (maternal uncle) who has a child B. If we refer to either A or B as C, what is C’s relation to R using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: A is the child of R’s paternal aunt, B is the child of R’s maternal uncle. In both cases C is the child of one of R’s parents’ siblings, which by definition makes C a first cousin of R. The relation is identical regardless of which child is chosen.

question: John is the son of Mary. Mary’s sister Anne is married to Peter. Peter’s brother Paul is married to Susan, who is the mother of John’s wife Lisa. What is Paul’s relation to John, using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: Paul is the brother of John’s uncle‑by‑marriage (Peter). This creates an affinal chain beyond the defined in‑law scope, yielding no standard direct kin term between Paul and John. Hence the only correct description is that there is no standard direct relation.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: P and Q are each the child of a married couple. P's mother is the sister of Q's father, and P's father is the brother of Q's mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relationship between P and Q?
explanation: P and Q share both sets of grandparents: one through their mothers (who are sisters) and one through their fathers (who are brothers). Hence they are double first cousins, a more specific term than ordinary first cousins.

question: Emma's mother has a brother named Victor. Emma's father has a sister named Lydia, and Victor is married to Lydia. Who is Emma's daughter Zoe to Victor, using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses)?
explanation: Victor is Emma's maternal uncle (brother of Emma's mother). Zoe is Emma's child, i.e., the grandchild of Emma's mother. To Victor, Zoe is the child of his niece (Emma), making Zoe his great‑niece. The precise term is great‑aunt/uncle for the older generation, so Zoe is Victor's great‑niece.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: John has a sister Mary. John’s son is Peter. Mary’s son is Tom. Peter’s daughter is Sarah. What is the precise blood‑relation between Tom and Sarah using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Tom is Mary’s child, making him John’s nephew. Sarah is Peter’s child, making her John’s granddaughter. The child of a sibling (Tom) and the grandchild of that sibling’s brother (Sarah) are first cousins once removed. No other standard term fits more precisely.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: Emma’s mother has a brother Victor. Victor and his wife Nora have a daughter Lily. Lily’s only child is Sam. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is Sam’s precise relation to Emma?
explanation: Victor is Emma’s maternal uncle, making Lily Emma’s first cousin. Sam, as Lily’s child, is one generation below a first cousin, therefore Emma’s first cousin once removed. No other blood link changes this classification.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N is married to P and they have a son Q. O and Q marry and have a child R. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, no remarriage, in‑law limited to spouse, parents, siblings, children), what is the precise relation of R to N?
explanation: R is N’s grandchild through N’s son Q, and also N’s great‑niece/nephew through N’s sibling M’s daughter O. Because two distinct standard terms apply, a single precise kinship label cannot be assigned.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: R’s father has a sister (paternal aunt) who is married to S. S’s mother is R’s maternal grandmother. S and the paternal aunt have a son T. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, in‑law limited to spouse), what is the most precise relation of T to R?
explanation: S is a child of R’s maternal grandmother, so S is R’s maternal aunt by blood. S’s wife is R’s paternal aunt. Their son T is the child of both R’s maternal aunt and paternal aunt, making T R’s first cousin on both sides – the precise term is simply “first cousin.”
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has two children: a son P and a daughter R. R has a child Q. What is the precise blood relation of O to Q (ignoring the later marriage between O and Q)?
explanation: M and N are siblings, so M is aunt/uncle of R. Therefore O (M’s child) and R are first cousins. Q is R’s child, making O a first cousin once removed to Q. No closer term applies.

question: Person X’s mother has a brother A, and X’s father has a sister B. A and B are married and have a child C. What is the precise kinship term for C’s relation to X, using standard English kinship vocabulary?
explanation: The child of X's maternal uncle and paternal aunt shares one grandparent pair with X through the mother and a different grandparent pair through the father; each line yields a first‑cousin link, and because the two parental lines are unrelated the relation is simply a first cousin.

question: In a family with monogamous marriages and no adoption: John and Mary are full siblings. John has a daughter Lily. Mary has a half‑brother Peter (they share the same mother but have different fathers). Peter has a son Sam. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for Lily relative to Sam?
explanation: John and Peter share only their mother, making them half‑siblings. Lily and Sam are each children of those half‑siblings, so they are children of half‑siblings. The exact term for such a relationship is “half‑first cousins.”

question: M is the only child of his mother A. A has a brother S. S is married to T and they have a son R. R is married to Q. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the most precise term for Q’s relation to M?
explanation: M’s mother’s brother S is M’s maternal uncle. S’s son R is M’s first cousin. Q is R’s spouse. Standard kinship terms cover only spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses. The spouse of a first cousin falls outside this scope, so there is no direct term; Q is related to M only through an affinal chain.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, N marries P, and O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their parents are two pairs of siblings. This makes them double first cousins—their relationship is first cousin on both maternal and paternal sides, a precise term distinct from ordinary first cousins.

question: L’s father M has a brother O, whose daughter is A. L’s mother N has a brother P, whose son is B. If we select either A or B and call that person C, what is C’s precise relationship to L using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: A is the child of L’s paternal uncle O, and B is the child of L’s maternal uncle P. In either case C is the child of a sibling of one of L’s parents, which by definition makes C a first cousin of L. The relation is the same regardless of which child is chosen.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P. O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father M and Y’s father N are brothers, and X’s mother O and Y’s mother P are sisters. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, giving them the exact term “double first cousins.”

question: John, Mary, and Peter are three siblings. John marries Anna, who is Peter’s daughter. Mary marries Michael, who is Anna’s brother (also Peter’s son). What is Michael to John using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Peter is John’s sibling, so his children Anna and Michael are John’s niece and nephew. Michael also becomes John’s brother‑in‑law by marrying John’s sister Mary, but when a person has both a blood and an affinal link, the blood term is primary. Hence Michael is John’s nephew.

question: Brother A marries sister C and brother B marries sister D (no other marriages). A and C have a son X; B and D have a daughter Y. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: the parents of A/B and the parents of C/D. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than ordinary first cousins.

question: L’s father has exactly one sister, and L’s mother has exactly one brother. The child of that sister and the child of that brother are the same person, M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s paternal aunt and also of L’s maternal uncle. Thus M shares both of L’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: In a family with monogamy, no adoption and no intermarriage, let S be the child of the only brother of J’s mother and also the child of the only sister of J’s father. What is S to J?
explanation: The brother of J’s mother is J’s maternal uncle; his child is J’s first cousin. The sister of J’s father is J’s paternal aunt; her child is also J’s first cousin. Regardless of which side, S is always a first cousin of J.

question: L’s father has exactly one brother, and L’s mother has exactly one sister. A child M is born to that brother and that sister (who are not related to each other). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship of M to L?
explanation: M’s father is L’s paternal uncle, so M is L’s first cousin on the father’s side. M’s mother is L’s maternal aunt, so M is also L’s first cousin on the mother’s side. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: M is married to N. N's mother is O. O's brother is P. P's daughter is Q, who is married to R. R's father is S, whose sister is T. T's son is U. Using only standard English kinship terms (blood and immediate affinal relations: spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the relation of U to M?
explanation: M’s links stop at N’s mother O (mother‑in‑law) and O’s brother P (uncle‑in‑law). All further persons are beyond the immediate affinal scope and have no blood connection to M. Therefore no standard direct kin term applies; the relationship exists only as an extended affinal chain.
choices: A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John’s mother has exactly one brother, and Mary’s father has exactly one sister. John’s mother’s brother is not blood‑related to Mary’s father’s sister. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the relationship between John and Mary?
explanation: John’s mother’s brother is John’s maternal uncle; Mary’s father’s sister is Mary’s paternal aunt. Since those two relatives are unrelated, John and Mary are children of unrelated individuals, giving them no blood kinship at all.

question: Man M and woman N are married and have a son S. M’s sister A marries N’s brother B, and they have a daughter D. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the exact relation between S and D?
explanation: S’s father M is the brother of D’s mother A, and S’s mother N is the sister of D’s father B. Thus S and D share both sets of grandparents. The precise term for such cousins who share both grandparent pairs is “double first cousins”.

question: P is the child of the only brother of Q’s mother, and also the child of the only brother of Q’s father. Assuming no adoption, monogamy, and that no two persons share both parents, what is the precise kinship term for P relative to Q?
explanation: If the two brothers are the same individual (i.e., Q’s parents are siblings), P is Q’s half‑sibling. If they are distinct brothers, P is Q’s first cousin. Both possibilities satisfy the given conditions, so the precise relation cannot be uniquely determined.

question: M is the mother of N and O. N is married to P. O has a son R. R’s spouse is Q. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Q’s relation to N?
explanation: N and O are siblings, so O’s son R is N’s nephew. The spouse of a nephew is a niece‑in‑law. Hence Q is N’s niece‑in‑law.

question: N has a father and a mother. P is the child of the only brother of N's father and also the child of the only sister of N's mother. No marriage occurs between the two sibling lines. What is the most precise standard kinship term for P relative to N?
explanation: P is the child of N's paternal uncle and maternal aunt. Thus P shares both of N's grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the exact term for cousins who share both sets of grandparents.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions, let M be the child of the only sibling of L's mother, and let L be the child of the only sibling of M's father. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between M and L?
explanation: M is the child of L's maternal aunt/uncle, making M L's first cousin. Likewise, L is the child of M's paternal aunt/uncle, making L M's first cousin. Since the two cousin links involve both parental lines, they share both sets of grandparents, which is precisely a "double first cousin".

question: John and Mary are brother and sister. John has one child, Anna. Mary has one child, Ben. Ben’s brother, Carl, marries Anna’s sister, Dana. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise blood relation between Carl and Dana?
explanation: Carl and Dana are each children of siblings (Mary and John). Children of siblings are first cousins, regardless of their spouses. Hence Carl and Dana are first cousins.
choices: D) No direct blood relation (in‑law only)

question: Adam and Ben are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and Ben marries Diana. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Ben and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the most precise blood relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents: Adam’s parents and Clara’s parents. Hence they are first cousins through two independent lines, i.e., double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: M is the mother of N. N’s paternal aunt is O. O’s daughter is P. P’s spouse’s sister is Q, and Q’s brother is R. What is R’s relation to M using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: O is sister of N’s father, so P is N’s first cousin. R is sibling of P’s spouse, giving only an affinal chain (cousin’s spouse’s sibling). No blood link and no direct in‑law term exists, so R has no standard direct relation to M.
choices: A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: Brother A and sister B are children of couple G1. Their spouses C and D are siblings, children of couple G2. A + C have child X; B + D have child Y. X and Y each have a child with unrelated partners, producing P and Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: A and B share both parents; C and D share both parents. X and Y are therefore double first cousins (they share both grandparent pairs). Their children P and Q share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins. No other term captures the double lineage.

question: Adam and Ben are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a son Ethan; Ben marries Diana and they have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona each marry unrelated partners and have children G and H respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between G and H?
explanation: Adam–Ben and Clara–Diana make Ethan and Fiona double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). The children of double first cousins share both pairs of great‑grandparents, which is expressed as double second cousins. No other term is more exact.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a daughter X; N and P have a son Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their parents are two pairs of siblings. Hence they are double first cousins—the only term that captures the dual shared lineage.

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamous marriages, let X be a person. X’s mother’s brother is Y. Y’s daughter is Z. Z’s husband is W. W’s mother is V, who is the sister of X’s father. What is V’s relation to X?
explanation: V is the sister of X’s father, so she is X’s paternal aunt. The other connections (through Y, Z, W) do not alter this direct blood link.

question: L has one sister S and one brother B. S has exactly one son C, and B has exactly one daughter D. C and D marry each other and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is M’s relation to L?
explanation: C is L’s nephew (son of sister) and D is L’s niece (daughter of brother). C and D are first cousins. Their child M is the child of L’s nephew and niece, which makes M L’s grandniece or grandnephew.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: John and Mary are full siblings. Mary’s only child is Tom. John’s only child is Anna. Tom marries Anna, and they have a daughter Lily. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Lily’s precise relation to John?
explanation: Lily is John’s granddaughter through his daughter Anna. She is also John’s great‑niece because Tom is John’s nephew (son of his sister Mary) and Lily is Tom’s daughter. The only term capturing both lines is the combined description.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed
D) D) Both granddaughter and great‑niece

question: M’s mother has a brother. That brother’s daughter (M’s first cousin) marries M’s father’s sister. What is the exact relationship, using standard English kinship terms, of the child of this couple to M?
explanation: The daughter is M’s first cousin (maternal side). Her husband is M’s paternal aunt, so their child is M’s first cousin through the aunt (same generation). The same child is also the child of M’s first cousin, making it a first cousin once removed. The closest, most precise term is therefore “first cousin”.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard term (affinal only)

question: A and B are siblings. C is the child of A. D is the child of B. E is the child of D. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of C to E?
explanation: C is A's child; D is B's child, making C and D first cousins. E is D's child, so C is one generation above E, i.e., a first cousin once removed.

question: In a family with no intermarriage, N has one paternal uncle (the only sibling of N’s father) and one maternal aunt (the only sibling of N’s mother). M is the child of both of those siblings (i.e., M is the child of N’s paternal uncle and also the child of N’s maternal aunt). What is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to N?
explanation: M shares both sets of grandparents with N because one parent of M is N’s paternal uncle and the other is N’s maternal aunt. Thus they are double first cousins, the most specific standard term.

question: A and B are married and have a child F. A has a brother C; B has a sister D. C and D marry each other and have a child E. Using only standard English kinship terms (no adoption, no remarriage), what is the most precise relation between E and F?
explanation: E is the child of A's brother (C) and B's sister (D). Thus E is A's niece/nephew and B's niece/nephew. F is the child of A and B. Consequently, E and F share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins on both parental lines – i.e., double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamy, let X be the child of the only brother of Y’s mother and also the child of the only sister of Y’s father. What is the most precise standard kinship term for X’s relation to Y?
explanation: X’s father is Y’s maternal uncle and X’s mother is Y’s paternal aunt. Thus X shares both of Y’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the only term that captures the doubled shared ancestry.

question: A and B are half‑siblings who share only their mother. A has a child C, and B has a child D. Assuming no other intermarriages in the family, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between C and D?
explanation: C and D are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent (the mother of A and B). The precise term for such a pair is “half‑first cousins”. Full first cousins share both grandparents, which is not the case here.

question: In a family with no adoptions or multiple births, N’s mother has exactly one sibling and N’s father has exactly one sibling. The child of the mother’s sibling is also the child of the father’s sibling. What is the precise kinship term for that child (call them M) to N, using standard English kinship vocabulary?
explanation: M is the child of N’s maternal uncle and also the child of N’s paternal uncle. Thus M shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making M and N double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: John is the son of Mary and Michael. Mary’s brother is Peter. Peter’s daughter Lisa is married to Tom. Tom’s mother Susan is Michael’s sister. What is the precise relationship between Lisa and Michael using standard English kinship terms (in‑law terms allowed, no adoption)?
explanation: Lisa is Peter’s daughter, so she is John’s maternal first cousin. Tom, Lisa’s husband, is Susan’s son; Susan is Michael’s sister, making Tom Michael’s nephew. Therefore Lisa is the wife of Michael’s nephew, i.e., Michael’s niece‑in‑law. The other options do not capture this marital‑in‑law link.

question: Consider persons M, A, and B with the following facts (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed): A is the only sibling of M's mother. B is the only sibling of M's father. C is the child of A and B. Using standard English kinship terminology (including doubled ancestry where appropriate), what is the precise relation of C to M?
explanation: A is M's maternal aunt/uncle, B is M's paternal aunt/uncle. Their child C shares both sets of grandparents with M, i.e., all four grandparents are common. That makes C a double first cousin of M, the most precise term.

question: M is the mother of N. N’s father is O. O’s sister is P. P’s son is Q. Q’s daughter is R. R’s husband is S. S’s mother is T. T’s brother is U. U’s daughter is V. What is V’s relation to M using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Trace: M→N (child). N’s paternal aunt P → cousin Q → cousin’s child R → R’s husband S → S’s mother T → T’s brother U → U’s daughter V. All links after R are by marriage, never introduce a blood connection to M. Hence V has no standard direct kinship term to M; only an affinal chain exists.
choices: A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: N’s mother has exactly one brother (her only sibling) and N’s father has exactly one brother. The two brothers marry each other and have a child M. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for M relative to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s maternal uncle and also the child of N’s paternal uncle. Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making M a double first cousin—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: R has a mother who has exactly one brother, and a father who has exactly one brother. Let X be the child of R’s maternal uncle and Y be the child of R’s paternal uncle. If we pick either X or Y and call that person Z, what is Z’s precise kinship to R using standard English terms?
explanation: Both X and Y are children of a parent’s brother, i.e., an uncle. Regardless of which uncle, the child is a first cousin of R. No other relationship applies, so Z is always R’s first cousin.

question: P is the child of X. X has a sister Y. Y is married to Z. Z's brother is W, whose daughter is Q. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: X and Y are blood sisters. Y’s husband Z is X’s brother‑in‑law. Z’s brother W is also X’s brother‑in‑law, but there is no blood link between X and W. Consequently P (X’s child) and Q (W’s child) share only an affinal chain of length three, which exceeds the immediate in‑law scope. No standard direct kin term exists.
choices: C) C) No relation (neither blood nor affinal)
D) D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, N marries P, and O and P are siblings. M and O have a daughter X; N and P have a son Y. X and Y marry each other and have a child Z. In standard English kinship terms (blood only, in‑law limited to spouse), what is the most precise description of Z’s relation to M?
explanation: Through X, Z is M’s grandchild. Through Y, Z is M’s great‑niece/nephew (child of M’s niece/nephew). The only term that captures both lines is “grandchild (also great‑niece/nephew)”. No single standard term covers both, so the most precise answer must state both relations.

question: N is married to S. The parent of S has a sibling, and that sibling has a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (allowing only spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses), what is M to N?
explanation: S’s parent’s sibling is S’s aunt/uncle; their child M is S’s cousin. N is related to M only through the marriage to S, and English kinship provides no term for a spouse’s cousin within the allowed in‑law scope. Hence M has no standard direct relation to N.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: A's mother has exactly one brother, B, whose daughter is C. A's father has exactly one sister, D, whose son is E. C and E marry and have a child X. What is X's relation to A using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed)?
explanation: B is A's maternal uncle, so C is A's first cousin. D is A's paternal aunt, so E is also A's first cousin. C and E are unrelated to each other, so X is the child of A's first cousin. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed, regardless of which side the cousin comes from.

question: Let N be a person. P is the child of the only brother of N’s mother, and also the child of the only brother of N’s father (i.e., the same individual is both the child of N’s maternal uncle and the child of N’s paternal uncle). What is the precise standard English kinship term for P to N?
explanation: P is the child of an uncle on either side of N. Regardless of whether the uncle is maternal or paternal, the relation to N is always a first cousin. No other qualifier applies, so the exact term is "first cousin".

question: M has a daughter D. M's brother B has a son C. B is M's only sibling. Additionally, M's sister S is married to N; N's brother T is married to D. T's daughter E is married to C. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no adoption), what is the precise relation of C to D?
explanation: C is the child of B, who is M's brother, making B D's uncle. Therefore C is the child of D's uncle, i.e., D's first cousin. Other connections (marriages) do not affect the blood relationship.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Ben, marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Ben and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Ethan’s child is Greg, and Fiona’s child is Hannah. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relationship between Greg and Hannah?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins; their children share both great‑grandparent pairs, making them double second cousins, which is the most precise term.

question: X’s mother has a brother A, and X’s father has a sister B. A’s daughter is C; B’s son is D. C and D marry and have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Y’s precise relation to X?
explanation: C is X’s maternal first cousin; D is X’s paternal first cousin. Y is the child of each of those cousins, making Y a first cousin once removed to X on both sides. The single standard term covering both is “first cousin once removed.”
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard direct relation

question: L’s mother has exactly one brother, and L’s father has exactly one sister. M is the child of that brother and also the child of that sister (the two cousins are unrelated). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M to L?
explanation: The child of L’s maternal uncle is L’s first cousin; likewise the child of L’s paternal aunt is also L’s first cousin. Both statements refer to the same person M, so M is uniquely a first cousin of L.

question: Person A’s mother has exactly one brother B, and A’s father has exactly one sister C. B’s only child and C’s only child are the same individual, D. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring adoption), what is the most precise term for D’s relation to A?
explanation: D is the child of A’s maternal uncle (B) and simultaneously the child of A’s paternal aunt (C). Thus D shares both of A’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the exact term for this doubled first‑cousin relationship.

question: Alex’s mother, Maya, has exactly one brother, Ben. Alex’s father, Raj, has exactly one brother, Dev. Ben and Dev are married and have a single child, Sam. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relationship between Alex and Sam?
explanation: Ben is Maya’s brother (maternal uncle) and Dev is Raj’s brother (paternal uncle). Their marriage makes Sam the child of both Alex’s maternal and paternal uncles. Thus Alex and Sam share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins. Hence the exact term is “double first cousin.”

question: M is the mother of N. N has a sibling O, whose child is P. M has a sibling R, and R’s child is Q. P and Q are married. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no in‑law), what is the precise relationship between Q and N?
explanation: M is N’s mother, so R (M’s sibling) is N’s aunt/uncle. R’s child Q is therefore N’s first cousin. The marriage of Q to P does not affect their blood relationship; the exact term is first cousin.

question: L has one brother and one sister. The brother has exactly one child, who in turn has a child M. The sister also has exactly one child, who in turn has a child N. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise blood relation between M and N?
explanation: L’s brother’s child and L’s sister’s child are first cousins (they share L’s parents). M and N are each the child of those first cousins, so they share L’s great‑grandparents. The correct term for children of first cousins is second cousins.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: M and N are siblings. M’s son marries N’s daughter and they have a child X. M’s daughter marries N’s son and they have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring any in‑law extensions), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: Both of X’s parents (M’s son and N’s daughter) are siblings, and both of Y’s parents (M’s daughter and N’s son) are also siblings. Hence X and Y share both pairs of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the exact term.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a son Ethan; Brian marries Diana and they have a son Felix. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Ethan and Felix?
explanation: Ethan and Felix share both sets of grandparents: their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. Therefore they are double first cousins, not merely first cousins or half‑cousins.

question: In a family, X has a sister Y. Y has two children, Z and T. X has a daughter W. T has a child V. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no adoption), what is the precise relation of V to W?
explanation: Y is X's sibling, so Z and T are X's nieces/nephews and first cousins of W. V, being T's child, is the child of W's first cousin, making V W's first cousin once removed.

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoption, let X be the child of the only brother of Y’s mother, and let Y be the child of the only brother of X’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle, making them first cousins on Y’s mother’s side. Y is the child of X’s paternal uncle, making them first cousins on X’s father’s side. Sharing both sets of grandparents, they are double first cousins – the only term that captures this dual lineage.

question: Anna is an only child. Her mother has exactly one sibling, a brother who has a daughter Clara. Her father has exactly one sibling, a sister who has a son David. If we pick either Clara or David and call that person Sam, what is Sam’s relation to Anna?
explanation: Clara is the child of Anna’s maternal uncle; David is the child of Anna’s paternal aunt. In either case Sam is the child of a parent’s sibling, which is precisely a first cousin to Anna.

question: L has one sister S and one brother B. S has exactly one son X, and B has exactly one daughter Y. X and Y marry each other and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is M's relation to L?
explanation: X is L's nephew (sister's son) and Y is L's niece (brother's daughter). Their child M is therefore the child of L's nephew/niece, i.e., L's grand‑nephew or grand‑niece (great‑nephew/great‑niece).
choices: D) No standard direct kinship term

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamy, let Q be a person. Q's father has exactly one sister, who has exactly one child C. C has exactly one child P. Using standard English kinship terms, what is P's relation to Q?
explanation: Q's father's sister is Q's paternal aunt. Her child C is Q's first cousin. P is the child of that cousin, placing P one generation below Q's cousin. Hence P is Q's first cousin once removed.

question: Let N be a person. M is the child of the only brother of N’s father and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother (the two brothers are married to each other). What is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to N, using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: M’s father is N’s paternal uncle and M’s mother is N’s maternal uncle. Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making them first cousins on both parental lines – the exact term is “double first cousin.”

question: In a family with no adoptions, divorces or remarriages, L’s mother has exactly one brother and L’s father has exactly one sister. The brother and the sister are married to each other and have a single child M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between M and L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, who are spouses. M therefore shares both of L’s grandparent pairs, making them first cousins on both sides. The exact term is double first cousin.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions, let R be a person. X is the child of the only brother of R’s mother, and Y is the child of the only sister of R’s father. If either X or Y is called S, what is S’s precise relation to R using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Both X and Y are children of a parent’s sibling (maternal uncle’s child or paternal aunt’s child). A child of any sibling of a parent is a first cousin, regardless of which side. Hence S is always a first cousin of R.

question: M is married to H. H has a brother B, whose daughter is L. M also has a sister S, whose son is J. J is married to L. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of L to M?
explanation: L is the daughter of H’s brother, making her H’s niece by blood. Since M is H’s spouse, L becomes M’s niece‑in‑law. The other connections (through S’s son J) also make L the spouse of M’s nephew, which yields the same term. No other standard term fits more precisely.

question: L has one sister and one brother. The only son of L's sister marries the only daughter of L's brother, and they have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is M's relation to L?
explanation: L's sister's son is L's nephew; L's brother's daughter is L's niece. Their child M is the child of L's nephew and niece, i.e., one generation down from L's siblings' children. Thus M is L's grandniece or grandnephew.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed
D) D) No uniquely determinable relation

question: P is the only child of Q’s father. R is the daughter of Q’s mother’s brother. Assuming the statements are true, what is the precise relationship of P to R?
explanation: Since Q’s father has only one child, that child must be both Q and P; thus Q = P. Q’s mother’s brother is Q’s maternal uncle, whose daughter R is Q’s (and therefore P’s) first cousin. Hence P is R’s first cousin.

question: Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses): R is married to S; S’s brother is T; T’s wife is U; U’s brother is V; V’s daughter is W. What is W to R?
explanation: R → S (spouse) → T (brother‑in‑law) → U (sister‑in‑law) → V (brother of that sister‑in‑law) → W (V’s daughter). The chain moves beyond the immediate in‑law scope and never creates a blood link, so no standard direct kinship term exists between R and W.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a family with no adoptions or remarriages, L is a man who has exactly one sister S and exactly one brother B. S has a son T. B has a daughter R. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between R and T?
explanation: T is the son of L’s sister, making him L’s nephew. R is the daughter of L’s brother, making her L’s niece. Children of siblings are first cousins, so R and T are first cousins. No other option fits.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: Anna and Ben share the same mother but have different fathers. Anna’s son Carl and Ben’s daughter Dana meet. Using standard English kinship terms and not ignoring the half‑sibling link, what is the most precise blood relationship between Carl and Dana?
explanation: Anna and Ben are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. Their children therefore share only one grandparent, making them half‑first cousins—the most exact term.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a daughter X; N and P have a son Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y each have a parent who is a sibling of the other's other parent, so they share both sets of grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than ordinary first cousins.

question: Two brothers, A and B, each marry a woman; A marries C and B marries D, where C and D are sisters. A and C have a child X; B and D have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two pairs of siblings (A–B and C–D). They share both sets of grandparents, giving them the exact term “double first cousins.”

question: M and N are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). M has a child A, and N has a child B. No other intermarriages exist. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between A and B?
explanation: M and N share a single parent, making them half‑siblings. Their children each inherit the shared grandparent from that one parent, so A and B have exactly one common grandparent. This yields the term half‑first cousins, distinct from full first cousins which require both grandparents.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter A. N has a son B, who marries C. C is the daughter of D, where D is the sister of A’s husband. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is C’s relation to M?
explanation: A’s husband’s sister D is A’s sister‑in‑law. D’s daughter C is therefore the daughter of A’s sister‑in‑law. C is the niece‑in‑law of A, but there is no direct blood or immediate affinal term linking C to M, who is A’s mother. Hence the relationship is not covered by a standard term.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John and Mary are married. Mary's brother Tom marries Lisa, who is John's sister; they have a child Emma. John's brother Mark marries Susan, who is Mary's sister; they have a child Noah. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Emma and Noah?
explanation: Emma's father Tom is Mary's brother, and her mother Lisa is John's sister, so Emma's paternal grandparents are Mary's parents and her maternal grandparents are John's parents. Noah's father Mark is John's brother, and his mother Susan is Mary's sister, giving him the same two sets of grandparents. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

question: John and Peter are brothers. Mary and Linda are sisters. John marries Mary and they have a son M. Peter marries Linda and they have a son N. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between M and N?
explanation: M and N share both paternal and maternal grandparents: their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. Thus they have the same two sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: Let N be a person. X is the child of N's father's only sister and also the child of N's mother's only brother. Assuming no intermarriage among the relatives, what is the precise kinship term for X to N?
explanation: X is the child of N's paternal aunt (father's sister) and also the child of N's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Thus X shares both of N's grandparent pairs, making X a double first cousin of N.

question: In a family, M and N are twins. M has a son O with his wife P. N has a daughter Q with her husband R. O and Q marry each other and have a child S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation of S to M?
explanation: O is M’s son, Q is M’s niece (daughter of M’s twin sister N). Their marriage makes S both M’s grandchild (through O) and great‑niece (through Q). The only term that captures both lines is “grandniece‑grandchild”, which is not a standard single word; thus S’s relation to M is not uniquely expressible by a standard term.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary’s son Tom marries John’s daughter Lisa. Tom and Lisa have a child Emma. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between Emma and John’s mother?
explanation: John’s mother is Lisa’s mother, making her Emma’s maternal grandmother. She is also Mary’s mother, so she is Tom’s grandmother, which makes her Emma’s paternal great‑grandmother. Because the two sides give different generational distances, no single standard term captures both; the relation is both grandmother and great‑grandmother.
choices: A) A) No single standard term (both grandmother and great‑grandmother)

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father; N’s mother is the sister of O’s father; O’s mother is the sister of M’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between M and O?
explanation: M’s father is O’s maternal uncle, making M and O first cousins. The other statements also create first‑cousin links, confirming the same relation. No half‑ or removed status applies.

question: M is married to N. M has a brother O, who is married to P. P’s sister is Q. N has a sister S, whose son is R. R is married to Q. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Q’s precise relation to M?
explanation: R is N’s nephew (son of N’s sister S). Since M is N’s spouse, R is M’s nephew‑in‑law. Q is R’s spouse, making Q the niece‑in‑law of M. No other path creates a standard kin term.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a family with monogamy (remarriage allowed) and no adoption, X is the mother of Y. Y’s father is Z. Z’s sister is W. W’s son is V. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is V’s precise relation to X?
explanation: Z is X’s spouse (or former spouse). W, as Z’s sister, is X’s sister‑in‑law. V, being W’s son, is therefore X’s nephew‑in‑law. No blood link exists, and the term “nephew‑in‑law” is the exact standard label.

question: M’s father is the brother of N’s mother, and M’s mother is the sister of N’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relationship between M and N?
explanation: M and N share both paternal and maternal grandparents because each of their parents are siblings of the opposite sex. This makes them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: R’s mother has exactly one sibling, a brother A. R’s father also has exactly one sibling, a sister B. A and B are married and have a single child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no extra intermarriages), what is the precise relation of C to R?
explanation: C is the child of both R’s maternal uncle (A) and paternal aunt (B). Being the child of a sibling of each parent makes C a first cousin on both sides, i.e., a double first cousin.

question: M is mother of siblings N and O. N is married to P. P's sister R is married to S. O is married to T, and they have a child Q. S is the brother of T. What is the precise kinship term for R in relation to Q, using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: S is T's brother, so S is Q's paternal uncle. R, as S's wife, is Q's aunt by marriage. The exact term that distinguishes the non‑blood link is “aunt‑in‑law.”

question: A and B are brothers. C and D are sisters. A marries C and B marries D. A and C have a daughter E; B and D have a son F. E and F marry each other and have a son G. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for G’s relationship to A’s mother?
explanation: A’s mother is the grandmother of both E (her daughter’s child) and F (her son’s child). Therefore G, the child of E and F, is one more generation down: the great‑grandchild of A’s mother. No other kin term captures this exactly.

question: Let Y be a person. X is the child of the only brother of Y's mother, and also the child of the only sister of Y's father. No adoption, monogamy, and X's two parents are different individuals. What is X's precise kinship to Y?
explanation: The mother’s brother is Y’s maternal uncle; the father’s sister is Y’s paternal aunt. X is the offspring of Y’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, making X the child of two of Y’s parents’ siblings. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of first cousins.

question: A and B share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). A has a child X and B has a child Y; there are no other intermarriages. What is the precise kinship term for the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent pair. The exact term for such relatives is “half‑first cousins,” distinguishing them from full first cousins who share both grandparent pairs.

question: M and N are brother‑and‑sister. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also brother‑and‑sister. M + O have a child X; N + P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s parents are M (brother of N) and O (sister of P). Y’s parents are N and P. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents—M’s parents and O’s parents—making them double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled ancestry.

question: My father’s brother (my paternal uncle) married my mother’s sister (my maternal aunt). They have a child X. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is X’s precise relation to me?
explanation: X is the child of both my paternal uncle and my maternal aunt. Because my parents are siblings of X’s parents on both sides, X shares both sets of grandparents with me, making X my double first cousin.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: Let Z be a person. T is the child of the only brother of Z’s mother, and U is the child of the only brother of Z’s father. If you pick either T or U and call that person X, what is X’s relation to Z using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Both T and U are children of Z’s maternal or paternal uncle. A child of an uncle is always a first cousin, regardless of which side. Hence X is Z’s first cousin.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: Liam is the son of the only brother of Maya's mother, and Maya is the daughter of Liam's father's sister. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between Liam and Maya?
explanation: Liam is the child of Maya's maternal uncle (her mother's brother) → first cousin. He is also the child of Maya's paternal aunt (his father's sister) → first cousin on the other side. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most exact term.

question: Two brothers, X and Y, each marry a sister, A and B, respectively. X and A have a son C; Y and B have a daughter D. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no in‑law extensions), what is the most precise term for the relation between C and D?
explanation: X and Y are brothers and A and B are sisters, so C and D share both sets of grandparents. They are therefore double first cousins—the only term that captures the dual shared ancestry.

question: X and Y are siblings. X marries W, and Y marries Z. W and Z are also siblings (but not otherwise related to X or Y). X and W have a child A; Y and Z have a child B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents: X’s parents are also B’s maternal grandparents, and W’s parents are B’s paternal grandparents. Hence they are double first cousins.

question: Man R has a sister S and a brother T. Woman U has a brother V and a sister W. S marries V and they have a child X. T marries W and they have a child Y. What is the precise kinship term between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two couples who are each other's siblings (R’s sister with U’s brother, and R’s brother with U’s sister). They share both pairs of grandparents, so they are first cousins on both sides – i.e., double first cousins, the most precise standard term.

question: Using only standard English kinship terms (allowing spouse, parents, siblings, children, and their spouses), X’s mother has a brother who is married to Y’s father’s sister. What is the most precise term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: The brother of X’s mother is X’s maternal uncle; his wife is Y’s paternal aunt. Their link is purely affinal, and standard kin terms stop at immediate in‑laws. Hence there is no direct standard kinship term between X and Y.
