question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a sister, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam's child is Ethan, Brian's child is Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Adam and Brian are brothers; Clara and Diana are sisters. Their children Ethan and Fiona each have both sets of grandparents in common, so they share two grandparent pairs. The most precise term is double first cousins.

question: Mia and Noah share the same mother but have different fathers. Noah’s daughter Zoe is married to Mia’s son Liam. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between Mia and Zoe?
explanation: Mia and Noah are half‑siblings because they share only one parent. Zoe is Noah’s child, so she is Mia’s half‑niece. The exact term is half‑aunt/uncle, not the full aunt/uncle term.

question: John married Alice and had a daughter Emma. After Alice died, John married Beth, who already has a son Liam from a previous marriage. John and Beth later have a son Noah. Using standard English kinship terms (including half‑, step‑, and in‑law where appropriate), what is the precise relationship between Emma and Noah?
explanation: Emma and Noah share only one parent (John); they are half‑siblings. No other relation applies.

question: P is the child of the only brother of Q’s mother and also the child of the only sister of Q’s father. Assuming no incest and monogamy, what is the most precise standard kinship term for P’s relation to Q?
explanation: Q’s mother’s only brother is Q’s maternal uncle, so P is Q’s first cousin on the mother’s side. Q’s father’s only sister is Q’s paternal aunt, so P is also Q’s first cousin on the father’s side. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes P a double first cousin of Q, the most exact term.

question: Let N be a person. M is simultaneously the child of the only brother of N’s father and the child of the only sister of N’s mother. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for M with respect to N using standard English relations?
explanation: M is the offspring of N’s paternal uncle (father’s brother) and also of N’s maternal aunt (mother’s sister). Thus M shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most specific term that reflects the doubled ancestry.

question: L has a full brother M and a half‑sister P (they share only one parent). N is the child of M. O is the child of P. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between N and O?
explanation: N and O are children of a full sibling and a half‑sibling of L. They share exactly one grandparent (the parent common to L and P). Hence they are half‑first cousins, not full first cousins.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Ben, each marry a sister, Claire and Diana respectively. Adam and Claire have a son Ethan; Ben and Diana have a son Felix. Ethan and Felix later marry each other and have a child. What is the most precise standard kinship term for the relationship between Ethan and Felix before they marry?
explanation: Ethan and Felix share both sets of grandparents (the parents of Adam/Ben and the parents of Claire/Diana). This makes them double first cousins, the exact term for cousins who are related through both paternal and maternal lines.

question: Adam and Frank are brothers. Their sister Beth has a son Carl. Carl marries Diana. Ethan, who is Diana’s brother, is the son of Frank. What is Diana’s precise relation to Adam?
explanation: Frank is Adam’s brother, so his children are Adam’s nieces/nephews. Ethan is Frank’s son and Diana’s brother, so Diana also shares Frank as a parent. Therefore Diana is Adam’s niece.

question: M and S are married and have twin children N and O. N marries P. P has a brother Q. Q’s mother is R, who is S’s sister. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise blood relation between P and O?
explanation: R is S’s sister, so R’s children (P and Q) are nieces/nephews of S. Therefore P is the child of S’s sibling, making P a first cousin of S’s children N and O. Hence P and O are first cousins.

question: R’s father has a sister who has a child A. R’s mother has a brother who has a child B. If we select either A or B and denote that person as S, what is S’s precise relation to R using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: A is the child of R’s paternal aunt, B is the child of R’s maternal uncle. Both are children of a parent’s sibling, which makes each of them R’s first cousin. The relation does not depend on which child is chosen, so the unique correct term is "first cousin".

question: Anna and Ben are siblings. Carla and Dan are also siblings. Anna marries Carla and they have a son Ethan. Ben marries Dan and they have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents: the parents of Anna/Ben and the parents of Carla/Dan. Sharing two grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than ordinary first cousins.

question: M is the mother of N. N is married to O. O’s sister is P, who is married to Q. Q’s father is R. R’s only son is S, who is the brother of T. T is the mother of N’s child U. What is the precise kinship term for U’s relation to R?
explanation: R is parent of T; T is mother of U. Therefore U is the child of R’s child, i.e., R’s grandchild.

question: M’s mother has exactly one brother. That brother is married to M’s father’s sister. Who is M’s mother’s brother’s wife to M?
explanation: M’s mother’s brother is M’s maternal uncle. His wife is also M’s father’s sister, i.e., a paternal aunt by blood. Thus she is simultaneously an aunt by marriage on the maternal side and a blood aunt on the paternal side.
choices: C) No blood relation, only an aunt by marriage
D) Both maternal aunt by marriage and paternal aunt by blood

question: M and N are siblings. M's daughter is A. N has two children: a son B and a daughter D. D's son is C. What is the precise standard English kinship term for the relation between A and C?
explanation: A is two generations down from the common grandparents (G → M → A). C is three generations down (G → N → D → C). The nearest common ancestor is G, so they are first cousins (min‑1) with a one‑generation difference, i.e., first cousins once removed.

question: John is the son of Mary's brother. Mary is the daughter of Peter's sister. Peter is the father of Lisa, and Lisa is the mother of Sam. What is Sam's precise relation to John using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Peter's sister's children are Mary and Mary's brother. Lisa, Peter's child, is first cousin to Mary's brother. Their children John and Sam are therefore children of first cousins, i.e., second cousins.

question: John is married to Mary. Mary’s sister Anna is married to Tom. Tom’s brother Peter is married to Lisa, who is the daughter of John’s brother Mark. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Lisa to Mary?
explanation: Lisa is Mark’s daughter, making her John’s niece. Mary is John’s spouse, so Lisa is Mary’s niece‑in‑law. The precise standard term is “niece‑in‑law.”
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation

question: Two sisters, M and N, each marry two brothers, P and Q. M + P have a son A; N + Q have a daughter B. A and B later marry each other and have children C and D. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring adoption, monogamy allowed, but accounting for doubled ancestry), what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: A and B are double first cousins because they share both sets of grandparents. Their children C and D therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins – the exact term for this doubled relationship one generation down.

question: In a family with monogamy (remarriage allowed) and no adoptions, X’s mother has a brother who is married to Y. Y’s brother is X’s father’s brother. What is Y’s precise kinship term to X using standard English relations?
explanation: X’s mother’s brother is X’s maternal uncle; his wife Y is therefore X’s aunt‑in‑law. Y’s brother is X’s paternal uncle, making Y the sister of X’s paternal uncle, i.e., X’s paternal aunt by blood. The standard term that covers both facts is simply “aunt”.

question: John is the son of Mary and Peter. Mary has a brother Alan, who is married to Susan. Susan's sister Laura is the mother of Kevin. Kevin is married to Emily, who is the daughter of Peter's sister Rachel. What is Kevin's relation to John using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Kevin is Laura's son; Laura is Susan's sister; Susan is Alan's wife, and Alan is Mary's brother, John’s maternal uncle. The chain John → uncle → aunt → her sister → her son is purely affinal with no blood link, and standard kinship terms stop at aunt/uncle, so no direct term exists.
choices: D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: Two brothers, A and B, marry two sisters, C and D, respectively. A and C have a son X; B and D have a son Y. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because each pair of parents are siblings on both the paternal and maternal sides. Hence they are first cousins with doubled ancestry, correctly called “double first cousins.”

question: L’s father has one sister, A. A has exactly one child, C. C has exactly one child, D. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is D’s precise kinship term to L?
explanation: A is L’s paternal aunt, so her child C is L’s first cousin. D is the child of L’s first cousin, which makes D L’s first cousin once removed. No other relations apply.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: X’s mother has a brother (X’s maternal uncle). The uncle is married to Y. Y’s brother has a daughter Z. Using only standard English kinship terms (blood and immediate in‑law relations), what is Z’s relation to X?
explanation: Y is X’s aunt‑by‑marriage; her brother is unrelated to X, and his daughter Z is only connected through that non‑blood chain. No standard term covers a kinship beyond one step of in‑law, so Z has no defined relation to X.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, S’s father’s sister has a brother. That brother has a child named T. What is the precise kinship term for T in relation to S, using standard English blood‑relation terminology?
explanation: S’s father’s sister is S’s paternal aunt. Her brother is S’s paternal uncle (the father’s brother). The child of that uncle is S’s first cousin. No other blood link is involved, so the exact term is “first cousin”.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary’s son is Tom. Tom’s daughter is Lily. John also has a son Kevin, and Kevin is married to Lily. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Lily to John?
explanation: Mary is John’s sister, so her son Tom is John’s nephew. Lily, being Tom’s daughter, is John’s grand‑niece (great‑niece). Thus the precise term is grand‑niece.

question: R’s father has a sister A. R’s mother has a brother B. A and B are married and have a son C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is C’s precise relation to R?
explanation: C is the child of R’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and also the child of R’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus C is both a paternal first cousin and a maternal first cousin, i.e., a double first cousin.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter A. A has a daughter C. N has a son B, and B marries C. Using standard English kinship terms only (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the most precise relation between C and N?
explanation: C is N’s grandniece (child of N’s niece) and also N’s daughter‑in‑law (wife of N’s son). No single standard term covers both blood and affinal links, so there is no standard direct relation.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M and N are full siblings. P and Q are also full siblings (different families). M marries Q, and N marries P. A is the child of M and Q, and B is the child of N and P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of P/Q. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a stricter term than ordinary first cousins.

question: L’s mother has a sister S, and L’s father has a brother B. S and B are married and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relationship of M to L?
explanation: S is L’s maternal aunt, B is L’s paternal uncle. Their child M is a child of both an aunt and an uncle, sharing both sets of grandparents with L. Hence M is a first cousin on the mother’s side and also a first cousin on the father’s side – a double first cousin.

question: X and U are brothers; Y and V are sisters. X marries Y and they have a child P. U marries V and they have a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relationship between P and Q?
explanation: P and Q share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. This makes them first cousins on the paternal side and first cousins on the maternal side simultaneously, i.e., double first cousins.

question: M is the only child of his mother. M’s mother has a sister who married M’s father’s brother. That couple’s daughter is N. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: M’s mother’s sister is M’s maternal aunt; M’s father’s brother is M’s paternal uncle. Their child N is therefore the child of both M’s aunt and uncle, sharing both sets of grandparents with M. This makes M and N double first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has two children: a son P and a daughter R. R has a child Q, who marries O. In standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Q’s relation to O?
explanation: M and N are siblings, so O is first cousin of R. Q is R’s child, making O first cousin once removed to Q. No closer term applies.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard direct kin term

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother, U, and R’s father has exactly one sister, V. U’s only child is M; V’s only child is N. If we select either M or N and call that person S, what is S’s precise relation to R using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: U is R’s maternal uncle, so M is R’s maternal first cousin. V is R’s paternal aunt, so N is R’s paternal first cousin. Regardless of which child is chosen, S is always a first cousin of R. No other blood link is involved, making "first cousin" the unique correct term.

question: M is the mother of N. N’s father is O. O has a sister P, who is married to Q. P and Q have a child R. What is the precise relation of R to M using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: P is O’s sister, so she is N’s paternal aunt. R, P’s child, is therefore N’s first cousin. M is N’s mother, i.e., the mother of a first cousin. No standard English term exists for the mother of one’s cousin; the relationship exists only through an affinal chain.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: L’s father has exactly one brother, F, and L’s mother has exactly one sister, G. F’s child is X and G’s child is also X (the same person). Using standard English kinship terms, what is X’s precise relation to L?
explanation: X is the child of L’s paternal uncle and also the child of L’s maternal aunt. Thus X shares both sets of grandparents with L, making X a double first cousin—the most specific term for this dual first‑cousin relationship.

question: John and Mark are brothers. Anna and Beth are sisters. John marries Anna and they have a son Carl. Mark marries Beth and they have a daughter Dana. Carl and Dana each marry unrelated partners and have children: Ethan (son of Carl) and Fiona (daughter of Dana). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: John and Mark are brothers and Anna and Beth are sisters, so Carl and Dana are double first cousins (they share both grandparent pairs). Their children Ethan and Fiona therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins. No other listed term fits precisely.

question: A and B are brothers. A marries C and B marries D, where C and D are sisters. A and C have a son P; B and D have a daughter Q. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: P and Q are children of two brothers (A,B) who married two sisters (C,D). Thus they share both paternal and maternal grandparents, giving them the precise term double first cousins.

question: M is the child of the only sibling of N’s father, and also the child of the only sibling of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal aunt/uncle, making M a first cousin. M is also the child of N’s maternal aunt/uncle, another first‑cousin link. Sharing both grandparent pairs yields the exact term “double first cousin.”

question: In a family with monogamous marriages and no adoptions, R is the sibling of S. R has exactly one child Q, and S has exactly one child T. Q has exactly one child P. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of P to T?
explanation: R and S are siblings, so Q (R’s child) is a first cousin of T (S’s child). P, being Q’s child, is one generation below Q, making P a first cousin once removed of T. No other kinship fits.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has a son P and a daughter R. R has a child Q. What is the precise kinship term (using standard English) for the relation between O and Q?
explanation: O and R are first cousins (children of siblings M and N). Q is R’s child, one generation below. Therefore O and Q are first cousins once removed. No other option captures this exact relationship.

question: M’s mother is N. N’s brother is O. O’s daughter is P. P’s son is Q. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of Q to M?
explanation: O is N’s brother, so O is M’s maternal uncle. P, O’s daughter, is M’s first cousin. Q, the son of that cousin, is one generation below the cousin, making Q M’s first cousin once removed.

question: M and N are brother and sister. M marries O and N marries P. O and P are also brother and sister (no other intermarriages). X is the child of M & O, Y is the child of N & P. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their parents are two pairs of siblings. That makes them double first cousins, a stricter term than ordinary first cousins.

question: Person P’s father is the brother of Person Q’s mother, and P’s mother is the sister of Q’s father. No other intermarriages exist. Using standard English kinship terms (excluding in‑law extensions), what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: P and Q share both paternal and maternal grandparents because each of P’s parents is a sibling of one of Q’s parents. Hence they are first cousins on two independent lines, i.e., double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: In a family with monogamy (remarriage allowed) and no adoption, let Y’s mother have exactly one brother and Y’s father have exactly one sister. Those two siblings marry each other and have a child X. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for X in relation to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, who are married. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled shared ancestry.

question: Tom’s mother has a brother Alan. Alan has a daughter Beth. Tom also has a sister Clara, who is married to Beth’s brother David. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, and in‑law terms limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of Tom to Beth?
explanation: Alan is Tom’s maternal uncle, so his daughter Beth shares Tom’s maternal grandparents. That makes Tom and Beth first cousins. The marriage between Clara and David creates only an affinal link; it does not alter the blood relationship.

question: Alan’s mother has only one brother, Brian. Brian’s daughter Clara is married to David, who is the son of the only sister of Alan’s father, Edward. What is the precise kinship term between Clara and David?
explanation: Clara is Alan’s maternal first cousin (daughter of his mother’s brother). David is Alan’s paternal first cousin (son of his father’s sister). Their parents are unrelated, so Clara and David share no common ancestor; there is no standard blood relation between them.

question: L has exactly one sister and exactly one brother. The sister’s only son is X, and the brother’s only daughter is Y. Both X and Y are parents of the same individual M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption), what is M’s relation to L?
explanation: L’s sister’s son X is L’s nephew; X’s child M is L’s grandnephew/niece. Similarly, L’s brother’s daughter Y is L’s niece; Y’s child M is again L’s grandniece/nephew. Both lines give the same precise term, so M is L’s grandniece (if female) or grandnephew (if male).

question: M is the child of the only brother of N’s mother, and also the child of the only sister of O’s father. If N and O are siblings, what is M’s precise relation to N?
explanation: The brother of N’s mother is N’s maternal uncle; his child is N’s first cousin. The sister of O’s father is O’s paternal aunt; her child is also O’s first cousin. Since N and O share both parents, M is first cousin to N on both sides – still a first cousin (double first cousin).

question: In a family with no adoptions: A is the only child of B. B is married to C. C has a brother D. D is married to E, who is the sister of F. F is the only child of G, who is B's sibling. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, in‑law limited to spouse), what is the precise relation of E to G?
explanation: E is the spouse of D, who is C's brother. G is B's sibling. There is no blood connection between E and G; the only link is through marriage, which does not produce a standard kin term. Hence no direct relation exists.
choices: D) No standard direct relation (affinal only)

question: Let Y be a person. Y’s mother has a brother (M) and Y’s father has a sister (F). A child, X, is born to the union of M and F. Using only standard English kinship terms (no adoption, no remarriage), what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: M is Y’s maternal uncle, so X is Y’s first cousin on the mother’s side. F is Y’s paternal aunt, so X is also Y’s first cousin on the father’s side. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes X and Y double first cousins, the most exact term.

question: John’s mother Mary has a brother Tom. Tom’s daughter Lisa marries John’s son Mark. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for Lisa’s relation to John?
explanation: Tom is Mary’s brother, so Lisa is John’s first cousin. By marrying John’s son Mark, Lisa also becomes John’s daughter‑in‑law. In kinship terminology the affinal (marital) relationship is the operative one, making daughter‑in‑law the most precise term.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: M and N are half‑siblings (they share only a mother). M has a child A and N has a child B. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent. The correct term for such a pair is "half‑first cousins"; full first cousins require both grandparents, and no generational offset exists.
choices: C) C) Half‑first cousins once removed

question: Let Y be a person. Y’s mother has exactly one brother. That brother has exactly one son. The child of that son is X. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is X’s relation to Y?
explanation: Y’s mother’s brother is Y’s maternal uncle. His only son is Y’s first cousin. X is the child of that cousin, making X a first cousin once removed to Y. No other relationship fits the description.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a son Ethan. Brian marries Diana and they have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins. Ethan later has a daughter Maya with another partner, and Fiona has a son Noah with another partner. What is the most precise standard English blood relation between Maya and Noah?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. Their respective children, Maya and Noah, therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents. The correct term for such a relationship is "double second cousins".

question: In a monogamous family tree with no adoptions: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has a son P. O marries a man Q, who is the only child of P’s sister R. Who is Q to O?
explanation: R is N’s daughter, so R is O’s first cousin. Q, being R’s only child, is O’s first cousin once removed. No other kinship applies, so the precise term is "first cousin once removed".
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: In a family, two brothers A and B each marry two sisters C and D respectively (A‑C and B‑D). A and C have a child X; B and D have a child Y. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two sibling couples. They share both sets of grandparents (A‑B’s parents and C‑D’s parents). Hence they are not merely first cousins; they are double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled ancestry.

question: In a family where there is no adoption or remarriage, let N be a person. M is the child of the only sibling of N's father and also the child of the only sibling of N's mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M’s father is N’s paternal uncle and M’s mother is N’s maternal aunt. Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making them double first cousins—the most specific term for this doubly shared lineage.

question: John is the son of Mary. Mary has a brother Peter, who is married to Linda. Linda's sister Susan is the mother of Tom. Tom is married to Alice, who is the daughter of John's sister Emma. What is the precise kinship term for Peter in relation to Alice?
explanation: Peter is Mary's brother, making him John’s maternal uncle. Emma, John’s sister, is Alice’s mother, so Alice’s grandmother is Mary. Therefore Peter is the brother of Alice’s grandmother, i.e., her great‑uncle. No other option matches.

question: M and N are brothers. S and T are sisters. M marries S and N marries T. M and S have a son X; N and T have a daughter Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two pairs of siblings (brothers and sisters). They share both paternal and maternal grandparents, giving them the exact term “double first cousins.” No other listed term captures the doubled shared ancestry.

question: Alice and Bob have one child, P. Alice’s brother Carl marries Bob’s sister Diana, and they have a child, Ethan. Ethan later has a child, Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise term for Fiona’s relationship to P?
explanation: Carl (Alice’s brother) and Diana (Bob’s sister) make Ethan a double first cousin of P because he shares both sets of grandparents. Fiona, Ethan’s child, is one generation younger, so she is a double first cousin once removed to P. No other standard term is more specific.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed
B) B) Double first cousin once removed

question: John and his sister Mary are siblings. Lisa and her brother Tom are siblings. John marries Lisa, and Mary marries Tom. John and Lisa have a son Adam; Mary and Tom have a daughter Beth. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring adoption and remarriage), what is the most precise relation between Adam and Beth?
explanation: John‑Lisa and Mary‑Tom are each pair of first cousins who married each other. Their children therefore share both sets of grandparents, giving Adam and Beth the exact relationship of double first cousins.

question: M is the only child of his mother. M’s mother has a sister (M’s maternal aunt) who is married to M’s paternal uncle (the brother of M’s father). The aunt and her husband have a son N. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: M’s mother and aunt are sisters, so N is M’s maternal first cousin. N’s father is M’s paternal uncle, so N is also M’s paternal first cousin. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the exact term.

question: M is the only child of his mother. N is the son of M's father's sister. O is the daughter of N's mother's brother. What is O's precise relation to M?
explanation: M's father's sister is his paternal aunt; her son N is M's first cousin. N's mother is that aunt, whose brother is M's father. The daughter of M's father is O, making her M's half‑sister (they share a father but have different mothers).

question: A is married to B. B's brother C is married to D. D's sister E is married to F, who has a son G. A and B have a daughter H. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children's spouses), what is the precise relation between G and H?
explanation: G and H share no common ancestor; the only link is a chain of marriages (B’s brother’s wife’s sister’s husband). Standard kinship provides no term for such an affinal chain, so they have no defined blood relation.

question: M and N are siblings. M has two children, A (with spouse S1) and D (with spouse S2). N has one child B (with spouse S3). A and B (first cousins) marry and have a child C. D has a child E. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between C and E?
explanation: A and B are first cousins who marry, so their child C is grandchild of both siblings M and N. D, another child of M, makes E a grandchild only of M. Thus C and E share a single grandparent (M) but not the other, giving them the precise term half‑first cousins.

question: Mary and John have a child X. After John dies, Mary marries Peter. Peter already has a daughter Anna from his previous marriage, and Mary and Peter have no children together. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise term for the relationship between X and Anna?
explanation: X and Anna share no blood; their parents are married to each other. The only kinship that connects them is the marriage of their respective parents, making them step‑siblings.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, the only child of P. N marries Q, the only child of R. P and R are siblings. M + O have a son S; N + Q have a daughter T. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between S and T?
explanation: M and N share parents A‑B. O and Q are first cousins, sharing grandparents C‑D (because P and R are siblings). S’s grandparents are A‑B (paternal) and C‑D (maternal); T’s grandparents are the same two sets. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes S and T double first cousins.

question: I have a father's brother (paternal uncle) whose daughter has a child, and I also have a mother's sister (maternal aunt) whose son has a child. If the two children described are the same person, what is my precise relation to that person?
explanation: My paternal uncle's daughter is my first cousin; her child is my first cousin once removed. Likewise, my maternal aunt's son is my first cousin; his child is also my first cousin once removed. Both descriptions point to the same individual, so the exact kinship term is first cousin once removed.

question: M is married to N. N’s mother is O, whose husband P is not N’s father. P has a son Q from an earlier marriage. Q is married to R, who is the sister of M’s mother S. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Q’s relation to M?
explanation: Q is the husband of M’s maternal aunt (sister of S) and also the spouse of N’s step‑brother. Both links go beyond the allowed in‑law scope, so no standard direct kinship term exists.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: P’s mother is the sister of Q’s father. R is the child of Q’s sister. What is R’s precise relationship to P using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: P’s mother and Q’s father are siblings, so P and Q are first cousins. Q’s sister is also a first cousin of P. R, being the child of that cousin, is one generation down, making R P’s first cousin once removed.

question: L's mother has a brother named N. N's daughter is O, and O has a son named P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of P to L?
explanation: N is L's maternal uncle, so O is L's first cousin. P is O's child, therefore P is the child of L's first cousin, i.e., L's first cousin once removed.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: In a family with no adoptions and monogamous marriages: M is the mother of A. M has a sister S. S is married to a man who has a son C from a previous marriage. C is married to D. D's brother is E, and E's mother is S. What is the precise blood relation of E to A?
explanation: S is M's sister, making S A's maternal aunt. E is the child of S, so E is the child of A's aunt, which is the definition of a first cousin. No other blood link exists.

question: John’s mother has a brother Mark. Mark’s daughter Lisa is John’s maternal first cousin. John’s father has a brother Peter; Peter’s son Tom is John’s paternal first cousin. Lisa and Tom marry and have a child Emily. What is Emily’s precise blood relation to John?
explanation: Lisa is John’s first cousin on his mother’s side; Tom is his first cousin on his father’s side. Their child Emily is one generation below each cousin, making her John’s first cousin once removed (through either line). No closer term applies.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: John and Mary are siblings. Their brother Peter is also their sibling. Peter has a daughter Anna. John marries Anna, and they have a son Sam. Mary has a daughter Lisa. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of Sam to Lisa?
explanation: John and Mary are siblings, so Sam (John’s child) and Lisa (Mary’s child) are first cousins. The extra link via Anna (Peter’s child) makes Sam also a first‑cousin‑once‑removed of Lisa, but the nearest blood link is the first‑cousin relationship, which is the most precise term.

question: R is married to S. S's brother is T. T's wife is U. U's sister is V. Who is V to R?
explanation: R → S (spouse) → T (brother‑in‑law) → U (sister‑in‑law) → V (sister of that sister‑in‑law). This chain goes beyond the scope of standard English kinship terms, which stop at immediate in‑law relations. Therefore V has no direct standard kinship label to R.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses): A is married to B. B’s sister is C. C’s husband is D. D’s sister is E. What is E to A?
explanation: A → B (spouse); C is B’s sister (sister‑in‑law); D is C’s husband (spouse of sister‑in‑law); E is D’s sister. E is linked to A through two successive in‑law steps, which exceeds the standard in‑law scope, so no direct kin term exists. Hence the only correct description is that there is no standard direct relation (affinal only).
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a family with no adoption or polygamy, let S be the only sister of T’s father. U is the child of S, and V is the child of U. What is V’s precise relation to T using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: S is T’s paternal aunt. U, as S’s child, is T’s first cousin. V, being the child of that cousin, is one generation below T’s cousin, making V T’s first cousin once removed. No other standard term fits more precisely.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions, let N be a person. N’s father has a sister who is married and has a child X, and N’s mother has a brother who is married and has a child X as well (the same X). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between N and X?
explanation: X is the child of both N’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle. Hence X shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most specific term beyond simple first cousin.

question: John is married to Mary. Mary's brother Tom is married to Linda. Linda's sister Eva is married to Mark, who is John's brother. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children's spouses), what is Eva to Mary?
explanation: Mary → John (spouse) → Tom (brother‑in‑law) → Linda (Tom’s spouse) → Eva (Linda’s sister). This chain never creates a blood link and exceeds the immediate in‑law scope defined in standard kinship, so there is no specific term for Eva’s relation to Mary.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: L’s mother has a brother M, and L’s father has a sister A. M and A are married and have a single child P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of P to L?
explanation: M is L’s maternal uncle and A is L’s paternal aunt. Their child P shares both sets of grandparents with L, giving P the status of a double first cousin – the most specific term for this dual‑line first‑cousin relationship.

question: Two brothers, Alan and Brian, each marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Alan and Clara have a child X; Brian and Diana have a child Y. No other intermarriages occur. Using standard English kinship terms without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of a brother‑brother pair and a sister‑sister pair. They share both sets of grandparents, not just one, making them double first cousins—the most specific standard term.

question: R is married to S. S’s sister T is married to U. U’s brother V is married to W. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is W’s relation to R?
explanation: R → S (spouse) → T (sibling‑in‑law) → U (that sibling’s spouse) → V (that spouse’s sibling) → W (that sibling’s spouse). The chain extends beyond the immediate in‑law scope and never creates a blood link, so no standard direct kin term applies.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: X and Y are children of two siblings who share exactly one parent (the siblings are half‑brothers/sisters). No other intermarriages exist. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: The two siblings share only one parent, so they have a single common grandparent. Their children therefore share that one grandparent, making them half‑first cousins. Full first cousins require both grandparents, and second cousins require shared great‑grandparents. Hence the precise term is half‑first cousins.

question: In a monogamous, non‑adoptive family tree, let R be a person. R’s mother has exactly one brother, who is the father of L. Also, L’s father has exactly one sister, who is the mother of R. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between L and R?
explanation: L is the child of R’s maternal uncle, making them first cousins on the maternal side. R is the child of L’s paternal aunt, making them first cousins on the paternal side as well. Sharing both sets of grandparents yields the precise term “double first cousins.”

question: In a family with no adoptions and monogamous marriages, let Z be the child of the only son of A’s mother and also the child of the only daughter of B’s father. Assuming all persons mentioned are distinct, what is Z’s precise relation to A?
explanation: If A’s mother’s only son is A’s brother, Z is A’s niece/nephew. If that son is A’s half‑brother (different father), Z becomes A’s half‑first cousin. Without knowing whether A’s mother’s son shares both parents with A, the exact kinship cannot be fixed, so the relation is not uniquely determinable.

question: Man A is married to E. A has a sister B. B's son C is married to D. D's mother is the sister of E. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the most precise term for the relation between C and E?
explanation: C is the son of A's sister, i.e., A's nephew. Because E is A's spouse, C is E's nephew‑in‑law. No direct blood term fits, and calling C simply a 'nephew' would ignore the affinal connection.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother (U1) and R’s father has exactly one brother (U2). U1 and U2 are married to each other and have a single child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relationship between C and R?
explanation: U1 is R’s maternal uncle, U2 is R’s paternal uncle. Their child C is the child of both a maternal uncle and a paternal uncle, thus sharing both sets of grandparents with R. This makes C a double first cousin of R, the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: In a family with no adoptions, monogamy, and no remarriages, B and C are siblings (share both parents). A is the child of B’s paternal aunt and also the child of C’s maternal uncle. What is the precise kinship term for A in relation to B?
explanation: B’s paternal aunt is B’s father’s sister; C’s maternal uncle is C’s mother’s brother. Since B and C share the same parents, that aunt and that uncle are the same two individuals – the sister of B’s father and the brother of B’s mother. A is therefore the child of B’s aunt/uncle, i.e., B’s first cousin.

question: John is the father of Mary. Mary’s brother is Peter. Peter’s wife is Laura. Laura’s mother is Susan. Susan’s son Michael is the father of Anna. Using only standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, in‑law terms limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Anna’s relation to John?
explanation: Peter is John’s son; Laura is John’s daughter‑in‑law. Michael is Laura’s brother, i.e., Peter’s brother‑in‑law. No blood link exists between John and Michael, nor a direct in‑law term beyond the affinal chain. Hence Anna, Michael’s daughter, has no standard direct kinship term to John.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M is the child of a woman who is the sister of N’s mother, and also the child of a man who is the brother of N’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M’s mother is N’s maternal aunt, making M a first cousin on the mother’s side. M’s father is N’s paternal uncle, making M a first cousin on the father’s side as well. Sharing both grandparent pairs, M and N are double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: The Smith family has two children, Adam (son) and Beth (daughter). The Jones family has two children, Carl (son) and Dana (daughter). Adam marries Dana, and Beth marries Carl. Adam and Dana have a son Ethan; Beth and Carl have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Adam and Beth are siblings; Carl and Dana are siblings. Their cross‑marriages make Ethan's parents Adam (Smith) and Dana (Jones) and Fiona's parents Beth (Smith) and Carl (Jones). Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents (the Smiths and the Joneses), so they are double first cousins, the exact term.

question: A’s mother has a brother B, whose daughter is C. A’s father has a sister D, whose son is E. Using only standard English kinship terms (no invented affinal chains), what is the precise relationship between C and E?
explanation: C is A’s maternal first cousin; E is A’s paternal first cousin. B and D are unrelated siblings of A’s parents, so C and E share no blood ancestor. Their link is solely through the affinal chain (cousin‑in‑law), for which standard kinship provides no direct term. Hence there is no standard direct relation.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal only)

question: X's mother and Y's father are siblings. X's father is married to Z, who is the sister of Y's mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise blood relation between X and Y?
explanation: X's mother and Y's father are siblings, so they share the same parents. Therefore X and Y are children of two siblings, making them first cousins. The additional marital connections involve no blood ties and do not alter this relation.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary’s daughter Lisa marries Tom, who is the son of John’s brother Mark. Tom and Lisa have a child Anna. What is Anna’s precise relation to John using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Tom is John’s nephew (son of his brother). Lisa is John’s niece (daughter of his sister). Their child Anna is the child of both a nephew and a niece, making her John’s grandniece. No other term fits precisely.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: Let L be a person. M is the child of the only sister of L’s father, and N is the child of the only brother of L’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of both M and N to L?
explanation: L’s father’s only sister is L’s paternal aunt; her child M is a first cousin on the paternal side. L’s mother’s only brother is L’s maternal uncle; his child N is a first cousin on the maternal side. Both are therefore first cousins of L, regardless of which side.

question: L has one sister S and one brother B. S has exactly one child X, and B has exactly one child Y. X and Y marry and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is M's precise relation to L?
explanation: X is L's niece/nephew (child of sister). Y is also L's niece/nephew (child of brother). Their child M is the child of L's niece/nephew, i.e., L's great‑niece (or great‑nephew). This is the most specific standard term.

question: John and Mary are married and have a son Paul. John's brother Mark marries Mary's sister Lisa, and they have a daughter Anna. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between Paul and Anna?
explanation: Paul and Anna share both sets of grandparents: John and Mark share the same parents, and Mary and Lisa share the same parents. Hence they are children of two sibling pairs, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: Emma is the child of the only brother of Sarah’s mother, and Sarah is the child of the only sister of Emma’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is Emma’s relation to Sarah?
explanation: Emma’s mother’s brother is Sarah’s maternal uncle, so Emma is Sarah’s first cousin on the maternal side. Sarah’s father’s sister is Emma’s paternal aunt, making Sarah Emma’s first cousin on the paternal side. Both statements describe the same first‑cousin relationship, uniquely determined.

question: L is the only child of his mother. L's mother has a brother R. R's daughter is S, and S has a son T. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between L and T?
explanation: R is L's maternal uncle, making S L's first cousin. T is S's son, one generation below L's first cousin, so L and T are first cousins once removed.

question: M is the mother of J. J is married to L. L's mother is N, and N's brother is O, whose daughter is P. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of M to P?

question: Tom has a son Alex with his first wife Sara. After Sara’s death Tom marries Linda, who already has a daughter Maya from a previous marriage. Tom and Linda later have a child Sam. What is the precise blood relation between Alex and Sam?
explanation: Alex and Sam share the same father Tom but have different mothers (Sara and Linda). They therefore have one common parent only, which makes them half‑siblings. No other parent is shared, so they are not full siblings.

question: M and N share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). M has a child P; N has a child Q. No other intermarriages occur. What is the precise kinship term for the relationship between P and Q?
explanation: Half‑siblings share only one grandparent. Their children therefore share only that single grandparent, making them half‑first cousins—the exact term for cousins who share just one grandparent pair.

question: Y’s mother has exactly one brother and Y’s father has exactly one sister. The brother of Y’s mother marries the sister of Y’s father, and they have a child named X. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no other intermarriage), what is the precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and paternal aunt (father’s sister). question: Using standard English kinship terms only (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted): Person A's father is B. B has a sister C. C's son is D, and D's daughter is E. What is the precise relationship of E to A?
explanation: B and C are siblings, so C is A's aunt. D, C's child, is A's first cousin. E, D's daughter, is one generation below that cousin, making E A's first cousin once removed.

question: M and N are siblings. M has two children: a daughter A and a son D. N has a son B. B marries C, who is the daughter of D. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is C's relation to M?
explanation: C is the daughter of D, who is M's son. Therefore C is M's granddaughter. No other blood link changes this relation.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary’s son is Alex. John’s daughter Emma has a daughter Lily. Alex and Lily marry. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no in‑law), what is the precise relation of Alex and Lily’s child to John?
explanation: Lily is John’s granddaughter (Emma’s daughter). Her child is therefore John’s great‑grandson. Through Alex the child is also John’s great‑nephew, but when both lineal and collateral apply the lineal term is used, giving great‑grandson as the precise relation.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a woman who is the sister of the other's wife. Adam's wife is Clara and Brian's wife is Dana, and Clara and Dana are sisters. explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters, so they are first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides, i.e., double first cousins.

question: J’s father has a sister, and J’s mother has a brother. The sister and the brother are married and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of M to J?
explanation: M is the child of J’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Hence M shares both sets of grandparents with J, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: In a family, Y’s mother has exactly one brother and Y’s father has exactly one sister. That brother and that sister are married to each other and have a child X. Using standard English kinship terms (including ‘double’ qualifiers), what is the most precise term for X’s relation to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, who are spouses. Thus X shares both sets of grandparents with Y, making them first cousins on both parental lines – the precise term is “double first cousin”.

question: In a family with no adoptions, X’s mother has a brother who is married to Y’s sister. Y is the child of X’s father’s sister. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise blood relation between X and Y?
explanation: Y is the child of X’s paternal aunt, so they share a set of grandparents on X’s father’s side, making them first cousins. The marriage of X’s maternal uncle to Y’s sister is only an affinal link and does not affect the blood relation.

question: X's mother has a brother (her maternal uncle). That uncle is married to Y. Y has a brother, and that brother has a daughter Z. question: In a family: L is the only child of his mother M. M has a sister N, who is married to O. O's brother is P. P has a daughter Q, whose mother is R, the sister of L's father S. question: John has a sister Anna. Mary has a brother Ben. Anna marries Ben, and John marries Mary. Emma is the child of John and Mary, and Liam is the child of Anna and Ben. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between Emma and Liam?
explanation: Emma and Liam share both sets of grandparents: John and Anna are siblings, and Mary and Ben are siblings. Hence they are first cousins on their fathers' side and also first cousins on their mothers' side, giving the precise term “double first cousins.”

question: John has a brother Peter. Peter is married to Mary. Mary has a sister Lisa. John’s only child, Kevin, marries Lisa. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law relations limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses), what is Lisa to John?
explanation: Kevin is John’s son. Lisa is Kevin’s spouse, which makes her John’s child’s spouse. The precise term is daughter‑in‑law.

question: Alan and Beth are siblings. Beth’s only child is Carl. Alan’s only child is Dana. Dana’s only child is Eva. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between Carl and Eva?
explanation: Beth and Alan are siblings, so their children Carl and Dana are first cousins. Eva is Dana’s daughter, one generation below Dana. Thus Carl is a first cousin of Eva’s parent, making Carl a first cousin once removed of Eva. No other standard term applies.

question: In standard English kinship terms (allowing only spouse, parents, siblings, children and their spouses), let X be a person. X's mother has a brother A. A is married to C. C's brother is B. B has a daughter Y. What is the precise relation of Y to X?

question: M and N are siblings. N has a son Q, who in turn has a son P. M’s daughter D is married to P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relationship of M to Q?
explanation: M and N share both parents, so M is the sibling of Q’s parent N. That makes M the aunt (or uncle) of Q. No other blood link (through marriage) changes this primary relation.

question: Using standard English kinship terms only (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), consider: M is married to N. N’s brother is O. question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father. M has a child K. N has a child L. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between K and L?
explanation: M’s mother and N’s father are siblings, so M and N are first cousins. The children of first cousins are second cousins. Therefore K and L are second cousins, a uniquely defined relationship.

question: L’s father has exactly one brother, and L’s mother has exactly one sister. Both of those siblings each have a single child, and those two children are the same person, M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s paternal uncle and also the child of L’s maternal aunt. Therefore M shares both of L’s grandparent pairs, making M a double first cousin of L—the most specific term for this doubled ancestry.

question: L has exactly one sister and one brother. The sister has exactly one son, X; the brother has exactly one daughter, Y. X and Y marry and have a child M. In standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is M’s relation to L?

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamous marriages, let Y be the child of the only brother of L’s mother and also the child of the only sister of L’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Y to L?
explanation: Y’s father is L’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and Y’s mother is L’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Therefore Y shares both of L’s grandparent pairs, making Y a double first cousin of L.

question: In a family, M's father (F) has a brother (B). M's mother (M1) has a sister (N). B is married to N, and they have a child O. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for O's relation to M?
explanation: O is the child of M's paternal uncle (B) and maternal aunt (N). Because B and N are siblings of M's parents, O shares both sets of grandparents with M, making O a double first cousin – the most specific standard term.

question: X's mother has exactly one brother, and X's father has exactly one sister. The brother of X's mother has a daughter Y, and the sister of X's father has a son Z. If Y and Z are the same person, what is the precise kinship term for that person to X (using standard English kinship terminology, without ignoring doubled ancestry)?
explanation: Y is the daughter of X's maternal uncle (first cousin). Z is the son of X's paternal aunt (first cousin). If Y and Z are the same individual, that person is simultaneously a maternal and paternal first cousin, i.e., a double first cousin of X.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, R’s mother has exactly one brother, U. U’s only child is V. What is the precise kinship term for V in relation to R, using standard English blood‑relation terminology?
explanation: U is R’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). V, being the child of R’s maternal uncle, is R’s first cousin. No other information can alter this relationship, making “first cousin” the unique correct term.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, and N marries P. O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise blood relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two couples that are both brother‑sister pairs. They share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through two independent lines – the exact term is double first cousins.

question: Let Y have a sister S and a brother B. S has exactly one son, who in turn has a child X. B has exactly one daughter, who in turn has a child Z. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relationship between X and Z?
explanation: S’s son is Y’s nephew; his child X is Y’s grand‑nephew/niece. B’s daughter is Y’s niece; her child Z is also Y’s grand‑nephew/niece. The nephew and niece are first cousins, so their children X and Z are second cousins. No other term fits more precisely.

question: N’s father has exactly one sister and N’s mother has exactly one brother. The only child of that sister‑brother pair is M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation of M to N?
explanation: The sister of N’s father is N’s paternal aunt; the brother of N’s mother is N’s maternal uncle. Their child M is a cousin on both the paternal and maternal sides, sharing both sets of grandparents. The precise term is “double first cousin”.

question: M is the child of the only sister of L’s father, and also the child of the only brother of L’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s relation to L?
explanation: L’s father’s sister is L’s paternal aunt; her child is L’s first cousin. L’s mother’s brother is L’s maternal uncle; his child is also a first cousin. Both possibilities give the same relation, so M is a first cousin of L.

question: M has two children by different fathers: daughter L and son J. M’s sister S has a son K. L marries K. S’s husband H previously had a daughter T from another marriage; T is not biologically related to S. J marries T. What is the precise blood‑relation between L’s child A and J’s child B?
explanation: L and J share only their mother M, making them half‑siblings. Their children A and B are therefore children of half‑siblings, which in standard kinship terms are half‑first cousins. No other blood link exists; the marriages add no blood relation.

question: John and Linda are siblings. John’s only child is Mary. Mary’s brother is Tom. Linda is married to Mark, who has a daughter Susan from an earlier marriage (Susan is Linda’s step‑daughter, not blood‑related to John). Tom marries Susan. Mary has a son Kevin. Using standard English kinship terms (spouse, parents‑in‑law, siblings‑in‑law, children‑in‑law only), what is Susan’s precise relation to Kevin?
explanation: Susan is married to Kevin’s maternal uncle Tom, giving her the status of aunt by marriage. She shares no blood link with Kevin, so the only correct standard term is aunt‑in‑law.

question: Alice's mother is the sister of Bob's father, and Alice's father is the brother of Bob's mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Alice and Bob?
explanation: Alice's mother and Bob's father are siblings, and Alice's father and Bob's mother are also siblings. Thus Alice and Bob are children of two sibling pairs, sharing both sets of grandparents. The exact term for this is double first cousins, which is more precise than simply first cousins.

question: Using standard English kinship terms only, let A be the child of B. B has a sister C. C’s child is D, and D’s child is E. What is the most precise relation of E to A?
explanation: C is A’s aunt, so D is A’s first cousin. E, being D’s child, is one generation removed from that cousin level, making E A’s first cousin once removed—the only exact term.

question: R has a paternal grandfather G. G has exactly one brother B. B has exactly one child C, and C has exactly one child S. Assuming no adoption, monogamy, and no remarriages, what is S’s precise relation to R?
explanation: B is R’s great‑uncle (brother of his paternal grandfather). C, B’s child, is R’s father’s first cousin. S, the child of that cousin, is one generation below R’s father’s cousin, making S R’s first cousin once removed.

question: Person X has a mother who has exactly one brother and a father who has exactly one sister. Those two siblings are married to each other and have a single child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption), what is the most precise blood relation between X and Y?
explanation: The brother (maternal uncle) and sister (paternal aunt) share no blood with each other, but each is a sibling of one of X's parents. Their child Y therefore shares both sets of grandparents with X, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: M and N are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). M has a child P, and N has a child Q. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise relationship between P and Q?
explanation: P and Q are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent (the common mother’s parent). That makes them half‑first cousins, a distinct term from full first cousins.

question: John is married to Mary. Mary’s brother Tom is married to Linda, who is John’s sister. John and Mary have a daughter Anna; Tom and Linda have a son Ben. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Anna and Ben?
explanation: Anna and Ben share both sets of grandparents: John’s parents (through John) and Mary’s parents (through Mary). Their parents are sibling pairs, so the children are double first cousins, not merely first or half‑cousins.

question: Let X be a person. X’s mother has a sister A, and A’s son is P. X’s father has a brother B, and B’s daughter is Q. Assuming no intermarriages, what is the precise relationship between P and Q using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: P descends from X’s maternal aunt, Q from X’s paternal uncle. Their lineages share no common ancestor, so they are not blood‑related. No standard kin term exists for such a pair.

question: A is the child of B. B and C are siblings. C has a daughter D, who in turn has a son E. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the precise relationship of E to A?
explanation: B and C are siblings, so A and D are first cousins. E is D’s child, one generation below A, making E A’s first cousin once removed.

question: A’s mother and B’s father are siblings, and A’s father and B’s mother are also siblings (no other intermarriages). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A shares both sets of grandparents with B because each of A’s parents is a sibling of one of B’s parents. Thus they are first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides, i.e., double first cousins – the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: John’s father Michael has a brother Tom. Tom is married to Susan. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Susan’s relation to John?
explanation: Tom is John’s paternal uncle because he is Michael’s brother. Tom’s spouse Susan is therefore John’s aunt by marriage, i.e., a paternal aunt‑in‑law. No blood link exists, so the precise term is ‘aunt‑in‑law’.

question: A person R has exactly one sibling, whose gender is unknown. That sibling has exactly one child, whose gender is also unknown. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no step‑relations), what is the precise term for that child in relation to R?
explanation: If R’s sibling is a brother, the child is R’s nephew; if the sibling is a sister, the child is R’s niece. Because both the sibling’s and child’s genders are unspecified, a single kin term cannot be assigned; the relation is not uniquely determinable.

question: M and P are full siblings. M’s brother N (same parents) marries L. L’s sister O (unrelated to M’s family) marries P. N and L have a child X. O and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: N is M’s brother, so X’s paternal grandparents are M’s parents. O is L’s sister, so Y’s maternal grandparents are L’s parents. Because P (M’s sister) married O, Y’s paternal grandparents are also M’s parents. Hence X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures both shared grandparent pairs.

question: X’s mother has exactly one brother (M) and X’s father has exactly one sister (S). M and S marry each other and have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of Y to X?
explanation: Y is the child of X’s maternal uncle (M) and paternal aunt (S). Hence Y is X’s first cousin on the mother’s side and also first cousin on the father’s side, making Y a double first cousin of X.

question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father. N is the child of the only brother of M’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relationship between M and N?
explanation: Let A be N’s father and B be M’s mother. The statements say B is the only sister of A and A is the only brother of B. Thus A and B are siblings. M is B’s child, N is A’s child, so they are children of siblings – exactly first cousins. No other kin term fits.

question: M is the child of the sister of P’s father and also the child of the brother of P’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation of M to P?
explanation: M is the offspring of P’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and also of P’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with P, making M a double first cousin – the exact term.

question: P and Q are each the child of a different sibling. Those two siblings share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). No other intermarriages occur. What is the precise kinship term for the relationship between P and Q?
explanation: The children of half‑siblings inherit only one common grandparent pair, so they are not full first cousins. The exact term for such a pair is "half‑first cousins".

question: M and N are half‑siblings who share only their mother. M has a daughter A; N has a son B. There are no other intermarriages or adoptions. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent (their common maternal grandmother). The correct term for such a pair is "half‑first cousins"; full first cousins require both grandparents, and other options are inaccurate.

question: Alex’s mother has exactly one brother, Ben, and Alex’s father has exactly one sister, Clara. Ben and Clara are married and have a single daughter, Dana. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation of Dana to Alex?
explanation: Ben is Alex’s maternal uncle and Clara is Alex’s paternal aunt. Their daughter Dana is the child of both an uncle and an aunt of Alex, sharing both of Alex’s grandparent pairs. The exact term is “double first cousin.”

question: Two brothers, P and Q, each marry a woman from the same family: P marries R and Q marries S, where R and S are sisters. P and R have a daughter X; Q and S have a son Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both paternal grandparents (P and Q are brothers) and both maternal grandparents (R and S are sisters). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a stricter term than ordinary first cousins.

question: P’s father has a sister who is married, and P’s mother has a brother who is married. Their respective spouses each have a child: M is the child of the sister of P’s father, and also the child of the brother of P’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation of M to P?
explanation: M is the child of P’s paternal aunt and also the child of P’s maternal uncle. Thus M shares both of P’s grandparent pairs, making M a double first cousin of P, the most specific term.

question: M is the only child of his mother. M’s father has a sister N, who is married and has one child P. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of P to M?
explanation: N is M’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Her child P is therefore M’s first cousin. No half‑ or double‑relationship exists, so the exact term is “first cousin”.

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father, and M’s father is the brother of N’s mother. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for the relation between M and N using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: M’s mother and N’s father are siblings, and M’s father and N’s mother are siblings. Hence M and N share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins on both parental sides – the exact term is double first cousins.

question: John and Mary are siblings. Their spouses, Paul and Lisa, are also siblings. John and Paul have a daughter Anna. Mary and Lisa have a son Ben. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between Anna and Ben?
explanation: Anna and Ben share both sets of grandparents: John‑Mary’s parents and Paul‑Lisa’s parents. That makes them first cousins through two independent sibling pairs, i.e., double first cousins. No other term is more exact.

question: L has one sister and one brother. M is the child of the only son of L’s sister. N is the child of the only daughter of L’s brother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise blood relationship between M and N?
explanation: L’s sister’s son is L’s nephew; L’s brother’s daughter is L’s niece. Those two (nephew and niece) are first cousins because their parents (sister and brother) are siblings. M and N are the children of those first cousins, making them second cousins. No other shared ancestors exist beyond that generation.

explanation: S is the child of R’s maternal uncle, making S R’s first cousin. U is R’s child, one generation below R. Therefore S is one generation above U but shares the same grandparent pair, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed.
