question: M’s mother has exactly one brother, who has a daughter A. M’s father has exactly one brother, who has a son B. If we pick either A or B and call that person C, what is C’s relation to M using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed)?
explanation: Both A and B are children of a parent’s brother—M’s maternal uncle’s daughter and paternal uncle’s son. A child of a parent’s sibling is, by definition, a first cousin. Hence C is always M’s first cousin.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, N marries P, and O and P are also siblings. M and O have a daughter X; N and P have a son Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: Both of X’s parents are siblings of both of Y’s parents, so X and Y share both sets of grandparents. That makes them double first cousins—the most precise term.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a child Ethan. Brian marries Diana and they have a child Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are children of two sibling pairs. They share both sets of grandparents (Adam‑Brian’s parents and Clara‑Diana’s parents). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than ordinary first cousins.

question: Let Q be a person. P is the child of the only brother of Q’s mother, and also the child of the only sister of Q’s father. Assuming no adoptions or step‑relations, what is the precise kinship term for P’s relation to Q?
explanation: P’s mother is Q’s maternal uncle’s wife, making P a first cousin on the mother’s side. P’s father is Q’s paternal aunt’s husband, making P a first cousin on the father’s side. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes P a double first cousin of Q, the most exact standard term.

question: Two brothers, A and C, each marry two sisters, B and D, respectively (A‑B and C‑D). A and B have a son E; C and D have a daughter F. E and F each have one child, G and H. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between G and H?
explanation: E and F are double first cousins because they share both sets of grandparents. Their children G and H therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the most specific term available.

question: John and Kate are siblings. Kate marries Michael. Michael’s sister, Laura, marries Peter, who is John’s son. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Laura’s relation to John?

question: Z’s mother is the sister of W’s father, and Z’s father is the brother of W’s mother. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between Z and W?
explanation: Each pair of parents are siblings, so Z and W share both sets of grandparents. That makes them double first cousins, but the conventional single term is simply “first cousins.”

question: X and Y are half‑siblings who share only their mother. X has a child M and Y has a child N. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relationship between M and N?
explanation: M and N are each the child of a half‑sibling. They share exactly one grandparent (the mother’s parent) and not the other. The correct term for such a pair is “half‑first cousins,” distinguishing them from full first cousins who share both grandparents.

question: Using standard English kinship terms only (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), Emma is the daughter of John’s father’s sister, and Kevin is Emma’s husband. What is Kevin’s relation to John?
explanation: Emma is John’s first cousin (child of his paternal aunt). Kevin is related to John only through marriage to that cousin. Standard kinship terms do not cover a cousin’s spouse, so no direct term exists. Hence the correct description is ‘no standard direct relation (affinal chain only)’.

question: M’s father has a sister (paternal aunt) who is married to M’s mother’s brother (maternal uncle). What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the child of that couple relative to M?
explanation: The couple shares both of M’s parents as siblings, so their child is M’s cousin through the father and also through the mother. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes the child a double first cousin of M.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries P, who is the sister of Q. N marries Q. M and P have a daughter R. N and Q have a son S. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the most precise relation between R and S?
explanation: R’s parents (M and P) and S’s parents (N and Q) each come from two sibling pairs. Thus R and S share both sets of grandparents, giving them the exact term “double first cousins.” No other term is as specific.

question: R’s mother has one brother, Tom, and R’s father has one sister, Sara. Tom’s daughter is Alice; Sara’s son is Bob. If you pick either Alice or Bob and call that person S, what is S’s relation to R?
explanation: Alice is the child of R’s maternal uncle and Bob is the child of R’s paternal aunt. In both cases S is the child of a parent’s sibling, which is precisely a first cousin.

question: M and N share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). M has a child X and N has a child Y. No other intermarriages occur. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent. The exact term for such descendants is “half‑first cousins”.

question: L has one sister S and one brother B. S’s only child (S1) and B’s only child (B1) marry each other and have a child M. What is the precise standard kinship term for M’s relation to L?
explanation: S1 is L’s niece, so M (her child) is L’s grand‑niece (great‑niece). B1 is L’s nephew, making M also L’s grand‑nephew (great‑nephew). The single term that covers both is grand‑niece/grand‑nephew (great‑niece/great‑nephew). No other option fits.

question: M has a maternal uncle (her mother’s only brother) who has a child A, and a paternal uncle (her father’s only brother) who has a child B. If either A or B is selected and called X, what is X's relation to M?
explanation: Both A and B are children of M's parents' brothers, making each a first cousin of M. Whichever child is chosen, the relationship is identical.

question: E’s paternal grandfather has exactly two sons: E’s father and his brother. That brother has a daughter, F. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of F to E?

question: X’s mother has a brother (her maternal uncle) and X’s father has a sister (his paternal aunt). Those two siblings marry and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise term for M’s relation to X?

question: John’s father is the brother of Mary’s mother, and John’s mother is the sister of Mary’s father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relationship between John and Mary?
explanation: John shares one set of grandparents with Mary through his father and her mother, and a second set through his mother and her father. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: A's mother and B's father are siblings, and A's father and B's mother are also siblings (no other intermarriages). A and B each have one child, C (child of A) and D (child of B). What is the most precise kinship term for the relation between C and D?

explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and also the child of N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus M shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

explanation: The child of L’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and paternal aunt (father’s sister) shares both of L’s grandparent pairs. Hence P is a double first cousin of L, the most specific standard term.

explanation: L’s mother is R’s paternal aunt and L’s father is R’s maternal uncle, so L shares both sets of grandparents with R. The exact term for this relationship is double first cousin.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John has a son Peter. Mary has a daughter Susan. Peter has a child Alan. Susan has a child Betty. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, ignoring remarriage), what is the precise relation between Alan and Betty?
explanation: John and Mary are siblings, so their children Peter and Susan are first cousins. Alan (Peter’s child) and Betty (Susan’s child) are therefore children of first cousins, which makes them second cousins. No other connections are present, so the exact term is second cousins.

question: M and N are full siblings. M is married to Q, whose sibling is P. N marries P. M and Q have a child A; N and P have a child B. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the most precise relationship between A and B?

question: M and N are siblings. M’s only child is X. N’s only child is Y. Y marries X’s child Z (who is the only child of X). Assuming monogamy, no adoption, and that all marriages are legal, what is the precise kinship term for Z to N?

question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M’s mother is N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and M’s father is N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Therefore M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making them double first cousins—the exact term for this doubled first‑cousin relationship.

question: M and N are siblings who share the same mother G. M has a daughter O; N has a son P. O and P marry and have a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relationship between G and Q?
explanation: G is mother of M and N. Q is grandchild of M (through O) and also grandchild of N (through P). Hence G is the parent of Q’s grandparents, making G Q’s great‑grandmother. No closer term applies.

question: In a family with no adoptions or remarriages, let J be a person. M is the child of the sister of J’s maternal grandfather. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for M’s relation to J?
explanation: J’s maternal grandfather’s sister is J’s maternal great‑aunt. Her child is the first cousin of J’s mother, i.e., one generation above J. Therefore M is J’s first cousin once removed, the exact term for this relationship.

question: In a family, X is the son of Y’s father’s sister, and also the son of Z’s mother’s brother. If Y and Z are siblings, what is the most precise kinship term for X to Y (using standard English kinship terms, no adoption)?
explanation: Y’s father’s sister is Y’s paternal aunt; her son is Y’s paternal first cousin. Z’s mother’s brother is Z’s maternal uncle; his son is Z’s maternal first cousin. Since Y and Z share both parents, X is simultaneously Y’s paternal and maternal first cousin, i.e., a double first cousin.

question: In a family with no inter‑marriage among relatives, X is the child of the only brother of Y's mother and also the child of the only sister of Y's father. What is the precise kinship term for X relative to Y?
explanation: X is simultaneously the child of Y's maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Hence X shares both sets of Y's grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific standard term.

question: John’s mother has a brother Peter, whose daughter is Anna. John’s father has a sister Mary, whose son is Brian. Anna and Brian marry and have a child Clara. What is Clara’s relation to John (using standard English kinship terms, no adoption, monogamy allowed)?
explanation: Anna is John’s maternal first cousin and Brian his paternal first cousin. Their child Clara is the child of a first cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed. No other option matches.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Ben, marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Ben and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona each have a child with unrelated partners: Ethan’s child is Greg, Fiona’s child is Hannah. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between Greg and Hannah?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins because they share both sets of grandparents. Their children, Greg and Hannah, therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the most exact term.

question: P’s mother is the sister of Q’s father. Q’s mother is the sister of R’s father, and R is the child of P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Q’s relation to R?
explanation: P and Q are first cousins because each is the child of a sibling of the other's parent. R is P’s child, one generation down. Hence Q is the first cousin of R’s parent, making Q R’s first cousin once removed.

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother, A, and R’s father has exactly one sister, B. A’s daughter is C and B’s son is D. If C and D are the same person, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for that person’s relation to R?
explanation: C/D is the child of R’s maternal uncle and also the child of R’s paternal aunt, so they share both of R’s grandparents. This makes them a double first cousin of R, the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: N’s father has exactly one brother, and N’s mother has exactly one sister. The father’s brother is married to the mother’s sister, and they have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring adoption), what is the most precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal uncle and maternal aunt, who are married to each other. Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making M a double first cousin—the exact term for this doubled relationship.

question: John and Michael are brothers. Their sister Mary is also their sibling. Mary’s son Peter marries Susan, who is Michael’s daughter. Peter and Susan have a child Anna. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Anna’s most precise relation to John?
explanation: Peter is John’s nephew (sister’s son) and Susan is John’s niece (brother’s daughter). Their child Anna is therefore the child of both a nephew and a niece, making her John’s grandniece on two independent lines – a double grandniece, the most specific term.

question: L and M share the same mother but have different fathers (they are half‑siblings). L has a son N and M has a daughter O. N and O marry and have a child P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, and only spouse as in‑law), what is the most precise relationship between N and O?
explanation: L and M are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. Their children N and O therefore share only one grandparent (the common mother), making them half‑first cousins. They are not full first cousins (which require both grandparents), nor double first cousins, nor second cousins.

question: X is simultaneously the child of the sister of A’s mother and the child of the brother of A’s father. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise term for X’s relation to A?
explanation: The sister of A’s mother is A’s maternal aunt, so X is A’s first cousin on the mother’s side. The brother of A’s father is A’s paternal uncle, making X also A’s first cousin on the father’s side. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes X a double first cousin of A.

question: M is the child of the sister of P’s father and also the child of the brother of P’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s precise relation to P?
explanation: M is the child of P’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and also the child of P’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Hence M is P’s first cousin on both sides, i.e., a double first cousin. No other standard term captures this dual relationship.

question: Couple A (brother) and B (sister) have a son C. Couple D (sister of A) and E (brother of B) have a daughter F. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between C and F?
explanation: C’s father A and F’s mother D are siblings, sharing the same set of paternal grandparents. Likewise, C’s mother B and F’s father E are siblings, sharing the same set of maternal grandparents. Thus C and F share both pairs of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures this double shared ancestry.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions, person A’s father is the brother of person B’s mother, and A’s mother is the sister of B’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between A and B?
explanation: A shares one set of grandparents with B through their fathers’ sibling link and another set through their mothers’ sibling link. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a stricter term than plain first cousins.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let X be a person. X’s father’s sister (X’s paternal aunt) is married to Y. Y’s mother is the sister of X’s mother. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation of Y to X?
explanation: Y is married to X’s paternal aunt, so Y is X’s uncle‑in‑law. Y’s mother is X’s maternal aunt, making Y the child of that aunt – a first cousin of X. Blood relationships take precedence over affinal ones, so the most precise term is “first cousin.”

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, and N marries P. O and P are also siblings. M and O have a daughter X; N and P have a son Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s parents are M (child of grandparents G1) and O (child of grandparents G2). Y’s parents are N (M’s sibling) and P (O’s sibling). Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, giving them the exact term “double first cousins.”

question: John and Mary are siblings. John’s son Michael has a daughter Lisa. Mary’s son Peter marries Lisa. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise blood relation of Peter to Lisa?
explanation: Mary and John are siblings, so their children Peter and Michael are first cousins. Lisa is Michael’s daughter, placing her one generation below Peter. Hence Peter is Lisa’s first cousin once removed.

question: L’s mother has exactly one brother, and L’s father has exactly one sister. Both of these relatives are married to each other and have a single child M. What is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to L, using standard English blood‑relation terminology?
explanation: M is the child of L’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, who are spouses. Therefore M shares both of L’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most specific term for this relationship.

question: In a family, X is the child of the only brother of Y’s mother and also the child of the only sister of Y’s father. No intermarriage occurs among the relatives mentioned. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law designations), what is the most precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and simultaneously the child of Y’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Therefore X shares both sets of grandparents with Y, making X a double first cousin—the most specific term available.

question: Y’s mother has exactly one brother, and Y’s father has exactly one sister. Those two siblings are married and have a child X. What is the most precise standard kinship term for X’s relation to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, who are spouses. Therefore X shares both of Y’s grandparent pairs, giving them the relationship of double first cousins, the only term that captures the dual shared ancestry.

question: Emma's mother has a brother Tom, who has a daughter Lily. Emma's father has a sister Sara, who has a son Mark. If we pick either Lily or Mark (the description does not tell us which) and call that person Q, what is Q's relationship to Emma?
explanation: Lily is the child of Emma's maternal uncle and Mark is the child of Emma's paternal aunt. In either case Q is the child of a sibling of one of Emma's parents, which by standard kinship is a first cousin.

question: Alice and Bob are siblings. Alice has a daughter Clara. Bob has two children: a son David and a daughter Fiona. Fiona has a son Edward. Who is Edward to Clara?
explanation: Alice and Bob are siblings, so their children Clara and David are first cousins. Fiona, another child of Bob, is also Clara’s first cousin. Edward is Fiona’s son, i.e., one generation below Clara’s first cousin, making him Clara’s first cousin once removed.

question: My father’s sister (my paternal aunt) is married to my mother’s brother (my maternal uncle). They have a child X. What is the most precise standard kinship term for X’s relation to me?
explanation: X is the child of my paternal aunt (father’s sister) and my maternal uncle (mother’s brother). My parents are siblings of X’s parents on opposite sides, so X shares both sets of grandparents with me, making X a double first cousin – the only term that captures this doubled ancestry.

question: In a lineage, X's mother has a brother who is also Y's father. Y has a daughter Z. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the precise relation of Z to X?
explanation: X's mother's brother is X's maternal uncle. As Y's father, Y is the child of that uncle, making Y X's first cousin. Z, being Y's daughter, is X's first cousin once removed – the exact term.

question: I have a father and a mother. My father's sister has exactly one son; that son has a child named M. My mother's brother has exactly one daughter; that daughter also has a child named M (the same M). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M's relation to me?
explanation: My father's sister's son is my paternal cousin; his child M is my first cousin once removed. My mother's brother's daughter is my maternal cousin; her child M is also my first cousin once removed on the maternal side. Both descriptions refer to the same person, so M is uniquely my first cousin once removed.

question: L has exactly one brother and exactly one sister. The brother has only one child, a daughter named N. The sister has only one child, a son named M. N and M marry and have a child named X. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is X's relation to L?
explanation: N is L’s niece (child of L’s brother) and M is L’s nephew (child of L’s sister). Their child X is one generation below L’s niece/nephew, which is the definition of a grandniece/grandnephew (great‑niece/nephew).

question: John and Mark are brothers. John marries Alice and Mark marries Beth, who are sisters. John and Alice have a son Carl; Mark and Beth have a daughter Dana. Carl and Dana each marry unrelated partners and have children Emma and Felix respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Emma and Felix?
explanation: Carl and Dana share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. Their children Emma and Felix therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, which is described as double second cousins. No closer term applies.

question:

explanation: C is A’s child. H is the child of C, so H is one generation below C and two generations below A. That makes H A’s grandchild (grandson or granddaughter). No other chain creates a different blood link.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let P be the child of the only brother of Q’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of P to Q?
explanation: Q’s mother’s only brother is Q’s maternal uncle. That uncle is P’s father, making P the child of Q’s maternal uncle. Therefore P and Q are first cousins.

question: M is described as (i) the child of the sister of N’s father, and (ii) the child of the brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: M is the offspring of N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and also of N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus M shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the exact term for cousins related through both parents’ sides.

question: L’s father has a sister S who is married to a man whose brother is T. T’s sister is the mother of L’s mother. The child of S and her husband is M. What is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to L, using only standard English blood‑relation terminology?

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has a son P and a daughter R. R has a child Q. O marries Q. Ignoring the marriage, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the blood relationship between O and Q?
explanation: O and R are first cousins (children of siblings M and N). Q is R's child, so O is one generation above Q but shares the same grandparent pair, making O Q's first cousin once removed. No closer term applies.

question: Anna’s mother has exactly one brother, Ben, who has exactly one daughter, Clara. Anna’s father has exactly one sister, Diana, who also has exactly one daughter, Clara (the same Clara). explanation: Clara is the child of Anna’s maternal uncle (Ben) and also the child of Anna’s paternal aunt (Diana). She therefore shares both of Anna’s grandparent pairs, making her a double first cousin – the most specific standard term.

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother, M, whose only child is S. R’s father has exactly one sister, N, whose only child is T. If we pick either S or T and call that person U, what is U’s relation to R?
explanation: Both S and T are children of R’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt respectively, making them first cousins regardless of which is chosen.

question: W married H1 and had a son S. After H1's death she married H2 and had another son T. S and T are thus half‑brothers (they share only their mother). S later had a daughter A. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of A to T?
explanation: S and T share only one parent, so they are half‑siblings. A is the child of S, making her T's half‑niece. A full niece would require T to be a full sibling of A's parent.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a sister, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the relationship between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are children of two brothers who married two sisters. They share both paternal and maternal grandparents, making them first cousins through two distinct lines. The exact term is double first cousins.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let Y be a person. Y’s father has a brother. That brother has a sister. X is the child of that sister. What is X’s precise kinship term for Y?
explanation: Y’s father’s brother is Y’s paternal uncle. The uncle’s sister is Y’s paternal aunt (the same as his father’s sister). X, being the aunt’s child, is Y’s first cousin. No other blood link exists, so the exact term is “first cousin.”

question:

question: In a monogamous family, N’s mother’s spouse has a sibling called M. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is M to N?
explanation: N’s mother’s spouse is N’s father. The sibling of N’s father is N’s paternal aunt or uncle. No other in‑law steps are involved, so the precise term is aunt/uncle.

question: M is the mother of N. N’s spouse is O. O’s mother is P. P’s brother is Q. Q’s daughter is R, who is married to S. S’s father is T, and T’s sister is U. What is U’s relation to M using standard English kinship terms?

question: M’s father’s sister (paternal aunt) is married to N. N’s mother is the sister of M’s mother’s brother (maternal uncle). What is the precise blood relationship between M and N’s daughter?

question: Two brothers, P and Q, each marry a sister; P marries R and Q marries S, where R and S are sisters. P and R have a child X; Q and S have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father is P, Y’s father is Q – brothers sharing the same parents. X’s mother is R, Y’s mother is S – sisters sharing the same parents. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the exact term.

question: Alex’s mother has exactly one brother and Alex’s father has exactly one brother. The child of Alex’s mother’s brother is Sam, and the child of Alex’s father’s brother is also Sam (i.e., both statements refer to the same person). explanation: If the maternal uncle and paternal uncle are the same individual, his child is both Alex’s maternal cousin and paternal cousin. That makes Sam a double first cousin of Alex – a first cousin with shared grandparents on both sides.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions or remarriages, X’s mother’s brother has a daughter Y, and X’s father’s sister has a son Z. Y and Z marry and have a child C. explanation: Y is X’s maternal first cousin; Z is X’s paternal first cousin. Their child C is the child of X’s first cousin on each side, making C a first cousin once removed to X (the “once removed” comes from being one generation down).

question: M is the mother of N and O. N is married to P. P’s sister Q is married to R, who is O’s son. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Q’s relation to N?
explanation: N is the sibling of O, so N is aunt/uncle of O’s child R. Q is R’s spouse, i.e., the spouse of N’s nephew. By the in‑law convention, the spouse of a nephew is a niece‑in‑law. Thus Q is N’s niece‑in‑law.

question: Two brothers, Alan and Brian, each marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Alan and Clara have a child Emma; Brian and Diana have a child Frank. Using standard English kinship terms (excluding in‑law extensions), what is the most precise relationship between Emma and Frank?
explanation: Emma and Frank share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. This makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: L has one brother B and one sister S. B has exactly one daughter D, and S has exactly one son N. D and N marry and have a single child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is M’s relation to L?

question: P's father has a sister (P's paternal aunt). That aunt has a daughter Q, and Q has a son R. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of R to P?

question: M's mother has a brother U, whose daughter is V. M's father has a sister W, whose son is X. V and X marry and have a child Y. What is the precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between M and Y?

question: M’s mother has a brother who married a woman whose sister is M’s father’s sister. The couple’s child is N. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation between M and N?

question: X’s mother M has a brother U. X’s father F has a sister V. U and V are married and have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is Y’s relation to X?
explanation: U is X’s maternal uncle, V is X’s paternal aunt. Their child Y is the child of both an uncle and an aunt of X, making Y a first cousin of X on both sides. The precise term is simply “first cousin.”

question: L’s mother has exactly one son, and L’s father has exactly one daughter. A child M is born to the union of that son and that daughter. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: The son is L’s maternal uncle; the daughter is L’s paternal aunt. Their child is a child of an aunt or uncle, which makes M a first cousin of L. No other blood link exists, so the relation is uniquely first cousin.

question: M and N are siblings. M’s daughter, D, is married to P, who is the son of N’s son Q. What is the precise blood relation between D and Q using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: M and N are siblings, so their children are first cousins. D is M’s daughter; Q is the child of N’s son, i.e., the child of D’s first cousin. Hence D is a first cousin once removed of Q.

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother M who shares both of her parents. R’s father has exactly one brother N who shares only one parent with him (a half‑brother). question: In a family with no adoptions or multiple marriages, let M be a person. M’s father has a sister (M’s paternal aunt) who has a son N. N has a daughter O. What is O’s precise relationship to M using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: M’s paternal aunt is his father’s sister. Her son N is M’s first cousin. N’s daughter O is the child of M’s first cousin, making O M’s first cousin once removed. No other shared ancestors affect this classification.

question: M and N are siblings (they share at least one parent, but it is not specified whether they are full or half siblings). M has a child X; N has a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: If M and N are full siblings, X and Y are first cousins. If they are half‑siblings, X and Y are half‑first cousins. Because the sibling type is unknown, the exact term cannot be fixed; it is not uniquely determinable.

question: Alice and Ben are siblings. Alice is married to Carl. Carl’s sister is Dana. Dana is married to Ethan. Ethan’s brother is Frank, who has a daughter Gina. question: Emma’s mother has a brother Carl. Carl’s daughter is Nina. Nina has a son Sam. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is Sam’s precise relation to Emma?
explanation: Carl is Emma’s maternal uncle, so Nina is Emma’s first cousin. Sam is Nina’s child, i.e., the child of Emma’s first cousin, which makes Sam Emma’s first cousin once removed. No other blood link exists.

question: Anna’s mother has exactly one brother, who has a daughter named Lily. Anna’s father has exactly one sister, who also has a daughter named Lily. If we refer to either Lily as Z, what is Z’s relationship to Anna?
explanation: Both possible Lilys are children of a sibling of one of Anna’s parents. A child of a parent’s brother or sister is a first cousin. Hence, regardless of which Lily is meant, Z is Anna’s first cousin.

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father. N’s mother is the sister of O’s father. O’s mother is the sister of P’s father. What is the precise blood relation of P to M using standard English kinship terms?
