question: John and Mark are brothers. Anna and Beth are sisters. John marries Anna and they have a son Carl. Mark marries Beth and they have a daughter Dana. Before Carl and Dana marry each other, what is the most precise blood‑relationship term for Carl and Dana?
explanation: John and Mark share both parents; Anna and Beth share both parents. Consequently Carl’s paternal grandparents equal Dana’s paternal grandparents, and Carl’s maternal grandparents equal Dana’s maternal grandparents. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: I have a paternal aunt (my father’s sister) who has exactly one son, and a maternal uncle (my mother’s brother) who has exactly one daughter. Their children each have one child, and those two grandchildren happen to be the same person, M. What is M’s precise relationship to me using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: My paternal aunt’s son is my first cousin; his child M is my first cousin once removed. Similarly, my maternal uncle’s daughter is also my first cousin, and her child M is again my first cousin once removed. Both descriptions refer to the same person, so M is uniquely a first cousin once removed.

question: John and Mark are brothers. Anna and Beth are sisters. John marries Anna and they have a son Carl; Mark marries Beth and they have a daughter Dana. Carl and Dana each marry unrelated partners and have children Ethan and Fiona respectively. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, ignoring in‑law extensions), what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Carl and Dana are double first cousins, sharing both grandparent pairs. Their children Ethan and Fiona therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins – the only term that reflects the doubled ancestry at the second‑cousin level.

question: John is the son of Mary. Mary’s sister Linda is married to Tom, who is Paul’s brother. Paul has a daughter Emma. Linda and Tom have a son Kevin. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the relation between Emma and Kevin?
explanation: Linda and Mary are sisters, so their children are first cousins. Tom is Paul’s brother, making Emma Tom’s niece. Kevin is Tom’s son, so Emma and Kevin are first cousins. No other connections alter this.

question: Person P's mother has a brother whose daughter is Q. P's father has a sister whose son is R. Q and R marry and have a child S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relationship between P and S?
explanation: Q is P's maternal first cousin; R is P's paternal first cousin. S is the child of each of P's first cousins, making S a first cousin once removed to P on both sides. No doubling occurs, so the exact term is "first cousin once removed".

question: M and N share only one parent (they are half‑siblings). M has a child X and N has a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share only one parent, making them half‑siblings. Their children X and Y each inherit the grandparent that M and N share, but not the other grandparent. Thus X and Y share exactly one grandparent, which is the definition of half‑first cousins. No other kinship term fits more precisely.

question: M and N are siblings. M has two children: daughter A and son D. N has a son B. D has a daughter C, who later marries B. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise blood relationship between B and C?
explanation: M and N are siblings, so their children (A, D, B) are first cousins. D is B's first cousin, and C is D's daughter. Therefore B is one generation above C relative to the same ancestor, making B C's first cousin once removed. No other blood link exists.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: M is the mother of N and O. N is married to P. P's sister Q is married to O's son R. What is the precise kinship term for Q in relation to M?
explanation: M’s children are N and O. N’s husband P is M’s son‑in‑law. P’s sister Q is not blood‑related to M. Q marries O’s son R, who is M’s grandson. Therefore Q is the spouse of M’s grandson, i.e., M’s granddaughter‑in‑law. No other listed term fits.

question: N’s father has exactly one sister and N’s mother has exactly one brother. The sister and the brother each marry unrelated partners and together have a single child M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and also the child of N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Hence M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making M a double first cousin of N.

question: Alex’s mother has a brother Ben, whose daughter is Clara. Alex’s father has a sister Dana, whose son is Ethan. Ethan marries Clara. Alex and Ethan each have one child: Alex’s child is Fiona, Ethan’s child is George. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between Fiona and George?
explanation: Ethan and Clara are Alex’s paternal and maternal first cousins respectively. Their child George is therefore the child of two of Alex’s first cousins, sharing both sets of great‑grandparents with Alex. Hence George (and likewise Fiona) is Alex’s double first cousin once removed, making Fiona and George double first cousins once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: X’s mother has a brother M and a sister S. M is married to a woman who is the sister of X’s father. S is married to a man who is the brother of X’s father’s sister. Who is the child of M and his wife to X, using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted)?
explanation: M is X’s maternal uncle; his wife is X’s paternal aunt. Their child shares both sets of grandparents with X, making them double first cousins.

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamy, each parent has exactly one sibling. Let X be the child of the only sibling of Y’s mother, and also the child of the only sibling of Y’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (excluding any “in‑law” designations), what is the precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X is simultaneously the child of Y’s maternal uncle and paternal uncle. Therefore X shares both pairs of grandparents with Y, making them first cousins on both sides—i.e., double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: M is the mother of J. J is married to L. L’s brother is K. K is married to N, who is the daughter of M’s brother. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is N to J?
explanation: J’s spouse L has a brother K, making K J’s brother‑in‑law. N is K’s wife, i.e., the spouse of J’s brother‑in‑law. No standard term exists for the spouse of a brother‑in‑law, so the relation is only an affinal chain with no direct kinship label.
choices: A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M and N share only the same mother (they are half‑siblings). M has a daughter A, and N has a son B. There are no other family intermarriages. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between A and B?
explanation: M and N are half‑siblings, so they share one parent. Their children therefore share only that one grandparent, not a full pair. The exact term for such children is "half‑first cousins".

question: John and Paul are brothers. John is married to Mary and Paul is married to Anna. Mary and Anna are sisters. John and Mary have a son Mark; Paul and Anna have a daughter Lily. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring any special “double‑cousin” jargon), what is the most precise term for the relationship between Mark and Lily?
explanation: Mark and Lily share both sets of grandparents: John‑Paul’s parents (paternal side) and Mary‑Anna’s parents (maternal side). Hence they are first cousins on two independent lines, i.e., double first cousins, the most specific label available.

question: John’s mother has a brother Mike. John’s father has a sister Lisa. Mike marries Lisa, and they have a daughter Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring any remarriage or adoption), what is Emma’s precise relation to John?
explanation: Mike is John’s maternal uncle, making Emma his first cousin on that side. Lisa is John’s paternal aunt, making Emma also his first cousin on that side. Because the same child is the offspring of both a maternal uncle and a paternal aunt, Emma is a double first cousin of John.

question: N's father has exactly one sibling, a brother F; N's mother has exactly one sibling, a sister M. F and M are married and have a child X. Using standard English kinship terms, what is X's precise relation to N?
explanation: X is the child of N's paternal uncle (F) and maternal aunt (M). Since those two relatives are married, X is simultaneously N's first cousin on the father's side and on the mother's side, making X a double first cousin of N.

question: M is the mother of N. N’s sister (by the same mother) is O. O’s child is P. M’s brother’s child is Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of P to Q?
explanation: O is M’s daughter, so Q (child of M’s brother) is O’s first cousin. P is O’s child, making P the child of a first cousin of Q, i.e., first cousin once removed.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed

question: M is the child of the only sister of N's father and also the child of the only brother of N's mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relationship between M and N?
explanation: M’s mother is N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and M’s father is N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus M is the child of both a paternal aunt and a maternal uncle, making M a double first cousin of N—the only precise term.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, N marries P, and O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child A; N and P have a child B. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relationship between A and B?
explanation: A’s father and B’s father are brothers, and A’s mother and B’s mother are sisters. Thus A and B share both sets of grandparents, giving them the exact term “double first cousins,” which is more specific than merely “first cousins.”

question: Arrange A–J in a straight row of nine seats numbered left‑to‑right 1 through 9. H sits in seat 1; A sits immediately to H’s right; I sits immediately to A’s right; J sits in seat 9; D sits in seat 8; the block B–E–G occupies three consecutive seats in that order, entirely within seats 4–7; and C sits somewhere to the left of D but is not adjacent to A or to B. Which set lists all and only the seats that C can occupy?
explanation: Seats 1‑3 and 8‑9 are fixed. The block B‑E‑G can be placed either at 4‑6 (leaving seat 7 free) or at 5‑7 (leaving seat 4 free). In the second placement C would be at 4, adjacent to B at 5, which is forbidden. Hence only the first placement works, forcing C to seat 7. So the only possible seat for C is 7.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Their wives, Emily and Fiona, are also sisters. Adam and Emily have a daughter Clara. Brian and Fiona have a son Daniel. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relationship between Clara and Daniel?
explanation: Clara and Daniel are children of two brothers (paternal side) and also children of two sisters (maternal side). They share both sets of grandparents, giving them the exact term “double first cousins.”

question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Assuming those two spouses are married to each other, what is the precise kinship term for M in relation to N?
explanation: M is the offspring of N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Because those two are married, M shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making M N’s double first cousin.

question: M and N are brother and sister. M marries O, and N marries P. O and P are also brother and sister (no other intermarriages). X is the child of M and O; Y is the child of N and P. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share both parents, and O and P share both parents. Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents (paternal and maternal). They are first cousins through two independent lines, i.e., double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: R’s mother has a brother M who is married to R’s father’s sister F. M and F have a child S. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the most precise relation of S to R?
explanation: M is R’s maternal uncle; F is R’s paternal aunt. Their marriage makes S the child of both R’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, so S shares both sets of grandparents with R. This is exactly a double first cousin, the most specific label.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter D. N has a son Q, who in turn has a son P. D marries P. Using standard English kinship terms (blood and affinal limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is D's relation to Q?
explanation: D is the spouse of Q's child P, making her Q's daughter‑in‑law. Although D is also Q's first cousin by blood, the affinal term is the single, precise kinship label required here; it directly defines the relationship without ambiguity.

question: M and N are siblings. M has two children, A and D; N has two children, B and E. A marries B and they have a child C. D marries E and they have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between C and F?
explanation: A and D are siblings; B and E are siblings. Each sibling from M marries a sibling from N, so the two couples are two pairs of siblings. Their children (C and F) therefore share both grandparents M and N, making them double first cousins.

question: R’s mother has one brother U, and R’s father has one sister V. U’s only child is X; V’s only child is Y. If we select either X or Y and call that person S, what is S to R (using standard English kinship terms, no adoption, monogamy allowed)?
explanation: Both X and Y are children of R’s parental siblings (maternal uncle and paternal aunt). A child of any parent’s sibling is a first cousin, regardless of which side. Hence S is always R’s first cousin.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let A be a man. A's only brother is B, who has a daughter C. A is married to D, whose only brother is E, who has a son F. C and F marry and have a child G. What is the precise standard English kinship term for G's relation to A?
explanation: C is A's niece (daughter of his brother). G is the child of A's niece, which makes G A's grandniece. The term “grandniece” is the exact standard label; other options describe different generations or add an in‑law element.

question: Emma and Noah are siblings. Noah has a son Victor. Emma has a daughter Clara, who marries Victor. Victor and Clara have a son Ethan. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Ethan's relation to Emma's mother?
explanation: Emma's mother is the grandmother of Clara (her daughter) and the great‑grandmother of Ethan through Clara. question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions, let Z be the child of the only sibling of L’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Z’s exact relation to L?
explanation: Z is the offspring of L’s maternal uncle (the mother’s only sibling). The child of a parent’s sibling is always a first cousin, regardless of gender. No other blood link is introduced, so the precise term is “first cousin.”

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter A; N has a son B. A marries C, who is the only child of D. D is the sister of B’s wife E. What is C’s precise kinship to E?
explanation: M and N are siblings, so A and B are first cousins. D is sister of E, making D E’s sibling. C is D’s child, therefore C is the niece/nephew of E by blood. No other blood link exists, so the exact term is niece/nephew.

question: M's mother has a sister (M's maternal aunt) who is married to M's father's brother (M's paternal uncle). Their daughter is N. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of N to M?
explanation: N is the child of M's maternal aunt and paternal uncle, so N shares both of M's sets of grandparents. This makes N and M double first cousins, the exact term for cousins who share both grandparent pairs.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary is married to Tom. Tom’s brother Peter marries John’s daughter Anna. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is Peter’s relation to Anna?
explanation: Peter is married to Anna, making him Anna’s husband. No other blood or affinal link exists between them, so the precise term is son‑in‑law (to John) and husband (to Anna). Hence the correct choice is D.

question: Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law beyond spouse), let A be a person. A’s mother and B’s father are siblings. B’s mother and C’s father are siblings. C is married to A. What is the precise blood relation between A and B?
explanation: A’s mother and B’s father being siblings makes B’s father A’s maternal uncle. B, as child of that uncle, is A’s first cousin. The extra information about C does not alter this blood link, so the only correct term is “first cousin.”

question: Let X be a person such that X is the child of the only brother of Y’s mother and also the child of the only brother of Y’s father. Assuming monogamy, no adoption, and that the two uncles are distinct individuals, what is the precise kinship term for X relative to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and also the child of Y’s paternal uncle (father’s brother). In either case X is the child of a parent’s sibling, which is the definition of a first cousin. The uncles are different, so there is no doubling; the relation is simply first cousin.

question: M is married to N. N’s sister O is married to P. P’s brother Q is married to R, who is the daughter of M’s brother S. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Q’s relation to O?
explanation: O is married to P, who is Q’s brother; thus O is the wife of Q’s brother, i.e., Q’s sister‑in‑law. No blood link or other in‑law chain changes this.

question: Grandparents G₁ & G₂ have children A (son) and B (daughter). Grandparents H₁ & H₂ have children C (daughter) and D (son). A marries C and B marries D. A + C have a child X; B + D have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents (G₁‑G₂ and H₁‑H₂) because their parents are cross‑siblings. They are therefore double first cousins, a term more precise than plain first cousins, half‑first cousins, or second cousins.

question: M is the only child of his mother. His mother’s sister (M’s maternal aunt) is married to M’s father’s brother (paternal uncle by marriage). M’s father’s sister (paternal aunt) is married to M’s mother’s brother (maternal uncle by blood). Who is M’s father’s sister’s husband to M?
explanation: M’s father’s sister is his paternal aunt. She is married to M’s mother’s brother, who is M’s maternal uncle by blood. Hence the relation is maternal uncle.

question: L’s mother has exactly one brother, and L’s father has exactly one sister. The brother and the sister marry each other and have a single child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s maternal uncle (first‑cousin connection) and also the child of L’s paternal aunt (another first‑cousin connection). Being a first cousin through both parental lines makes M a double first cousin of L.

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoption, let Z be the child of the only brother of L’s mother and also the child of the only sister of L’s father. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for Z in relation to L?
explanation: Z’s mother is the sister of L’s father, making Z a first cousin on the paternal side. Z’s father is the brother of L’s mother, making Z a first cousin on the maternal side as well. Sharing both grandparent pairs yields the exact term “double first cousin.”

question: John and his sister Mary share the same parents. Mary’s son Peter marries Susan, who is the daughter of John’s son Michael. Using standard English kinship terms and assuming no adoption, what is the most precise blood relationship between Peter and Susan?
explanation: Peter is Mary’s son, making him a grandchild of John’s parents. Susan is Michael’s daughter, a great‑grandchild of the same parents. They share the same set of grandparents but are offset by one generation, which is defined as first cousins once removed.

question: Adam and Beth are siblings. Adam’s son is David. Beth’s daughter is Clara, whose sister is Emma. Emma’s son is Frank, and Frank’s son is George. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, and no in‑law extensions), what is the precise relationship of George to David?

explanation: Z is X’s nephew (child of X’s sister). U is the daughter of X’s brother‑in‑law, making her X’s niece‑in‑law. There is no blood link between Z and U, and the affinal chain exceeds the allowed in‑law scope, so no standard direct kin term exists.

question: In a traditional monogamous family, M is the sibling of Q’s parent. No information is given about the gender of M or the gender of Q’s parent. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no in‑law extensions), what is the precise term for M’s relation to Q?
explanation: M is the brother or sister of Q’s parent, so M could be an aunt or an uncle. Without gender information the exact term cannot be fixed; the only correct description is that the relation is not uniquely determinable.

question: In a family with monogamy, no adoptions, and no multiple births, let X be the child of the only sibling of Y’s father and also the child of the only sibling of Y’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s paternal uncle (father’s sibling) and also the child of Y’s maternal uncle (mother’s sibling). Thus X is a first cousin on both sides, i.e., a double first cousin. No other term is more specific.

question: In a family with no adoptions or multiple marriages, let R be a person. A is the only brother of R’s mother, and B is the only sister of R’s father. explanation: Both S and T are children of R's parent's siblings—one a maternal uncle, the other a paternal aunt. In either case they share a set of grandparents with R, so X is a first cousin of R.

question: John has a son Michael with his first wife Anna. After Anna dies, John marries Lisa, who already has a daughter Sarah from a previous marriage. Michael and Sarah later marry and have a child Emma. What is Emma's relation to Lisa?
explanation: Lisa is Michael's step‑mother and Sarah's biological mother, so Emma is simultaneously her step‑granddaughter (via Michael) and granddaughter (via Sarah). Hence the precise kin term is ambiguous.

question: Person X’s mother is the sister of A, and X’s father is the brother of B. There are no adoptions, no incest, and all individuals are distinct. Using standard English blood‑relation terms, what is the precise relationship between A and B?
explanation: A is the maternal aunt/uncle of X; B is the paternal aunt/uncle of X. They share no common ancestor, so there is no blood kinship term linking A and B. Hence they are unrelated by blood.

question: Alex’s mother has a brother (Alex’s maternal uncle). That uncle’s son marries Alex’s father’s sister (Alex’s paternal aunt). The couple’s child is Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no in‑law extensions), what is Emma’s relation to Alex?
explanation: Emma is the child of Alex’s paternal aunt, making her Alex’s first cousin. She is also the child of Alex’s maternal cousin, which would be a first cousin once removed, but the closest blood link (first cousin) prevails as the most precise term.

question: Emma's father's brother (her paternal uncle) married a woman who is also the sister of Emma's mother's brother (her maternal uncle). Emma's cousin Lily is the child of that couple. What is Lily's precise relation to Emma?
explanation: Lily is the child of Emma’s paternal uncle (father’s brother) and her maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Therefore Lily shares both of Emma’s grandparents on the father's side and both on the mother’s side, making her a double first cousin of Emma.

question: Person X’s mother is the sister of Person Y’s father. Person X has a child Z. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Z’s precise relation to Person Y?

question: Brothers Alan and Brian each marry sisters Clara and Diana respectively. Alan and Clara have a son Ethan. Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than ordinary first cousins.

question: My father's sister's son is married to my mother's brother's daughter. What is the precise kinship term for that spouse with respect to me, using standard English blood‑relation terminology only?
explanation: Father's sister's son = my paternal first cousin. Mother's brother's daughter = my maternal first cousin. They are married, so the spouse of my paternal cousin is my maternal cousin, i.e., a first cousin. Hence the correct answer is B.

question: In a family, a brother B and his sister S are siblings. B marries a woman W, whose brother is K. S marries K. B and W have a daughter D1; S and K have a son S1. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between D1 and S1?

question: M is the child of the only brother of L’s mother and also the child of the only sister of L’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: M’s mother is L’s maternal uncle (her mother’s brother) and M’s father is L’s paternal aunt’s brother (her father’s brother). Thus M is the child of a sibling of L’s mother and a sibling of L’s father, sharing both sets of grandparents. The exact term is double first cousin.

question: John is married to Mary. Mary’s sister Anna is married to Peter. Peter’s brother Luke is married to Susan, who is the daughter of John’s brother Michael. What is the precise standard English kinship term for the relation between Luke and Mary?
explanation: Susan is John’s niece (child of his brother Michael). As Mary is John’s wife, Susan is also Mary’s niece by marriage. Luke, being Susan’s husband, is therefore Mary’s nephew‑in‑law. No blood relation exists, only this affinal link.

question: M is the mother of N. N’s sibling is O. O’s child is P. P’s spouse is Q. Q’s mother, R, is M’s sister. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no in‑law extensions), what is Q’s relation to N?
explanation: R is M’s sister, so R is N’s aunt. Q is R’s child, making Q N’s first cousin. The marriage of Q to N’s niece/nephew (P) does not affect the blood relation.

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamy, let R be any person. Define S as the child of the only brother of R’s mother, or alternatively the child of the only brother of R’s father (you may pick either cousin). Who is S to R?
explanation: Whether S is the child of R’s maternal uncle or paternal uncle, S is always the child of a parent’s brother. That makes S a first cousin of R.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John has two sons, Tom and Mark. Mary has a daughter, Lisa. Lisa marries Tom. What is the precise kinship term for the relation between Mark and Anna, the child of Tom and Lisa?
explanation: Mark is Tom's brother, so he is Anna's paternal uncle. Although Mark is also a first cousin of Lisa, the most specific term for his relation to Anna is "uncle".

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P. O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: M and N share parents, O and P share parents, and the two sibling pairs married each other. Thus X and Y are first cousins through both paternal and maternal lines, i.e., double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), A is married to B. B’s sister is C. C’s husband is D. D’s sister is E. What is E to A?

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Adam marries Clara and Brian marries Diana, who are sisters. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. explanation: Ethan’s father Adam and Fiona’s mother Diana are siblings, and Ethan’s mother Clara and Fiona’s father Brian are also siblings. Thus Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy, and no incest, let A and B be two distinct individuals. A is the child of the only brother of B’s mother. B is the child of the only brother of A’s mother. What is the precise kinship term for the relation between A and B?
explanation: If the two maternal uncles are the same person (the mothers are sisters), A and B are double first cousins. question: John has a sister Mary. John’s son is Michael; Mary’s son is Peter. Michael’s daughter is Lisa. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise blood relation of Peter to Lisa?
explanation: Peter is Mary’s son, making him John’s nephew. Michael is John’s son, so Peter and Michael are first cousins. Lisa is Michael’s daughter; therefore Peter is the first cousin of Lisa’s father, which makes him Lisa’s first cousin once removed. This is the most specific standard term.

question: Brothers John and James each marry sisters Mary and Margaret, respectively. John and Mary have a son Peter; James and Margaret have a daughter Paula. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is the most precise relation between Alan and Betty?
explanation: Peter and Paula are double first cousins, sharing both sets of grandparents. Their children, Alan and Betty, therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the most specific term.

question: In a family with monogamous marriages and no adoptions, J’s mother is married to her husband. The brother of that husband has a child named M. What is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to J?
explanation: J’s mother’s husband is J’s father. His brother is J’s paternal uncle. The uncle’s child is J’s first cousin on the paternal side. No other blood links are involved, so the exact term is “first cousin.”

question: M and N are full siblings. M marries X and they have a daughter A. N marries Y (who is X’s sister) and they have a son B. A and B marry each other and have a child C. explanation: Peter and Paula are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent. The exact term for such children is “half‑first cousins”.

question: P is the child of the only brother of Q’s mother and also the child of the only sister of Q’s father. Assuming the two parents are married (or otherwise co‑parents), what is the precise kinship term for P’s relation to Q using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: The mother’s brother is Q’s maternal uncle; the father’s sister is Q’s paternal aunt. Their union produces P, who is simultaneously the child of Q’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Thus P shares both sets of grandparents with Q, making P a double first cousin of Q.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?

question: N’s mother has a brother who is married to N’s father’s sister. They have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring adoption, remarriage, and in‑law extensions), what is M’s precise relation to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Because those two relatives are married, M shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making M a double first cousin of N—the most specific term.

question: John’s mother has a brother named Tom. Tom has a daughter Lisa, and Lisa has a son Mark. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Mark’s precise relationship to John?
explanation: Tom is John’s maternal uncle, so his daughter Lisa is John’s first cousin. Lisa’s son Mark is one generation younger than a first cousin, making him John’s first cousin once removed.

question: R is the child of S. S and T are siblings. T is the parent of U, and U is the parent of V. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between R and V?
explanation: S and T are siblings, so R (S’s child) and U (T’s child) are first cousins. V is U’s child, making V one generation below U. Therefore R and V are first cousins once removed, the exact standard term.

question: M and N are married. M has a brother O. N has a sister P. O marries P, and they have a daughter Q. M and N have a son R. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation between Q and R?
explanation: O is M’s brother, so Q shares M’s parents as grandparents. P is N’s sister, so Q also shares N’s parents as grandparents. R’s grandparents are exactly M’s and N’s parents. Thus Q and R share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: Two brothers each marry two sisters. The first couple has a son P; the second couple has a son Q. P and Q are therefore double first cousins. P has a daughter A and Q has a son B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between A and B?

explanation: X is the child of both P’s maternal uncle and paternal uncle, sharing all four grandparents with P. This makes X a double first cousin of P, the most specific standard term.

question: R is the child of the only child of S's mother, and also the child of the only child of T's father. No adoptions, monogamy, and no multiple births are assumed. What is R's precise kinship relation to S?

question: M’s mother has exactly one brother, who has a son S. M’s father has exactly one sister, who also has a son S (the same S). There are no other intermarriages. What is the precise kinship term for S in relation to M, using standard English terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry?
