explanation: E and F share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins. Their children G and H therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins, the most precise standard term.

question: L has one child X. M is X’s son. L’s sister is N. N’s daughter is O, and O’s son is P. What is the precise relationship between M and P using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: X and O are children of siblings (L and N), so they are first cousins. Their children, M and P, are therefore children of first cousins, which makes them second cousins. No half‑blood or removal applies.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: Let L be a person. L’s mother has exactly one brother, and L’s father has exactly one sister. A child, M, is the offspring of the brother of L’s mother and also the offspring of the sister of L’s father (the two spouses are unrelated). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: M could be the child of L’s maternal uncle (making M a first cousin) or the child of L’s paternal aunt (also a first cousin). Since the two spouses are unrelated, M is simultaneously the child of an uncle and an aunt, but the direction (maternal vs paternal) is unspecified, so the exact term cannot be fixed beyond “first cousin”. Hence the relation is not uniquely determinable.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M and N are half‑siblings (they share only a mother). M has a daughter X, and N has a son Y. No other intermarriages exist. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent. The precise term for such a relationship is "half‑first cousins"; full first cousins require both grandparents, and any more distant term would be inaccurate.

question: Two brothers, Alan and Brian, each marry a sister, Clara and Diana, respectively (Clara and Diana are sisters). Alan and Clara have a child, Emma; Brian and Diana have a child, Frank. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Emma and Frank?
explanation: Emma and Frank share both sets of grandparents: Alan and Brian share the same parents, and Clara and Diana share the same parents. Hence they are first cousins through two independent lines, i.e., double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: M is the child of the only sibling of N’s father and also the child of the only sibling of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M’s father (or mother) is N’s paternal aunt/uncle, and M’s mother (or father) is N’s maternal aunt/uncle. Thus M shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: M is the child of the only son of R’s father’s sister. N is the child of the only daughter of R’s mother’s brother. What is the precise blood relationship between M and N?
explanation: R’s father’s sister is R’s paternal aunt; her only son is R’s male first cousin, whose child M is R’s first cousin once removed. R’s mother’s brother is R’s maternal uncle; his only daughter is R’s female first cousin, whose child N is also R’s first cousin once removed. The two cousins come from unrelated paternal and maternal lines, so M and N share no common ancestor.

question: Mike and Tom are brothers. Anna and Beth are sisters. Mike marries Anna and they have a son Carl. Tom marries Beth and they have a daughter Dana. Carl and Dana each marry unrelated partners and have children: Carl’s child Eva and Dana’s child Frank. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Eva and Frank?
explanation: Mike‑Anna and Tom‑Beth are double sibling couples, so Carl and Dana are double first cousins (they share both grandparent pairs). Their children Eva and Frank therefore share both great‑grandparent pairs, making them double second cousins—the most specific term.

question: A is the son of B’s mother‑in‑law. Using only standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is A’s relation to B?
explanation: B’s mother‑in‑law is the mother of B’s spouse. A is her son, so A is the sibling of B’s spouse. The sibling of one’s spouse is a brother‑in‑law (if male) or sister‑in‑law (if female). Hence A is B’s brother‑in‑law.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: P is the child of the only brother of Q’s mother. Q is the child of the only sister of P’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: P is the child of Q’s maternal uncle, making P and Q first cousins. Likewise, Q is the child of P’s paternal aunt, also making them first cousins. Both statements guarantee a first‑cousin relationship; no further precision (half‑cousin, double cousin) is implied.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a son Ethan. Brian marries Diana and they have a daughter Fiona. Ignoring any other relatives, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Adam and Brian share both parents; Clara and Diana share both parents. Their children Ethan and Fiona therefore share both sets of grandparents, i.e., they have the same four grandparents. The precise term for such cousins is double first cousins.
choices: C) C) First cousins once removed

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father M and Y’s father N are brothers, and X’s mother O and Y’s mother P are sisters. Therefore X and Y share both paternal and maternal grandparents, making them double first cousins—the exact term for this doubled ancestry.

question: John and Lisa are half‑siblings, sharing only their father Mark. John and his wife Emma have a son Aaron. Lisa and her husband Paul have a daughter Bella. No other intermarriages exist. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Aaron and Bella?
explanation: Aaron and Bella are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent (Mark). The exact term for such children is “half‑first cousins”. Full first cousins require both grandparents in common, which they do not have.

question: Person A has one sibling, a brother, and one sibling, a sister. Person Z is known to be the child of either A's brother or A's sister, but Z's gender is not given. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Z's relation to A?
explanation: If Z is the brother's child, Z is A's nephew; if Z is the sister's child, Z is A's niece. Without Z's gender the precise term cannot be fixed, making the relation indeterminate among nephew or niece.

question: Tom's mother has a brother named Jeff. Sarah's father has a sister named Laura. Jeff and Laura are married and have a son named Ethan. Assuming no other blood connections among Tom, Sarah, Jeff, and Laura, what is Ethan's relationship to Tom?
explanation: Jeff is Tom's maternal uncle, so his child Ethan is Tom's first cousin. Ethan is not Tom's uncle, half‑cousin, or unrelated; a standard kin term (first cousin) applies uniquely.

question: M's mother has exactly one brother, A, and M's father has exactly one sister, B. A and B are married and have a single child, C. What is C's most precise relation to M using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: C is child of M's maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Through the uncle, C shares M's maternal grandparents; through the aunt, C shares M's paternal grandparents. Thus C shares both grandparent pairs with M, making them double first cousins—the most specific standard term.

question: P and Q are each the child of a different couple. P’s father is the sole son of R, and P’s mother is the sole daughter of S. Q’s father is the same sole son of R, while Q’s mother is the sole daughter of T. No other marriages or adoptions occur. What is the precise blood relation between P and Q?
explanation: Both P and Q share the same father (the only son of R) but have different mothers. Sharing exactly one parent makes them half‑siblings, and no other shared ancestors exist, so the correct term is “half‑siblings.”

question: Anna and Ben are siblings. Clara is the only child of Anna's brother. David is the only child of Ben's sister. Emma is Clara's child. Fiona is David's child. What is the precise kinship term between Emma and Fiona?
explanation: Anna and Ben are siblings, so Anna's brother is Ben and Ben's sister is Anna. Clara (Ben's child) and David (Anna's child) are first cousins. Their children, Emma and Fiona, are therefore second cousins.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P. O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: M and N share parents, and O and P share parents. Hence they are children of two couples who are each other's siblings, making X and Y double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: L’s mother and N’s father are half‑siblings (they share only a mother). There are no other intermarriages. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between L and N?
explanation: L’s mother and N’s father share only one parent, so L and N share only one grandparent. That makes them half‑first cousins; full first cousins would require both grandparents in common.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: X’s mother has a brother who is married to Y’s mother. Y’s father is the brother of X’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father’s brother is Y’s father, so X and Y share the same paternal grandparents, making them first cousins. The maternal uncle is only an aunt by marriage, adding no blood link. Hence the precise term is first cousins.

question: E and F are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). E has a child G, and F has a child H. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise kinship term for G and H?
explanation: E and F share one parent, so they are half‑siblings. Their children each have only one grandparent in common (the shared parent’s parent). Thus G and H are first cousins who share only a single grandparent, i.e., half‑first cousins. No other relationship applies.

question: Two brothers, Tom and Victor, each marry a woman who is the sister of the other's wife. Tom marries Anna, Victor marries Beth, and Anna and Beth are sisters. Their respective children are Maya (Tom and Anna’s child) and Victor Jr. (Victor and Beth’s child). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Maya and Victor Jr.?
explanation: Maya and Victor Jr. share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. This makes them double first cousins – first cousins with doubled ancestry.

question: Emily's mother has a brother named Tom. Tom has a daughter named Sara. Sara has a son named Leo. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Leo to Emily?
explanation: Emily’s mother’s brother is Emily’s maternal uncle. His daughter Sara is Emily’s first cousin. Sara’s son Leo is one generation younger, making him Emily’s first cousin once removed.

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father, and M’s father is the brother of N’s mother. Assuming monogamy, no adoption, and that all individuals are distinct, what is the precise kinship term for the relationship between M and N?
explanation: M’s mother and N’s father are siblings, making M the child of N’s paternal aunt. Simultaneously, M’s father and N’s mother are siblings, making M the child of N’s maternal uncle. Thus M and N are children of two sibling pairs who married each other, which defines double first cousins.

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoption, X's mother has a brother whose daughter is Y. X's father has a sister whose son is Z. Y and Z marry and have a child W. Using standard English kinship terms, what is W's relation to X?
explanation: Y is X's maternal first cousin; Z is X's paternal first cousin. Their child W is one generation below X, making W the child of X's first cousins. The precise term for a child of one's first cousin is "first cousin once removed."
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: John is the son of Mary. After John’s birth, Mary marries Peter, whose sister is Susan. Susan is the mother of Lisa, and Lisa is married to Tom. Tom is the son of Michael, who is John’s half‑brother. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Tom’s relation to Peter?
explanation: Tom is the child of John’s half‑brother, making him John’s half‑nephew. Peter is John’s step‑father and has no blood tie to John’s siblings. Because step‑relations are not counted as in‑law beyond the spouse, Tom’s precise kinship to Peter cannot be fixed; it varies with the unknown parent of Michael. Hence the relation is not uniquely determinable.

question: M and N are full siblings. O and P are full siblings. M marries O and N marries P. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. X and Y (who are double first cousins) marry and have a child Z. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for Z’s relation to M’s mother?
explanation: M’s mother is grandmother of both X and Y (each is her grandchild via a different child). Z is the child of those grandchildren, so she is a great‑grandchild through two independent lines, i.e., a double great‑grandchild. Simpler terms ignore the duplication, but the precise label is “double great‑grandchild.”

question: M is the son of father A and mother F. A has a sister B. B’s son is C. C is married to D, who is the daughter of E. E is the brother of M’s mother F. What is D’s precise relationship to M using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed)?
explanation: E is M’s maternal uncle, so his daughter D is M’s first cousin by blood. The marriage of D to C does not alter the blood relationship, so D is M’s first cousin.

question: L is the only child of M. M has a sister N, who together with her husband O has a daughter P. P is married to Q, and they have a son R. Using only blood relations (ignore spouses), what is the precise relation of L to R?
explanation: M’s sister N is L’s aunt. N’s daughter P is L’s first cousin. P’s son R is therefore the child of L’s first cousin, i.e., L’s first cousin once removed. No closer blood term applies.

question: R’s mother has a brother named M. M’s daughter is S. R’s father has a sister named N. N’s son is T. S and T marry each other. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise blood relation between R and S?
explanation: S is the child of R’s maternal uncle (the brother of R’s mother). That makes S R’s first cousin. Their marriage to T does not change the blood link.

question: P’s father has a sister who is married, and P’s mother has a brother who is married. Their respective spouses each have a child: M is the child of P’s paternal aunt and also the child of P’s maternal uncle. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of M to P?
explanation: M is the child of P’s father’s sister (paternal aunt) → first cousin, and also the child of P’s mother’s brother (maternal uncle) → first cousin. Being a first cousin through both parents makes M a double first cousin of P, the most specific term.

question: Anna's mother has a brother named Tom. Tom's only child, Sam, marries the only son of Anna's father. What is Sam to Anna, using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed)?
explanation: Tom is Anna's maternal uncle, so Sam is Anna's first cousin. Sam marries Anna's only brother, making Sam the spouse of Anna's brother, i.e., Anna's brother‑in‑law. The affinal term uniquely captures the relationship.

question: In a monogamous family without adoption, let X be the child of the only brother of Y’s father, and also the child of the only sister of Y’s mother. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for X relative to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s paternal uncle and also the child of Y’s maternal aunt. Thus X shares both sets of grandparents with Y, making them double first cousins—the most specific standard term.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question:
In a family:
- A and B are full siblings.
- B is married to C.
- C's mother is D.
- D is the sister of A's father.
- E is the child of B and C.
Using standard English blood‑kin terms only (spouse allowed but no extended in‑law terms), what is the precise relation of E to D?
explanation: D is the sister of A's father, making her the paternal aunt of A and also of B. B's child E is therefore the grand‑child of D's sibling, i.e., D is E's great‑aunt. The exact term is great‑niece or great‑nephew, depending on E's gender.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: R's paternal grandmother has a brother G, and R's maternal grandfather has a brother H. G's son is A; H's son is B. If we pick either A or B and call that person S, what is S's precise relation to R using standard English blood‑kin terms?
explanation: G is the brother of R's paternal grandmother, making G R's great‑uncle; his son A is first cousin of R's father, thus A is R's first cousin once removed. Likewise, H is brother of R's maternal grandfather, so H is R's great‑uncle; his son B is first cousin of R's mother, also R's first cousin once removed. Hence whichever person S is chosen, the relation to R is first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a daughter X; N and P have a son Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their parents are double siblings (M–N and O–P). Therefore they are not merely first cousins; the exact term is double first cousins.

question: John and Mary are full siblings. John marries Anna, whose brother is Ben. Mary marries Ben. John and Anna have a daughter Lily; Mary and Ben have a son Mark. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Lily and Mark?
explanation: Lily’s father John is sibling of Mark’s mother Mary, giving them first‑cousin status. Simultaneously Lily’s mother Anna is sibling of Mark’s father Ben, providing a second, independent first‑cousin link. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the only term that captures both lines of descent.

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted, let A be the child of a man whose sister is B’s mother. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between A and B?
explanation: A’s father’s sister is B’s mother, so A and B are children of siblings. That makes them first cousins. No half‑sibling or double‑cousin conditions are present, so the precise term is simply "first cousin".

question: M is the only child of his mother N. N’s mother is O. O also has another child Q (different from N). P is the child of Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of P to M?
explanation: N and Q are siblings, both children of O. M is N’s child, P is Q’s child. Children of siblings are first cousins. Hence P is M’s first cousin.

question: Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage possible): X is the son of the sister of Y’s mother. X is married to Z, who is the daughter of W. W is the brother of Y’s father. What is X’s relation to Y?
explanation: X is the son of Y’s mother’s sister, i.e., the child of Y’s maternal aunt. That makes X Y’s first cousin regardless of X’s marriage to Z, who is Y’s paternal cousin. Hence the precise kin term is “first cousin”.

question: N’s father has exactly one sister, and N’s mother has exactly one brother. The sister and the brother marry each other and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus M shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making M a double first cousin of N. No other term is more precise.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P. O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: M and N share parents, and O and P share parents. Thus each child receives the same maternal and paternal grandparents, making them double first cousins—the exact term for this doubled ancestry.

question: G has two children, a son B and a daughter A. B’s child is C. A’s child is D. C and D marry and have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms, what is E’s relation to G?
explanation: B and A are G’s children, so C and D are G’s grandchildren. Their child E is one generation below the grandchildren, making E a great‑grandchild of G. No other standard term fits.
choices: C) C) No direct blood relation

question: In a family, X's mother has a brother A. X's father has a sister B. A is married to C, and C is the sister of B. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of C to X?
explanation: C is the sister of X’s father’s sister, making her X’s paternal aunt by blood, and she is also married to X’s mother’s brother, making her X’s maternal aunt by marriage. Having both relations, the precise term is “double aunt.”

question: John and Peter are brothers. Their sisters‑in‑law, Mary and Anne, are also sisters. John marries Mary and Peter marries Anne. John and Mary have a daughter Lisa; Peter and Anne have a son Mark. Lisa and Mark each marry unrelated partners and have children. What is the most precise standard kinship term for the relationship between Lisa’s child and Mark’s child?
explanation: Lisa and Mark share both sets of grandparents (their parents are sibling pairs), making them double first cousins. Their children therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, which is precisely described as double second cousins.

question: L's father's sister (L's paternal aunt) has a child H. H later has a child K. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted), what is K's precise relation to L?
explanation: L's paternal aunt's child H is L's first cousin. K is H's child, so K is the child of L's first cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed.

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy allowed and remarriage permitted: B is the mother of A. B's brother is C. C's daughter is D. D's son is E. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only), what is the relation of E to A?
explanation: B is A's mother. C, B's brother, is A's maternal uncle. D, C's daughter, is A's first cousin. E, D's son, is the child of A's first cousin, i.e., A's first cousin once removed.

question: M is the only child of P. P has a brother Q. Q’s son R has a daughter S. What is the precise kinship term for S with respect to M?
explanation: P and Q are brothers, so Q is M’s paternal uncle. Q’s son R is therefore M’s first cousin. R’s daughter S is one generation below that cousin, making S M’s first cousin once removed. No closer or different term applies.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard relation (affinal only)

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother, and R’s father has exactly one sister. Both of these siblings have the same daughter, S (i.e., S is the child of R’s maternal uncle and also the child of R’s paternal aunt). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of S to R?
explanation: S is the child of R’s maternal uncle (brother of R’s mother) and also the child of R’s paternal aunt (sister of R’s father). She therefore shares both of R’s grandparent pairs, making her a double first cousin – the most specific term.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: Let B be a person. B’s paternal grandmother has exactly one child, and B’s maternal grandfather has exactly one child. A is the child of that only child of B’s paternal grandmother, and also the child of that only child of B’s maternal grandfather. What is A’s precise relation to B?
explanation: The only child of B’s paternal grandmother is B’s father; the only child of B’s maternal grandfather is B’s mother. A is the child of B’s father and also the child of B’s mother, making A B’s sibling (brother or sister).

question: Brothers Adam and Brian each marry sisters Clara and Diana respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona (who are double first cousins) each later marry unrelated partners and have children Liam and Grace respectively. What is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between Liam and Grace?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins. Their children Liam and Grace each inherit the same pair of great‑grandparent couples, making them second cousins with the same double ancestry—i.e., double second cousins. No other term is more precise.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: Two brothers, Alan and Brian, each marry a sister, Clara and Diana, respectively. Alan and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). Ethan's child George and Fiona's child Hannah are what precise kinship relation?
explanation: Since Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins, they share both pairs of grandparents. Their children therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins – the most specific term.
choices: C) C) First cousins once removed

question: Person X is the child of the only brother of Y’s mother, and also the child of the only sister of Y’s father. Assuming no intermarriage among relatives, what is the precise kinship term for X in relation to Y?
explanation: The brother of Y’s mother is Y’s maternal uncle; his child is Y’s first cousin. The sister of Y’s father is Y’s paternal aunt; her child is also Y’s first cousin. Both lines give the same standard term, with no extra distinction required. Hence X is Y’s first cousin.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: John and Mark are brothers; Anna and Beth are sisters. John marries Anna and they have a son Carl. Mark marries Beth and they have a daughter Dana. Carl and Dana (double first cousins) marry and have a child Ethan. Also, John marries Beth and they have a daughter Fiona; Mark marries Anna and they have a son George. Fiona and George (also double first cousins) marry and have a child Hannah. What is the most precise standard kinship term for Ethan and Hannah?
explanation: Carl and Dana share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins; their child Ethan inherits that doubled ancestry. Fiona and George are the same type, and their child Hannah shares the identical doubled grandparent pairs with Ethan. Thus Ethan and Hannah are double second cousins – children of double first cousins who themselves are double first cousins.
choices: A) A) First cousins once removed

question: In a family with no adoptions, let R be a person. The only brother of R's mother has a child X, and the only brother of R's father has a child Y. If one of X or Y (but not both) is selected and called S, what is the precise kinship term for S relative to R?
explanation: Whether S is X (child of R's maternal uncle) or Y (child of R's paternal uncle), S is always the child of a parent’s brother. That makes S a first cousin of R. No other relation fits uniquely.

question: M is the mother of two children, A and B, who have different fathers. A has a child C, and B has a child D. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for the relationship between C and D?
explanation: A and B are half‑siblings, sharing only M. Their children C and D therefore share a single grandparent (M) but not a full pair, making them half‑first cousins—the exact term.

question: W has one child, M. W’s brother, U, also has one child, N. M’s son is X, and N’s daughter is Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N are first cousins because their parents (W and U) are siblings. X is the child of M and Y is the child of N, so X and Y are the children of first cousins, which makes them second cousins. No half‑blood or doubled ancestry is involved.

question: In a family, a man P has a sister Q. Q marries R, who is the brother of P's wife S. P and S have a daughter T. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relationship of R to T?
explanation: R is the brother of T's mother S, making him T's maternal uncle. Although R is also married to P's sister Q, that does not change the blood relation; the only direct kin term is maternal uncle.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a sister, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a child, Ethan; Brian and Diana have a child, Fiona. Using only standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents: Adam and Brian’s parents as paternal grandparents, and Clara and Diana’s parents as maternal grandparents. The exact term for such a pair is “double first cousins.”

question: M is the brother of P's mother, and S is the sister of P's father. M and S are married to each other and have a child C. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between P and C?
explanation: M is P's maternal uncle and S is P's paternal aunt. Their child shares both of P's grandparents on the maternal side (through M) and on the paternal side (through S). Thus the child is related to P through two independent first‑cousin lines, i.e., a double first cousin. No other term fits more precisely.

question: Anna is the only child of Michael. Michael’s sister Clara is the mother of Ben. Ben has a daughter Dana. What is Dana’s relation to Anna using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Clara is Anna’s aunt, so Ben is Anna’s first cousin. Dana, as Ben’s daughter, is one generation below a first cousin, i.e., Anna’s first cousin once removed.

question: John's mother has a brother named Mark. John's father has a sister named Lisa. Mark and Lisa are married and have a child named Sam. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between John and Sam?
explanation: Mark is John’s maternal uncle, Lisa is John’s paternal aunt. Their child Sam is therefore John’s first cousin on his mother’s side and also his first cousin on his father’s side. When the same person is a cousin through both parental lines, the exact term is “double first cousin.”

question: M and N are married. M has a brother O, whose daughter is P. N has a sister Q, whose son is R. P and R marry and have a child S. What is the precise relation between S and M’s mother?
explanation: M’s mother is the grandmother of O’s daughter P, so P is her grandchild. S is P’s child, one generation further, making S the mother’s great‑grandchild. No other choice fits.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries P and N marries Q. P and Q are also siblings (no other intermarriages). M and N each have one child, X and Y respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of P/Q. This makes them first cousins on two separate lines, i.e., double first cousins. No other term captures the doubled shared ancestry.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents (the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P). Hence they are first cousins through two independent lines, i.e., double first cousins. No other term captures this dual shared ancestry.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, N marries P, and O and P are also siblings. M and O have a son X; N and P have a daughter Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father M and Y’s father N are brothers, and X’s mother O and Y’s mother P are sisters. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures this doubled ancestry.

question: John and Mark are brothers. Anna and Beth are sisters. John marries Anna and they have a son Carl. Mark marries Beth and they have a daughter Diana. Using standard English kinship terms without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between Carl and Diana?
explanation: Carl and Diana share both sets of grandparents: John‑Mark’s parents and Anna‑Beth’s parents. Hence they are first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides, i.e., double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: M is the only child of L. L has a sister N. N’s son is O, and O has a daughter P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of P to M?
explanation: L and N are sisters, so N is M’s aunt. O, N’s son, is M’s first cousin. P is O’s daughter, i.e., the child of M’s first cousin, making P M’s first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: Man A’s mother had two children, A and his half‑sister C (different father). Woman B’s father had two children, B and his half‑brother D (different mother). C marries D and they have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of E to A?
explanation: E is the child of A’s half‑sister C, sharing only one grandparent with A. Thus E is A’s half‑niece. No other blood link exists, so the term is uniquely determined.

question: Two brothers each marry two sisters. Each couple has exactly one child. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between the two children?
explanation: Each child’s father is the brother of the other child’s father, and each child’s mother is the sister of the other child’s mother. Thus they share both paternal and maternal grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures this doubled ancestry.

question: R is married to S. S’s father has a brother (S’s paternal uncle) who is married to T. T’s sister is U. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is U to R?
explanation: U is the sister of T, who is the wife of S’s paternal uncle. This makes T R’s aunt‑in‑law, but U is merely T’s sister, with no blood or direct affinal link to R. No standard term exists for this relationship; it is an affinal chain only.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John’s mother has a brother Tom. Tom’s daughter Alice is therefore John’s maternal first cousin. John’s father has a brother Mark, making Mark John’s paternal uncle. Alice and Mark marry and have a child Sam. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Sam’s precise relation to John?
explanation: Alice is John’s maternal first cousin and Mark is his paternal uncle. Their child Sam is therefore the child of John’s first cousin (making Sam a first cousin once removed) and also the child of John’s paternal uncle (making Sam a first cousin). Since Sam shares both of John’s sets of grandparents—maternal via Alice and paternal via Mark—the precise term is double first cousin.

question: Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses), consider: A is married to B; B’s brother is C; C’s wife is D; D’s brother is E; E is married to F; F’s mother is G; G’s brother is H. What is H to A?
explanation: The chain A→B (spouse) →C (spouse’s sibling) →D (that sibling’s spouse) →E (spouse’s sibling) →F (spouse) →G (spouse’s mother) →H (spouse’s mother’s brother). It never introduces a blood link and exceeds the immediate in‑law scope, so no standard kin term applies.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary’s daughter Lisa marries John’s son Mark. Lisa and Mark have a child Anna. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, but remarriage allowed), what is Anna’s relation to John?
explanation: John is Mark’s father, so Anna is his granddaughter. John is Mary’s brother, making Lisa his niece; thus Anna is also John’s great‑niece. The only precise description combines both lines of descent.
choices: D) D) Both granddaughter and great‑niece

question: P’s father has a sister who is married to Q’s mother’s brother. The child of that couple is M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation of M to P?
explanation: P’s paternal aunt’s child is a first cousin. The same child is also the child of P’s maternal uncle, giving a second, independent first‑cousin link. Because the two cousin relationships involve both shared grandparent pairs, the relationship is a double first cousin, the most specific term.

question: Arrange A–J in a straight row of ten seats numbered 1 (leftmost) to 10 (rightmost): H sits in seat 1; A sits immediately to H’s right; I sits immediately to A’s right; D sits in seat 9; F sits in seat 10; the block B–E–G occupies three consecutive seats in that left‑to‑right order somewhere within seats 4–8; and C sits somewhere to the left of D but is not adjacent to A or to B. Which set lists all and only the seats that C can occupy?
explanation: With H1–A2–I3 and D9–F10 fixed, the B‑E‑G block must occupy seats 4‑6, 5‑7, or 6‑8. C must be left of D, not next to A (seat 2) or B (the leftmost seat of the block). Checking each placement shows C can only be in seats 4, 7, or 8.

question: L’s mother has a brother M; M’s daughter is N, whose son is O. L’s father has a sister P; P’s son is Q. Q and O marry and have a child R. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise description of the relation between L and R?
explanation: N is L’s first cousin (maternal). O is N’s son, so O is L’s first cousin once removed (maternal). Q is L’s first cousin (paternal). R is child of Q (first cousin) and O (first cousin once removed). R is simultaneously L’s first cousin once removed (through Q) and L’s second cousin (through O). No single standard term captures both, so the precise answer is that there is no single standard kinship label.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed
C) C) No single standard kinship term (double relationship)

question: E and F are half‑siblings: they share the same father but have different mothers. E has a daughter G; F has a son H. No other intermarriages exist in the family. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between G and H?
explanation: G and H are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent (their common paternal grandfather). The exact term for such relatives is “half‑first cousins”. Full first cousins would share both grandparents, which they do not.

question: M is the mother of N. N’s sibling is P. P’s child is Q. Q is married to R. R’s mother, S, is the sister of M. What is the precise kinship term for S in relation to Q?
explanation: S is sister of M, who is mother of P, making S the aunt of P. Since Q is P’s child, S is the aunt of Q’s parent, i.e., Q’s great‑aunt. No other standard term fits more precisely.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry one of two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan’s parents (Adam and Clara) and Fiona’s parents (Brian and Diana) are two pairs of siblings. Thus Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: X’s mother Y has exactly one sister Z. X’s father V has exactly one brother U. Z and U are married and have a single child W. Assuming no adoption, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between X and W?
explanation: W is the child of X’s maternal aunt (Z) and paternal uncle (U). Thus W shares both of X’s grandparents, making W a double first cousin of X – the exact term.

question: R’s mother has a brother (R’s maternal uncle) who is married to S. S’s brother is the only child of R’s father’s brother (R’s paternal uncle). Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only; spouses are not counted as blood), what is the most precise relation of S to R?
explanation: S is sibling of the child of R’s paternal uncle, so she shares that uncle as a parent. Hence she is also a child of R’s paternal uncle, making her R’s first cousin. The marital link to the maternal uncle is an affinal relation and does not affect the blood term, which is uniquely “first cousin.”
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a sister, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona marry each other and have children G and H. What is the most precise kinship term for the relation between G and H?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins (their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters, sharing both grandparent pairs). Their children therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, which makes G and H double second cousins. This is the most specific standard term.

question: Alice and Bob share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). Alice has a daughter Clara, and Bob has a son David. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise relationship between Clara and David?
explanation: Clara and David are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent. The exact term for such cousins is “half‑first cousins,” distinguishing them from full first cousins (who share both grandparents) and from more distant cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries P and N marries Q, where P and Q are also siblings. M and N each have one child (A and B) who marry each other. Using standard English kinship terms without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the precise relation between A’s child C and B’s child D?
explanation: A and B are double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). Their children therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins – the most specific term.

question: Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law relations limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses): Person A is married to B. B’s mother is C. C’s brother is D. D’s daughter is E, and E is married to F. What is the relation of F to A?
explanation: A’s spouse is B. B’s mother C is A’s mother‑in‑law. C’s brother D is B’s maternal uncle, which is not a recognized in‑law term under the given limits. D’s daughter E is B’s cousin, also outside the allowed scope. Therefore F, E’s spouse, has no standard direct kinship term to A.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John and Jim are brothers. Anna and Amy are sisters. John marries Anna and they have a daughter Clara. Jim marries Amy and they have a son Daniel. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Clara and Daniel?
explanation: Clara and Daniel each have a father who is a brother of the other's father and a mother who is a sister of the other's mother. They share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

question: Alice's father has exactly one brother, and Alice's mother has exactly one sister. Those two siblings marry each other and have a child named Ben. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between Ben and Alice?
explanation: Alice's paternal uncle’s child is her first cousin; her maternal aunt’s child is also her first cousin. Because the uncle and aunt are married, the same child Ben fulfills both roles, giving Alice a double first cousin. No other term is more precise.

question: P and Q are siblings. P has a daughter R. Q has a son S. R and S marry each other and have a child T. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of T to P?
explanation: T is the child of R, who is P's daughter, giving a direct line P → R → T. That makes T P's grandchild. Although T is also the child of P's nephew/niece (S), the direct descendant term "grandchild" is the most precise.
choices: D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: N's mother has exactly one brother, and N's father has exactly one sister. M is the child of that brother and also the child of that sister (no other intermarriages). What is the precise kinship term for M's relation to N, using standard English blood‑relation terminology?
explanation: M is the child of N's maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Thus M shares both of N's grandparents on the mother's side and both on the father's side. Sharing two full grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the most specific standard term.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: A’s father has a sister (F) and A’s mother has a brother (M). F and M are married and have a child X. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between X and A?
explanation: F is A’s paternal aunt and M is A’s maternal uncle. Their child X is simultaneously the child of A’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle, sharing both of A’s grandparent pairs. The exact term is “double first cousin.”
choices: D) D) First cousin once removed

question: John is the son of Mary's brother. Mary's sister is married to Paul's father, and Paul is the father of Susan. Susan is the mother of Tim. What is Tim's relation to John?
explanation: John and Paul are first cousins because their parents are siblings of Mary. Susan, as Paul's daughter, is John's first cousin once removed. Tim, being Susan's son, is one more generation down, making him John's first cousin twice removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin twice removed

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary’s son Peter marries John’s daughter Anne. Peter and Anne have a child Lily. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no adoption), which of the following best describes Lily’s relation to John?
explanation: Anne is John’s daughter, so Lily is John’s granddaughter. Mary is John’s sister, making Peter John’s nephew; therefore John is Lily’s great‑uncle, and Lily is John’s great‑niece. Both relations hold simultaneously, so the most precise description is the double relation.
choices: D) Both granddaughter and great‑niece (double relation)

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted: X is described as the child of the only child of A’s mother, and also the child of the only child of A’s father. Who is X to A?
explanation: A’s mother’s only child can be A or a sibling; likewise for the father. If the only child is A, X is A’s child. If it is a sibling, X is A’s niece/nephew. Both possibilities satisfy the statement, so the precise kinship cannot be fixed.

question: John’s father is the only son of his paternal grandfather, and Maya’s mother is the only daughter of her maternal grandmother. John’s paternal grandfather and Maya’s maternal grandmother are siblings. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between John and Maya?
explanation: John’s father (son of his paternal grandfather) and Maya’s mother (daughter of her maternal grandmother) are first cousins because their parents are siblings. John and Maya are each one generation below those first cousins, making them second cousins.

question: M is the child of the sister of P’s father and also the child of the brother of Q’s mother. Assuming all individuals are distinct and monogamous, what is the precise kinship between P and Q?
explanation: M is P’s first cousin through P’s paternal aunt and Q’s first cousin through Q’s maternal uncle. This only tells that P and Q share a common cousin; it gives no information about any direct blood link between them. Their relation can vary, so it is not uniquely determinable.

question: M is the mother of A. M’s sister is S, whose daughter is D. A is married to B. B’s father, F, also fathered C with another woman (so B and C are half‑siblings). C is married to D. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is C to A?
explanation: C is the half‑brother of A’s spouse B. A sibling of one’s spouse—full or half—is called a brother‑in‑law (or sister‑in‑law). No blood link exists beyond that, so the precise term is brother‑in‑law.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: M is the child of P’s father’s sister and also the child of P’s mother’s brother. Assuming monogamy and no adoption, what is the exact kinship term for M’s relation to P?
explanation: The father’s sister (paternal aunt) and the mother’s brother (maternal uncle) must be married. Their child M shares both pairs of grandparents with P, making M P’s double first cousin, the most precise label.

question: M and N are full siblings. P is the child of M. Q is the child of N, and R is the child of Q. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of R to P?
explanation: M and N are siblings, so P and Q are first cousins. R, being Q's child, is one generation removed from P, making R P's first cousin once removed.

question: R is married to S. S's sister is W. W's husband is X. X's mother is Y. Y's brother is Z. In standard English kinship terms (allowing only spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses as in‑laws), what is Z to R?
explanation: The link goes: R→S (spouse) →W (sibling‑in‑law) →X (that sibling’s spouse) →Y (that spouse’s mother) →Z (her brother). This chain goes beyond immediate in‑law relations and introduces no blood link, so no standard direct kin term applies.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a family with monogamy, no adoption, and no multiple births, let X be a person. Y is the child of the only son of X’s maternal aunt, and also the child of the only daughter of X’s paternal uncle. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Y’s precise relation to X?
explanation: The only son of X’s maternal aunt is X’s maternal first cousin; his child is X’s first cousin once removed. Likewise, the only daughter of X’s paternal uncle is X’s paternal first cousin; her child is also X’s first cousin once removed. Both descriptions refer to the same person, so Y is X’s first cousin once removed.

question: John’s parents are Mary and Peter. Mary’s brother Tom is married to Linda. Linda’s sister Sue is married to Mark, who is Peter’s brother. Sue and Mark have a daughter Emma. What is Emma’s precise kinship to John using standard English terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, in‑laws limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: Mark is Peter’s brother, making him John’s paternal uncle; his child Emma is therefore John’s first cousin. All other links are affinal and do not add blood relation, so the most precise term is "first cousin".
choices: C) C) No standard blood relation

question: A man says: “My mother’s brother’s daughter is married to my father’s brother’s son.” Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the precise blood relation between the two spouses?
explanation: My mother’s brother is my maternal uncle; his daughter is my maternal first cousin. My father’s brother is my paternal uncle; his son is my paternal first cousin. The two cousins descend from unrelated sibling pairs, so they share no common ancestor. Hence the spouses have no blood relation.

question: L’s father has exactly one sister, and L’s mother has exactly one brother. The sister and the brother are married and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) – a first cousin on the father's side – and also the child of L’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) – a first cousin on the mother’s side. Being a first cousin through both parents makes M a double first cousin of L, the most specific term.

question: My mother has a sister; that sister’s only son, Tom, has a daughter Lily. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is Lily’s precise relation to me?
explanation: My mother’s sister is my maternal aunt. Her son Tom is my first cousin. Tom’s daughter Lily is one generation below my cousin, making her my first cousin once removed. No other standard term applies.

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father. N’s mother is the sister of O’s father. O’s mother is the sister of P’s father. If Q is the child of M and P, what is Q’s precise blood relation to N (using standard English kinship terms, ignoring any in‑law connections)?

question: R is married to S. S’s sister is T. T’s husband is U. U’s sister is V. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is V to R?

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let X be a person. Y is the child of the sister of X’s father and also the child of the brother of X’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the precise relation of Y to X?
explanation: Y is the child of X’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) making Y a first cousin on the father’s side, and also the child of X’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) making Y a first cousin on the mother’s side. The most specific standard term is simply “first cousin”.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries P, while N marries Q, and P and Q are sisters. M and P have a child X; N and Q have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of P/Q. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a distinct term from ordinary first cousins.

question: L has one sister and one brother. The sister’s only son and the brother’s only daughter each have a child, and both children are the same person M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: L’s sister’s son is L’s nephew; the brother’s daughter is L’s niece. Those two are first cousins, and their common child M is one generation below them. Thus M is the child of L’s nephew and niece, making M L’s grand‑niece or grand‑nephew (also called great‑niece/nephew).

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N is married to P and they have a son Q. O has a daughter R, and R marries Q. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only), what is R's relationship to Q?
explanation: M and N share parents, so O (M's daughter) is Q's first cousin. R, O's daughter, is therefore Q's first cousin once removed. The marriage adds the spousal link, but the precise blood term is first cousin once removed.

question: M and N are full siblings. M marries P and N marries Q. P and Q are also full siblings (but unrelated to M and N). M and P have a child X; N and Q have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of P/Q. This makes them double first cousins, the exact term for cousins linked through two independent sibling pairs.

question: X's mother has exactly one brother, who is married to Y. Y's sister has a son Z. Z is also the child of X's father's only sister. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Z's relation to X?
explanation: Z is child of X's paternal aunt (father's sister) → first cousin. The other description only gives Z a non‑blood connection via the maternal uncle’s wife, which does not affect the blood relation. Hence Z is X's first cousin.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a sister, Clara and Diana respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents: Adam and Brian share the same parents, and Clara and Diana share the same parents. Therefore they are first cousins through both paternal and maternal lines, i.e., double first cousins.

question: P's father has a sister who is married to X, and P's mother has a brother who is married to Y. Their respective children are the same person M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of M to P?
explanation: M is the child of P's paternal aunt (father's sister) and also the child of P's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with P, making M a double first cousin of P.

explanation: O is child of M, who is sibling of N. Thus O is first cousin to N's children P and R. Q is R's child, making Q the child of O's cousin. Therefore O and Q are first cousins once removed.

question: M's mother is the sister of N's father, and M's father is the brother of N's mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise blood relation between M and N?
explanation: M's mother and N's father are siblings, making N's father M's maternal uncle. Likewise, M's father and N's mother are siblings, making N's mother M's paternal aunt. question: M's mother and N's father are siblings, and M's father and N's mother are also siblings (no intermarriage beyond these). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: M and N share both sets of grandparents: one through their mothers' sibling link and another through their fathers' sibling link. Thus they are first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins, the most specific term.

explanation: M’s maternal aunt’s child is a first cousin on the mother’s side; the same child is also the offspring of M’s paternal uncle, making it a first cousin on the father’s side. Sharing both grandparent pairs yields the specific term “double first cousin.”

question: Let X be the child of the only brother of Y’s mother, and let Y be the child of the only brother of X’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is X’s relation to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle, while Y is the child of X’s paternal uncle. In both cases each is the child of a sibling of the other’s parent, which is precisely a first cousin. The relation is uniquely determined.

question: In a family, F’s mother has exactly one brother, and F’s father has exactly one brother. Both of these brothers have a single child, and these two children are the same person, E. explanation: E is the child of F’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and also the child of F’s paternal uncle (father’s brother). Hence E shares both sets of grandparents with F, making them double first cousins—the most precise label.

question: In a family, X is the child of the only brother of Y’s mother, and also the child of the only sister of Y’s father. Assuming monogamy and no adoption, what is the precise kinship term for X’s relation to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and also the child of Y’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Those two relatives must be married, so X descends from both of Y’s grandparent pairs. This makes X and Y double first cousins – they share both sets of grandparents.

question: John’s mother has a brother Mark. Mark is married to Sarah. Sarah’s sister is Linda, who is married to Tom. Tom’s father is the brother of John’s father. explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their parents are two pairs of siblings. This double sharing makes them double first cousins, not merely first cousins or half‑cousins.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary’s daughter Lisa marries John’s son Mark. Lisa and Mark have a child Sam. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Sam’s precise relation to John?
