explanation: If B and C are full siblings, D and E are first cousins; if they are half‑siblings, D and E are half‑first cousins. Because the paternal relationship is unknown, the exact term cannot be fixed, so the relation is not uniquely determinable.

question: P is the child of the only child of his father's sister. Q is the child of the only child of his mother's sister. Assuming no intermarriage between the two sides of the family, what is the precise blood relationship between P and Q?
explanation: P is the grand‑child of his paternal aunt; Q is the grand‑child of his maternal aunt. The two aunts are unrelated, so P and Q share no common ancestor. Therefore they have no blood relationship.

question: X is the son of Y. Y has a sister Z. Z is the mother of W. W has a daughter V. Using standard English kinship terms, what is V to X?
explanation: Y’s sister Z is X’s aunt. Z’s child W is X’s first cousin. W’s daughter V is one generation below that cousin, making V X’s first cousin once removed. No other listed term fits precisely.

question: X’s mother has a brother A, whose daughter is Y. X’s father has a sister B, whose son is Z. Y and Z marry and have a child W. What is the precise kinship term for the relation of X to W using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: Y is X’s maternal first cousin; Z is X’s paternal first cousin. Their child W is one generation below X’s first cousins, making W a first cousin once removed of X. No other standard term fits more precisely.

question: Two brothers, P and Q, each marry a woman; P marries S and Q marries T. S and T are sisters. P and S have a child A; Q and T have a child B. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: P and Q are siblings and S and T are siblings, so each pair of parents shares both parents. Their children therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: A and B are half‑siblings who share the same mother but have different fathers. A has a child C, and B has a child D. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relationship between C and D?
explanation: A and B share only one parent, so their children share only one grandparent. Children of half‑siblings are therefore half‑first cousins, a distinct term from full first cousins.

question: M and N share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). M has a child A, N has a child B, and there are no other intermarriages or adoptions. Using standard English kinship terminology, what is the precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent. The correct term for such relatives is "half‑first cousins"—they are first cousins with a single shared grandparent, not full first cousins (which require both grandparents) nor second cousins.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions, L has exactly one brother B and exactly one sister S. B has exactly one daughter D, and S has exactly one son E. M is the child of D, and N is the child of E. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between M and N?
explanation: B and S are siblings, so their children D and E are first cousins (they share L's parents). M and N are the children of those first cousins, making them second cousins, sharing the same great‑grandparents.

question: Leah and Omar are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). Leah has a son Sam. Omar has a daughter Maya. What is the precise kinship term for Sam and Maya?
explanation: Sam and Maya are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent. The correct term for such a relationship is “half‑first cousins”. Full first cousins require both grandparents in common, which they lack.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a son Ethan. Brian marries Diana and they have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan’s father is Adam, whose brother is Brian, Fiona’s father. Ethan’s mother is Clara, whose sister is Diana, Fiona’s mother. They share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides – double first cousins.

question: M is the mother of N and O. O has a son R. P is married to N, and P’s sister Q is married to R. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses), what is Q’s relation to N?
explanation: N is the sibling of R’s mother O, so N is R’s aunt. Q is R’s spouse, making Q the spouse of N’s nephew. The correct term for the spouse of one’s nephew is “niece‑in‑law.”

choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M and her spouse have two children N and O. P and his spouse have two children Q and R. N marries Q and O marries R. Their children are S (of N & Q) and T (of O & R). question: Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), R’s mother has exactly one brother, who is married to the only sister of R’s father. Their child is S. What is S’s precise relation to R?
explanation: R’s mother’s brother is R’s maternal uncle; his wife is R’s paternal aunt. Their child S is the child of both a maternal uncle and a paternal aunt, so S shares both sets of grandparents with R – a double first cousin.

question: In a family with no intermarriage, let Q be a person. P is the child of the brother of Q’s mother and also the child of the sister of Q’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of P to Q?
explanation: P is the child of Q’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and also the child of Q’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Those two parents are unrelated, so P shares both sets of grandparents with Q, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John marries Anna, whose brother is Peter. Mary marries Peter. John and Anna have a daughter Lily; Mary and Peter have a son Mark. Lily marries Mark’s son Kevin. What is the precise standard kinship term for Lily’s relation to Kevin?
explanation: John and Mary are siblings; Anna and Peter are siblings. Their children Lily and Mark share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. question: M and N are full siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also full siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y’s parents are two pairs of full siblings, so X and Y share both sets of grandparents. That makes them double first cousins—the only term that captures sharing both grandparent pairs.

question: F1 and F2 are brothers. M1 and M2 are sisters. F1 marries M1 and they have a child P. F2 marries M2 and they have a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between P and Q?
explanation: P and Q share both sets of grandparents (the parents of F1/F2 and the parents of M1/M2). Hence they are first cousins with a double line of descent, called double first cousins. No other listed term captures this exact double ancestry.

question: P is the child of the brother of Q’s mother, and also the child of the sister of Q’s father. Assuming no adoption or remarriage, what is the precise kinship term for P to Q?
explanation: If Q’s mother’s brother and Q’s father’s sister are different people, P is the child of Q’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt – a first cousin. question: A and B are married. A’s only brother C marries B’s only sister D. C and D have a son E. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relationship of E to A?
explanation: E is the child of A’s brother, so E is A’s nephew by blood. E is also the child of B’s sister, making E A’s nephew‑in‑law. When a person is both a blood nephew and a nephew‑in‑law, the most specific standard term is “double nephew.”

question: Lena’s mother has exactly two children: Lena and her half‑brother Mark (they share only their mother). Mark’s daughter Zoe marries Lena’s son Sam. question: In a family, Alex has a brother Ben. Ben’s daughter Clara marries Alex’s son David. Clara and David have a child Eva. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of Eva’s relation to Alex?
explanation: David is Alex’s son, so Eva is Alex’s grandchild. Clara is Alex’s niece (daughter of his brother), making Eva the child of his niece, i.e., Alex’s great‑niece. Both relations apply, and no single term covers both, so the precise description is “grandchild and great‑niece.”

question: In a family tree: Z and W are siblings. Z has a single child Y; Y has a single child X. W has a single child V; V has a single child U. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between U and X?
explanation: Y and V are first cousins (children of siblings Z and W). Their children X and U are therefore second cousins, sharing the same great‑grandparents (Z and W’s parents). No other listed term fits.

question: A has a sister S. S’s only son is X. B has a brother T. T’s only daughter is Y. X and Y marry and have a child C. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise standard English kinship term for C’s relation to A?

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoption, L’s paternal grandfather has exactly one sibling, a brother named G. G has a daughter S. What is S’s precise relation to L?
explanation: G is L’s great‑uncle (sibling of a grandparent). His daughter S is therefore the child of L’s great‑uncle, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed. No other kin term fits more precisely.

question: M has two sisters, S1 and S2. S1 marries A and they have a child C. S2 marries B, who is A’s brother, and they have a child D. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: C and D’s mothers are sisters and their fathers are brothers, so they share both sets of grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, the exact term for such a relationship.

question: Person X’s mother has exactly one brother, who has a daughter Y. X’s father has exactly one sister, who has a son Z. Y and Z are married to each other. What is the precise relation between Y and X?
explanation: Y is the daughter of X’s maternal uncle (the mother’s brother). The child of a parent’s sibling is a first cousin, irrespective of any other connections. Hence Y is X’s first cousin.

question: Let L be a person. L’s father has exactly one sibling, a brother named F. L’s mother has exactly one sibling, a sister named M. A child named X is born to F and to a spouse unrelated to L’s family, and another child named Y is born to M and an unrelated spouse. If X and Y are the same individual, what is the precise kinship term for X (or Y) to L using standard English blood‑relation terminology?
explanation: X/Y is the child of L’s paternal uncle and also the child of L’s maternal aunt. Hence X/Y shares both sets of grandparents with L, making them a double first cousin—the most specific term for this doubled first‑cousin relationship.

question: J’s mother has a brother who is married to K’s mother. J and K are of the same generation. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of J to K?
explanation: J’s maternal uncle (his mother’s brother) is married to K’s mother, making K the step‑child of J’s uncle. No blood link exists, and the affinal chain exceeds the immediate in‑law scope, so standard kinship provides no direct term.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary's son Peter marries John's daughter Alice. Peter and Alice have a child Sam. explanation: Sam is the child of John’s daughter, making him John’s grandchild. He is also the child of John’s nephew, which would label him great‑nephew, but grandchild is the closest and most precise standard term.

question: Let J be a person. M is described as both (i) the child of the only sister of J’s father, and (ii) the child of the only brother of J’s mother. Assuming no adoption or multiple births, what is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to J?
explanation: J’s father’s only sister is J’s paternal aunt; her child is J’s paternal first cousin. J’s mother’s only brother is J’s maternal uncle; his child is J’s maternal first cousin. The same person M satisfies both, making M a double first cousin of J—sharing both sets of grandparents.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries X and N marries Y, where X and Y are also siblings. M and X have a child A; N and Y have a child B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B are children of two couples that are both brother‑sister pairs, so they share both paternal and maternal grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, the most exact term.

question: R's mother and S's father are siblings, and R's father and S's mother are also siblings. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between R and S?
explanation: R and S share both sets of grandparents because each of their parents are siblings with the other's opposite parent. This makes them double first cousins, the exact term for cousins related through both parental lines.

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoption, let A be a person. A's father's sister (his aunt) has a son B. B has a daughter C. What is the precise kinship term for the relation of C to A?
explanation: A's father's sister is A's paternal aunt. Her son B is A's first cousin. B's daughter C is one generation below B, making her A's first cousin once removed. No other blood link exists, so this term is uniquely correct.

question: R's mother has a brother U, whose daughter is V. R's father has a sister W, whose son is X. Apart from these connections there is no other intermarriage. What is the precise standard English kinship term for V in relation to X?
explanation: V is the child of R's maternal uncle, making V R's first cousin. X is the child of R's paternal aunt, also R's first cousin. V and X share no common ancestor, so they are not blood relatives; there is no standard direct kin term for them.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let M be a person. M’s mother’s brother has a daughter, and that daughter has a son. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of that son to M?
explanation: M’s mother’s brother is M’s maternal uncle. His daughter is M’s first cousin. Her son is one generation below that cousin, making him M’s first cousin once removed. No other standard term applies.

question: John and Lisa are full siblings. John marries Anna, who is the daughter of Mark. Mark is the brother of Lisa’s husband, Peter. John and Anna have a child Sam; Lisa and Peter have a child Tom. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Sam and Tom?
explanation: Sam’s paternal grandparents are John and Lisa’s parents, which are Tom’s maternal grandparents. Sam’s maternal grandparents are Mark’s parents, which are Tom’s paternal grandparents. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes Sam and Tom double first cousins, the exact term.

question: Sam is married to Lily. Sam's sister Anna is married to Tom, and Tom is Lily's brother. Ben is the child of Sam and Lily. What is Tom to Ben?
explanation: Tom is Lily's brother, so he is Ben's maternal uncle by blood. Although Tom is also Sam's brother‑in‑law, the direct blood link determines the kin term. Hence Tom is Ben's uncle.

question: Two sisters, Maya and Nina, marry two brothers, Leo and Omar, respectively. Maya and Leo have a daughter, Tara; Nina and Omar have a son, Sam. explanation: Maya‑Leo and Nina‑Omar are sibling‑spouse pairs, so Tara and Sam are double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). Their children, Alex and Bella, therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins – the exact term required.

question: In a traditional family tree (no adoption, monogamy, and using standard English kinship terms), X is the child of Y's father's sister. What is the precise relationship of X to Y?
explanation: Y's father's sister is Y's paternal aunt. The child of a paternal aunt is a first cousin of Y. No other qualifiers apply, so the exact term is "first cousin".

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted, X's mother has a brother who married X's father's sister. They have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the precise relation of Y to X?
explanation: Y is the child of X's paternal aunt, making Y X's first cousin. The same Y is also the child of X's maternal cousin, which makes Y X's first cousin once removed. Both relations hold and no single standard term covers both, so the precise kinship is not uniquely determinable.

question: M is married to N. N has a sister S, and S is married to O. O's mother is P, and P's brother is Q. Q has a daughter R. Using standard English kinship terms limited to blood, spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses, what is R to M?

question: Anna and Brian are siblings. Anna’s child is Carla; Brian’s child is David. Carla has one child, Emma, and David has one child, Frank. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Emma and Frank?
explanation: Anna and Brian share parents, so Carla and David are first cousins (they share grandparents). Emma and Frank, being children of first cousins, share the same great‑grandparents, making them second cousins. No nearer standard term applies.

question: M and N are full siblings. M marries W1 and has a child A. N marries W2 and has a child B. W1 and W2 are sisters. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B are first cousins through their fathers (M and N) and also first cousins through their mothers (W1 and W2). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a distinct and more precise term than plain first cousins.

question: John has a sister Mary. John’s son Peter marries Anna, who is Tom’s sister. Tom is Mary’s brother‑in‑law (married to Mary’s sister‑in‑law). Who is Anna to Mary?
explanation: Peter, John’s son, is Mary’s nephew (her brother’s child). Anna is Peter’s wife, making her the spouse of Mary’s nephew, i.e., Mary’s niece‑in‑law.

question: Anna and Ben are siblings. Anna marries Carl, and Ben marries Diana. Carl and Diana are also siblings. X is the child of Anna and Carl, and Y is the child of Ben and Diana. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?

question: John has a sister Mary. John’s daughter Sarah marries Alan. Alan is the brother of Tom, who is Mary’s husband. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Alan’s relation to Mary?

question: John’s mother has a brother Peter, whose daughter is Lisa. John’s father has a sister Mary, whose son is Tom. Tom marries Lisa. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is Tom’s relation to John?

question: Two brothers marry two sisters: Brother 1 marries Sister A and Brother 2 marries Sister B. Brother 1 and Sister A have a child X; Brother 2 and Sister B have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the exact relationship between X and Y?

question: Let R be a person. X is the child of R's maternal uncle (the brother of R's mother). Y is the child of the sister of R's paternal aunt (the sister of R's father's sister). If we select either X or Y and call that person S, what is S's relation to R?

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoption, X’s mother is an only child. X’s father has a sister who is married to X’s maternal uncle (the brother of X’s mother). Who is the husband of X’s father’s sister to X?
explanation: X’s father’s sister is X’s paternal aunt. She is married to X’s maternal uncle, the brother of X’s mother. Thus her husband is X’s maternal uncle. The correct relation is maternal uncle.

question: John is married to Anna. John’s sister Mary is married to Tom. Tom’s brother is Sam, who is married to Lisa. Lisa’s mother is also Anna’s mother. Who is Sam to John?

question: L’s father has exactly one sister and L’s mother has exactly one brother. Those two siblings (the aunt and the uncle) are married and have a single child M. question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, X's mother has exactly one brother, and X's father has exactly one sister. The brother's daughter (Y) and the sister's son (Z) marry and have a child W. What is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between W and X?

question: John has a sister Mary who is married to Peter. Peter’s sister Laura is married to John’s brother Michael, and Laura and Michael have a daughter Emma. What is Emma’s relation to John?
explanation: Michael is John’s brother, making Emma his daughter. A brother’s daughter is a niece, regardless of the aunt’s in‑law connections. Therefore Emma is John’s niece.

question: L and M share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). L has a daughter X and M has a son Y; there are no other marriages linking the families. Using standard English kinship terminology, what is the most precise term for the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent. The correct specific term is “half‑first cousins,” which denotes cousins who share a single grandparent rather than a full pair.

question: John is married to Mary. Mary’s sister Anna is married to John’s brother Peter. Anna and Peter have a daughter Lily. John and Mary have a son Sam. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Lily and Sam?

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, N’s father has a sister A and N’s mother has a brother B. A and B marry each other and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between M and N?

question: M and N are half‑siblings who share only their mother. M has a daughter X; N has a son Y. There are no other intermarriages in the family. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?

question: Let A be a person. B is the child of the only brother of A’s mother. C is the child of the only brother of A’s father. If we select either B or C and call that person X, what is X’s precise relation to A using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed)?
explanation: Whether X is B (child of A’s maternal uncle) or C (child of A’s paternal uncle), X is always the child of a parent’s brother. In standard kinship that makes X a first cousin of A, regardless of which side the uncle is on.

question: In a family, Person A’s mother is the sister of Person B’s father, and Person A’s father is the brother of Person B’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the most precise blood relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents: A’s mother and B’s father are siblings, and A’s father and B’s mother are siblings. Thus they are first cousins on both parental sides, i.e., double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries A and N marries B, where A and B are also siblings. M and A have a child X; N and B have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no ignoring doubled ancestry), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father M and Y’s father N are brothers, sharing the same paternal grandparents. X’s mother A and Y’s mother B are also sisters, sharing the same maternal grandparents. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the exact term.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a sister, Clara and Diana, respectively (Adam–Clara and Brian–Diana). Adam and Clara have one child, Ethan; Brian and Diana have one child, Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Adam and Brian share both parents, as do Clara and Diana. Therefore Ethan and Fiona share all four grandparents, not just one pair. The exact term for such relatives is "double first cousins."

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has a son P. O and P marry and have a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Q’s relation to N?
explanation: N is the father of P, who is Q’s father, so Q is N’s grandson. The fact that Q’s mother is M’s daughter does not change the term.

question: M and N are brother and sister. P and Q are another brother‑sister pair. M marries P and N marries Q. Their children, X (child of M & P) and Y (child of N & Q), are born. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of P/Q. Because both of their parents are siblings, they are double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled ancestry.

question: M and his sister S each marry a sibling pair: M marries Anna, S marries Ben, and Anna and Ben are siblings. M and Anna have a child X; S and Ben have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two sets of siblings who married each other. They share both paternal and maternal grandparents, so they are first cousins with doubled ancestry—precisely called double first cousins.

question: L’s father has exactly one sister, and L’s mother has exactly one brother. M is the child of that sister and also the child of that brother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s relation to L?
explanation: The sister of L’s father is L’s paternal aunt; her child is L’s paternal first cousin. The brother of L’s mother is L’s maternal uncle; his child is L’s maternal first cousin. In either case M is a first cousin of L. No closer or half‑relation exists, so the precise term is "first cousin".

question: M and N are half‑siblings who share only their mother. M has a child G; N has a child H. G and H each marry unrelated partners and have children I and J respectively. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between I and J?
explanation: G and H are half‑first cousins (they share one grandparent). Their children I and J therefore share only one great‑grandparent, making them half‑second cousins. Full second cousins would require both great‑grandparents to be common.

question: Two brothers marry two sisters. The elder brother (M) and elder sister (N) have a son X. The younger brother (P) and younger sister (Q) have a daughter Y. Before X and Y marry each other, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between X and Y, considering doubled ancestry?
explanation: M and P are brothers; N and Q are sisters. X is child of M & N, Y child of P & Q. X and Y share both paternal grandparents (parents of M & P) and maternal grandparents (parents of N & Q). Thus they have the same two grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the most precise label.

question: M is mother of twins N and O. N is married to P. O is married to T and they have a child Q. P's sister is R, who is married to S. S is the brother of T. What is the precise kinship term for R in relation to Q, using standard English kinship terminology (in‑law terms limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses)?
explanation: Through N–P–R, R is sister‑in‑law of N and thus sister‑in‑law of O, giving no direct term to Q. Through S (brother of Q’s father) R is aunt‑in‑law of Q. The two legitimate paths yield different standard terms, so the relation cannot be uniquely identified.

question: M is the child of the sister of P’s father and also the child of the brother of P’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is M’s precise relation to P?
explanation: The sister of P’s father is P’s paternal aunt; her child is P’s paternal first cousin. The brother of P’s mother is P’s maternal uncle; his child is P’s maternal first cousin. M occupies both positions, sharing both sets of grandparents, making M a double first cousin of P.

question: Anna’s mother has exactly one brother, who is married and has a child named Sam. Anna’s father has exactly one sister, who also has a child named Sam (the same Sam). Using standard English kinship terms, what is Sam’s relation to Anna?
explanation: The person is the child of Anna’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and also the child of Anna’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Thus they share both of Anna’s grandparents, making them Anna’s first cousin (double first cousin). The most precise standard term is first cousin, so option B is correct.
choices: D) D) Relation not uniquely determinable

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a sister, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona marry each other. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, and in‑law terms limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the most precise description of the relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. Hence they are double first cousins, a term that captures the doubled shared ancestry.

question: M and N are siblings. M’s child is O. N is married to P. P’s sibling is Q, who is married to R. R’s child is S. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only, in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation between O and S?
explanation: O is a blood descendant of M. S is a blood descendant of R. All links between the two lines are through marriage (N‑P, P‑Q, Q‑R). No common ancestor exists, so there is no standard blood kin term; the connection is purely affinal.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions, let Y be a person. X is described as the child of the only brother of Y’s mother and also the child of the only brother of Y’s father. The two brothers are different individuals. What is X’s precise relationship to Y using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle and also the child of Y’s paternal uncle. Because the uncles are unrelated, X shares both sets of grandparents with Y, making them double first cousins—the exact term for this relation.

question: Person X has a paternal aunt (father’s only sister) whose son is Y, and a maternal uncle (mother’s only brother) whose daughter is Z. Y and Z marry and have a child W. Using standard English kinship terms, what is W’s relation to X?
explanation: Y is X’s paternal first cousin; Z is X’s maternal first cousin. Their child W is one generation down from each cousin, making W a first cousin once removed to X on both sides. No closer or doubled term applies.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard direct kinship term

question: Brothers John and Mark each marry sisters Alice and Beth, respectively (John↔Alice, Mark↔Beth). John and Alice have a child Carl; Mark and Beth have a child Dana. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relationship between Carl and Dana?
explanation: Carl and Dana share both sets of grandparents: John and Mark share the same parents, and Alice and Beth share the same parents. Hence they are first cousins through two distinct parental lines, i.e., double first cousins. This is more specific than merely "first cousins".
choices: D) D) First cousins once removed

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a son Ethan. Brian marries Diana and they have a daughter Fiona. Before Ethan and Fiona marry each other, what is the most precise standard kinship term describing their relationship?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents: Adam and Brian’s parents (paternal) and Clara and Diana’s parents (maternal). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the exact term required.

question: Let R be a person. R's mother has exactly one brother, U. R's father has exactly one sister, V. U is married to V's daughter, W. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise term for W's relation to R?
explanation: W is the child of R's paternal aunt V, making her R's first cousin by blood. At the same time, she is the spouse of R's maternal uncle U, which makes her R's aunt‑in‑law by marriage. No single standard term covers both aspects, so the relation is not uniquely determinable.

question: R’s mother has a brother A, and R’s father has a sister B. A’s daughter is C; B’s son is D. C and D marry and have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation of E to R?
explanation: C is R’s maternal first cousin; D is R’s paternal first cousin. Their child E is each of their children’s first cousin once removed. Because E is related to R in the same way through both parental lines, the precise term is a double first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
C) C) Double first cousin once removed

question: A is married to B. B’s sister is C. C’s husband is D. D’s sister is E. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is E to A?
explanation: A → B (spouse) → C (sister‑in‑law) → D (brother‑in‑law to B, thus also to A) → E (sister of that brother‑in‑law). The chain goes beyond the immediate in‑law scope, and no blood link exists, so there is no standard direct kin term for E relative to A.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: A and C are brothers; B and D are sisters. A marries B and they have a son E. C marries D and they have a daughter F. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between E and F?
explanation: E and F share both paternal grandparents (parents of A and C) and both maternal grandparents (parents of B and D). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: Two brothers, Alan and Brian, each marry a woman who is the sister of the other's wife. Alan marries Clara, Brian marries Diana, and Clara and Diana are sisters. Alan and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. What is the most precise standard English kinship term describing the relationship between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Alan and Brian share the same parents, and Clara and Diana share the same parents. Ethan and Fiona therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: M and N are full siblings. Their sister Q is also a sibling of M and N. M has a child A. Q has a child P. N marries P and they have a child B. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A is M’s child. B’s father N is M’s sibling, and B’s mother P is Q’s child, where Q is also M’s sibling. Thus B’s both parents are children of the same grandparents as M, making B share both grandparent pairs with A. The exact term is double first cousins.

question: J has a sister K who is married to L. J’s child is M, and L’s child is N. M and N get married. What is the precise kinship term for the relation of J to N?
explanation: M is J’s child. N is M’s spouse. Therefore J is the parent of M’s spouse, i.e., the parent‑in‑law of N. The standard term is father‑in‑law (or mother‑in‑law depending on J’s gender).

question: Mary has a brother John. Mary’s only child is Kevin. Kevin is married to Anne, whose sister is Lisa. Lisa is John’s wife. What is the precise kinship term for Anne’s relation to John, using standard English kin terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: John’s sibling Mary makes Kevin John’s nephew. Anne, as Kevin’s spouse, is therefore John’s niece‑in‑law. No other standard term applies.
choices: D) D) No direct kinship term

question: P’s father has a sister W and P’s mother has a brother H. W and H marry and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between M and P?
explanation: W is P’s paternal aunt, so M is P’s first cousin on the father’s side. H is P’s maternal uncle, so M is also P’s first cousin on the mother’s side. Because M shares both sets of grandparents with P, the exact term is double first cousins.

question: S1 and S2 are siblings. S1 marries A and they have a child C. S2 marries B and they have a child D. C and D each marry unrelated partners and have children X and Y respectively. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no other intermarriages), what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: C and D are first cousins because their parents are siblings. The children of first cousins are second cousins. No additional blood links exist, so X and Y are exactly second cousins.

question: M and N are full siblings. O, P and Q are full siblings. M marries O, N marries Q. M‑O have a daughter A; N‑Q have a son B. A and B each have one child with unrelated partners: A’s child is C, B’s child is D. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: M and N share both parents; O and Q share both parents. Thus A and B share both sets of grandparents – they are double first cousins. Their children therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making C and D double second cousins. No other term is more exact.

question: John and Mary are siblings. Their other sibling, Peter, has a daughter Anna. John marries Anna and they have a child Sam. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relationship of Sam to Peter?
explanation: Peter is John’s brother, so Sam (John’s child) is Peter’s nephew. Anna is Peter’s daughter, so Sam is also Peter’s grandchild. The term that simultaneously reflects both lines and is the most specific recognized kinship label is “grandnephew” (the child of a nephew).
choices: D) D) No standard term (relationship ambiguous)

question: M is the child of the sister of P’s father and also the child of the brother of P’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between M and P?
explanation: M is the offspring of P’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle, sharing both sets of grandparents with P. Hence M and P are double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled relationship.

question: L has one sister and one brother. The only child of L’s sister has a child M, and the only child of L’s brother also has a child M (the same person). What is M’s precise relation to L using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: M is the child of L’s niece (through the sister) and also the child of L’s nephew (through the brother). In both lines M is the child of L’s sibling’s child, making M L’s great‑niece or great‑nephew. Hence the precise term is “grandniece/grandnephew”.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), consider the following statements: 1) B and C are siblings. 2) A is the only child of B. 3) D is the only child of C. 4) F is the child of A. 5) E is the child of D. What is the precise relation of E to F?
explanation: B and C are siblings, so A and D are first cousins. F is A's child and E is D's child. Children of first cousins are second cousins, making E and F second cousins. No other standard term fits.

question: In a family with no blood marriages, let X be a person. Y is the child of X’s mother’s brother, and Y is also the child of X’s father’s sister (the same Y). What is the most precise standard kinship term for Y relative to X?
explanation: Y is the child of X’s maternal uncle (first cousin) and also the child of X’s paternal aunt (first cousin). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes Y a double first cousin of X, the exact term required.

question: M and N are brother and sister. P and Q are brother and sister. M marries P and has a child A. N marries Q and has a child B. Assuming monogamy and no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between A and B?
explanation: M and N share both parents, as do P and Q. Thus A and B share all four grandparents, making them first cousins through two independent parental lines – i.e., double first cousins. No other standard term captures this exact relationship.

question: In a family with no adoption or remarriage, let X be the child of the brother of Y’s father, and also the child of the sister of Y’s mother. What is the most precise kinship term for X in relation to Y?
explanation: The brother of Y’s father is Y’s paternal uncle; his child is Y’s first cousin on the paternal side. The sister of Y’s mother is Y’s maternal aunt; her child is Y’s first cousin on the maternal side. Since X fulfills both roles, X is a double first cousin of Y.

question: John and Mary are half‑siblings, sharing only their mother. John has a daughter Lily; Mary has a son Peter. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Lily and Peter?
explanation: John and Mary share one parent, so their children share only one grandparent. Children of half‑siblings are therefore half‑first cousins, not full first cousins. The term “half‑first cousin” uniquely describes Lily’s relation to Peter.

question: M is the mother of N. N is married to O. O’s sister is P. P is the daughter of Q, who is the brother of M’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only), what is P’s relation to M?
explanation: M’s father’s brother Q is M’s paternal uncle; his daughter P is therefore M’s first cousin. Marriage ties do not affect the blood relationship, so P is precisely M’s first cousin.

question: M and N are brother and sister. P and Q are also brother and sister. M marries Q and N marries P. R is the child of M and Q, and S is the child of N and P. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between R and S?
explanation: M and N share the same parents; Q and P share another set of parents. R’s parents (M, Q) and S’s parents (N, P) are respectively siblings on both sides, so R and S share both grandparent pairs. This makes them double first cousins.

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamy, A is the only child of her mother M. M has a sister S. S has a son C, and C has a daughter D. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation of D to A?
explanation: M and S are sisters, so their children A and C are first cousins. D is C's daughter, making D one generation below C. Therefore D is the child of A's first cousin, i.e., A's first cousin once removed. No closer or alternative term applies.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamy, the only child of L’s father’s sister marries the only child of L’s mother’s brother, and they have a child M. What is M’s relationship to L using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: M is the child of L’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and L’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Those parents are siblings of L’s father and mother respectively, so M shares both sets of grandparents with L, making M a double first cousin of L.

question: Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses): M is married to N. N’s sister is O, who is married to P. P’s mother Q is the sister of R, who is the father of S. S is married to T. What is T to M?
explanation: M→N (spouse) →O (sibling‑in‑law) →P (spouse of that sibling‑in‑law) →S (first cousin of P) →T (spouse of that cousin). The chain passes beyond the allowed affinal links; no blood or direct in‑law term exists between M and T. Hence T has no standard direct kinship label to M.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M and N share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). M has a daughter A; N has a son B. Assuming no other marriages among relatives, what is the precise kinship term for the relationship between A and B?
explanation: A and B are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent. The exact term for such relatives is “half‑first cousins,” distinguishing them from full first cousins (who share both grandparents).

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, the only child of P. N marries Q, the only child of R. P and R are themselves siblings. M‑O have a daughter S; N‑Q have a son T. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between S and T?
explanation: S and T each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of P/R. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a distinct term from ordinary first cousins.

question: M, N and P are three siblings. M’s daughter is A; N’s son is B; P’s daughter is E. A and B each have one child, C and D respectively. C marries E. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of D to E?
explanation: E is the child of P, a sibling of N, so E is first cousin to B. D is B’s child, thus one generation below B. Therefore D is the first cousin once removed of E. No shared half‑relationship or double‑cousin condition exists.
choices: D) D) First cousin once removed

question: M and N share only their mother (they are half‑siblings). M is married to A and has a child X; N is married to B and has a child Y. There are no other intermarriages. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: M and N are half‑siblings, so they share one parent. Their children X and Y therefore share only that one grandparent, not a full grandparent pair. The exact term is half‑first cousins; full first cousins require both grandparents in common.

question: Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), R is married to S; S’s brother is T; T’s wife is U; U’s brother is V. What is V to R?
explanation: R→S (spouse) →T (spouse’s sibling) →U (that sibling’s spouse) →V (that spouse’s sibling). This chain exceeds the defined in‑law scope and introduces no blood link, so no standard direct kin term exists between V and R.
choices: A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: G1 and G2 have two children: a son S and a daughter D. S has a child P; D has a child Q. P has a child X. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is X’s relation to Q?
explanation: P and Q are first cousins because their parents are siblings. X is the child of P, putting X one generation below P. A child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed to the original cousin, so X is Q’s first cousin once removed.

question:
Using only standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), consider the following description:

- R’s mother has a brother, call him M.
- M is married to S.
- S has a sister T.
- T is the mother of the only child U of R’s father’s sister.

What is the precise relationship of U to R?
explanation: R’s father’s sister is R’s paternal aunt. Her child U is therefore the child of R’s aunt, which makes U a first cousin of R. The extra information about M, S, and T does not affect this direct blood link.

question: L’s father has exactly one sister, and L’s mother has exactly one brother. A child M is born to the union of that sister and that brother. In standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus M shares both of L’s grandparent pairs, making M a double first cousin of L—the most specific term.

question: R’s paternal aunt (his father’s sister) has a son A. R’s maternal uncle (his mother’s brother) has a daughter B. A and B marry and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only), what is C’s relation to R?
explanation: A is R’s paternal first cousin; B is R’s maternal first cousin. Their child C is one generation below each first cousin, making C a first cousin once removed of R. This holds from both sides, so the precise term is first cousin once removed.

question: A and B are siblings. B has a daughter C. A marries D. D’s brother is E, who is C’s husband. The mother of D and E is F, and F is also the mother of G, who is A’s son with D. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents, siblings, and children’s spouses), what is the precise relationship of F to C?
explanation: C’s husband is E; E’s mother is F, making F C’s mother‑in‑law. No blood link exists, and the only standard term for this connection is “mother‑in‑law.”

question: John and Tom are brothers. Their sister Mary has a son Peter. Tom has a daughter Susan. Peter marries Susan. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only), what is Peter's relation to Tom?
explanation: Peter is the child of Mary, who is Tom's sister. Therefore Peter is Tom's nephew. The marriage to Susan does not change the blood relationship.

question: John and Mary are siblings. Mary’s son Peter marries John’s daughter Susan. Peter and Susan have a child Emma. What is the precise kinship term for Emma’s relation to Mary?
explanation: Peter is Mary’s son, so Emma is Mary’s granddaughter. Susan is John’s daughter; John is Mary’s brother, making Susan Mary’s niece. Hence Emma, as Susan’s child, is also Mary’s grandniece. The only term that captures both links is ‘granddaughter and grandniece’.

question: X's mother has a brother M, and X's father has a sister F. M's daughter is Y, and F's son is Z. Assuming no intermarriage among these families, what is the precise standard English kinship term (if any) for the relation between Y and Z?
explanation: Y is the child of X's maternal uncle, Z is the child of X's paternal aunt. Their only common individual is X, who is not an ancestor of either. Therefore Y and Z share no blood ancestor and have no standard kinship term.
choices: A) No blood relationship (no standard kinship term)

question: Anna and Brian are brother and sister. Anna has a daughter Clara. Brian has a son David. David marries Clara's daughter Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Brian's precise relation to Emma?
explanation: Brian is Anna's brother, so he is Clara's uncle. Emma is Clara's daughter, making Emma Brian's grandniece. The standard term for the male relative of a grandniece is great‑uncle (also called granduncle). Therefore Brian is Emma's great‑uncle.
choices: D) No standard direct kinship term

question: Man X and woman Y are married. X’s mother is the sister of Y’s father, and X’s father is the brother of Y’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between the children of X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are each other's cross‑siblings: they share both a maternal aunt/uncle pair and a paternal aunt/uncle pair. Their children therefore have the same set of four grandparents, i.e., they share both grandparent pairs. The exact term for such children is “double first cousins”.

question: X’s mother has a brother Y whose daughter is Z. X’s father has a sister W whose son is V. Z and V marry each other. What is the relationship between X and the child of Z and V, using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: Z is X’s maternal first cousin; V is X’s paternal first cousin. Their child is one generation down from each cousin, so to X it is a first cousin once removed. Both lines give the same relation.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions, R’s mother has exactly one brother. That brother is married to R’s father’s sister. Using standard English kinship terms, who is R’s father’s sister to R?
explanation: R’s father’s sister is the sibling of R’s father, making her R’s paternal aunt. The marriage of the maternal uncle to her does not change this direct blood relation.

question: In a family, X’s mother has exactly one brother and X’s father has exactly one sister. The brother (X’s maternal uncle) marries the sister (X’s paternal aunt), and they have a single child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of Y to X?
explanation: Y is child of X’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and X’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Thus Y shares both of X’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins, the most specific standard term.

question: Z has two children with different partners: with W he has a son Y; with U he has a daughter V. Y's child is X. V's child is Q. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise blood relation between X and Q?
explanation: X and Q are children of half‑siblings (Y and V share only father Z). They share a single grandparent, not a full pair, so they are half‑first cousins.

question: R is married to S. S’s brother is T. T’s son is U. What is U’s relation to R?
explanation: S is R's spouse. T is S's brother, so T is R's brother‑in‑law. U is T's son, making U the son of R's brother‑in‑law, i.e., R's nephew‑in‑law. No blood link exists, and "nephew‑in‑law" is the precise standard term.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M has two children, A and B. A’s child is C, and B’s child is D. C and D each marry unrelated partners and have children E and F respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between E and F?
explanation: A and B are siblings, so C and D are first cousins. Their children E and F are the children of first cousins, which makes them second cousins. No closer term applies.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a woman who are sisters, Alice and Betty respectively. Adam and Alice have a son Carl; Brian and Betty have a son David. Later the brothers swap spouses and each has another child with the new spouse, but the first children remain unchanged. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation between Carl and David?
explanation: Carl and David share both paternal grandparents (their fathers are brothers) and both maternal grandparents (their mothers are sisters). Sharing the full set of grandparents on both sides defines them as double first cousins, a tighter relation than ordinary first cousins.

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father. N’s mother is the sister of O’s father. O is the child of M. What is the precise kinship term for N’s relation to O using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: M’s mother and N’s father are siblings, so N is M’s first cousin. O is M’s child, making O one generation below M. Therefore N is the first cousin of O’s parent, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No direct kinship term

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother, and his only child is A. R’s father has exactly one sister, and her only child is also A. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise term for A’s relation to R?
explanation: A is the child of R’s maternal uncle and also the child of R’s paternal aunt. Thus A shares both sets of grandparents with R, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: Emily's mother has only one brother, Tom. Tom's only child is Adam. Adam has a daughter Zoe. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is Zoe's relation to Emily?
explanation: Tom is Emily's maternal uncle, so his child Adam is Emily's first cousin. Zoe, being Adam's daughter, is one generation below Adam, making her Emily's first cousin once removed. This is the most precise standard term.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M and N are siblings. M marries P and has a son R. N marries Q and has a daughter S. R and S (who are first cousins) marry and have a child T. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, ignoring no doubled ancestry), what is the most precise relation of T to M?
explanation: M is R’s father, so M is T’s paternal grandfather. M is also N’s brother, making him S’s maternal great‑uncle, but the closer generational link (grandparent) prevails. Hence the most precise term is grandfather.

question: In a family with no adoptions, monogamy allowed but remarriage possible: X is the child of the sister of Y’s mother, and X is also the child of the brother of Y’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law terms limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal aunt and also the child of Y’s paternal uncle. Thus X shares both sets of grandparents with Y, making X a double first cousin—the most specific term available.

question: K and J have a single child L. L’s child is M. K also fathers N with another partner. N marries O, whose sister is P. P is the mother of Q. Using standard English kinship terms (blood and immediate in‑law only), what is the precise relation of Q to M?
explanation: L and N share father K, so N is M’s half‑uncle. N’s wife O is an aunt‑in‑law to M. O’s sister P is only a sibling of M’s aunt‑in‑law, giving no direct blood or immediate in‑law link to M. Therefore P’s child Q is related to M solely through this extended affinal chain, for which English kinship provides no standard term.
choices: C) C) Second cousin once removed
D) D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a family, X's mother has a brother (M) who has a daughter Y. X's father has a sister (N) who has a son Z. Y and Z marry and have a child W. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the precise relation of W to X?
explanation: Y is X's maternal first cousin; Z is X's paternal first cousin. Their child W is the child of X's first cousins, making W X's first cousin once removed. The double‑cousin nature does not change the basic term.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, X is the only child of Y's mother's brother, and Z is the only child of Y's father's sister. If X and Z are the same individual, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for X's relation to Y?
explanation: Y's mother's brother is Y's maternal uncle; his only child is a maternal first cousin. Y's father's sister is Y's paternal aunt; her only child is a paternal first cousin. Being the same person makes X both a maternal and paternal first cousin, i.e., a double first cousin. No other term is more precise.

question: Emma’s mother has a brother whose daughter is Lily. Emma’s father has a sister whose son is Mark. Lily and Mark marry and have a child named Sam. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation between Sam and Emma?
explanation: Lily is Emma’s maternal first cousin; Mark is Emma’s paternal first cousin. Sam is the child of two first cousins who are unrelated to each other, so Sam is Emma’s first cousin once removed on both sides. The precise term is “double first cousin once removed.”
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed
C) C) Half‑first cousin once removed
D) D) Double first cousin once removed

question: In a family with no adoptions, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted, Person X’s mother is the half‑sister of Person Y’s grandfather. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s mother and Y’s grandfather share exactly one parent, so they are half‑siblings. X is therefore the child of Y’s grandfather’s half‑sister, making X a half‑first cousin of Y’s parent. Consequently X is a half‑first cousin once removed to Y, which is the most specific term.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed
D) D) Half‑first cousin once removed

question: Brothers A and B and sisters C and D each marry across the families: A marries C and they have a child X; B marries D and they have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring the doubled ancestry, what is the most precise term for the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents (A’s parents and C’s parents) because their parents are two pairs of siblings. The exact term for such a pair is “double first cousins”.

question: M has a sister N and a brother R. N is married to O. R has a daughter Q. What is the precise standard English kinship term for Q's relation to O?
explanation: N is Q's aunt (sibling of Q's parent R). O is N's spouse, making him the husband of Q's aunt, i.e., an uncle‑in‑law. No blood link exists, and the term ‘uncle‑in‑law’ is the only standard label that fits.

question: M has a sister N. N is married to O. O’s brother P is married to Q. Q shares a mother with R (they are half‑siblings). R is the father of S. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the relation of M to S?
explanation: M is linked to S only through a series of marriages and a half‑sibling connection. There is no blood relationship, and the affinal chain passes beyond immediate in‑law scope, so no standard kin term applies.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John is the son of Mary and Peter. Mary has a sister Anna, who is married to Thomas, Peter’s brother. Anna and Thomas have a daughter Lily. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation between John and Lily?
explanation: John’s mother Mary and Lily’s mother Anna are sisters, sharing the same maternal grandparents. John’s father Peter and Lily’s father Thomas are brothers, sharing the same paternal grandparents. Thus John and Lily share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the most specific standard term.

question: R’s mother has a brother who has a daughter S. R’s father has a sister who has a son T. If we pick either S or T and call that person X, what is X’s relation to R?
explanation: S is the child of R’s maternal uncle; T is the child of R’s paternal aunt. In both cases X is the child of one of R’s parents’ siblings, which is precisely a first cousin. The relation is the same regardless of which child is chosen.

question: In a family, M is the only sister of N. N is married to O. M’s only brother is P. O’s only brother is Q. P has a son R, and Q has a son S. If we select either R or S and call that person T, what is T’s precise relation to O’s child?
explanation: R is the child of M’s brother (maternal uncle of O’s child) and S is the child of O’s brother (paternal uncle of O’s child). Either way T is the child of a parent’s sibling, which is exactly a first cousin.

question: Emma is married to Frank. Frank’s sister is Grace. Grace is married to Henry. Henry’s brother is Ian. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), who is Ian to Emma?
explanation: Emma → Frank (spouse) → Grace (sibling‑in‑law) → Henry (spouse of that sibling‑in‑law) → Ian (brother of Henry). This chain extends beyond the allowed in‑law scope, so no standard direct kin term exists.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M is the child of the sister of the father of J's mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, in‑law terms limited to spouse and parents' siblings), what is M's relation to J?
explanation: J's mother’s father is J’s maternal grandfather. His sister is J’s maternal great‑aunt. The child of that sister is J’s mother’s first cousin. A first cousin of one’s parent is a first cousin once removed to the child. Hence M is J’s first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: A and B are siblings. D and C are also siblings. A marries D, and B marries C. The child of A and D is X; the child of B and C is Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, but remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of A/B and the parents of C/D. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than ordinary first cousins.

question: A is the son of B’s father’s sister. In standard English kinship terminology (ignoring marriage links), what is A’s relation to B?
explanation: B’s father’s sister is B’s paternal aunt. Her son is therefore B’s first cousin. No other blood link exists, so the precise term is “first cousin.”

question: M and N are full siblings. M marries O, who is the sister of P. N marries Q, who is the brother of O. Their children are X (child of M + O) and Y (child of N + Q). Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise blood relationship between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share both parents, and O and Q are also full siblings. Thus X and Y have the same paternal grandparents (M/N’s parents) and the same maternal grandparents (O/Q’s parents). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: X’s father has exactly one sister and X’s mother has exactly one brother. The sister’s child and the brother’s child are the same person, Z. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Z’s precise relation to X?
explanation: The sister is X’s paternal aunt, so her child is X’s paternal first cousin. The brother is X’s maternal uncle, so his child is X’s maternal first cousin. Because the two cousins are the same individual, Z shares both sets of grandparents with X, making Z a double first cousin – the most specific standard term.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard direct relation

question: Two brothers marry two sisters. Brother 1 (John) and Sister 1 (Anna) have a son Carl. Brother 2 (Mike) and Sister 2 (Beth) have a son Dan. Carl’s child is Emma; Dan’s child is Fiona. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise kinship term for Emma and Fiona?
explanation: John and Mike share both parents; Anna and Beth share both parents. Hence Carl and Dan share both sets of grandparents – they are double first cousins. Their children Emma and Fiona therefore share both great‑grandparent pairs, making them double second cousins.

question: John is married to Mary. Mary's sister Anna is married to John's brother Peter. Anna and Peter have a daughter Lily; John and Mary have a son Sam. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Lily and Sam?
explanation: Lily's father Peter is John's brother, and Lily's mother Anna is Mary's sister. Thus Lily and Sam share both sets of grandparents—paternal and maternal—making them double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled relationship.

question: A and D are siblings, B and C are siblings. M is the child of A and B. N is the child of C and D. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: M’s parents are A (child of grandparents P) and B (child of grandparents Q). N’s parents are C (child of Q) and D (child of P). Thus M and N share both sets of grandparents P and Q, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled shared ancestry.

question: L’s mother has exactly one brother, and L’s father has exactly one sister. The child of that brother and the child of that sister are the same person, M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s maternal uncle and also the child of L’s paternal aunt. Therefore M shares both sets of grandparents with L, making M a double first cousin—the most specific term.

question: John and Mary are siblings. Anna and Peter are siblings. John marries Anna and they have a daughter Lily. Mary marries Peter and they have a son Mark. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Lily and Mark?
explanation: John and Mary are siblings; Anna and Peter are siblings. Lily’s paternal grandparents are John’s parents, Mark’s maternal grandparents are the same persons. Lily’s maternal grandparents are Anna’s parents, Mark’s paternal grandparents are the same persons. Thus Lily and Mark share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most precise term.

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy allowed and remarriage permitted: R’s father’s sister has a child named A. R also has a child named B. What is the precise kinship term between A and B?
explanation: R’s father’s sister is R’s paternal aunt, so her child A is R’s first cousin. B is R’s child, one generation below R. Hence A is one generation above B, making A and B first cousins once removed.

question: Brother A marries sister C, and brother B marries sister D. A and C have a son X; B and D have a daughter Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two brother–sister couples. They share both paternal grandparents (parents of A and B) and both maternal grandparents (parents of C and D). Hence they are first cousins through both parents, i.e., double first cousins, the most exact label.

question: X's mother has a brother U and X's father has a brother V. U and V are married to each other and have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is Y's precise relation to X?
explanation: U is X's maternal uncle, V is X's paternal uncle. Their child Y shares both sets of grandparents with X, making Y a double first cousin of X—the most specific term for this relationship.

question: X's father's sister (paternal aunt) married Y, who is the son of X's mother's brother (maternal uncle). They have a child Z. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted), what is Z's relation to X?
explanation: Z is the child of X's paternal aunt, who is a sibling of X's father; thus Z is X's first cousin. Although Y is X's first cousin, the nearest blood link for Z is through the aunt, giving the precise term "first cousin".
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed

question: M’s mother is T. M has a sister O. O is married to P, whose brother is Q. Q is the father of R, and R is married to S, the only child of T. What is the precise kinship term for S with respect to M (using standard English blood‑relation terms only)?
explanation: Both M and S are children of T, but the father of S is not identified. Since they share a mother, they are at least half‑siblings; they could be full siblings if they share the same father. The information does not determine this, so the relation cannot be uniquely specified beyond “sibling”.
choices: C) Not uniquely determinable (could be full or half sibling)

question: T's mother has a brother U, and T's father has a sister V. U and V are married to each other. W is the child of U and V. What is W's precise kinship term to T using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: U is T's maternal uncle and V is T's paternal aunt. Their child W therefore shares both of T's grandparent pairs, making W and T double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: M is the mother of N. N is married to O. O's sister is P. P's husband is Q. Q's mother is R, and R is the paternal aunt of M. What is Q's relation to M using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: R is M's father's sister, i.e., M's aunt. Q is R's child, making Q the child of M's aunt, which is the definition of a first cousin. No other listed relation fits.
choices: C) C) No direct relation (affinal only)

question: Adam and his sister Beth each marry a sibling from another family: Adam marries Carol and Beth marries Dan, where Carol and Dan are full siblings. Adam and Carol have a son Ethan; Beth and Dan have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Adam and Beth are full siblings; Carol and Dan are full siblings. Their children Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through both parents—double first cousins, the most precise term.

question: A's mother has a brother named M, and A's father has a sister named N. M's child is X, and N's child is Y. If either X or Y is selected and called Z, what is Z's precise relationship to A using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed)?
explanation: Both M and N are A's maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Their children, X and Y, are each the child of a sibling of one of A's parents, which by definition makes them A's first cousins. Regardless of which child is chosen, Z is always a first cousin of A.

question: Using standard English kinship terms only (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), consider the following: X’s mother has a brother A. A’s daughter is B. B is married to C. C’s mother is the sister of X’s father. What is B’s relation to X?
explanation: A is X’s maternal uncle, so B is X’s maternal first cousin. C is the child of X’s paternal aunt, making C X’s paternal first cousin. B’s marriage to C does not alter B’s blood relation to X. The only applicable term is ‘first cousin.’

question: M and N are siblings. M’s daughter is married to P, who is the son of N’s son Q. If R is the child of P and M’s daughter, what is the precise kinship term for R to Q?
explanation: M and N are siblings, so Q is N’s son and M’s nephew. P, Q’s son, is M’s grandson-in-law. M’s daughter (R’s mother) is Q’s niece. Their child R is therefore the child of Q’s niece, making R Q’s grand‑niece (the child of a niece).
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let X be the child of the sister of Y’s father, and let Y be the child of the brother of X’s mother. Using standard English blood‑kin terms (in‑law relations excluded), what is the precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X’s mother is the sister of Y’s father, so X is Y’s first cousin through Y’s paternal side. Conversely, Y’s father is the brother of X’s mother, giving the same first‑cousin link from X’s maternal side. No other parental sibling pairs exist, so the unique term is “first cousin”.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries P and N marries S, where P and S are sisters (both daughters of Q and R). M and P have a child X; N and S have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise term for the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: M and N share parents, and P and S share parents. Hence they are first cousins on two independent lines, which is called "double first cousins"—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: M and N are full siblings. O, P and Q are full siblings (O is sister of P; Q is brother of O). M marries O and they have a child X. N marries Q and they have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share both grandparents A and B; O, P, Q share both grandparents C and D. X’s parents are M and O; Y’s parents are N and Q. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, giving them the exact term “double first cousins.”

question: M and N are siblings. M's daughter A marries an unrelated man P. N's son B marries an unrelated woman Q. A and B each have one child, X and Y respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: A and B are first cousins, sharing the same grandparents. The children of first cousins are second cousins, sharing great‑grandparents only. No other blood link exists, so X and Y are precisely second cousins.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoption, X is the child of the only brother of Y’s mother and also the child of the only brother of Y’s father. What is X to Y?
explanation: X is the child of a sibling of Y’s mother (maternal uncle) and also of a sibling of Y’s father (paternal uncle). In either case X is the child of a parent’s brother, which is the definition of a first cousin. The relation is the same regardless of which side, so X is Y’s first cousin.

question: R’s mother has a brother (R’s maternal uncle) who has a daughter A. R’s father has a sister (R’s paternal aunt) who has a son B. A and B marry and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is C’s relation to R?
explanation: A is R’s maternal first cousin; B is R’s paternal first cousin. Their child C is one generation below each cousin, so C is a first cousin once removed to R (through either side).

question: Let Q be a person. P is the child of the sibling of Q’s father, and also the child of the sibling of Q’s mother. Assuming monogamy, no incest, and no adoption, what is the precise kinship term for P relative to Q?
