question: M and N are siblings. M is married to S, and N is married to T. S and T are sisters. M and S have a child P; N and T have a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: M and N share both parents, giving P and Q common maternal grandparents. S and T share both parents, giving P and Q common paternal grandparents. Thus P and Q share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins. No other term captures this exact double lineage.

question: Person P’s father has a brother (P’s paternal uncle) who has a daughter Q. P’s mother has a sister (P’s maternal aunt) who has a son R, and R is married to Q. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise blood relation of R to P?
explanation: R is the child of P’s maternal aunt, so they share one set of grandparents. That makes R P’s first cousin regardless of R’s marriage to Q.

question: A is the son of B’s sister. B is the daughter of C’s brother. C is the mother of D, and D is married to A. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is D’s blood relation to B?
explanation: C is the sibling of B’s father, making C B’s aunt/uncle. D, as C’s child, is therefore B’s first cousin. Marriage to A (B’s nephew) does not alter the blood relationship.

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamy (remarriage allowed), X is the child of the sister of Y’s mother, and X is also the child of the brother of Y’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal aunt (first cousin) and also the child of Y’s paternal uncle (first cousin). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the exact term.

question: M is the child of the sister of P’s father and also the child of the brother of Q’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: M’s mother is P’s paternal aunt; M’s father is Q’s maternal uncle. For M to have both parents, that aunt and uncle must be the same individual, meaning P’s father and Q’s mother are siblings. Hence P and Q are children of siblings – i.e., first cousins. No other blood link is guaranteed.

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father. M has a brother; his child is P. N has a sister; her child is Q. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: M’s mother and N’s father are siblings, so M and N are first cousins. Consequently M’s brother and N’s sister are also first cousins. The children of first cousins (P and Q) are second cousins. No other relationship fits.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has a son P. P marries R, whose brother is S. S has a son Q. What is the precise blood‑relationship term between O and Q (ignoring the marriage between O and Q)?
explanation: O is the daughter of M; P is the son of N, so O and P are first cousins. Q is the son of S, who is the brother of P’s wife R and has no blood link to O. Hence O and Q share no consanguinity.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, N marries P, and O and P are also siblings. M and O have a son X; N and P have a daughter Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters; therefore they are double first cousins, the most precise term.

question: Mary has two children, John and Anna. Mary’s brother Peter has a daughter Lisa. Anna’s son is Tom. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of Lisa to Tom?
explanation: Lisa is John’s first cousin (child of Mary’s brother). Anna, John’s sister, is also Lisa’s first cousin. Tom is Anna’s son, making Tom a first cousin once removed of Lisa. No closer term exists.

question: A is married to B. B’s brother C is married to D, who is A’s sister. E is the child of C and D. What is E’s precise relation to A using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: D is A’s sister, so any of D’s children are A’s nieces or nephews regardless of D’s spouse. Therefore E is A’s niece/nephew. The marriage to C (B’s brother) does not create a blood link.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary's son Tom marries John’s daughter Lisa. Tom and Lisa have a child Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), which single term best describes Emma’s relation to John?
explanation: Lisa is John’s daughter, making Emma his granddaughter. Tom is John’s nephew, making Emma his great‑niece. The only term that captures both lines of descent is the combined description “granddaughter and great‑niece.”

question: Grandfather G1 and Grandmother GM1 have two sons, Adam and Brian. Grandfather G2 and Grandmother GM2 have two daughters, Clara and Diana. Adam marries Clara and Brian marries Diana. Adam and Clara’s child is X; Brian and Diana’s child is Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents (G1/GM1 and G2/GM2). Hence they are first cousins through both parents, i.e., double first cousins. The other terms omit one shared grandparent pair.

question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father, and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M’s mother is N’s paternal aunt, making M a first cousin on the father's side. M’s father is N’s maternal uncle, making M a first cousin on the mother's side as well. Sharing both sets of grandparents, M and N are double first cousins, the only term that captures this exact relationship.

question: In a family with no adoption, L's father has a sister whose son is N. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of N to L?
explanation: L's father's sister is L's paternal aunt. Her son is therefore L's first cousin. No half‑relationship or other qualifier applies, making "first cousin" the exact term.

question: A man’s brother marries a woman’s sister; each couple has one child. Those two children are double first cousins. Each of those children has one child, C and D. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: Double first cousins share both sets of grandparents. Their children therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the precise term for this doubled lineage.

question: M is the child of P's paternal aunt (the sister of P's father) and also the child of P's maternal uncle (the brother of P's mother). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between M and P?
explanation: M is a child of both P's father's sister and P's mother's brother, making M simultaneously a first cousin on the paternal side and a first cousin on the maternal side. The exact term is "double first cousin".

question: Two brothers, R and S, each marry two sisters, T and U respectively. R and T have a child V; S and U have a child W. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between V and W?
explanation: V and W are children of two brothers who married two sisters. They share both paternal grandparents (through R and S) and both maternal grandparents (through T and U). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

question: M is the child of the sister of P’s father and also the child of the brother of P’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring marriage ties), what is the precise relation of M to P?
explanation: M is the offspring of P’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus M shares both of P’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: A has a brother B. B's daughter C marries A's son D, and they have a child E. What is the precise standard English kinship term for E's relationship to A's mother?
explanation: A's mother is the maternal grandmother of D, so through D, E is her great‑grandchild. Through C she would be a great‑niece, but that term is not a direct blood line. The most precise standard term is great‑granddaughter.

question: John is the son of Mary. Mary is the sister of Tom. Tom is the father of Susan. With no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for John relative to Susan using standard English kinship?
explanation: Mary and Tom are siblings, so their children John and Susan share the same set of grandparents. Children of siblings are first cousins. No other connections are introduced, making "first cousin" the exact term.

question: Lara and Maya are half‑sisters who share only their mother. Lara has a daughter, Nina; Maya has a son, Omar. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relationship between Nina and Omar?
explanation: Nina and Omar are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent. The correct term is “half‑first cousins,” which denotes cousins who share a single grandparent rather than a full pair.

question: John has a sister Mary. John marries Anna, whose brother is Paul. Paul marries Lisa, who is Mary’s daughter. Using standard English kinship terms (excluding extended affinal chains), what is Lisa’s relation to John?
explanation: Mary is John’s sister, so her daughter Lisa is John’s niece by blood. Lisa’s marriage to Paul (John’s brother‑in‑law) does not alter the blood relationship; the precise term remains "niece".

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother (M), and R’s father has exactly one sister (F). M’s son (C1) marries F’s daughter (C2). Their child is S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relationship of S to R?

question: John’s mother has a brother named Tom. Tom has a daughter named Lily. Lily has a son named Mark. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is Mark’s relation to John?
explanation: Tom is John’s maternal uncle, so Lily is John’s first cousin. Mark is Lily’s son, i.e., one generation below John’s cousin. The child of a first cousin is called a first cousin once removed. No other standard term fits.

question: John’s mother has a brother Mike, whose daughter Anna marries Tom, the son of John’s father’s brother. Anna and Tom have a daughter Lily. What is Lily’s precise relation to John using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Anna is John’s maternal first cousin; Tom is his paternal first cousin. Lily is the child of John’s first cousins, making her a first cousin once removed on both sides. No double‑cousin term applies because the cousins share different grandparent pairs.

question: John and Tom are brothers. John marries Mary, and Tom marries Lisa, who is Mary’s sister. John’s child is Anna and Tom’s child is Ben. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between Anna and Ben?
explanation: John and Tom share the same parents, and Mary and Lisa share the same parents. Therefore Anna and Ben share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term for this situation.

question: John’s mother has a brother Mark. Mark’s daughter Lisa marries John’s father’s brother Peter. Lisa and Peter have a child Emma. What is Emma’s precise relation to John using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Lisa is John’s maternal first cousin; Peter is John’s paternal first cousin. Emma is the child of those two first cousins. question: L’s mother has a brother M whose daughter is N. L’s father has a sister O whose son is P. N and P marry and have a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relationship of Q to L?

question: Let me be the speaker. M is the child of the only son of my father’s sister. N is the child of the only daughter of my mother’s brother. If I pick either M or N and call that person X, what is X to me using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: My father’s sister is my paternal aunt; her only son is my first cousin. His child (M) is the child of a first cousin, i.e., my first cousin once removed. Similarly, my mother’s brother is my maternal uncle; his only daughter is also my first cousin, and her child (N) is likewise my first cousin once removed. Thus X is always a first cousin once removed.

question: John and Mary are brother and sister. Mary has a daughter Lily. John has a son Mark, and Mark has a son Sam. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is Lily's relation to Sam?
explanation: Lily and Mark share both grandparents, making them first cousins. Sam is Mark's son, one generation younger. Therefore Lily is Sam's first cousin once removed, the precise term for a cousin separated by one generation.

question: R’s mother has a brother T, whose daughter is S. R’s father has a sister U, whose son is V. S and V marry and have a child W. Using standard English kinship terms, what is W’s relation to R?
explanation: S is R’s maternal first cousin; V is R’s paternal first cousin. Their child W is the child of R’s first cousin on each side, which is precisely a first cousin once removed. No closer or different term applies.

question: Assume monogamy and no adoption. X is the child of the only sister of Y’s father and also the child of the only brother of Y’s mother. What is the precise kinship term for X in relation to Y?
explanation: The sister of Y’s father is Y’s paternal aunt; her child is a paternal first cousin. The brother of Y’s mother is Y’s maternal uncle; his child is a maternal first cousin. Since the aunt and uncle are married, X is both a paternal and maternal first cousin – a double first cousin.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John marries Anna, who is the daughter of Mary's brother‑in‑law (i.e., Mary's husband's brother). John and Anna have a child, Lily. What is the most precise kinship term for Lily's relation to Mary's son, Peter?

question: Let Q be a person. Q’s mother has exactly one brother, and Q’s father has exactly one sister. A child P is simultaneously the child of that brother and the child of that sister. explanation: P is the offspring of Q’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, who must be married to each other. Therefore P shares both of Q’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: A is married to B. B's sister is C. C's husband is D. D's sister is E. What is E to A, using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, who has a brother P. N marries Q, who is the sister of O. If R is the child of M and O, and S is the child of N and Q, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between R and S, assuming no adoption and monogamy?
explanation: M and N are siblings, O and Q are siblings, and the two couples cross‑marry. R and S are children of double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). Hence R and S are double first cousins, the most precise term.

question: Y’s mother has exactly one brother, B, and Y’s father has exactly one sister, S. Z is the child of B and also the child of S (i.e., B and S are Z’s parents). Using standard English kinship terms, what is Z’s precise relation to Y?

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, A and B are siblings. B has a child C, and C has a child D. Using standard English kinship terms, what is D’s precise relation to A?
explanation: A is the aunt/uncle of C (sibling’s child). D is the child of C, making D the grand‑child of A’s sibling. The exact term is great‑niece (or grand‑niece), the child of one’s niece/nephew.

question: John and Mark are brothers. John’s daughter is Anna. Mark’s daughter is Lisa. John’s sister Mary has a son Tom, and Tom’s cousin is Lisa. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the precise relation of Lisa to Anna?
explanation: Anna and Lisa are each children of two brothers (John and Mark). Children of siblings are first cousins. No other blood link exists, making "first cousin" the exact term.

question: A and B are siblings. B is married to C. C has exactly one sibling, D, who is married to A. E is the child of A and D. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the relation of E to C?
explanation: D is C’s sibling and also E’s parent, making C E’s aunt by blood. Additionally, C is spouse of B, who is A’s sibling, so C is also aunt‑in‑law. The most precise standard term covering both is simply “aunt.”

question: L has one sister and one brother. The sister has exactly one son, who has exactly one child M. The brother has exactly one daughter, who also has exactly one child M (the same person). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M's relation to L?
explanation: L's sister’s son is L’s nephew; his child is L’s great‑nephew/niece. L's brother’s daughter is L’s niece; her child is also L’s great‑nephew/niece. Both lines converge on M, so M is precisely L’s great‑nephew/niece.

question: M and N are brother and sister. M marries P, who is the daughter of Q. N marries R, who is the son of S. P and R are first cousins (i.e., Q and S are siblings). Each couple has exactly one child: X (child of M & P) and Y (child of N & R). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: M and N are siblings, so their children X and Y are first cousins. Additionally, P and R are first cousins, making X and Y also second cousins through that line. The closest degree of kinship is first cousins, which is the most precise single term.

question: Person X has a mother whose brother (maternal uncle) with a daughter Y, and a father whose brother (paternal uncle) with a son Z. Y and Z marry and have a child W. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of W to X?
explanation: Y is X's maternal first cousin; Z is X's paternal first cousin. Their child W is the child of X's first cousins, making W X's first cousin once removed on both sides. The standard term is simply "first cousin once removed".

question: M’s mother has exactly one brother, who is married and has a single child named N. What is N’s precise relation to M using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: N is the child of M’s maternal uncle (the brother of M’s mother). The child of a parent’s sibling is a first cousin. Therefore N is M’s first cousin.

question: M is the child of the only son of A’s sister, while N is the child of the only daughter of B’s brother. If A and B are siblings, what is the precise kinship between M and N?
explanation: M and N’s relation depends on whether A’s sister and B’s brother are the same sibling or different ones. That uncertainty yields multiple possible connections (first cousins, half‑first cousins, etc.). Therefore the exact relation cannot be uniquely determined.

question: M is the father of N. N is the mother of O. O is the father of P. P is married to Q, who is the daughter of R. R is the sister of M. What is the precise kinship term for Q relative to N, using standard English blood relations only?
explanation: M is N's father, so R, M's sister, is N's aunt. Q, being R's daughter, is therefore N's first cousin. No other direct blood link exists.

question: Rachel’s mother has a brother named Sam. Sam’s daughter is Linda. Linda’s son is Mark. What is Mark’s relationship to Rachel?
explanation: Sam is Rachel’s maternal uncle; his daughter Linda is Rachel’s first cousin. Mark is Linda’s son, i.e., the child of Rachel’s first cousin, which makes him Rachel’s first cousin once removed.

question: In a family, Y’s mother has exactly one brother. That brother has a single child X. Using standard English kinship terms, what is X’s relation to Y?
explanation: Y’s mother’s brother is Y’s maternal uncle. His child X is therefore the child of Y’s uncle, which makes X Y’s first cousin. No other relation applies.

question: In a family with no adoption, X’s mother has exactly one brother (her maternal uncle) and X’s father has exactly one sister (his paternal aunt). explanation: Y is the child of X’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, who are spouses. Thus Y shares both sets of grandparents with X, making Y a double first cousin—the only term that captures the dual shared‑grandparent relationship.

question: In a family where there is no adoption or remarriage, let N be a person. N's father has exactly one sibling, and N's mother also has exactly one sibling. The child of the father's sibling and the child of the mother's sibling happen to be the same individual, M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of M to N?

question: R’s father has a sister named A. A’s only child is B. B has a daughter C. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the precise relation of C to R?
explanation: A is R’s paternal aunt. Her child B is R’s first cousin. B’s daughter C is one generation below that cousin, making C R’s first cousin once removed. No other standard term applies.

question: Emma's mother has exactly one sibling, a brother named Alan. Emma's father has exactly one sibling, a sister named Beth. Alan and Beth are married and have a daughter, Lily. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is Lily to Emma?
explanation: Alan is Emma's maternal uncle; Beth is Emma's paternal aunt. Their daughter Lily is child of both Emma's maternal uncle and paternal aunt, sharing both sets of grandparents with Emma. This makes Lily a double first cousin of Emma.

question: John is the only child of Mary and Peter. Mary has a brother Tom, who is married to Linda. Linda's sister Susan is the mother of Alex. Alex's father is Peter's brother. question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, M is the child of the sister of the spouse of L’s father. What is M’s relation to L?
explanation: L’s father’s spouse is L’s mother. Her sister is L’s maternal aunt. The child of that aunt is L’s first cousin. No other kinship fits.

question: M and N are brothers. M marries O, who is the sister of P. N marries P. Their only children are X (child of M and O) and Y (child of N and P). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?

question: J's mother has a brother K. J's father has a sister L. K and L are married and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M to J?
explanation: K is J's maternal uncle; L is J's paternal aunt. Their child M shares both sets of grandparents with J, making M J's double first cousin—the only precise term.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a daughter Emma. Brian marries Diana and they have a son Frank. explanation: Laura is sister of both Clara and Diana, making her the maternal aunt of Emma and also of Frank. Since George is the child of Emma and Frank, Laura is great‑aunt to George through two independent lines, i.e., a double great‑aunt.

question: John and Paul are brothers. John has a daughter Anna; Paul has a son Brian and a daughter Diana. Anna marries Brian (first cousins) and they have a son Carl. Diana has a son Ethan with an unrelated spouse. Before Ethan and Carl marry, what is Ethan's precise blood relation to Carl?
explanation: Brian and Diana are siblings (both children of Paul). Their children Carl and Ethan are therefore children of siblings, which makes them first cousins. No other shared ancestors alter this relationship.

question: L has exactly two children: a daughter and a son. The daughter’s only child is M, and the son’s only child is N. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relationship between M and N?
explanation: M and N are each the child of one of L’s children, who are siblings. Children of siblings are first cousins. No other qualifying relationship (e.g., half‑cousin) applies because L’s two children share both parents.

question: M and N are married. M’s sister O is married to P, who is N’s brother. O and P have a child Q. M and N have a child R. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relationship between Q and R?
explanation: Q’s mother O and R’s mother M share the same parents, and Q’s father P and R’s father N share the same parents. Thus Q and R share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the most precise term.

question: In a family with no adoptions, L is a woman who had two children with different fathers: N (father P) and M (father Q). Thus N and M are half‑siblings. N’s only child is A; M’s only child is B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent (L) and not the other. The correct term for such children is “half‑first cousins,” distinct from full first cousins which require both grandparents in common.

question: Two brothers, M and N, each marry a sister, O and P, respectively, where O and P are also sisters. M and O have a child A; N and P have a child B. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relationship between A and B?
explanation: M and N are brothers and O and P are sisters, so A and B are children of double first cousins. They share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry precisely.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: M’s mother has a brother whose only child is A. M’s father has a sister whose only child is B. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term between A and B?
explanation: A is the child of M’s maternal uncle, making A a first cousin of M on the mother’s side. B is the child of M’s paternal aunt, making B a first cousin of M on the father’s side. Two people who are each a first cousin of the same person are themselves first cousins. Hence A and B are first cousins.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: M is the mother of N. N is married to O. O's mother is P, who is the sister of Q. Q is the father of R, and R is the spouse of S. S is the sibling of M. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is O's relation to S?
explanation: M and S are siblings, so N (M's child) is S's niece/nephew. O is the spouse of that niece/nephew, making O S's niece‑in‑law, the precise term allowed by the in‑law scope.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: R’s father has a sister (paternal aunt) who marries R’s mother’s brother (maternal uncle). Their only child is S. Using standard English kinship terms, what is S’s precise relation to R?
explanation: S shares both of R’s sets of grandparents because the parents of S are R’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle. Hence S is a double first cousin of R, the most specific term.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: Let R be a man. R’s paternal grandfather has exactly one sister; her only child is A. R’s maternal grandmother has exactly one brother; his only child is B. If we select either A or B and call that person S, what is S’s relation to R using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: A is the child of R’s great‑aunt (paternal), making A the cousin of R’s father; thus A is R’s first cousin once removed. The same logic applies to B via R’s great‑uncle (maternal). Hence, regardless of the choice, S is always R’s first cousin once removed.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M and N are each the child of a different woman; those two women are half‑sisters (they share exactly one parent and have different other parents). No other intermarriages exist. What is the precise relationship between M and N?
explanation: M’s mother and N’s mother share only one parent, so M and N share exactly one grandparent. Children sharing a single grandparent are half‑first cousins, distinct from full first cousins who share both grandparents.

question: A and B are siblings. B is married to C. C has one sibling, D, who is married to E. E’s only child is F. A’s only child is G. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only, in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation between G and F?
explanation: A and B share parents. B’s spouse C is not blood‑related to A. D is C’s sibling, also not blood‑related to A. E, married to D, is likewise unrelated by blood. Their child F is therefore connected to G only through a chain of spouses and siblings‑in‑law, with no common ancestor. No standard direct kin term exists for such an affinal chain.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: L has one sister and one brother. The only son of L’s sister (L’s nephew) marries the only daughter of L’s brother (L’s niece), and they have a child M. What is M’s precise kinship term to L using standard English kinship?
explanation: The child of L’s nephew (or niece) is L’s grand‑nephew or grand‑niece (also called great‑nephew/niece). Both parent lines give the same relation, so M is precisely L’s grand‑nephew/niece.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed

question: Two brothers, John and Mark, each marry a sister, Anna and Beth respectively. John + Anna have a son Paul. Mark + Beth have a daughter Maya. Assuming no other marriages or adoptions, what is the precise standard kinship term for the relation between Paul and Maya?
explanation: John and Mark share the same parents, and Anna and Beth share the same parents. Therefore Paul and Maya share both sets of grandparents. When two people share both grandparent pairs, the correct term is “double first cousins.”

question: M and N are siblings. M has a child X. M's brother (their sibling) has a son who in turn has a child Z. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between X and Z?
explanation: M’s brother’s son is M’s nephew; his child Z is M’s grandnephew. X, as M’s child, is first cousin to M’s nephew. Therefore X is one generation above Z, making X and Z first cousins once removed, the exact term required.

question: X is married to Y. Y’s sister is Z. Z is married to W. W’s mother is V, and V’s brother is U. Using only standard English kinship terms (blood and in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is U to X?
explanation: Y’s sister Z is X’s sister‑in‑law; Z’s husband W is X’s brother‑in‑law. V is the mother of that brother‑in‑law, not a parent of X’s spouse, so she has no direct term to X. U, V’s brother, is one step further removed; no standard kin term exists for this affinal chain.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John is the only child of Tom and Mary. Mary has a brother Peter, who is married to Susan. Susan’s sister Lisa is married to Mark, who is Tom’s brother. What is Lisa’s precise kinship term to John, using standard English kinship (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: Peter is John’s maternal uncle; his wife Susan is John’s aunt‑in‑law. Susan’s sister Lisa is Susan’s blood sister, not directly related to John. Lisa’s husband Mark is Tom’s brother, i.e., John’s paternal uncle. Therefore Lisa is Mark’s wife, making her John’s paternal aunt‑in‑law. The single correct term is “Aunt (by marriage)”.

question: In a family with no adoptions and monogamy, let X be a person. X’s mother has a brother named U. U has a daughter V, and V has a son W. What is the precise standard English kinship term for the relation of W to X?
explanation: U is X’s maternal uncle, so V (U’s daughter) is X’s first cousin. W is V’s son, i.e., the child of X’s first cousin, making W X’s first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: John and Anna are married. John’s sister Mary is married to Tom, who is Anna’s brother. John and Anna have a daughter Lily. Mary and Tom have a son Sam. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Lily and Sam?
explanation: Lily’s mother Anna is Tom’s sister, so Lily and Sam share Anna’s parents as grandparents. Lily’s father John is Mary’s brother, so they also share John’s parents as grandparents. Because they share both sets of grandparents, they are double first cousins—the most specific standard term.

question: R is married to S. S’s father has a daughter T from an earlier marriage (so T is S’s half‑sister). T is married to U, who is the brother of R’s mother. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is T’s relation to R?
explanation: T is the spouse of R’s maternal uncle. The allowed in‑law scope does not include a spouse of an uncle, so no standard direct kinship term applies. The relationship exists only through an affinal chain beyond the defined limits.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father, and M’s father is the brother of N’s mother. Assuming no adoption or remarriage, what is the most precise kinship term for the relationship between M and N?
explanation: Each of M’s parents is a sibling of one of N’s parents, so the two children share both sets of grandparents. That makes them double first cousins – the exact term for cousins with doubled ancestry.

question: R’s mother has exactly one sibling, a brother named U. U has a single child V. No adoptions, no inter‑marriage among cousins, and monogamy are assumed. Using standard English kinship terms, what is V’s precise relation to R?
explanation: U is R’s maternal uncle. His child V is therefore the child of a parent’s sibling, which by definition is a first cousin. The lack of other ties does not change this classification.
choices: D) D) Relation not uniquely determinable

question: Brothers A and B each marry sisters C and D respectively. A and C have a son E; B and D have a daughter F. E and F later marry each other and have a child G. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no in‑law), what is the most precise relation between G and A?
explanation: A is E’s father. E and F are double first cousins because their parents are two sets of siblings. Their child G therefore descends from A through both paternal and maternal lines, making A G’s great‑grandfather on two separate lines. The only term that captures this double descent is “great‑grandfather (double‑related)”, which is option D.

question: John marries Mary. Mary's brother Peter marries John’s sister Anna. Peter and Anna have a daughter Lily. John and Mary have a son Mark. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between Lily and Mark?
explanation: Lily’s mother Anna is John’s sister, so Lily is John’s niece; Lily’s father Peter is Mary’s brother, so Lily is Mary’s niece. Mark is John and Mary’s child. Thus Lily and Mark share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

question: L has a brother and a sister. The brother has exactly one daughter, and the sister has exactly one son. M is the child of that daughter, and N is the child of that son. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between M and N?
explanation: The brother’s daughter and the sister’s son are first cousins (they share L’s parents as grandparents). Their children, M and N, are therefore the children of first cousins, which makes them second cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. M has children A and D; N has children B and E. A marries B and they have a child C. D marries E and they have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between C and F?
explanation: A and B are first cousins (their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters). D and E are likewise first cousins. Thus C and F are children of double first‑cousin marriages, sharing both sets of grandparents, which makes them double first cousins.

question: I have a paternal aunt (my father’s sister) whose son is C1, a paternal uncle (my father’s brother) whose son is C2, and a maternal uncle (my mother’s brother) whose son is C3. All three cousins are unrelated to each other. If any one of them has a child Y, what is Y’s precise relationship to me using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Each cousin is a first cousin of me (they share a grandparent pair). The child of a first cousin is one generation down, making Y my first cousin once removed. No other blood link exists, so this is the most precise term.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed
C) C) Half‑first cousin once removed

question: Anna and Ben are siblings. Carl and Dana are also siblings. Mia is the child of Anna and Carl, while Lily is the child of Ben and Dana. No other marriages exist in the families. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between Mia and Lily?
explanation: Mia’s mother (Anna) is the sister of Lily’s father (Ben), and Mia’s father (Carl) is the brother of Lily’s mother (Dana). Thus Mia and Lily share both pairs of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the exact term for cousins with two common grandparent sets.

question: Two brothers, John and Jim, each marry one of two sisters, Anna and Beth, respectively. John and Anna have a child, C; Jim and Beth have a child, D. No other marriages or children exist. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: C and D share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. This dual shared ancestry makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: M and N are brother and sister. M marries O and N marries P. O and P are also brother and sister. X is the child of M and O; Y is the child of N and P. Using only standard English kinship terms (no “double‑cousin” synonyms), what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father (M) is sibling of Y’s mother (N) and X’s mother (O) is sibling of Y’s father (P). Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the only term that captures the dual shared lineage.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry one of two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan; Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Adam and Brian share the same parents, and Clara and Diana share the same parents. Their children Ethan and Fiona therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled shared ancestry.

question: A and B are half‑siblings who share only their mother M. A has a child C, and B has a child D. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for the relation between C and D?
explanation: A and B share one parent, so they have only one common grandparent. Their children therefore share that single grandparent, making C and D half‑first cousins—the exact term for cousins who share only one grandparent pair.

question: M has a sister S. S marries N. N’s sister T marries M’s brother B. B and T have a child C. M and N have a child D. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation between C and D?
explanation: C’s parents (B and T) are respectively the brother and sister of D’s parents (M and N). Hence C and D share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father, and M’s father is the brother of N’s mother. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between M and N?
explanation: M and N share both sets of grandparents: one through their mothers’ siblings and one through their fathers’ siblings. This makes them double first cousins, a distinct term from ordinary first cousins or half‑first cousins.

question: John and Paul are brothers. Mary and Nina are sisters. John marries Mary and Paul marries Nina. John and Mary have a daughter Lily; Paul and Nina have a son Mark. Lily and Mark marry each other and have a child Sam. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for Sam’s relation to John?
explanation: Sam is the child of Lily, who is John’s daughter, making Sam John’s grandchild. Although Sam is also John’s grand‑niece (child of his nephew Mark), the direct line through his own child gives the precise term “grandchild.”
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: P is the child of the only brother of Q’s father and also the child of the only sister of Q’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: P’s father is Q’s paternal uncle, and P’s mother is Q’s maternal aunt. Thus P is a child of both a sibling of Q’s father and a sibling of Q’s mother, sharing both sets of grandparents with Q. The exact term is double first cousin.

question: In a monogamous (remarriage allowed) family with no adoption, let M be the mother of person X. M’s only brother U is married to S. S’s sister T is married to the only brother of X’s father. T and that brother have a child C. What is the precise kinship term for C relative to X?
explanation: C is the child of X’s paternal uncle, so C is X’s first cousin. The extra link through the maternal side does not affect the direct blood relation; no half‑ or double‑cousin situation arises.

question: Emma and Noah are siblings. Emma marries Paul, and Noah marries Rachel. Paul and Rachel are first cousins (their mothers are sisters). Emma and Paul have a son Alex; Noah and Rachel have a daughter Bella. What is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between Alex and Bella?
explanation: Alex and Bella are children of siblings (Emma and Noah) and also children of first cousins (Paul and Rachel). They share both sets of grandparents, so the exact term is double first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a child P. N has a child Q, and Q has a child R. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of P to R?
explanation: M and N are siblings, so their children P and Q are first cousins. R is Q's child, making R the next generation. A first cousin of a parent is a first cousin once removed. Hence P is the first cousin once removed of R.

question: Two brothers marry two sisters. Each couple has exactly one child. The two children then marry each other. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the relationship between those two children?
explanation: Each child is the offspring of a brother‑sister pair, so they share both paternal grandparents (the brothers' parents) and both maternal grandparents (the sisters' parents). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, not merely first or half‑first cousins.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a son Ethan. Brian marries Diana and they have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona each marry unrelated partners and have one child each, X and Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law terms), what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins because they share both sets of grandparents. Their children X and Y therefore share both great‑grandparent pairs, which makes X and Y double second cousins—the most precise term.

question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father, and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship of M to N?
explanation: M is child of N's paternal aunt and also child of N's maternal uncle, so M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making them double first cousins—the most precise term.

question: In a family, Emma and Liam are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). Emma has a daughter, Zoe. Liam has a son, Noah. Assuming no other intermarriages or adoptions, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between Zoe and Noah?
explanation: Zoe and Noah are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent. The correct term is “half‑first cousins”, which denotes cousins who share only one common grandparent.

question: A is the child of B’s brother. C is the child of D’s sister. B and D are married. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only, in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the relation of A to C?
explanation: A is B’s niece/nephew (child of B’s brother). C is D’s niece/nephew (child of D’s sister). Since B and D are spouses, their siblings are siblings‑in‑law, not blood relatives. Thus A and C share no blood link and exceed the permitted in‑law scope, giving no standard direct kin term.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal only)

question: A man A marries a woman B. A's sister C marries B's brother D. A and B have a child F. C and D have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between E and F?
explanation: E's parents (C and D) are respectively the sister of A and the brother of B. Thus E shares both of A’s parents (through C) and both of B’s parents (through D) with F. They have the same two sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: M and N are siblings. M has children A and D; N has children B and E. A marries B and they have child C. D marries E and they have child F. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between C and F?
explanation: A and D are siblings; B and E are siblings. Thus C’s parents (A, B) and F’s parents (D, E) are two pairs of siblings. Children of such unions share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. No other option captures the double shared ancestry.

question: Let X be the child of Y. Y is a sibling of Z, and Z is the parent of W. Assuming no adoption, monogamy, and that Y and Z could be either full siblings or half‑siblings, what is the most precise standard kinship term describing the relationship between X and W?
explanation: If Y and Z are full siblings, X and W are first cousins; if they are half‑siblings, X and W are half‑first cousins. Because the sibling status is unspecified, the exact relation cannot be uniquely determined.

question: A is married to B. B’s brother C is married to D. D’s sister E has a child F. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the relation of F to A?
explanation: B’s brother C is A’s brother‑in‑law; C’s wife D is also A’s sister‑in‑law (spouse of a brother‑in‑law). D’s sister E is unrelated to A by blood or marriage, so E’s child F has no direct kin term for A. The connection exists only through a chain of affinal links.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: Two brothers, M and N, each marry two sisters, U and V. M + U have a son A; N + V have a daughter B. A and B marry unrelated partners and have children C and D respectively. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: A and B are double first cousins: they share both sets of grandparents (M‑N’s parents and U‑V’s parents). Their children C and D therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins. No other term is more exact.

question: John has a sister Mary and a brother Michael. Mary’s son Peter marries Anna, who is Michael’s daughter. Peter and Anna have a child Lily. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Lily’s relation to John?
explanation: Peter is John’s nephew (sister’s son) and Anna is John’s niece (brother’s daughter). Their child Lily is therefore the child of John’s nephew and niece, making her John’s great‑niece (the child of a niece or nephew).
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M is the child of the only son of A’s mother and also the child of the only daughter of B’s father. No adoption or polygamy is allowed, and A and B are not siblings. What is M’s relationship to A?
explanation: The only son of A’s mother is A’s brother. Hence M is the child of A’s brother, making M A’s nephew or niece. The other parent (the only daughter of B’s father) does not affect M’s relation to A. Thus the precise term is nephew/niece.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Ben, marry two sisters, Clara and Dana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a son, Ethan. Ben and Dana have a daughter, Fiona. Ethan and Fiona each marry unrelated partners and have one child each: Gage (Ethan’s child) and Hannah (Fiona’s child). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Gage and Hannah?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters, sharing both sets of grandparents. Their children Gage and Hannah therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins.

question: X’s mother has exactly one brother, and X’s father has exactly one sister. The child of X’s maternal uncle is Y, and the child of X’s paternal aunt is Z. If either Y or Z is selected (call that person S), what is S’s precise kinship term to X using standard English blood‑relation terminology?
explanation: Y is the child of X’s mother’s brother (maternal uncle) and Z is the child of X’s father’s sister (paternal aunt). Both are children of a parent’s sibling, which by definition makes each a first cousin of X. The relation is unique regardless of which child is chosen.

question: L has one sister and one brother. The only son of L’s sister has a child X, and the only daughter of L’s brother also has a child X (the same person). Using standard English kinship terms, what is X’s relation to L?
explanation: L’s sister’s son is L’s nephew; his child is L’s grand‑nephew/niece (great‑nephew/niece). L’s brother’s daughter is L’s niece; her child is also L’s grand‑nephew/niece. Both paths give the same precise term, so X is L’s grand‑niece/nephew.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed

question: Using standard English kinship terms (blood plus in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), consider: A is married to B; B’s sister is C; C is married to D; D’s brother is E; E is married to F; F’s mother is G. What is G to A?
explanation: A→B (spouse) →C (sister‑in‑law) →D (spouse of sister‑in‑law, also a brother‑in‑law) →E (sibling of that brother‑in‑law, no direct term) →F (spouse of that sibling, still no term) →G (mother of that spouse). The chain never produces a recognized kin term, so G has no standard direct relation to A.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: John and Mary are siblings. Mary has a daughter Anna. John has a son Peter, and Peter has a daughter Lily. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between Anna and Lily?
explanation: Anna and Lily share the same set of grandparents (John and Mary's parents). Anna is a child of John’s sibling, Lily is a child of John’s child. Thus they are one generation apart but share grandparents, making them first cousins once removed. No other listed term fits exactly.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: Emma’s father Frank has a sister Gina. Gina is married to Henry, and Henry’s brother is Ian. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Ian’s relation to Emma?
explanation: Frank’s sister Gina is Emma’s paternal aunt. Gina’s husband Henry is an uncle‑in‑law. Ian is Henry’s brother, i.e., the sibling of an uncle‑in‑law. This link exceeds the allowed in‑law scope, so no standard direct kin term exists. Therefore the precise answer is C.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted: Person A has a son B. B marries C. C’s mother D later marries E, who is A’s brother. What is E’s relation to B using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: E is the brother of A, who is B’s father, making E B’s paternal uncle. The other options either misstate the generational level or ignore the blood link.

question: In a family with no adoptions and monogamy, let Q be a person. Let X be the child of the only brother of Q’s mother, and let Y be the child of the only sister of Q’s father. If X and Y are the same individual, what is the relation of that individual to Q?
explanation: The only brother of Q’s mother is Q’s maternal uncle; his child is Q’s first cousin on the mother’s side. The only sister of Q’s father is Q’s paternal aunt; her child is Q’s first cousin on the father’s side. Since the same person fulfills both roles, they are Q’s first cousin.

question: Let Z be a person such that Z is the child of the only child of the sister of A’s mother, and also the child of the only child of the brother of A’s father. Assuming no adoption, monogamy, and that the two “only children” may be the same individual or different individuals, what is the precise kinship term for Z with respect to A?
explanation: If the two only‑children are the same person, Z is A’s first cousin (both parents are siblings of A’s parents). If they are different individuals, Z is A’s half‑first cousin (they share only one grandparent). Because the information does not specify whether the two only‑children coincide, the exact term cannot be uniquely determined.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: Alan has a sister Beth. Beth is married to Carl. Carl's sister Diane is married to Alan's brother Edward. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is Diane's relation to Alan?
explanation: Diane is married to Alan's brother Edward, making her Alan's sister‑in‑law. No blood link exists; the other described connections do not affect this relation.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions, R’s mother has exactly one brother and R’s father has exactly one sister. The mother’s brother (R’s maternal uncle) marries the father’s sister (R’s paternal aunt) and they have a child S. What is the most precise standard kinship term for S’s relation to R?
explanation: S is the child of R’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Therefore S shares R’s maternal grandparents (through the uncle) and paternal grandparents (through the aunt). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes S and R double first cousins, the most specific term.
choices: D) D) Relation not uniquely determinable

question: M's mother has a brother U. M's father has a sister V. U and V are married and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is C's relation to M?
explanation: U is M's maternal uncle, so C is M's first cousin on the mother’s side. V is M's paternal aunt, so C is also M's first cousin on the father’s side. The two cousin links are independent; the precise term remains "first cousin".

question: L’s father has a sister who is married to L’s mother’s brother. Their only child is M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: The child of L’s paternal aunt is a first cousin; the same child is also the child of L’s maternal uncle, another first cousin line. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes M a double first cousin of L.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: Z is the child of the only brother of A’s mother and also the child of the only sister of A’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is Z’s precise relation to A?
explanation: The brother of A’s mother is A’s maternal uncle; his child is A’s nephew/niece. The sister of A’s father is A’s paternal aunt; her child is also A’s nephew/niece. Since Z’s gender is unspecified, Z could be either a nephew or a niece, making the exact term indeterminable.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, who is the sister of P. N marries Q, who is the brother of O. M and O have a daughter A; N and Q have a son B. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the most precise relation of A to B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents: through M/N (their parents are siblings) and through O/Q (their parents are also siblings). Hence they are double first cousins, the most specific term available.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Ben, each marry sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a son, Ethan; Ben and Diana have a daughter, Fiona. Ethan and Fiona each marry unrelated partners and have children, Paul and Quinn respectively. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no in‑law extensions), what is the most precise relation between Paul and Quinn?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins because they share both sets of grandparents. Their children, Paul and Quinn, therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry at the second‑cousin level.

question: M is the child of the sister of P’s father and also the child of the brother of P’s mother. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is M’s precise kinship to P using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: M’s father is the brother of P’s mother, making M a first cousin on the maternal side. M’s mother is the sister of P’s father, making M a first cousin on the paternal side as well. Sharing both sets of grandparents defines a double first cousin, the most specific term.

question: John is married to Mary. Mary's brother Tom is married to Lisa. Lisa and Sarah share the same mother (they are half‑sisters). Sarah is married to Mark, who is John’s brother. Tom and Lisa have a daughter Emma. What is Emma's relation to Mark using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses)?
explanation: Lisa is Emma's mother. Lisa's half‑sister is Sarah, whose husband is Mark. Thus Mark is the husband of Emma's maternal half‑aunt, making him Emma's uncle by marriage – the standard term is "uncle‑in‑law".

question: In a family, let P be a person. P's mother's brother (her maternal uncle) has a daughter who is married to the son of P's father's brother (P's paternal uncle). What is the precise blood relation between that son and P, using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: P's maternal uncle's daughter is P's maternal first cousin. She marries P's paternal uncle's son, who is P's paternal first cousin. Thus that man is a first cousin of P by blood, making "first cousin" the exact term.

question: Two brothers each marry a different sister from another family (each brother marries one of the sisters). The first couple has a child X, and the second couple has a child Y. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share the same paternal grandparents (their fathers are brothers) and the same maternal grandparents (their mothers are sisters). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the exact term.

question: John and Mary are siblings. Mary marries Dave, who is Paul's brother; they have a daughter Lisa. Paul’s sister Anna marries Mark, who is John’s brother; they have a son Tom. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between Lisa and Tom?
explanation: Lisa’s mother Mary and Tom’s father Mark are both children of John’s parents, so Lisa and Tom share those grandparents. Their fathers Dave and Paul are also brothers, giving them the same set of grandparents on the other side. Thus they share both grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: R’s mother has a brother M, and R’s father has a sister S. M’s daughter is A; S’s son is B. A and B marry and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is C’s relation to R?
explanation: M is R’s maternal uncle, so A is R’s maternal first cousin. S is R’s paternal aunt, so B is R’s paternal first cousin. A and B’s child C is one generation below R’s first cousins, making C R’s first cousin once removed (via either side).

question: John and Mary are siblings. John marries Anna, who is the sister of Peter. Mary marries Peter. John and Anna have a son Sam; Mary and Peter have a daughter Lily. Before Sam and Lily marry each other, what is Lily’s precise kinship term to Sam using standard English blood‑relation terminology?
explanation: Sam and Lily share both sets of grandparents: John/Mary’s parents and Anna/Peter’s parents. Hence they are double first cousins, the only term that captures the dual shared ancestry.

question: Let L be a person. M is the child of the only son of L’s father. N is the child of the only daughter of L’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: The “only son of L’s father’’ could be L himself or a different male sibling/half‑sibling; likewise the “only daughter of L’s mother’’ could be L’s sister or a different female sibling/half‑sibling. Depending on which individuals these are, M and N may be first cousins, uncle‑nephew, or unrelated. Hence the relation cannot be uniquely determined.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary's son David marries Sarah, who is the daughter of John's son Michael. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation between David and Sarah?
explanation: David is Mary's son, making him John’s nephew. Michael is John’s son, so Michael and David are first cousins. Sarah is Michael’s daughter, one generation below Michael. Hence David (a first cousin of Michael) and Sarah (Michael’s child) are first cousins once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: M and N share only their mother (they are half‑siblings). M has a child X and N has a child Y. Assuming no other marriages or adoptions in the family, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent (the common mother’s parent). The correct term is “half‑first cousins,” which denotes first cousins with only a single shared grandparent pair.

question: In a family with no adoption, Person P’s mother has a brother M, and P’s father has a sister S. M and S marry and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of C to P?
explanation: M is P’s maternal uncle, S is P’s paternal aunt. Their child C is first cousin to P through the mother’s side and also first cousin through the father’s side, sharing both sets of grandparents. The term for this is “double first cousin.”

question: Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted): 1) A is the only child of B. 2) B has a sister C. 3) C is married to D. 4) D’s mother is E, who has exactly one child (D). 5) C and D have a daughter H. 6) H is the mother of I. What is the precise relation of I to A?
explanation: C is A’s maternal aunt. H, her daughter, is A’s first cousin. I, being H’s child, is the child of A’s first cousin, i.e., A’s first cousin once removed. No other link changes this relationship.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries P and N marries Q. P and Q are also siblings (but not related to M or N). Their children are A (child of M + P) and B (child of N + Q). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of P/Q. Hence they are first cousins through two distinct parental lines, i.e., double first cousins, the exact term for this relationship.

question: Person X is the child of a man who is the brother of Y’s mother, and also the child of a woman who is the sister of Y’s father. Assuming monogamy, no adoption, and using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father is Y’s maternal uncle and X’s mother is Y’s paternal aunt. Thus X’s parents are the siblings of Y’s parents, giving X and Y the same four grandparents. They are therefore double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled shared ancestry.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and they have a child R. O’s brother is P. P marries Q, who is N’s daughter. S is the child of P and Q. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law relations limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise blood relationship between R and S?
explanation: R is the child of M; Q is the child of N, M’s sibling, so R and Q are first cousins. S is Q’s child, one generation below R, making R and S first cousins once removed. No other blood link changes this.

question: Two brothers marry two sisters. The first brother and his wife have a daughter X; the second brother and his wife have a son Y. X and Y marry each other and each have one child. What is the most precise kinship term for the two grandchildren?
explanation: X and Y are double first cousins because they share both sets of grandparents. Their children therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins. No other standard term is more exact.

question: John’s mother has exactly one brother, Tom, and John’s father has exactly one sister, Mary. Tom has a daughter Alice; Mary has a son Bob. If we select either Alice or Bob and call that person X, what is X’s precise relation to John using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed)?
explanation: Alice is the child of John’s maternal uncle, Bob is the child of John’s paternal aunt. In either case X is the child of a parent’s sibling, which is the definition of a first cousin.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has two children: a son P and a daughter R. R has a child Q, who marries O. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only), what is the precise relation of O to Q?
explanation: M and N share both parents, so O (M’s child) and R (N’s child) are first cousins. Q is R’s child, making Q the first cousin once removed of O. Marriage does not affect the blood relationship, so O is O’s spouse’s first cousin once removed.

question: Let X be a person. X’s paternal grandfather has a brother. That brother has a grandchild Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is Y’s relation to X?
explanation: X’s paternal grandfather and his brother share the same parents. The brother’s child is X’s father’s first cousin. The child’s child (Y) is one generation further, so Y and X are of the same generation but are two generations removed from the common ancestors, making them second cousins.

question: Two brothers, A and B, each marry sisters: A marries C and B marries D, where C and D are siblings. A’s daughter is X and B’s daughter is Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. This makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother M, and R’s father has exactly one brother N. M and N are married to each other and have a single child S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, and in‑law terms limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of S to R?
explanation: S is the child of R’s maternal uncle (M) and also the child of R’s paternal uncle (N). In either case S is R’s first cousin. Because both uncles are blood‑related, S is a double first cousin, but the standard term remains “first cousin”.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a son Ethan. Brian marries Diana and they have a son Felix. Ethan and Felix each have a child with unrelated partners: Ethan’s child is Grace, Felix’s child is Helen. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Grace and Helen?
explanation: Ethan and Felix share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins. Their children therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making Grace and Helen double second cousins. The other options omit the doubling or mis‑place the degree.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions, let L be a person. L’s father has exactly one brother, and L’s mother has exactly one brother. The child of each of those two brothers is the same individual, M. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for M’s relation to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s paternal uncle and also the child of L’s maternal uncle. Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with L, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let L be the only child of M. M has exactly one sibling, N. N’s only child is O. What is the precise kinship term for O’s relation to L?
explanation: L and O are children of siblings (M and N). Children of siblings are first cousins; no other blood link exists, so the exact term is "first cousin".

question: Adam and Beth are full siblings. Adam marries Clara and they have a son Ethan. Beth divorces and later marries Daniel, who is Clara’s brother; Beth and Daniel have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents: Adam‑Beth’s parents (paternal side) and Clara‑Daniel’s parents (maternal side). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a finer term than plain first cousins.

question: John and Mary are married. John's mother, Linda, had two children with different fathers: John and his half‑brother Paul. Mary's father, Robert, had two children with different mothers: Mary and her half‑sister Susan. Paul marries Susan, and they have a daughter Emma. What is Emma's precise relationship to John?
explanation: Paul is John’s half‑brother (they share only their mother). Emma is Paul’s daughter, making her John’s half‑niece. Susan provides no blood link to John, so the only correct term is half‑niece.

question: R’s mother has a brother U, whose daughter is V. R’s father has a sister W, whose son is X. V and X are married. What is the relation of the child of V and X to R (using standard English kinship terms, in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: V is R’s maternal uncle’s daughter → first cousin. X is R’s paternal aunt’s son → first cousin. Their child is one generation below both V and X, i.e., one generation below R’s first cousins, making the child R’s first cousin once removed. Both lines give the same term.

question: M’s mother has exactly one brother and M’s father has exactly one brother. The child of the mother’s brother is the same person as the child of the father’s brother. What is the precise kinship term for that child relative to M?
explanation: The child is the offspring of both M’s maternal uncle and paternal uncle, meaning they share both sets of grandparents with M. This is the definition of a double first cousin – a first cousin through both parental lines.

question: M has one sister S. S is married to N. N’s brother is B, and B is married to D, who is M’s only daughter. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is B to M?
explanation: B is the husband of M’s daughter D, making him M’s son‑in‑law. No blood link exists, and no other in‑law category (nephew‑in‑law, brother‑in‑law) applies.

question: In a lineage with no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage possible, let Z be the child of the sole sibling of L’s mother and also the child of the sole sibling of L’s father. What is Z’s precise relationship to L?
explanation: Z is the child of L’s maternal aunt (or uncle) and also the child of L’s paternal aunt (or uncle). In either case Z is the child of a parent’s sibling, which makes Z a first cousin of L. No other kin term is more exact.

question: M’s mother has a half‑sister H (they share the same mother but have different fathers). H has a daughter C, and C has a son S. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of H to S?
explanation: H is the half‑sister of M’s mother, so she is M’s half‑aunt. Her daughter C is M’s half‑first cousin, making C’s son S a half‑first cousin once removed to M. Therefore H is the half‑great‑aunt of S – the only term that reflects the single‑shared‑grandparent link.

question: N’s father has exactly one sibling, a brother F. N’s mother has exactly one sibling, a sister M. F and M are married and have a child X. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is X’s precise relation to N?
explanation: X is the child of N’s paternal uncle (F) and maternal aunt (M). Thus X shares both of N’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: N’s mother has a sister named M. N’s father has a brother named O, and O is married to M. Using standard English kinship terms (allowing only spouse, parents, siblings, children, and their spouses), what is M to N?
explanation: M is the sister of N’s mother, so she is N’s maternal aunt by blood. She is also the wife of N’s paternal uncle, making her an aunt‑in‑law. The blood relation dominates, and the single precise term is simply “aunt.”
