question: John and Mary are siblings. John marries Anna, who is the daughter of Mary's brother Peter. John and Anna have a child Sam. Mary has a child Lisa with her husband Mark. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only), what is the precise relationship between Sam and Lisa?
explanation: John and Mary share both grandparents, so their children Sam and Lisa each inherit those grandparents. Therefore Sam and Lisa are first cousins. The marriage to a niece does not alter this cousin link.
choices: D) D) No blood relation (in‑law only)

question: M and N are siblings. P and Q are siblings. M marries Q, and N marries P. Their children are X (child of M and Q) and Y (child of N and P). Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share both parents (grandparents G1). P and Q share both parents (grandparents G2). X’s parents are M (grandchild of G1) and Q (grandchild of G2); Y’s parents are N (grandchild of G1) and P (grandchild of G2). Hence X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: R's mother has a brother M, and R's father has a sister S. M's daughter is X, and S's son is Y. Assuming no intermarriage between the two families, what is the most precise standard English kinship term describing the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: M and S are unrelated siblings of R's parents, so X and Y are children of unrelated individuals. They share no common ancestor, thus there is no direct blood kinship term for X and Y. The correct description is that they are unrelated in standard kinship terminology.

question: M is the only child of his father F. N is the only child of her mother G. M and N marry each other and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no “in‑law” extensions), what is C’s relation to F’s sister S?
explanation: S is F’s sister, i.e., M’s paternal aunt. C is M’s child, so S is the aunt of C’s parent. The child of a sibling’s child is a grand‑niece (or great‑niece). Therefore C is S’s grand‑niece.

question: M and N are siblings. M has two children: daughter A and son D. N has one child, son B. D marries and has a daughter C. Who is C to B using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: B is N’s child; D is M’s child, so B and D are first cousins. C is D’s daughter, making C the child of B’s first cousin – i.e., B’s first cousin once removed. No other listed relation fits.

question: M's mother has exactly one brother, and M's father has exactly one sister. The brother of M's mother marries the sister of M's father, and they have a child N. Using standard English kinship terms, what is N's relation to M?
explanation: Maternal uncle shares M’s maternal grandparents; paternal aunt shares M’s paternal grandparents. Their child N shares both grandparent pairs with M, so N is a double first cousin of M.

question: John’s father and Mary’s mother are half‑siblings (they share only one parent). John and Mary have no other common ancestors. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between John and Mary?
explanation: John’s father and Mary’s mother share a single parent, so John and Mary share only one grandparent. That makes them half‑first cousins, distinct from full first cousins (who share both grandparents) and from any more distant cousin category.

question: M and N are full siblings. M marries X and they have a child A. N marries Y and they have a child B. X and Y are also full siblings. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between A and B?
explanation: A’s father M and B’s father N are brothers, and A’s mother X and B’s mother Y are sisters. Thus A and B share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – a stricter term than ordinary first cousins.

question: In a monogamous family, J’s mother’s spouse has a sibling, and that sibling has a child named M. Using only standard English blood‑kin terms (in‑law terms limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is M’s precise relation to J?
explanation: M is the child of the sibling of J’s father (the spouse of J’s mother). That sibling is J’s paternal aunt/uncle, so M is J’s first cousin. No other relationship fits.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation

question: A has a brother B. B's daughter is C. A's son is D. D marries C and they have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse only), what is the most precise relation of E to A?
explanation: E is the child of A's son D, making E A's grandchild. Although E is also the child of A's niece C (which would make E a grandniece), kinship terms use the closest blood link, so the precise term is grandchild.

question: John’s mother has a brother Mike. Mike’s daughter Lisa is John’s first cousin. Lisa is married to Tom. Tom’s sister Sarah is the mother of Emma. Emma’s father is the only son of John’s father. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Emma to John?
explanation: Emma is the child of Sarah, who is Tom’s sister. Tom is Lisa’s husband, and Lisa is John’s first cousin. The chain John → cousin → cousin‑in‑law → niece‑in‑law exceeds the permitted in‑law scope, and there is no blood link. Hence no standard direct kin term exists.
choices: A) A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)
B) B) First cousin once removed

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary's son David marries John’s daughter Emma. David and Emma have a child Lily. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring adoption and polygamy), what is Lily’s most precise relation to her paternal grandfather John?
explanation: Lily is the child of John’s daughter, so she is his granddaughter. She is also the child of John’s nephew (David), making her his great‑niece. The only term that captures both lines of descent is “granddaughter and great‑niece (double relationship).”

question: Mike and Tom are brothers. Anna and Beth are sisters. Mike marries Anna and they have a son Carl; Tom marries Beth and they have a daughter Dana. Carl and Dana each marry unrelated partners and have one child each: Emma and Frank. Using standard English kinship terms without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the precise relationship between Emma and Frank?
explanation: Mike‑Anna and Tom‑Beth are double sibling marriages, so Carl and Dana are double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). Their children Emma and Frank therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins, the most specific term.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter A who marries X. X has a sister S, and S’s daughter is C. What is the precise standard English kinship term for C’s relation to M?
explanation: C is the daughter of X’s sister, i.e., the daughter of M’s son‑in‑law’s sister. This creates no blood link and lies beyond the usual in‑law scope, so no standard direct kin term applies.

question: M and N are siblings. M has two children, A and D; N has two children, B and E. A marries B and they have a child C. D marries E and they have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between C and F?
explanation: C and F are each the child of a pair of first cousins (A‑B and D‑E). Because the two cousin couples are themselves siblings, C and F share both sets of grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: M's mother has a brother who has a daughter X. M's father has a brother who has a son Y. X and Y marry and have a child Z. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, ignoring step relations), what is the precise relation between Z and M?
explanation: X is M's maternal first cousin; Y is M's paternal first cousin. Their child Z is one generation below each cousin, making Z a first cousin once removed to M via both lines. The standard term is simply “first cousin once removed.”

question: M and N are siblings. M has one child, P. N is married to Q. Q’s brother is R, who is married to S. S and P together have a child T. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is T’s precise relation to Q?
explanation: T is the child of Q’s sister‑in‑law (S) and Q’s niece (P). One line suggests a niece‑in‑law, another a great‑niece‑in‑law, but no standard term covers this mixed lineage. Hence the relation cannot be uniquely determined.
choices: C) C) No standard direct kinship term

question: L has one sister and one brother. The sister has exactly one son, and the brother has exactly one daughter. M is the child of either that nephew or that niece (but we do not know which). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M's precise relation to L?
explanation: If M is the nephew’s child, M is L’s grandnephew/niece (child of a nephew). If M is the niece’s child, M is also L’s grandnephew/niece (child of a niece). However, the gender of M is unspecified, so the exact term (grandnephew vs. grandniece) cannot be determined. Hence the relation is not uniquely determinable.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: Person X’s mother has exactly one brother Y. Y’s only child is a daughter Z, and Z’s only child is a son W. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of W to X?
explanation: Y is X’s maternal uncle, so Z is X’s first cousin. W, being Z’s child, is the child of X’s first cousin, which makes W X’s first cousin once removed.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, X's mother has exactly one brother and X's father has exactly one sister. That brother and that sister marry each other and have a single child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Y's precise relation to X?
explanation: The brother is X’s maternal uncle and the sister is X’s paternal aunt. Their child is the child of X’s maternal uncle (first cousin on the mother’s side) and also the child of X’s paternal aunt (first cousin on the father’s side). Hence Y is a double first cousin of X—the most specific standard term.

question: John and Mary are married. John’s sister Lisa marries Mary’s brother Tom. Lisa and Tom have a daughter Emma. John and Mary have a son Alex. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Emma and Alex?
explanation: Emma’s paternal grandparents are John’s parents; her maternal grandparents are Mary’s parents. Alex shares the same two sets of grandparents. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more precise term than ordinary first cousins.

question: M’s mother has a sister N. N’s child is O. O has a daughter P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is P’s relation to M?
explanation: N is M’s maternal aunt, making O M’s first cousin. The child of a first cousin (P) is one generation apart, so P is M’s first cousin once removed.

question: John and Mary are full siblings. John marries Lisa and they have a son Alan. Mary marries Tom and they have a daughter Beth. Alan and Beth each marry unrelated partners and have children: Alan’s child is Carla, Beth’s child is David. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption), what is the most precise relationship between Carla and David?
explanation: Alan and Beth are first cousins because their parents are siblings. Their children Carla and David are therefore children of first cousins, which makes Carla and David second cousins (they share the same great‑grandparents). No doubling occurs, so the precise term is second cousins.

question: Two brothers marry two sisters. The elder brother and elder sister have a son X; the younger brother and younger sister have a daughter Y. X and Y later marry each other. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of Y to X?
explanation: X and Y are children of two brother‑sister couples, so they share both paternal and maternal grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, the exact term required.

question: Brother A marries sister C, and his brother B marries sister D (C and D are sisters). A and C have a son X; B and D have a son Y. Using standard English kinship terms without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. Hence they are first cousins with doubled ancestry, called double first cousins, the most precise term.

question: Emma's mother has a brother Tom. Tom's daughter Sarah marries Mark, who is Emma's father's brother. Emma has a daughter Lily; Sarah and Mark have a daughter Rose. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the most precise description of the relationship between Lily and Rose?
explanation: Through Mark (Emma's paternal uncle) Rose is Emma's first cousin, making Lily and Rose first cousins. Through Sarah (Emma's maternal first cousin) Rose is Emma's first cousin once removed, making Lily and Rose first cousins once removed. Because the two lines give different precise terms, no single standard kinship term uniquely describes their relation.
choices: C) C) First cousins once removed

question: M and N are double first cousins (their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters). M has a child X; N has a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins. Their children X and Y therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, which makes them double second cousins – the only term that captures the doubled ancestry at the second‑cousin level.

question: M is the mother of N. N is married to O. O’s sister is P. P and R are the parents of Q. R is M’s brother. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for Q’s relation to N?
explanation: R is N’s maternal uncle, so Q is N’s first cousin by blood. P is N’s sister‑in‑law, making Q N’s niece‑in‑law by marriage. When a blood relationship exists, the kin term is given by that blood link, which is more specific than an affinal one. Hence the precise term is “first cousin.”

question: In a family, P's father has a sister (F) and P's mother has a brother (U). F and U marry each other and have a child M. Using only standard English blood‑kinship terms (no in‑law or step relations), what is the precise relationship between M and P?
explanation: M is the child of P's paternal aunt (father's sister) and maternal uncle (mother's brother). Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with P, making them double first cousins – first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides simultaneously.

question: Two brothers, Alan and Brian, marry two sisters, Clara and Diana respectively (Alan‑C​lara, Brian‑Diana). Alan and Clara have a son Paul; Brian and Diana have a daughter Quinn. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Paul and Quinn?
explanation: Paul and Quinn are children of siblings (Alan‑Brian) and siblings (Clara‑Diana). Hence they share both paternal and maternal grandparents, making them double first cousins – the most precise term.

question: P’s mother has a brother who is married to Q. Q’s sister is the sister of P’s father. What is the relationship of P to Q?
explanation: P’s mother’s brother is P’s maternal uncle. He is married to Q. Q’s sister being P’s father’s sister means Q is also a daughter of P’s paternal grandparents, i.e., a paternal aunt. Thus Q is P’s aunt both by marriage and by blood. No other standard term fits.

question: Emily's mother has a brother, Mark, whose daughter is Sara. Emily's father has a sister, Nina, whose son is Leo. Sara and Leo marry and have a child, Zoe. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Zoe's precise relationship to Emily?
explanation: Mark is Emily's maternal uncle, so Sara is Emily's first cousin. Nina is Emily's paternal aunt, so Leo is also Emily's first cousin. Zoe is the child of Emily's first cousin (through the mother) and also the child of another first cousin (through the father). The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed, regardless of which side the line comes from.

question: In a standard English kinship system (no adoption, monogamy), let M be a person. M’s mother has a brother named U. U has a daughter V. V has a son W. What is the precise relationship of W to M?
explanation: U is M’s maternal uncle, so V is M’s first cousin. W, being the child of that cousin, is one generation removed from M, making W M’s first cousin once removed. No other listed term fits exactly.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries X, and N marries Y, where X and Y are sisters. M and X have a daughter A; N and Y have a son B. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of X/Y. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more precise term than simple first cousins.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoptions, let B be a person. B’s father has exactly one sister, and B’s mother has exactly one brother. A child A is born to the union of that sister and that brother. What is the precise kinship term for A’s relation to B?
explanation: A’s father is B’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and A’s mother is B’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Therefore A shares both sets of grandparents with B, making them double first cousins—the most specific standard term.

question: L's mother has a brother named M. N's father has a sister named O. M and O are the same person. What is the precise kinship term for the relation between L and N?
explanation: M is L's maternal uncle and O is N's paternal aunt; since M = O, L's mother and N's father are siblings. Therefore L and N are children of siblings, i.e., first cousins.

question: Alice and Beth share exactly one parent (they are half‑sisters). Alice has a son Carl. Beth has a daughter Dana, and Dana has a child Ethan. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of Carl to Ethan?
explanation: Alice and Beth are half‑sisters, so their children Carl and Dana are half‑first cousins. Ethan is Dana’s child, one generation down, making Carl a half‑first cousin once removed of Ethan. This is the most specific standard term.
choices: A) A) First cousin twice removed
C) C) Half‑first cousin once removed

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Clara and Dana are sisters. Adam marries Clara and they have a daughter Emily. Brian marries Dana and they have a son Frank. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between Emily and Frank?
explanation: Adam and Brian share both parents; Clara and Dana share both parents. Emily is child of Adam+Clara, Frank of Brian+Dana. Thus Emily and Frank share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most precise term.

question: Adam and Brian are brothers. Adam marries Clara and Brian marries Diana, who are sisters. Adam and Clara have a child X; Brian and Diana have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: Adam‑Brian’s parents and Clara‑Diana’s parents. Hence they are first cousins through each parent pair, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled shared ancestry.

question: M and N are double first cousins (each is the child of a sibling of the other's parent, so they share both sets of grandparents). M has a son S, and N has a daughter D. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between S and D?
explanation: M and N share both grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins. Their children S and D therefore share both great‑grandparent pairs, which is exactly the definition of double second cousins, the most specific term.

question: P’s mother has a brother whose daughter is Q. P’s father has a sister whose son is R. Q and R marry and have a child S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, and in‑law terms limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is S’s relation to P?
explanation: Q is P’s maternal first cousin; R is P’s paternal first cousin. S is the child of a first cousin of P, so S is a first cousin once removed to P. The double line does not change the term; no closer or different standard term applies.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary marries Tom. Tom’s sister Anna marries John’s son Peter. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Anna’s relation to Mary?
explanation: Mary’s husband Tom is Anna’s brother. The sister of one’s spouse is a sister‑in‑law. No blood link exists, and other in‑law categories do not apply.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: M is the only child of his mother. M’s mother has a sister (M’s maternal aunt) who is married to a man who is the brother of M’s father. The aunt and uncle have a daughter N. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: M’s mother’s sister and M’s father’s brother are siblings of opposite parents, so their child N shares both sets of grandparents with M. Hence M and N are double first cousins – they are first cousins through both the maternal and paternal lines.

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother, whose daughter is S. R’s father has exactly one sister, whose son is T. S and T marry each other and have a child U. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of U to R?
explanation: S is R’s maternal first cousin; T is R’s paternal first cousin. Their child U is the child of R’s first cousin on both sides, which makes U R’s first cousin once removed. No closer or different term applies.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M and N are siblings. M marries X and N marries Y, where X and Y are also siblings. Their respective children are A (child of M & X) and B (child of N & Y). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between A and B?
explanation: A’s father and B’s father are brothers, and A’s mother and B’s mother are sisters, so A and B share both paternal and maternal grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, a stricter term than simple first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings (no other intermarriages). M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father M and Y’s father N are brothers, and X’s mother O and Y’s mother P are sisters. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – a distinct term from ordinary first cousins.

question: N's father has exactly one brother, and N's mother has exactly one brother. The child of that paternal uncle marries the child of that maternal uncle, and they have a child M. What is the precise kinship term for M relative to N, using standard English blood‑relation terminology?
explanation: N's paternal uncle and maternal uncle are unrelated, but their children are first cousins. Their marriage produces a child who shares both sets of grandparents with N, making M a double first cousin—first cousins on both parental sides.

question: P’s mother has exactly one brother, whose daughter is X. P’s father has exactly one sister, whose son is Y. X and Y marry and have a child Z. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Z’s relation to P?
explanation: X is P’s maternal uncle’s daughter, a first cousin. Y is P’s paternal aunt’s son, also a first cousin. Z is the child of P’s first cousins, placing Z one generation below them. Hence Z is a first cousin once removed of P, the precise term.

question: Anna’s mother has exactly one brother, who has a daughter named Lily. Anna’s father has exactly one sister, who also has a daughter named Lily. Assuming no adoption and monogamy, what is Lily’s most precise kinship term to Anna?
explanation: Lily is the child of Anna’s maternal uncle (first cousin) and also the child of Anna’s paternal aunt (first cousin). She shares both sets of grandparents with Anna, making her a double first cousin—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: M is the mother of J. J is married to L. L’s mother is N. N’s brother is O. O’s daughter is P. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is P’s relation to M?
explanation: M → J (child). J ↔ L (spouse). L → N (mother). N’s brother O is L’s maternal uncle. O’s daughter P is L’s first cousin. Thus P is the cousin of M’s daughter‑in‑law, a relationship with no direct standard term.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a sister, Clara and Diana respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan. Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Ethan and Fiona marry each other and have a son Gabriel. What is Gabriel's precise blood relationship to Adam's mother?
explanation: Adam's mother is Ethan's grandmother (her son Adam is Ethan's father). Ethan is Gabriel's father, so Gabriel is one generation further: Adam's mother is Gabriel's great‑grandmother, making Gabriel her great‑grandchild. No other blood line links Gabriel to her.

question: L has exactly one sister and one brother. The sister has only one son, X, and the brother has only one daughter, Y. X and Y marry and have a child, M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s relation to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s nephew (sister’s son) and niece (brother’s daughter). The child of a nephew or niece is a great‑nephew/niece, i.e., the grand‑child of L’s sibling. Hence M is L’s great‑nephew/niece.

question: M and N are married. M's sister O is married to N's brother P. O and P have a child X, while M and N have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: O is M's sibling and P is N's sibling, and they are married. Thus X's parents are the siblings of Y's parents on both sides. X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the only term that captures the double shared ancestry.

question: R's mother has exactly one brother, U, and R's father has exactly one brother, V. U and V are married to each other and have a child, W. Assuming no adoption, monogamy, and no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between W and R?
explanation: W is the child of R's maternal uncle (U) and also the child of R's paternal uncle (V). Thus W is a first cousin on the mother's side and a first cousin on the father's side, sharing both pairs of grandparents. The precise term is "double first cousin".

question: M is the mother of J and K. J is married to L. L's mother is N. N's brother is O, whose daughter is P. P is married to Q, who is the son of K. What is the precise kinship term for M's relation to Q?
explanation: K is M's child, so Q, as K's son, is M's grandchild. No other blood link changes this. Hence M is Q's grandmother.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John has one child, a daughter named Anna. Anna is married to Peter. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Peter's precise relation to Mary?
explanation: Anna is Mary's niece (daughter of Mary's brother). Peter, as Anna's spouse, is the husband of Mary's niece, i.e., Mary's nephew‑in‑law. He is not Mary's brother‑in‑law, son‑in‑law, or cousin‑in‑law.

question: P's mother has a brother (her maternal uncle) who is married to P's father's sister (his paternal aunt). The couple's child is Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation of Q to P?
explanation: Q is the child of P's maternal uncle (first cousin on the mother’s side) and also the child of P's paternal aunt (first cousin on the father’s side). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes Q a double first cousin of P, the only term that captures this doubled lineage.

question: M and N are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). M has a daughter A; N has a son B. If a person X is known to be either A or B (but we do not know which), what is X’s precise kinship term to the other’s parent?
explanation: Because we do not know whether X is A or B, X could be the child of M (making X a niece/nephew of N) or the child of N (making X a nephew/niece of M). The two possibilities give different standard terms, so the exact relation cannot be determined uniquely.

question: John and Mark are brothers. Anna and Beth are sisters. John marries Anna and they have a daughter Clara. Mark marries Beth and they have a son David. Clara and David each marry unrelated partners and have children Emma and Frank respectively. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between Emma and Frank?
explanation: Clara and David are double first cousins because they share both paternal and maternal grandparents. Their children Emma and Frank therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins—the most exact label.

question: A and B are married and have a child F. A has a brother C, and B has a sister D. C and D marry each other and have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, but remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation between E and F?
explanation: E is the child of A’s brother (paternal uncle) and B’s sister (maternal aunt). F is the child of A and B. Thus E and F are children of two siblings from opposite sides, making them double first cousins – they share both sets of grandparents.

question: Let Q be a person. Q’s mother has exactly one brother, and Q’s father also has exactly one brother. Both of these brothers are unrelated to each other. If a person P is the child of the brother of Q’s mother and also the child of the brother of Q’s father, what is P’s precise kinship term for Q using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: P is the child of a maternal uncle and also the child of a paternal uncle. In either case P is the child of a parent’s brother, which is the definition of a first cousin. No other qualifiers apply.

question: M is the mother of twins N and O. O is married to R. R’s brother is Q, whose son is P. N marries P and they have a child S. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for R relative to S?
explanation: N is S’s mother; O is N’s sister, so O is S’s aunt. R is O’s spouse, making him S’s uncle by marriage. The precise term is “uncle‑in‑law.”

question: Two brothers, John and Mark, each marry a sister—John marries Alice and Mark marries Beth. John and Alice have a son Carl; Mark and Beth have a daughter Dana. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Carl and Dana?
explanation: John and Mark share the same parents, and Alice and Beth share the same parents. Their children therefore share both sets of grandparents, making Carl and Dana double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: M and N are half‑siblings (they share exactly one parent). M has a child C and N has a child D, with no other intermarriages in the family. What is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between C and D?
explanation: C and D are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent. The exact term for such relatives is “half‑first cousins,” distinguishing them from full first cousins (who share both grandparents).

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. X and Y marry and have a child Z. What is the most precise standard kinship term for X and Y to each other?
explanation: X’s parents (M and O) and Y’s parents (N and P) each consist of a pair of siblings. M and N share one set of grandparents; O and P share another. Thus X and Y share both grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the exact term.

question: In a family, X’s mother is the sister of Y’s father, and X’s father is the brother of Y’s mother. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s mother and Y’s father are siblings, giving X and Y one shared set of grandparents. X’s father and Y’s mother are also siblings, giving a second shared set of grandparents. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes X and Y double first cousins.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, M is a woman whose only brother is A. F is a man whose only sister is B. A and B are married to each other. M and F have a child X. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse), what is X's relation to A?
explanation: A is the brother of X's mother, i.e., X's maternal uncle. The child of a sibling of one's parent is a niece or nephew. Marriage of A to B does not change this direct blood link.

question: John and Michael are brothers. John’s sister Mary is their sibling. Mary’s son Peter marries Lisa, who is Michael’s daughter. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between Peter and Lisa?
explanation: Peter is the child of Mary, Lisa is the child of Michael. Mary and Michael are siblings, sharing both parents. Therefore Peter and Lisa are children of siblings, i.e., first cousins. No half‑blood or double relations exist.

question: M is the only child of his mother. N is the only child of his father. M and N marry and have a child C. M's mother also gave birth to P (so P is M's half‑sibling). P has a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between C and Q?
explanation: M and N are unrelated; their child C is M’s offspring. P is M’s half‑sibling (same mother). Q is P’s child. C and Q share only one grandparent (their common mother), so they are half‑first cousins.

question: M is the only child of his mother. M’s father has a sister (his paternal aunt). That aunt has a son N. N’s mother is the aunt herself. P is a daughter of N’s mother. What is the precise kinship term for P’s relation to M, using standard English blood‑relation terminology?
explanation: M’s paternal aunt is both N’s mother and P’s mother. Thus N and P are siblings, each being children of M’s aunt, making them both first cousins of M. The only precise term for P’s relation to M is “first cousin.”

question: In a family with no adoptions, monogamy, and remarriage allowed, person J has a father who has exactly one brother. That brother’s only child is L. J’s mother has exactly one daughter other than J, and that daughter’s spouse is also L. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is L to J?
explanation: L is the son of J’s paternal uncle, so he is J’s first cousin. He is also the husband of J’s sister, making him J’s brother‑in‑law. The most precise standard term is brother‑in‑law.

question:
Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted):
1. A is the only child of B.
2. C is B's sister.
3. D is C's son.
4. E is D's spouse.
5. F is E's mother.
What is the precise relation of F to A?
explanation: B is A's parent; C is A's aunt; D is A's first cousin; E is D's spouse, so E is A's cousin‑in‑law. F is E's mother, i.e., the mother of A's cousin‑in‑law. No standard English kin term denotes this affinal chain; the relation is not a direct blood or immediate in‑law link.
choices: D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: Let L have a sister S and a brother B. S has exactly one son X, and B has exactly one daughter Y. X’s only child is M, and Y’s only child is N. What is the precise blood relation between M and N, using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: X (son of L’s sister) and Y (daughter of L’s brother) are first cousins because their parents are siblings. M and N are each the child of those first cousins, making M and N second cousins. No other qualifier applies.

question: R’s mother has a brother (M) and R’s father has a sister (F). M’s only child (C₁) and F’s only child (C₂) marry each other and have a child S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is S’s precise relation to R?
explanation: C₁ is R’s maternal first cousin; C₂ is R’s paternal first cousin. S is the child of each of those first cousins, so S is a first cousin once removed of R (the same for both maternal and paternal lines). No closer or doubled relationship exists.

question: M and S are brother and sister. A and B are brother and sister. M marries A and they have a son X. S marries B and they have a daughter Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father M is sibling of Y’s mother S, and X’s mother A is sibling of Y’s father B. Thus each of X’s parents is a sibling of one of Y’s parents, so X and Y share both sets of grandparents. The exact term is double first cousins.

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy, and no remarriage, N’s father has exactly one sister and N’s mother has exactly one brother. The sister and the brother marry each other and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (excluding any “double‑” modifiers), what is M’s precise relation to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Both of M’s parents are siblings of N’s parents, so M shares both sets of grandparents with N. The standard term for that relationship is first cousin.

question: M’s mother has exactly one brother, and M’s father has exactly one brother. Both of those brothers are married to unrelated women and each has a single child. If those two children are the same person L, what is the precise kinship term for L’s relation to M (using standard English kinship terms, no adoption, monogamy allowed)?
explanation: L is the child of M’s maternal uncle (first cousin) and also the child of M’s paternal uncle (first cousin). Being a first cousin on both sides makes L a double first cousin of M, the most specific standard term.

question: M is described as both the child of the only sister of N’s father and the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms and assuming monogamy, no adoption, and no incest, what is M’s relationship to N?
explanation: The father’s only sister is N’s paternal aunt; the mother’s only brother is N’s maternal uncle. For one person (M’s parent) to be both, the aunt and uncle must be the same individual, which would make N’s parents siblings—prohibited by the given constraints. Hence the description cannot occur.
choices: C) No valid kinship; the description is contradictory

question: L has one brother and one sister. The only daughter of L’s brother is X, and the only son of L’s sister is Y. A child M is born to both X and Y (i.e., X and Y are M’s parents). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: X is L’s niece and Y is L’s nephew. Their child M is therefore the child of L’s niece and nephew, which makes M L’s grandniece (if female) or grandnephew (if male). The relation is uniquely determined as grandniece/grandnephew.

question: R’s father has a sister whose son (P) marries the daughter (Q) of R’s mother’s brother. What is the precise kinship term for the child of P and Q with respect to R, using standard English blood‑relation terminology only?
explanation: P is R’s paternal first cousin; Q is R’s maternal first cousin. Their marriage links two unrelated first cousins. Their child is one generation below each cousin, i.e., one generation below R’s generation, making the child R’s first cousin once removed (the same on both sides). No more specific term applies.

question: John is the only child of his father's sister. Lisa is the child of John's mother's brother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Lisa to John?
explanation: John’s father’s sister is his paternal aunt; her child (John) and the child of his mother’s brother (maternal uncle) are first cousins. Lisa is that child, so John and Lisa are first cousins.

question: Tom is the brother of John's mother. Tom has a daughter Lisa. John has a daughter Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of Lisa to Emma?
explanation: Tom is John's maternal uncle, making Lisa John's first cousin. Emma is John's daughter, one generation below John. Therefore Emma is the child of John's first cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a daughter A; N and P have a son B. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P. Hence they are first cousins through two independent lines, i.e., double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: A and B are siblings. C and D are another pair of siblings. A marries C and B marries D. The child of A & C is X; the child of B & D is Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y each have the same two grandparents on both the paternal and maternal sides because both sibling pairs intermarried. Hence they share both grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: M is the only child of his mother. N is the only child of his father. M and N marry each other and have a child O. M’s mother has a sister; that sister’s child is P. What is the precise kinship term for the relation between O and P using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: M’s maternal aunt’s child (P) is M’s first cousin. O is M’s child. A child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed, so O and P are first cousins once removed.

question: Adam has two children, Beth and Carl, from his first marriage. Later Adam marries Diana, who already has a son Ethan from a previous marriage. Beth and Ethan marry and have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only, spouses excluded), what is the precise relation of Carl to Fiona?
explanation: Carl is Adam's son and Beth's half‑brother. Fiona is Beth's child, so Carl is the half‑brother of her mother. The correct term for a sibling of a parent who shares only one grandparent with the child is "half‑uncle" (or half‑aunt). No other answer fits this precise definition.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter D. N has a son S, and S has a son J. Before any marriage, what is the precise standard English kinship term for the relation between D and J?
explanation: M and N are siblings, so D (M’s child) and S (N’s child) are first cousins. J is S’s son, making J the child of D’s first cousin. That makes D and J first cousins once removed, the exact term.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: Adam and Ben are brothers. Adam has a daughter Clara. Ben has a son David. Clara marries Edward, and Edward is the brother of Fiona, who is David’s wife. What is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between Edward and David?
explanation: Clara and David are first cousins (their fathers are brothers). Edward is Clara’s husband, making him David’s cousin‑in‑law. Edward is also Fiona’s brother, and Fiona is David’s wife, so Edward is David’s brother‑in‑law. Both kin terms apply, so the precise relation cannot be uniquely determined.
choices: D) D) Not uniquely determinable (could be brother‑in‑law or cousin‑in‑law)

question: John’s mother Alice has a brother Robert. Robert is married to Susan. Susan’s sister Linda is the mother of Mark. What is Mark’s relation to John, using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: Robert is John’s maternal uncle; Susan is John’s aunt by marriage. Linda is Susan’s sister, having no blood or marriage link to John. Their child Mark is therefore connected to John only through a chain of affinal links beyond the immediate in‑law scope, for which no standard kin term exists.
choices: B) B) No standard direct kinship term

question: M and N are half‑siblings who share the same mother but have different fathers. M has a daughter A; N has a son B. No other marriages or adoptions occur. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B are the children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent (their common maternal grandmother). The correct term for such children is “half‑first cousins.” Full first cousins require both grandparents in common, which they lack.

question: Arrange A–H in a left‑to‑right line of eight seats numbered 1 (leftmost) to 8 (rightmost) with the following conditions: H occupies seat 1; G sits immediately to H’s right; D occupies seat 8; E sits immediately to the left of D; B and C are consecutive with B left of C; A sits somewhere between G and D but is not adjacent to either G or D; F sits somewhere to the right of A but left of D and is not adjacent to C. Which statement must be true?
explanation: The condition “E sits immediately to the left of D” forces seat 7 to be E, making statement B invariant. The other statements can change in different valid layouts, as the example arrangement H‑G‑B‑C‑A‑F‑E‑D shows.
choices: A) A) A is in seat 3.
B) B) The person immediately left of D is E.
C) C) B sits in seat 4.
D) D) F sits immediately to the right of C.

question: John’s mother has a brother Mike. Mike’s daughter Anna marries Peter, who is John’s father’s brother. Peter and Anna have a child Lily. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Lily’s relation to John?
explanation: Anna is John’s first cousin (maternal). Peter is John’s paternal uncle, so Lily, as Peter’s child, is John’s first cousin (paternal). The closest blood link is the paternal one, making Lily John’s first cousin. The maternal link would be first cousin once removed, but the nearer degree prevails.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No direct kinship term

question: John and Mary are married and have two children, Alice and Bob. Mary’s brother David has a son Carl, who marries Alice. John’s half‑brother Frank (sharing only their mother) has a daughter Eve, who marries Bob. Bob and Eve have a daughter Zoe. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Zoe’s precise relation to Carl?
explanation: Carl is Mary’s nephew, making him first cousin to Alice and Bob. Bob is Carl’s first cousin, so Bob’s child Zoe is one generation down: Carl is Zoe’s first cousin once removed. No other blood link exists.

question: John has a sister Mary. Mary’s son Peter marries John’s daughter Lisa. Their child is Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise term for Emma’s relation to John?
explanation: John is Lisa’s father, so he is Emma’s maternal grandfather. He is also Mary’s brother; Mary is Peter’s mother, making John Peter’s maternal uncle, thus Emma’s paternal great‑uncle. Between the two, the closest direct line is grandparent, so the precise standard term for Emma’s relation to John is “grandfather.”

question: L’s father has exactly one brother, and L’s mother has exactly one sister. M is the child of that brother and also the child of that sister. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: The only brother of L’s father is L’s paternal uncle; the only sister of L’s mother is L’s maternal aunt. Since M is child of both, the uncle and aunt must be married. M therefore shares both sets of grandparents with L, making M a double first cousin—the most specific term.

question: In a family with monogamy and no remarriages, A’s mother has a brother B. B is married to D, who is A’s father’s sister. B and D have a child C. What is the precise kinship term for C in relation to A?
explanation: B is A’s maternal uncle; D is A’s paternal aunt. Their child C is therefore the child of both A’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, sharing both pairs of grandparents with A. This makes C a double first cousin of A, the most specific standard term.

question: A’s mother has a brother B. B’s daughter C is married to D, who is the son of A’s father’s sister E. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations and in‑law relations limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of C to A?
explanation: C is the child of A’s maternal uncle B, making her A’s first cousin by blood. Her marriage to D (A’s paternal cousin) does not alter the existing blood relationship. Thus the most specific standard term is simply "first cousin".

question: M and N share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). M has a son S, N has a daughter D, and there are no other intermarriages. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between S and D?
explanation: S and D are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent. The exact term for such a pair is "half‑first cousins"; full first cousins require both grandparents.

question: M and N are married. M's sister is the mother of A, and N's brother is the father of B. No other intermarriages exist. What is the most precise standard kinship term for the relationship between A and B?
explanation: A's mother is M's sister, so A is M's niece. B's father is N's brother, so B is N's nephew. Since M and N are spouses, A and B share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the dual shared lineage.

question: M is the child of P's father's sister and also the child of P's mother's brother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation of M to P?
explanation: M is the offspring of P's paternal aunt (father's sister) and also of P's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Both relations make M a first cousin of P on each side, sharing both grandparent pairs, which is exactly a double first cousin.

question: M is the only child of his mother. His mother’s sister (M’s maternal aunt) has a child N. N’s father is the brother of M’s father (M’s paternal uncle). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between M and N?
explanation: M’s mother and her sister share the same parents, and M’s father and his brother share the same parents. Their children (M and N) therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the dual shared lineage.

question: M and N are siblings; P and Q are siblings. M marries Q and N marries P. Their children are X (child of M & Q) and Y (child of N & P). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share parents A and B; P and Q share parents C and D. X (child of M‑Q) and Y (child of N‑P) have grandparents A/B and C/D in common, i.e., they share both grandparent pairs. Hence they are first cousins on both sides, known as double first cousins.

question: A's mother is B. B has a brother C. C's daughter is D, and D's son is E. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of E to A?
explanation: C is B's brother, so he is A's maternal uncle. D, C's daughter, is A's first cousin. E, D's son, is the child of A's first cousin, which makes E A's first cousin once removed.

question: Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), L says: “My mother has no sons; I am my mother’s only child. My father’s sister has a son named K.” What is the exact relation of K to L?
explanation: L's father and his sister share the same parents. The sister's son K shares those grandparents with L, making them first cousins. No half‑blood or other link exists, so the precise term is first cousin.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a woman from the same pair of sisters, Clara and Diana. Adam marries Clara, Brian marries Diana. No other marriages occur. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between Adam and Clara's son Ethan and Brian and Diana's daughter Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona are children of two couples who are respectively brother–sister pairs. Their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters, so Ethan and Fiona share both paternal and maternal grandparents. Hence the precise term is double first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. O, P and Q are siblings. M marries O, N marries Q. M and O have a daughter A; N and Q have a son B. Using standard English kinship terms and not ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both pairs of grandparents: M and N share one pair, O and Q share another. Thus they have two common grandparent sets, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled lineage.

question: In a family with no adoption, let B be the brother of M. B has exactly one child C, and L is C’s son. M is married to N. N is the sister of O’s mother. O is the father of P. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of L to P?
explanation: B is M’s brother, so B is an uncle‑in‑law of O (through M’s marriage to O’s maternal aunt N). Hence B and O share no blood. Consequently L, B’s grandson, has no blood link to O or P; the only connection is an affinal chain, for which no standard kin term exists.
choices: C) No standard kinship term (affinal connection only)

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamy, L is a person. M is a person who is (i) the child of the only brother of L’s mother, and (ii) the child of the only sister of L’s father. What is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to L?
explanation: M’s father is L’s maternal uncle, making M a first cousin on L’s mother’s side. M’s mother is L’s paternal aunt, making M a first cousin on L’s father’s side. Sharing both grandparent pairs, M and L are double first cousins, the most specific standard term.

question: Man A and his sister B are children of parents P and Q. C and D are siblings, children of parents R and S. A marries C and B marries D. Their respective children are X (child of A and C) and Y (child of B and D). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: A and B are siblings (share both parents). C and D are siblings (share both parents). A marries C and B marries D. Their children X and Y each have one parent from each sibling pair, so X and Y share both paternal grandparents (parents of A and B) and both maternal grandparents (parents of C and D). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry a woman who are sisters, Clara and Diana. Adam marries Clara; Brian marries Diana. Their only children are X (child of Adam & Clara) and Y (child of Brian & Diana). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both paternal grandparents (parents of Adam and Brian) and both maternal grandparents (parents of Clara and Diana). Sharing the full set of grandparents makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption: A has exactly one sibling, C. C is married to D. D has exactly one sibling, E, who is married to F. G is the child of C and D, and H is the child of E and F. What is the precise blood relation between G and H?
explanation: G’s paternal grandparents are the parents of D, while H’s maternal grandparents are the same pair (parents of D and E). They share one set of grandparents and no others, making them first cousins. The relation is not halved or doubled.

question: In family Alpha, siblings Emma and Liam. In family Beta, siblings Noah and Olivia. Emma marries Noah and they have a child Maya. Liam marries Olivia and they have a child Ethan. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Maya and Ethan?
explanation: Maya and Ethan are each the child of a sibling from Alpha married to a sibling from Beta. They therefore share both sets of grandparents, giving them the exact term double first cousins.

question: John and Mark are brothers. Anna and Beth are sisters. John marries Anna and they have a son X. Mark marries Beth and they have a son Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise blood relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y’s fathers are brothers (sharing paternal grandparents) and their mothers are sisters (sharing maternal grandparents). Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the exact term for this doubled ancestry.

question: J’s father has exactly one sister, and J’s mother has exactly one brother. The child of that sister (the paternal aunt) is also the child of that brother (the maternal uncle). Who is that child to J?
explanation: The child is the offspring of J’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle, so the child shares both of J’s grandparent pairs. This makes the child J’s double first cousin, the most precise standard term.

question: In a family, A's father is the brother of B's mother. B's father is the brother of C's mother. C's father is the brother of D's mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between A and D?
explanation: A is a first cousin of B, B of C, and C of D. The chain does not ensure a single common ancestor pair for A and D; depending on whether the sibling links involve the same families, they may share none, one, or two grandparent pairs. Thus their exact kinship cannot be uniquely fixed.

question: A’s mother has a brother B. B is married to C. C’s brother D has a child E. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of E to A?
explanation: If D is also A’s maternal uncle (i.e., B and D are the same person), then E is A’s first cousin. If D is unrelated to A, then E is not blood‑related to A. Because the information does not specify whether D is A’s uncle, the exact kinship cannot be determined uniquely.

question: R's mother has exactly one brother, whose only child is S. R's father has exactly one sister, whose only child is T. S and T marry and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms, what is C's relation to R?
explanation: S is R's maternal first cousin; T is R's paternal first cousin. Their child C is one generation below each cousin, so C is a first cousin once removed to R on both sides. No closer term applies.

question: M is the son of A’s sister. He is also the grandson of B’s brother. A and B are unrelated by blood and are not married to each other. What is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to B?
explanation: A’s sister’s son makes M A’s nephew. B’s brother is M’s grandfather, so M is the child of B’s niece/nephew, i.e., B’s grand‑nephew (great‑nephew). This term uniquely fits the described connections.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: In a family, brother B1 marries sister S2, and sister S1 marries brother B2. B1 and S1 have child X; B2 and S2 have child Y. Using only standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: Each child's father is the brother of the other child's mother and each child's mother is the sister of the other child's father. Thus X and Y share both pairs of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the exact term.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries P, N marries Q, and P and Q are also siblings. M and P have a child A; N and Q have a child B. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents: M and N share parents, and P and Q share parents. Therefore they are first cousins through two independent sibling links, making them double first cousins—the most specific correct term.

question: J’s father has a sister A, and J’s mother has a brother B. A and B are married and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of M to J?
explanation: M is the child of J’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Hence M is J’s first cousin on both the father’s and mother’s sides, i.e., a double first cousin.

question: Mary and Anne are sisters. Mary’s son is John. Anne is married to Tom, who is Paul’s brother. Paul’s daughter Lisa marries Tom and Anne’s son Mark. What is Lisa’s precise relationship to Anne?
explanation: Anne is Mark’s mother; Lisa is married to Mark, therefore Lisa is Anne’s daughter‑in‑law, the only standard kinship term that applies.
choices: D) D) No standard kinship term

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother and R’s father has exactly one sister; there are no other siblings. It is unknown whether the mother’s brother is a full sibling of his sister or only a half‑sibling, and likewise for the father’s sister. If we take the child of the mother’s brother or the child of the father’s sister (whichever we pick) and call that person S, what is S’s precise relation to R?
explanation: If the mother’s brother (or father’s sister) is a full sibling, S is a first cousin; if a half‑sibling, S is a half‑first cousin. Because we lack information about the sibling‑type, the relationship cannot be fixed to a single standard term.

question: M and N are half‑siblings, sharing only their mother. M has a son S. N has a daughter D. Using standard English kinship terms and ignoring any adoption, what is the precise relation between S and D?
explanation: S and D are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent (their common mother’s parent). The correct term for such relatives is “half‑first cousins,” not full first cousins (which require both grandparents) nor second cousins.

question: John is married to Mary. Mary’s sister Lisa is married to Tom. Tom’s brother Kevin is married to Anna, who is the daughter of John’s brother Mark. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Kevin to John?
explanation: Anna is John’s niece (daughter of his brother). Kevin, as Anna’s husband, is the husband of John’s niece, which is precisely a nephew‑in‑law. No closer blood or direct in‑law term applies.

question: L has one child, M, and a brother N. N's daughters are O and R (who are sisters). O's son is P; R's only child is Q. M is married to Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relationship between P and Q?
explanation: O and R are sisters, so their children P and Q are first cousins. No blood link to M changes this; the marriage is irrelevant for their direct kinship.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: Two brothers, X and Y, each marry a woman who are sisters, M and N respectively. X and M have a son P; Y and N have a daughter Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: P and Q share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. This makes them double first cousins, a specific term beyond ordinary first cousins.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Ben, each marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a child, Eva; Ben and Diana have a child, Frank. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Eva and Frank?
explanation: Eva and Frank share both sets of grandparents (Adam’s parents and Clara’s parents) because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: M and N are full siblings. X and Y are also full siblings, unrelated to M and N. M marries X and N marries Y. M and X have a son A; N and Y have a daughter B. Using standard English kinship terms (no “double” prefixes unless required), what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A’s father and B’s mother are full siblings, and A’s mother and B’s father are also full siblings. Thus A and B share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: Emma's mother has exactly one brother, whose only child is Lily. Emma's father has exactly one sister, whose only child is Mark. Lily and Mark marry and have a child named Noah. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is Noah's relation to Emma?
explanation: Lily is Emma's maternal first cousin; Mark is Emma's paternal first cousin. Their child Noah is the child of Emma's first cousin, which makes Noah Emma's first cousin once removed. No closer or different term applies.

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother, M, whose only child is A. R’s father has exactly one brother, N, whose only child is B. A and B marry each other and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, and in‑law limited to spouse), what is C’s relation to R?
explanation: A is R’s maternal first cousin; B is R’s paternal first cousin. Their child C is the child of R’s first cousin on each side, which makes C a first cousin once removed to R (the “once removed” indicates a generational difference).

question: Emma is married to Tom. Tom’s sister Sara is married to Mike. Mike’s brother Alex has a daughter Zoe. Using standard English kinship terms limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses, what is Zoe to Emma?
explanation: Emma → Tom (spouse) → Sara (spouse’s sibling) → Mike (sibling’s spouse) → Alex (brother of that spouse) → Zoe (Alex’s daughter). The chain never creates a blood link and exceeds the allowed in‑law scope, so no standard direct kin term exists.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry one of two sisters, Clara and Diana (Adam + Clara, Brian + Diana). Their children are Ethan (Adam & Clara) and Fiona (Brian & Diana). Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relationship between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both paternal grandparents (through Adam and Brian) and both maternal grandparents (through Clara and Diana). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a more exact term than plain first cousins.

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoptions, X's mother has a brother U. X's father has a sister V. V's sister W (also X's father's sister) is married to U. Their child is Y. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for Y's relation to X?
explanation: U is X's maternal uncle; W is X's paternal aunt. Their child Y is simultaneously the child of X's maternal uncle and paternal aunt, sharing both sets of grandparents with X. Hence Y is X's double first cousin, the exact term for this doubled first‑cousin relationship.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: L’s father has exactly one sister, and L’s mother has exactly one brother. M is the child of that sister and also the child of that brother (the two are married to each other). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s relation to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s paternal aunt and also the child of L’s maternal uncle. Both are children of a parent’s sibling, so M is a first cousin of L on both sides. The precise term is simply "first cousin".

question: In a family, the mother of man A is the sister of the father of woman B, and the father of A is the brother of the mother of B. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between A and B?
explanation: A’s mother and B’s father are siblings, and A’s father and B’s mother are siblings. Thus A and B share both sets of grandparents—maternal and paternal—making them double first cousins, a relationship more specific than ordinary first cousins.

question: Mary has a brother and a sister. John is the son of Mary's brother. Mary's sister is married to Peter, and they have a daughter Lisa. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between John and Lisa?
explanation: John's father (Mary's brother) and Lisa's mother (Mary's sister) are siblings. Their children are therefore first cousins. No other blood link alters this relationship.

question: Two brothers, A and B, marry two sisters, C and D, respectively. A + C have a son X; B + D have a son Y. X and Y each marry unrelated spouses and have children P and Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: X and Y are double first cousins because they share both sets of grandparents. Their children P and Q therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, which makes them double second cousins – the most specific term.

question: R and S are siblings. R’s only child is Q, and Q’s only child is P. S’s only child is T. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of P to T?
explanation: R and S are same generation. Q is the child of R, so Q is the niece/nephew of S. P is Q’s child, making P one generation below Q. T, as S’s child, is the same generation as Q. Thus P and T are first cousins separated by one generation, i.e., first cousins once removed.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: X has a sister Y and a brother U. U’s daughter V is X’s niece. Y’s son Z is X’s nephew. Z is married to W, and W’s mother is V. What is W’s precise blood relation to X?
explanation: V is X’s niece (daughter of his brother). W is V’s child, so W is the child of X’s niece, i.e., X’s grandniece. No other blood link alters this relationship.

question: Two brothers, M and N, each marry a woman who is a sister of the other’s wife. M’s son is X and N’s son is Y. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. This makes them double first cousins, the exact term for cousins with two common grandparent pairs.

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father, and M’s father is the brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: M’s mother and N’s father are siblings, and M’s father and N’s mother are siblings, so M and N share both sets of grandparents. That makes them double first cousins.

question: A is the only child of his mother. B is the only child of his father. The mother of A and the father of B are siblings. C is the child of A. D is the child of B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between C and D?
explanation: A’s mother and B’s father are siblings, so A and B are first cousins (they share a set of grandparents). C and D are the children of those first cousins, which makes them second cousins. No other shared ancestors exist, so the most specific term is "second cousins".
choices: C) C) First cousins once removed
D) D) No standard direct relation

question: Y’s mother has exactly one brother and Y’s father has exactly one sister. The brother and the sister are married to each other and have a single child X. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, who are spouses. X therefore shares both of Y’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: M and N are siblings. O, P and Q are siblings (O and Q are sister and brother). M marries O and they have a daughter S. N marries Q and they have a son T. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between S and T?
explanation: S’s father M and T’s father N are siblings, giving them one shared set of grandparents. S’s mother O and T’s mother Q are also siblings, giving a second shared set of grandparents. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes S and T double first cousins, the exact term.

question: Brothers M and N each marry sisters O and P, respectively. M and O have child A; N and P have child B. A and B each marry unrelated partners and have children C and D. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption), what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: A and B are double first cousins because they share both sets of grandparents. Their children C and D therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, which makes them double second cousins—the most specific label.

question: In a family, M and N are siblings. M marries O, who is the sister of P. N marries Q, who is the brother of O. M and O have a daughter A; N and Q have a son B. What is the most precise kinship term for A and B?
explanation: M and N are siblings; O and Q are siblings. Thus A’s mother O and B’s father Q are siblings, making A and B double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). The precise term is double first cousins.

question: E and F are half‑siblings who share only their mother. E has a son G. F has a daughter H. Before any marriage, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between G and H?
explanation: G and H are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent. The correct term is “half‑first cousins”, which denotes cousins with a single shared grandparent pair.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries X and N marries Y, where X and Y are also siblings. M and X have a daughter A; N and Y have a son B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents because their parents are two pairs of siblings. This makes them double first cousins, the exact term required.

question: John has two children, Michael and Emily. John’s sister Anna has two children, Sarah and Tom. Michael marries Sarah. Emily marries David, who is Tom’s son. What is the precise blood relationship between Michael and David?
explanation: Michael is John’s son. Tom, Anna’s son, is Michael’s first cousin. David is Tom’s son, so David is the child of Michael’s first cousin – Michael’s first cousin once removed.

question: L has exactly one sister and exactly one brother. The sister’s only child is a son; the brother’s only child is a daughter. Those two children marry each other and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: L’s sister’s son is L’s nephew; the brother’s daughter is L’s niece. Their child M is the child of L’s niece and nephew, i.e., L’s grandniece or grandnephew. This term is the most specific standard kinship label.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let B be a person. B’s father has a sister who has exactly one child, C. A is the child of C. Using standard English kinship terms, what is A’s precise relation to B?
explanation: B’s father’s sister is B’s paternal aunt. Her only child C is B’s first cousin. A, being C’s child, is one generation below that cousin, making A B’s first cousin once removed. No other listed relations fit this exact generational offset.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has a son P, who has a daughter R. R’s son Q marries O. What is the precise blood relation between O and R?
explanation: M and N share the same parents. O is M’s child, R is N’s grandchild. Both O and R are grandchildren of the same couple, making them first cousins. The marriage to Q does not affect their blood relation.

question: M says, “My husband’s mother is also my mother’s sister.” Using only standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of M’s husband to M?
explanation: If the husband’s mother is the mother’s sister, then M’s mother and her mother‑in‑law are sisters. Thus the husband is the son of M’s maternal aunt, i.e., M’s first cousin. No other standard term fits.

question: A and B are brothers. C and D are sisters. A marries C and B marries D. E is the child of A & C, and F is the child of B & D. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relationship between E and F?
explanation: E and F share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. That makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: A is the only child of his mother. B is the only child of his father. A and B marry each other and have a child C. B has a sister who has a son N; N has a child D. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation between C and D?
explanation: B’s sister’s son N is B’s nephew. N’s child D is B’s grandnephew. C is B’s child. A child of B and a grandnephew of B are first cousins once removed (C is one generation above D).
