question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Assuming monogamy and no adoption, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for M’s relation to N?
explanation: The sister of N’s father is N’s paternal aunt; the brother of N’s mother is N’s maternal uncle. They are spouses, so M is the child of both N’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle. M therefore shares both sets of grandparents with N, making them double first cousins – the only term that captures this exact relationship.

question: John has a sister Mary and a brother Tom. Mary's son Peter marries Lisa, who is Tom's daughter. Peter and Lisa have a child Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is Emma's precise relation to John?
explanation: Peter is John’s nephew (sister’s son) and Lisa is John’s niece (brother’s daughter). Their child is the child of John’s niece (or nephew), which is called a grandniece (or great‑niece). No other standard term is more specific.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard direct relation

question: L’s father has one sister (FS) and L’s mother has one brother (MB). FS and MB marry each other and have a child M. What is the precise standard kinship term for the relationship between L and M?
explanation: L’s paternal aunt (FS) and maternal uncle (MB) are spouses, so L and M are children of two sibling pairs. They share both of L’s grandparents on the father’s side and both on the mother’s side, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John marries Anna, who is the sister of Mary's husband Peter. John and Anna have a daughter Lisa. Mary and Peter have a son Mark. Lisa and Mark marry each other and have a child Emma. What is the most precise standard kinship term for Emma's relationship to John?
explanation: Lisa is John’s daughter, so Emma is his granddaughter. Mark is John’s nephew (son of his sister Mary), so Emma is also John’s grandniece. The only term that captures both lines of descent is “both granddaughter and grandniece (double relation)”.
choices: D) Both granddaughter and grandniece (double relation)

question: John’s mother has a sister Mary. Mary’s son Peter is married to Lisa, who is the daughter of John’s father’s sister. Ignoring any marital links, what is the precise blood relation of Lisa to John?
explanation: John’s father’s sister is his paternal aunt; her daughter Lisa is therefore John’s paternal first cousin. The marriage to Peter (a maternal first cousin) does not affect the blood link. Hence Lisa is John’s first cousin.

question: R’s mother and S’s father are siblings, and R’s father and S’s mother are also siblings. Assuming monogamy and no adoption, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between R and S?
explanation: R and S share both sets of grandparents: one through their mothers (who are siblings) and one through their fathers (who are siblings). Hence they are first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins—the only term that captures the dual shared grandparentage.

question: John is the father of Mary. Mary’s sister is Lisa. Lisa’s husband is Tom. Tom’s mother is Susan. Susan’s brother is Robert, whose daughter is Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (blood and direct in‑law only), what is Emma’s relation to John?
explanation: Tom is John’s son‑in‑law. Emma is Tom’s first cousin (daughter of his maternal uncle Robert). The link from Emma to John passes only through a spouse’s cousin, giving no blood or direct in‑law connection. Hence there is no standard direct kin term.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: A’s mother M has exactly one brother U. A’s father F also has exactly one brother, who is the same person U. U has a child C. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring the doubled ancestry, what is C’s precise relation to A?
explanation: U is both A’s maternal and paternal uncle, so C is the child of both an aunt/uncle on each side. C shares both sets of grandparents with A, making them double first cousins.

question: M is the mother of N and O. N is married to P. P's sister Q is married to R, who together with O are the parents of S. What is the precise relationship between Q and S using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: O and R are S’s parents, so R is S’s father. Q is R’s spouse, i.e., the spouse of S’s parent. This connection is only affinal; standard kinship provides no direct term for the spouse of a parent’s spouse. Therefore Q has no standard direct relation to S.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M and N are brother and sister. M marries O and N marries P. O and P are also brother and sister. Their only children, X (child of M & O) and Y (child of N & P), grow up. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their parents are two pairs of siblings. This makes them double first cousins – first cousins with doubled ancestry. No other term captures the doubled shared lineage.

question: Two brothers, John and Mark, marry two sisters, Anna and Beth, respectively. John and Anna have a son Carl. Mark and Beth have a daughter Dana. Carl and Dana each marry unrelated partners and have children: Carl’s child Emma and Dana’s child Frank. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Emma and Frank?
explanation: John‑Anna and Mark‑Beth are sibling pairs, so Carl and Dana share both sets of grandparents—they are double first cousins. Their children Emma and Frank therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins, the exact term.

question: S’s mother has exactly one brother, U, and S’s father has exactly one sister, V. U and V are married to each other and have a single child, T. Assuming no adoption or polygamy, what is T’s precise kinship to S using standard English terms?
explanation: U is S’s maternal uncle and V is S’s paternal aunt. Their child T is the child of both S’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, making T S’s first cousin on both sides. The duplication does not change the basic term; T is simply S’s first cousin.

question: Emma’s mother Laura is the sister of Noah’s father Victor, and Noah’s mother Sarah is the sister of Emma’s father Thomas. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relationship between Emma and Noah?
explanation: Laura and Victor are siblings, so Emma is Victor’s niece; Thomas and Sarah are siblings, so Noah is Thomas’s nephew. Thus Emma and Noah share both sets of grandparents—one through their mothers and one through their fathers—making them double first cousins, the only term that captures both shared grandparent pairs.

question: M is the mother of N. M has a brother R, whose son is Q. N is married to O. O’s sister is P, who is married to Q. Using standard English kinship terms (blood and the in‑law relations limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the most precise relation of Q to N?
explanation: Q is the son of M’s brother, so he is N’s first cousin by blood. He is also married to P, who is the sister of N’s spouse O, making Q N’s brother‑in‑law. When a person is both a blood relative and an affinal relative, the blood term is the precise kinship. Hence the correct designation is “first cousin.”

question: A's father has one sister, S. B is the child of S. C is the child of B's mother’s brother. D is the child of C's father's sister. What is D's exact relation to A?
explanation: S is A's paternal aunt. B, her child, is A's first cousin. B's mother’s brother is S's brother, i.e., A's father, so C is a child of A's father – A's sibling (if any) or half‑sibling, but that does not affect the next step. C's father's sister is again S, whose child D is therefore another child of A's aunt, making D a first cousin of A. Hence the precise term is "first cousin".

question: A and B are married. A's brother C marries B's sister D. C and D have a child E, while A and B have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is the most precise relation of E to F?
explanation: E and F are children of two sibling pairs who married each other. They share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins on both maternal and paternal sides—i.e., double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: N's father has a sister who is married to a man; N's mother has a brother who is married to a woman. Their respective spouses have a child M. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise kinship term for M's relation to N?
explanation: M is the child of N's paternal aunt (father's sister) and also the child of N's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Thus M is N's first cousin on both sides, i.e., a double first cousin, the most specific standard term.

question: John is married to Mary. Mary's sister Lisa is married to Tom. Tom's brother Kevin is married to Anna, who is the daughter of Mark, John's brother. What is Kevin's precise kinship term to Mary using standard English kinship (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: Mark is John's brother, so Anna is John's niece. Kevin, married to Anna, is John's nephew‑in‑law. Since Mary is John's spouse, Kevin is also Mary's nephew‑in‑law. No blood term applies; the exact term is nephew‑in‑law.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, marry two sisters, Clara and Diana respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan. Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan’s father Adam is brother of Fiona’s father Brian, and Ethan’s mother Clara is sister of Fiona’s mother Diana. Thus Ethan and Fiona share both paternal and maternal grandparents, making them double first cousins.

question: In a family with no adoptions, X’s mother has exactly two children: X and his sister S. S is married to Y and they have a daughter D. X also has a son Z. D marries Z. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the precise relation of D to X?
explanation: By blood D is X’s niece (daughter of his sister). By marriage D is X’s daughter‑in‑law (wife of his son). No single standard term covers both roles, so the relation cannot be expressed uniquely with one word.

question: M and N are half‑siblings who share only their father. M has a child X and N has a child Y. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y each descend from one of the half‑siblings, so they share only a single grandparent (their father's parent). Children of half‑siblings are therefore half‑first cousins, not full first cousins.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John marries Lisa, who already has a daughter Emma from a previous marriage. Mary’s son Kevin (John’s nephew) marries Emma. Kevin and Emma have a child Sam. Using standard English kinship terms (blood and in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Sam’s relation to John?
explanation: Sam is the child of Kevin, who is John’s nephew (child of John’s sister). Therefore Sam is the child of John’s nephew, i.e., John’s great‑nephew (also called grand‑nephew). The step‑relationship via Emma does not affect the precise blood term.
choices: D) D) No standard single term

question: In a monogamous family tree, M and N are siblings. M marries O, and N marries P. O’s only sibling is Q, who is married to R. P’s only sibling is S, who is married to T. Q and S are first cousins. Who is the child of M and O to the child of N and P?
explanation: M and N are siblings, so their children are first cousins. The extra marriages do not affect that direct line. Hence the relationship is first cousins, which corresponds to choice B.

question: A person X has a paternal aunt (father’s sister) who has a child B, and a maternal uncle (mother’s brother) who has a child C. If Y is either B or C (unspecified which), what is Y’s precise relation to X using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Both B and C are children of a sibling of one of X’s parents, which by definition makes each a first cousin of X. No other listed term applies.

question: Emma's mother has a brother named Carl. Carl has a daughter Lily. Emma has a son Noah. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Lily's relation to Noah?
explanation: Carl is Emma's maternal uncle, so Lily is Emma's first cousin. A first cousin of a parent is a first cousin once removed to that parent's child. Therefore Lily is Noah's first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: Mona and Paul are half‑siblings (they share the same mother but have different fathers). Mona has a son Kevin, and Paul has a daughter Zoe. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Kevin and Zoe?
explanation: Kevin and Zoe are children of half‑siblings. Their parents share only one parent, so the cousins share only one grandparent. The exact term for such cousins is “half‑first cousins”.

question: In a family, X is the son of the sister of Y’s father, and also the son of the brother of Y’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and also the child of Y’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Therefore X shares both sets of grandparents with Y, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: In a family, person A’s mother (C) and person B’s father (D) are siblings, and person A’s father (E) and person B’s mother (F) are also siblings (C and D are a brother‑sister pair, E and F are a different brother‑sister pair). A and B marry each other. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the blood relationship between A and B?
explanation: A shares a set of grandparents with B through C‑D and another set through E‑F. Because they have both paternal and maternal grandparents in common, they are double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled first‑cousin relationship.

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother, whose daughter is S. R’s father has exactly one sister, whose son is T. S and T marry and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is C’s relation to R?
explanation: S is R’s maternal first cousin; T is R’s paternal first cousin. Their child C is one generation below a first cousin on either side, making C a first cousin once removed to R. The two cousin lines are independent, so no closer term applies.

question: A and B are siblings (they share at least one parent). A marries C and they have a child P. B marries D and they have a child Q. No other intermarriages occur. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between P and Q?
explanation: If A and B are full siblings, P and Q are first cousins. If they are only half‑siblings, P and Q are half‑first cousins. Because we are told only that A and B share at least one parent, the exact relation cannot be fixed; thus it is not uniquely determinable.

question: L and K have the same mother but different fathers. L’s daughter is S, and K’s son is T. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between S and T?
explanation: L and K are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. Their children therefore share exactly one grandparent, which makes S and T half‑first cousins—the precise term for this relationship.

question: M and N are full siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also full siblings. M + O have a child X; N + P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no “double‑cousin” slang), what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their parents are two pairs of siblings. Hence they are first cousins through the maternal line and also first cousins through the paternal line, i.e., double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: M and N are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). M has a child C and N has a child D. No other intermarriages exist in the family. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relationship between C and D?
explanation: C and D are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent (their common maternal grandmother). The correct term for such a pair is "half‑first cousins"—they are first cousins but with only one shared grandparent.

question: L's father has a sister M. M has a son N, and N has a daughter O. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is O's precise relation to L?
explanation: M is L's aunt (father's sister). Her son N is L's first cousin. N's daughter O is one generation below that cousin, making O L's first cousin once removed. No other term fits exactly.

question: M and N are full siblings. M’s only child is X. N marries O, whose only sibling is P. P’s only child is Y. Using standard English kinship terms only (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation of Y to X?
explanation: X is the blood child of M. Y is the child of P, who is only related to X through the marriage chain N‑O‑P. No blood link exists, and the allowed in‑law scope stops at a spouse’s sibling’s child. Hence there is no standard direct kin term; Y is related to X only by an affinal chain.
choices: A) A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: P is the only child of R, and Q is the only child of S. R and S are siblings. P and Q marry each other and have a child T. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relationship between R and S as relatives of T?
explanation: R and S are siblings to each other. Both are grandparents of T, but their mutual relation does not change; they remain brother‑and‑sister. The precise kin term for their mutual relation is "sibling".

question: M is the child of the only sister of N’s father and also the child of the only brother of N’s mother. Assuming no adoption or remarriage, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for M’s relation to N?
explanation: The sister of N’s father is N’s paternal aunt; her child is N’s first cousin. The brother of N’s mother is N’s maternal uncle; his child is also N’s first cousin. Because the same person M occupies both positions, M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making M a double first cousin—the only term that captures this doubled ancestry.

question: M is the child of the sister of N's father, and also the child of the brother of N's mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is child of N's paternal aunt (father's sister) and also child of N's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Both relations make M a first cousin on each side, sharing both sets of grandparents, i.e., a double first cousin. No other relation fits.

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoptions, T's mother has exactly one brother. That brother is married and has a single child named S. What is the precise kinship term for S in relation to T?
explanation: The brother of T's mother is T's maternal uncle. His child S is therefore the child of T's uncle, which makes S T's first cousin. No other direct blood link exists.

question: L has one sister S and one brother B. S’s only son X and B’s only daughter Y each have exactly one child, and both children are the same person M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation of M to L?
explanation: X is L’s nephew (son of sister) and Y is L’s niece (daughter of brother). Their common child M is therefore the child of both a nephew and a niece, making M L’s great‑nephew/niece on two independent lines – a double great‑nephew/niece. No other term captures this dual descent.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed

question: M is married to N. N’s sister O is married to P. P’s mother Q is the sister of M’s father R. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Q’s relation to M?
explanation: R is M’s father. Q is R’s sister, making Q M’s paternal aunt. No other connections alter this direct blood link, so the precise term is aunt.

question: M is married to N. M’s mother’s brother (M’s maternal uncle) is T, who is married to S. S’s sister is V, who is married to L. L is the father of N’s cousin (the cousin may be L’s biological child or a step‑child). Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is V’s relation to M?
explanation: V is the sister‑in‑law of M’s maternal uncle, but her link to M runs through L, whose relationship to N’s cousin is ambiguous (biological or step). Hence V could be an aunt‑in‑law or a step‑aunt‑in‑law, and no single standard term applies.

question: M is married to N. N's sister O is married to P. P's brother Q is the father of R. R is the mother of S. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is S to M?
explanation: M→N (spouse) →O (sibling‑in‑law) →P (that sibling’s spouse) →Q (spouse’s sibling, a blood relation) →R (child of Q) →S (grandchild). The chain passes beyond the immediate in‑law scope and never creates a direct blood link to M, so no standard term applies.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: A is married to B. B's sister is C, and C is married to D. D is the brother of E, who is the mother of F. F is married to G, who is the sibling of A's mother. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is D's relation to A?
explanation: A ↔ B (spouses). B’s sister C is A’s sister‑in‑law. C’s husband D is therefore A’s brother‑in‑law. The additional chain through E, F and G does not create a blood link or an allowed in‑law link, so the only precise term is brother‑in‑law.

question: X's mother has a brother named A. X's father has a sister named B. A is married to C, who is B's daughter. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only, spouses excluded), what is C's relation to X?
explanation: B is X's paternal aunt, so her daughter C is X's first cousin. The marriage of A (X's maternal uncle) to C does not change the blood relationship. Hence C is X's first cousin.

question: Person X's mother has a brother A (X's maternal uncle). A has a daughter B. X's father has a sister C (X's paternal aunt). C has a son D. B and D marry and have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of E to X?
explanation: B is X's first cousin (maternal) and D is X's first cousin (paternal). Their child E is one generation below X, making E X's first cousin once removed on both sides. The term "first cousin once removed" uniquely describes this relation; no more specific standard term exists.

question: Two brothers marry two sisters. The elder brother and his wife have a son A; the younger brother and his wife have a daughter B. A and B later marry each other and have children C (son) and D (daughter). Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: A and B are double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). Their children therefore share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making C and D double second cousins. No simpler term captures the doubled ancestry.

question: M and N are married. M has a daughter L from a previous marriage; N has a son K from a previous marriage. L and K marry and have a child Z. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Z's relationship to M's mother?
explanation: M's mother is the grandmother of M's daughter L. L is Z's mother, so M's mother is Z's great‑grandmother. The precise term for Z to M's mother is great‑grandchild.

question: Let Z be the child of the only brother of L’s mother and also the child of the only brother of L’s father. Assuming monogamy, no adoption, and that the two brothers are distinct individuals, what is Z’s precise relationship to L?
explanation: Z is the child of a sibling of L’s mother (maternal uncle’s child) and also the child of a sibling of L’s father (paternal uncle’s child). In either case Z is a child of a parent’s brother, which is exactly a first cousin of L. The double‑uncle situation does not change the basic term.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: M is married to N. N’s sister O is married to P. P’s mother Q is the aunt of R. R’s child S is the cousin of T. T is married to U. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is U’s relation to M?
explanation: M→N (spouse) →O (sibling‑in‑law) →P (that sibling’s spouse) →Q (parent‑in‑law) →R (aunt‑in‑law’s nephew/niece) →S (cousin‑in‑law) →T (cousin’s spouse) →U (spouse of a cousin‑in‑law). The chain never produces a blood link or an allowed in‑law link, so no standard direct kin term exists.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: L's mother has exactly one brother, and L's father has exactly one sister. Both of these siblings have a single child, and it happens to be the same person M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L's maternal uncle and also the child of L's paternal aunt. Thus M shares both of L's grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins – the most specific term for this doubled ancestry.

question: P and R are brothers; Q and S are sisters. P marries Q and they have a child M. R marries S and they have a child N. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: M and N share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. Hence they are first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides, i.e., double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: Y and Z are married and have a single child X. Y’s brother is W, and Z’s sister is V. W and V are married to each other and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and C?
explanation: W is Y’s brother → paternal uncle of X; V is Z’s sister → maternal aunt of X. Their marriage makes C the child of both X’s paternal uncle and maternal aunt, so C shares both sets of grandparents with X. The exact term is “double first cousin”.

question: A’s mother has a brother. B’s father has a sister. The brother of A’s mother and the sister of B’s father are the same person. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between A and B?
explanation: The shared sibling is both A’s maternal uncle and B’s paternal aunt, so A’s mother and B’s father are siblings. A and B are therefore children of siblings, i.e., first cousins.

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother, and R’s father has exactly one sister. Those two siblings are married and have a child S. What is the precise kinship term for S in relation to R?
explanation: R’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt are married, so their child S shares both sets of grandparents with R. Thus S is related to R through both the maternal and paternal lines, making S a double first cousin – the most precise standard term.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has a son P, who is married to R. R and P have a child Q. Using standard English blood‑relation terms only, what is the precise relationship of O to Q (ignoring the fact they later marry)?
explanation: M and N share both parents, so O and P are first cousins. Q is P’s child, making Q the child of O’s first cousin. Therefore O is a first cousin once removed of Q.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed
D) D) No direct blood relation

question: Eve’s mother is the sister of Frank’s father, and Eve’s father is the brother of Frank’s mother. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between Eve and Frank?
explanation: Eve and Frank share both sets of grandparents: one through their mothers’ siblings and one through their fathers’ siblings. This makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than ordinary first cousins.

question: R is married to S. S’s sister is T. T is married to U. U’s brother is V. What is V to R using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?
explanation: R→S (spouse) →T (sister‑in‑law) →U (her husband, also brother‑in‑law) →V (brother of that brother‑in‑law). The chain stays entirely affinal and never creates a blood link; standard kin terms stop at the spouse’s sibling’s spouse. Thus V has no direct kin term to R.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: A and B are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). A has a child C, and B has a child D. Assuming no other intermarriages or adoptions, what is the most precise kinship term for the relation between C and D?
explanation: C and D are each the child of a half‑sibling of the other’s parent, so they share exactly one grandparent. The correct term for children of half‑siblings is “half‑first cousins,” which is more precise than “first cousins.”

question: Using only standard English kinship terms (blood relations plus in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses), R is married to S; S’s brother is T; T is married to U; U’s sister is V; V is married to W. What is the relation of W to R?
explanation: R→S (spouse) →T (sibling‑in‑law) →U (that sibling’s spouse) →V (that spouse’s sibling) →W (that sibling’s spouse). This chain extends beyond the defined in‑law scope and never creates a blood link, so no standard direct kin term exists.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: Q’s mother has exactly one brother, and Q’s father has exactly one sister. P is the child of that brother, and R is the child of that sister. What is the precise blood relationship between P and R?
explanation: P is Q’s maternal first cousin; R is Q’s paternal first cousin. Their parents (Q’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt) are not related to each other, so P and R share no common ancestor. Hence they have no blood relationship.

question: M is the child of the only brother of N’s father and also the child of the only sister of N’s mother. Assuming no intermarriage, what is M’s relation to N?
explanation: M is the child of a sibling of N’s father (paternal uncle) and also the child of a sibling of N’s mother (maternal aunt). In either case M is the child of a parent’s sibling, which is precisely a first cousin of N.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: John’s mother has a brother Tom, and John’s father has a sister Mary. Tom and Mary marry each other and have a child Lily. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Lily’s precise relation to John?
explanation: Tom is John’s maternal uncle; Mary is John’s paternal aunt. Their child Lily is the offspring of both a maternal uncle and a paternal aunt, making her John’s first cousin on both sides – the exact term is “double first cousin.”

question: Person X’s mother has a brother whose daughter D marries the son S of X’s father’s brother. D and S have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms, what is C’s precise relation to X?
explanation: D is X’s first cousin (maternal side) and S is X’s first cousin (paternal side). Their child C is the child of X’s first cousin, which makes C a first cousin once removed to X. No double‑cousin term applies because D and S are unrelated.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No direct kinship term

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, a man M says: “My mother‑in‑law is also my father’s mother‑in‑law.” Using standard English kinship terms only, what is M’s relation to his wife W?
explanation: M’s mother‑in‑law is W’s mother. His father’s mother‑in‑law is his father’s wife’s mother, i.e., M’s maternal grandmother. Thus W’s mother equals M’s maternal grandmother, making W a daughter of M’s maternal grandmother – an aunt of M. Therefore M is W’s nephew (and W is M’s aunt).
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: Adam and Beth are brother and sister. Carl and Dana are also brother and sister. Adam marries Dana and Beth marries Carl. Adam and Dana have a son Ethan; Beth and Carl have a daughter Fiona. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relationship between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan’s father Adam and Fiona’s mother Beth are siblings, sharing one set of grandparents. Ethan’s mother Dana and Fiona’s father Carl are siblings, sharing another set of grandparents. Thus Ethan and Fiona share both pairs of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

question: T's paternal grandmother has a brother U. U's daughter V has a son W. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of W to T?
explanation: U is T's great‑uncle (grandparent’s sibling). V, U’s daughter, is T's father's cousin, i.e., T's first cousin. W, V’s son, is the child of T’s first cousin, which makes W T's first cousin once removed. No closer term applies.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: Brothers M and N each marry sisters O and P respectively. M and O have a daughter A; N and P have a son B. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents: M and N share the same father‑mother, and O and P share the same father‑mother. Thus they have two common grandparent pairs, which makes them double first cousins, not merely first cousins.

question: M's mother has exactly one brother, B. M's father has exactly one sister, S. B and S are married and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage), what is the precise relation between M and C?
explanation: B is M’s maternal uncle, S is M’s paternal aunt. Their marriage makes C the child of both an uncle and an aunt of M. C shares both sets of grandparents with M, i.e., both of M’s paternal and maternal grandparents, making C a double first cousin.

question: R’s mother has a brother A and a sister B. A’s daughter is C; B’s son is D. C and D (who are first cousins) marry and have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of E to R?
explanation: R, C and D are all first cousins (same generation, sharing the same pair of grandparents). E is the child of R’s first cousin, which makes E a first cousin once removed to R. No additional qualifying terms apply because the shared ancestors are a single grandparent pair.

question: Q’s mother has exactly one brother, M, and Q’s father has exactly one sister, S. M and S are married and have a single child, P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation of P to Q?
explanation: M is Q’s maternal uncle, making P Q’s first cousin on the mother’s side. S is Q’s paternal aunt, also making P Q’s first cousin on the father’s side. Because the same two individuals are both the maternal uncle and paternal aunt, P shares both sets of grandparents with Q, giving the exact term “double first cousin.”

question: L’s father has exactly one sibling, and L’s mother has exactly one sibling. M is the child of L’s father’s sibling and also the child of L’s mother’s sibling. Assuming monogamy and no inter‑marriage between the two siblings, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between M and L?
explanation: M’s father is L’s paternal uncle and M’s mother is L’s maternal aunt. Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with L, making them double first cousins – the only term that captures the dual shared lineage.

question: John has two children, Mary and Lisa. John’s brother Mark has a son Tom. Tom marries Lisa. Lisa and Tom have a daughter Anna. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Anna’s precise relation to John?
explanation: Anna is the child of John’s daughter (making her John’s grandchild) and also the child of John’s nephew Tom (making her John’s great‑niece). The only precise description acknowledges both links: she is both John’s grandchild and great‑niece.
choices: C) C) Both grandchild and great‑niece (double relation)

question: John and Mary are full siblings. John’s daughter is Emma; Mary’s son is Liam. Emma and Liam marry and have a son Noah. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise term for the relationship between Noah and John’s mother?
explanation: John’s mother is the grandmother of both Emma (through John) and Liam (through Mary). Noah is the child of Emma and Liam, making him the great‑grandchild of John’s mother on either line. The precise term is “great‑grandchild.”
choices: D) No standard direct term (descendant only)

question: M’s mother has exactly one brother, U, whose daughter is N. M’s father has exactly one sister, V, whose son is also N. Assuming no adoption and monogamy, what is the precise kinship term for N in relation to M?
explanation: N is the child of M’s maternal uncle (U) and also the child of M’s paternal aunt (V). Thus N shares both of M’s grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, whose brother is P. N marries Q, who is O’s sister. M and O have a son R; N and Q have a daughter S. Using standard English kinship terms (allowing doubled ancestry), what is the most precise relation between R and S?
explanation: R’s father (M) and S’s mother (N) are siblings, giving them one set of shared grandparents. R’s mother (O) and S’s father (Q) are also siblings, providing a second shared set. Thus R and S share both paternal and maternal grandparents – they are double first cousins.

question: M’s mother has a brother U1 who is married to W1. W1’s sister S is married to M’s father’s brother U2. C1 is the child of U1 & W1, and C2 is the child of U2 & S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation between C1 and C2?
explanation: W1 and S are sisters, so their children C1 and C2 share the same set of grandparents (the parents of W1/S). That makes them first cousins. No other blood link exists between them, so a more specific term (half‑, double‑) does not apply.

question: Eve and Adam are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). Eve’s son Ben and Adam’s daughter Clara each have one child with unrelated partners. What is the most precise standard kinship term for the relationship between Ben’s child and Clara’s child?
explanation: Ben and Clara are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent. Their children therefore share that same grandparent’s descendant as a parent, giving them half‑first‑cousin status. Full first cousins require two shared grandparents, which they lack.

question: M is the son of the sister of P’s mother, and P is the daughter of the brother of M’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation of M to P?
explanation: M’s mother is P’s maternal aunt and M’s father is P’s paternal uncle, so both of M’s parents are siblings of P’s parents. They share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

question: John and Mary are married. John's mother Linda has a brother Paul. Mary's father Robert has a sister Susan. Paul and Susan marry and have a daughter Emma. John and Mary’s only child is Kevin. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is Emma to Kevin?
explanation: Paul is John’s maternal uncle, so Emma is John’s first cousin. Susan is Mary’s paternal aunt, so Emma is also Mary’s first cousin. Thus Emma is a first cousin of both of Kevin’s parents. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed to the next generation, so Emma is Kevin’s first cousin once removed.

question: Father F had a child G with his first wife K. Mother N had a child H with her first husband L. Later F and N married and had a single child M. Thus G and H are each half‑siblings of M but share no parent with each other. G’s child is X and H’s child is Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise blood relationship between X and Y?
explanation: G and H share no common ancestor; they are unrelated half‑siblings of M via different parents. Consequently their children X and Y have no shared blood lineage, so there is no kinship term beyond "no blood relation".

question: X is the child of the only brother of Y’s mother, and also the child of the only brother of Y’s father. There are no other intermarriages in the family. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X’s mother’s brother and father’s brother are two distinct uncles of Y. Their children are first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., they share both sets of grandparents. The precise term is double first cousin.

question: M is the son of the sister of P’s mother, and P is the daughter of the brother of M’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between M and P?
explanation: M’s mother is the sister of P’s mother, making M a first cousin of P on the maternal side. P’s mother is the sister of M’s father’s brother, making P a first cousin of M on the paternal side as well. They share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins.

question: Using standard English kinship terms only (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses): X’s mother has a brother A. X’s father has a sister B. B’s daughter C is married to A. Who is C to X?
explanation: C is X’s first cousin (child of paternal aunt B) and simultaneously X’s aunt‑in‑law (spouse of maternal uncle A). Standard kinship provides separate terms for each role but none that combines them, so the precise relation cannot be expressed uniquely.

question: Let R be a person. R’s mother has exactly one brother, and R’s father has exactly one sister. The child of that brother is called S, and the child of that sister is called T. If we pick either S or T and call that person U, what is U’s exact relationship to R?
explanation: Both S and T are children of R’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt respectively. Each is the child of a parent’s sibling, which by definition is a first cousin to R.

question: John is married to Mary. Mary's sister Anna is married to John's brother Tom. John and Mary have a son Peter; Tom and Anna have a daughter Lily. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the exact relation between Peter and Lily?
explanation: John and Tom are brothers and Mary and Anna are sisters, so Peter and Lily share both sets of grandparents. The precise term for cousins who share all grandparents is double first cousins.

question: Tom’s mother has a brother Alan, whose daughter is Claire. Tom’s father has a sister Beth, whose son is David. Claire and David marry and have a child Emma. What is Emma’s precise relation to Tom, using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Alan is Tom’s maternal uncle, so Claire is Tom’s first cousin. Beth is Tom’s paternal aunt, so David is also Tom’s first cousin. Emma is the child of Tom’s first cousin, making her Tom’s first cousin once removed. No other blood link exists between Claire and David, so no doubling occurs.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: P is married to Q. Q’s mother has a brother R. R’s daughter is S. S’s husband is T. Using standard English kinship terms (blood and immediate in‑law only), what is T to P?
explanation: R is Q’s maternal uncle, so S is Q’s first cousin. T is the spouse of that cousin. Standard terminology has no direct term for the spouse of a cousin; the relationship exists only as an affinal chain.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: X and Y are siblings. X marries B, and Y marries A. A and B are also siblings. X and B have a son C; Y and A have a daughter D. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: X and Y share the same parents, as do A and B. C is child of X & B; D is child of Y & A. Thus C and D share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the exact term.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John marries Anna; Mary marries Ben. John and Anna have a son Carl. Mary and Ben have a daughter Dana. Carl and Dana marry and have a child Eve. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between John and Eve?
explanation: John is Carl's father, so he is Eve's paternal grandfather. He is also Mary’s brother, making him Dana's maternal uncle, thus Eve's maternal great‑uncle. Holding both roles simultaneously, no single standard kin term covers this combined relationship; option C is correct.
choices: C) C) No standard single kin term (both grandfather and great‑uncle)
D) D) First cousin twice removed

question: M and N are siblings. M marries X and N marries Y, where X and Y are also siblings. M and X have a child A; N and Y have a child B. A and B marry each other. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring any legal restrictions), what is the most precise term for the relationship between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents (their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters), so they are double first cousins. No other term conveys the double shared ancestry.
choices: D) D) No blood relation (spouses only)

question: Adam and Ben are brothers. Adam first marries Clara and they have a daughter Lily. After Clara dies, Adam marries Diana. Ben marries Diana's sister Eva, and they have a son Mark. What is the precise blood relation between Lily and Mark?
explanation: Lily’s father Adam and Mark’s father Ben are brothers, giving Lily and Mark the same set of paternal grandparents. Their mothers are unrelated, so there is no half‑relationship. Sharing both paternal grandparents makes them first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. P and Q are another pair of siblings. M marries P, N marries Q. Their children are X (child of M‑P) and Y (child of N‑Q). Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of P/Q. Hence they are first cousins on two distinct lines, i.e., double first cousins, the most exact term.

question: M and N are siblings. M’s child A marries N’s child B, and they have a child C. Using only standard English kinship terms (no “step‑” or “in‑law”), what is C’s relation to N?
explanation: N is aunt/uncle of A and also of B. The child of a niece or nephew is a grandniece/grandnephew. Since C is the child of both A and B, who are each N’s niece/nephew, C is N’s grandniece (if female) or grandnephew (if male). No closer term exists.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No direct kin term

question: Anna is the child of Paul and Mary. Paul has a sister Sarah. Mary’s mother is Linda, whose brother is George. Sarah marries George, and they have a son Kevin. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation between Anna and Kevin?
explanation: Anna’s paternal grandparents are Sarah’s parents; her maternal grandparents are Linda’s parents. Kevin’s paternal grandparents are the same as Anna’s maternal grandparents, and his maternal grandparents are Anna’s paternal grandparents. Thus they share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, B is married to C. B has exactly one sibling, and C has exactly one sibling. A is the child of B's sibling and also the child of C's sibling. What is A's relation to B?
explanation: A is the child of B's only sibling, making A B's niece or nephew. The fact that A is also the child of C's sibling is consistent because B and C are spouses; it does not change the direct blood relation between A and B.

question: Let X’s mother be Y. Y’s brother is Z. Z’s daughter is W. W’s son is V. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, in‑law terms limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is V’s precise relation to X?
explanation: Z is X’s maternal uncle, making W X’s first cousin. V, as W’s son, is one generation below that cousin, i.e., X’s first cousin once removed. No other listed term fits this exact generational offset.

question: M and N are brother and sister. P and Q are also brother and sister. M marries P and N marries Q. Their only children, X (child of M & P) and Y (child of N & Q), have no other relatives. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because each pair of parents are siblings on both sides. This makes them double first cousins, the exact term for cousins who have two common grandparent pairs.

question: M’s mother has a brother N. N’s son O has a daughter P. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relationship between M and P?
explanation: N is M’s maternal uncle; his son O is M’s first cousin. O’s daughter P is one generation younger than O, so she is M’s first cousin once removed. No other kin term fits more precisely.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John has a daughter Lisa. Mary has a son Peter. Peter marries Lisa and they have a child Anna. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, no in‑law), what is the most precise term for the relationship between Mary and Anna?
explanation: Through Peter, Anna is Mary's granddaughter. Through Lisa, Anna is Mary's grandniece. Standard kinship provides separate terms for each, but none that simultaneously captures both roles. Hence the precise relationship cannot be uniquely expressed with a single standard term.

question: John married two women, W1 and W2. With W1 he had a daughter Alice; with W2 he had a daughter Beth. Alice later had a son Carl. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relation of Beth to Carl?
explanation: Alice and Beth share only their father, making them half‑sisters. Beth is therefore the half‑sister of Carl’s mother, which makes Beth Carl’s half‑aunt—the exact term required.

question: John has a sister Mary and a brother David. Mary’s son Tom marries Sarah, who is David’s daughter. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise blood relation between Tom and Sarah?
explanation: Mary and David are siblings, so their children Tom and Sarah are the children of siblings. The exact term for such a pair is "first cousins".

question: M is the only child of L. L’s sister N is married to O. O’s brother P is married to Q, who is the mother of R. R’s father is S, and S is the brother of L. What is R’s precise relation to M using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: L and S are siblings, so S is M’s maternal uncle. R is the child of S, making R the child of M’s uncle. Therefore R is M’s first cousin. No other blood links alter this relationship.

question: A and B are siblings. A’s child is C; B’s child is D. C’s child is E; D’s child is F. E’s child is G. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of G to F?
explanation: A and B are siblings, so C and D are first cousins. E (child of C) and D are first cousins once removed; likewise F (child of D) and C are first cousins once removed. E and F are second cousins. G, as E’s child, is one generation below a second cousin of F, making G a second cousin once removed to F.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed
B) B) Second cousin once removed
D) D) No standard term (relation not determinable)

question: R is married to S. S’s mother is M. M’s brother is U. U’s daughter is V. V is married to W, and W’s sister is T. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is T’s relation to R?
explanation: M is R’s mother‑in‑law; her brother U is R’s uncle‑in‑law. V, U’s daughter, is S’s first cousin, which falls outside the allowed in‑law scope. W and T are further affinal links beyond the defined categories, so no standard direct kin term exists between R and T.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: Adam's mother Linda has a brother Carl, whose daughter is Emma. Adam's father Mark has a sister Nora, whose son is Leo. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only), what is the most precise description of the relationship between Emma and Leo?
explanation: Emma is Adam's maternal first cousin; Leo is Adam's paternal first cousin. They share no common ancestor, only the mutual cousin Adam, who is not an ancestor of either. Standard kinship terms cover blood links, so there is no direct term for their relation.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (they are not blood relatives)

question: John and Mary are brother and sister. John marries Anna, whose only sibling is Peter. Mary marries Peter. John and Anna have a child X; Mary and Peter have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two couples where each spouse is the sibling of the other spouse. They share both sets of grandparents, so they are double first cousins – the only term that reflects the doubled shared ancestry.

question: M is married to N. N’s sister is O, who is married to P. P’s brother is Q. Q is the father of R, and R is married to S. S’s mother is T, who is the sister of M. What is Q’s relation to S?
explanation: R is S’s spouse, making Q R’s father and therefore S’s father‑in‑law. No other blood or affinal link between Q and S changes this. Hence the precise standard term is father‑in‑law.

question: Y has a mother and a father. X is the son of the only brother of Y’s mother. Z is the daughter of the only sister of Y’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between X and Z?
explanation: The only brother of Y’s mother is Y’s maternal uncle; his son X is Y’s first cousin. The only sister of Y’s father is Y’s paternal aunt; her daughter Z is also Y’s first cousin. Therefore X and Z, both being children of a parent’s sibling, are first cousins to each other.

question: M and N are half‑siblings (they share only one parent). M has a child X and N has a child Y. Apart from this, there are no other marriages or adoptions. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share a single grandparent, so X and Y each inherit that one grandparent. They therefore share exactly one grandparent, which makes them half‑first cousins. Full first cousins would share both grandparents, which is not the case here.

question: Emma’s father and Liam’s mother are siblings, and Emma’s mother and Liam’s father are also siblings. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Emma and Liam?
explanation: Emma and Liam share both sets of grandparents because each of their parents are siblings on both sides. This makes them double first cousins, the exact term for such a relationship.

question: John and Mary are siblings. Mary marries Peter. Peter's sister is Linda, who has a son Kevin. John has a daughter Susan, and Susan marries Kevin. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Susan's relation to Linda?
explanation: Susan is married to Kevin, Linda’s son; thus Susan is Linda’s daughter‑in‑law. She is not a blood niece or cousin, and a relation does exist.

question: R’s mother has a brother M, and R’s father has a sister S. M’s daughter is A; S’s son is B. A and B marry and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of C to R?
explanation: A is R’s maternal first cousin (child of R’s maternal uncle). B is R’s paternal first cousin (child of R’s paternal aunt). C is the child of two of R’s first cousins, so C is one generation below a first cousin. The exact term is “first cousin once removed.”
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: L has one sister and one brother. The only son of L’s sister marries and has a single child M. Independently, the only daughter of L’s brother also marries and has a single child M (the same person). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the exact relation of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s nephew (the son of L’s sister) and also the child of L’s niece (the daughter of L’s brother). Both describe the same person, so M is the child of L’s sibling’s child – i.e., L’s grandniece – but through two independent lines, making her a double grandniece. Hence option C is the precise term.

question: M is the father of N and O (who are siblings). N is married to P. P's sister Q is married to R, who is O's son. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is Q's relation to N?
explanation: Q is the sister of N's spouse, making her N's sister‑in‑law. Though Q is also the spouse of N's nephew, the term for that is niece‑in‑law, which is less direct than the sibling‑in‑law connection. The most precise standard term is therefore sister‑in‑law.

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father. N’s mother is the sister of O’s father. O’s mother is the sister of P’s father. All eight individuals are distinct and there are no other marriages among them. What is the precise blood relation between M and P?
explanation: M is first cousin to N via their parents, N is first cousin to O, and O is first cousin to P. Each cousin link uses a different pair of siblings, so M and P share no common ancestor. Hence they are not blood‑related at all; no standard kin term applies.
choices: A) No blood relation (they are not related)

question: A has a son B from his first marriage. Later A marries C, who already has a daughter D from a previous marriage. B and D marry each other and have a child E. What is the most precise kinship term for the relationship between E and C?
explanation: C is mother of D (blood) and step‑mother of B. B and D, being step‑siblings, have child E. Through D, E is C’s biological grandchild; through B, E is C’s step‑grandchild. Hence the precise description is that E is both a grandchild and a step‑grandchild of C.
choices: C) C) No recognized kinship term
D) D) Both a grandchild (by blood) and a step‑grandchild

question: In a family with no adoptions and monogamous marriages, L has exactly one child, a daughter D. L's sister S also has exactly one child, a son S1. D’s child is M. S1’s child is N. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: D and S1 are first cousins (children of siblings L and S). Their children M and N are therefore second cousins, sharing a pair of great‑grandparents. No closer or more distant term applies.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a son P. N has a daughter Q. P and Q marry and have a child R. What is the precise kinship term for R with respect to M’s mother?
explanation: M’s mother is the grandmother of both P and Q. Their child R is one generation further, making R her great‑grandchild through either line. No other standard term applies.

question: Alan is the sole child of his mother. His mother’s brother is Brian. Brian’s daughter Clara has a son Daniel. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Daniel’s relation to Alan?
explanation: Brian is Alan’s maternal uncle, so Clara is Alan’s first cousin. Daniel, being Clara’s son, is one generation below Alan’s cousin, making him Alan’s first cousin once removed.

question: Alan's mother Beth has a brother Carl. Carl's daughter Dana is Alan's maternal first cousin. Alan's father George has a sister Fiona; Fiona's son Ethan is Alan's paternal first cousin. Dana and Ethan marry and have a son Henry. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation between Alan and Henry?
explanation: Henry is the child of Dana, Alan's maternal first cousin, making Henry Alan's first cousin once removed. The same holds via Ethan, Alan's paternal first cousin, but the term does not change. Thus the exact relationship is first cousin once removed.

question: John’s mother has a brother who married John’s father’s sister. Their only child is Lisa. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the most precise blood relationship between John and Lisa?
explanation: John’s mother’s brother is his maternal uncle; John’s father’s sister is his paternal aunt. Their child Lisa is the child of both a maternal uncle and a paternal aunt, making her John’s double first cousin – sharing both sets of grandparents.

question: M is married to N. N's sister O is married to P. P's brother Q is married to R, who is the daughter of M's brother S. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Q to O?
explanation: O's spouse is P. Q is P's brother, making Q O's brother‑in‑law by the definition of a spouse's sibling. The extra details about R and S do not affect this direct in‑law link.

question: W is a woman who is simultaneously the sister of N’s father and the aunt of N’s mother. M is the child of W. What is the exact kinship term for M’s relation to N, using standard English blood‑relationship terminology?
explanation: W being the sister of N’s father makes her N’s paternal aunt; being the aunt of N’s mother makes her N’s maternal aunt as well. In either case, W’s child M is N’s first cousin. The double‑aunt role does not change the degree, so the precise term is simply “first cousin.”

question: John’s mother is the sister of Mary’s father, and Mary’s mother is the sister of John’s father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise kinship term for the relationship between John and Mary using standard English kinship terminology (ignoring in‑law terms)?
explanation: John and Mary share both sets of grandparents, since each is the child of a sibling of the other's parent. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: Alex is married to Blake. Blake’s mother, Catherine, has a brother David. David is married to Fiona, who is the sister of Emma. Emma is the mother of George. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is George’s relation to Alex?
explanation: David is Blake’s maternal uncle (blood). His wife Fiona is Blake’s aunt‑in‑law. Fiona’s sister Emma is therefore also Blake’s aunt‑in‑law, making Emma’s child George a niece‑in‑law to Blake and, by marriage, to Alex. No blood link exists.

question: M is the mother of N and O. N is married to P. P’s sister Q is married to R, who is the son of O. What is the precise kinship term (using standard English kinship, with in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses) for the relation of Q to N?
explanation: O is N’s sibling, so R (O’s son) is N’s nephew. Q is married to R, making her the spouse of N’s nephew. The standard term for a spouse of a nephew/niece is "niece‑in‑law" (or "nephew‑in‑law").

question: M is the child of a woman who is the sister of N’s father, and also the child of a man who is the brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father, so M and N share N’s paternal grandparents as first cousins. M’s father is the brother of N’s mother, so they also share N’s maternal grandparents as first cousins. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries P and N marries Q, where P and Q are also siblings. M and P have a child X; N and Q have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. Therefore they are double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled ancestry.

question: Emma's father is the brother of Lucas's mother, and Emma's mother is the sister of Lucas's father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term between Emma and Lucas?
explanation: Emma’s father is sibling of Lucas’s mother, so they share maternal grandparents. Emma’s mother is sibling of Lucas’s father, so they share paternal grandparents. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes Emma and Lucas double first cousins, the most specific standard term.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O; N has a son P. O marries Q, who is the brother of P’s wife R. O and Q have a child S. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation between S and R?
explanation: R is the sister of Q, who is S’s father, making R S’s aunt‑in‑law (the father’s sister‑in‑law). No blood link exists, and the only standard term for this relationship is "aunt‑in‑law".

question: John is married to Mary. Mary’s brother is Tom. Tom is married to Lisa. Lisa’s mother, Susan, is also the mother of Emma, who is John’s sister. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is Emma’s relation to Tom?
explanation: Lisa is Tom’s wife, making Lisa’s siblings Tom’s sisters‑in‑law. Emma is Lisa’s sister (both daughters of Susan). Therefore Emma is Tom’s sister‑in‑law. No blood link exists, and other options (aunt, cousin, no term) do not fit.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation

question: M is the mother of N. N is married to O. O's sister is P, who is the mother of Q. Q is married to R, and R is the child of S. S is the brother of M. What is R's precise kinship term to M using standard English blood‑relation terminology?
explanation: S is M's brother, making S the uncle of N. R is S's child, so R is the child of M's brother, i.e., M's nephew or niece. All other links are through marriage and do not affect the blood relation.

question: Alice’s mother has exactly one brother, and Alice’s father has exactly one sister. Both of these siblings have a single child, and it is the same person, Sam. Using standard English kinship terms (without ignoring doubled ancestry), what is Sam to Alice?
explanation: Sam is the child of Alice’s maternal uncle and also the child of her paternal aunt. They share both sets of grandparents, so Sam and Alice are first cousins through both parental lines – a double first cousin.

question: L’s mother has a sister named S, and L’s father has a brother named B. A child, M, is simultaneously the child of S and also the child of B (through separate marriages). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s precise relationship to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s maternal aunt (S) and also the child of L’s paternal uncle (B). In either case M is the child of a parent’s sibling, which is the definition of a first cousin. The double link does not change the basic term.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O; N has a son P. O and P marry and have a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relationship of Q to N?
explanation: Q is the child of N’s son P, making Q N’s grandchild. Q is also the child of N’s niece O, so Q is N’s great‑niece. The single term that captures both links is “grandchild and great‑niece (double relationship).”

question: John’s mother Mary has a brother Peter. John’s father Robert has a sister Susan. Peter is married to Susan. Using standard English kinship terms (blood and in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the most precise term for Peter’s relation to John?
explanation: Peter is Mary’s brother, so he is John’s maternal uncle by blood. He is also Susan’s husband; Susan is Robert’s sister, making Peter John’s paternal uncle‑in‑law. Since the blood relationship already defines him as an uncle, the most precise standard term is simply “uncle”.

question: Y’s father has a sister (Y’s paternal aunt). That aunt has exactly one child, who in turn has a child named X. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: The aunt is Y’s paternal aunt, so her only child is Y’s first cousin. X is the child of that first cousin, placing X one generation below Y’s cousin. Hence X is Y’s first cousin once removed.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, N marries P, and O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y’s fathers are brothers (M and N) and their mothers are sisters (O and P). Thus they share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John marries Anna. Anna’s mother, Susan, has a sister named Lisa. Mary’s brother Peter (who is also John’s brother) is married to Lisa. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Lisa to John?
explanation: John’s brother Peter is married to Lisa, making Lisa his sister‑in‑law. Additionally, Lisa is Susan’s sister, i.e., the sister of John’s mother‑in‑law. The only term covering a spouse’s parent’s sibling is “aunt‑in‑law”. Hence Lisa is John’s aunt‑in‑law.

question: John’s sister Mary marries Tom, who is the brother of John’s wife Linda. John and Linda have a daughter Emma. Mary and Tom have a son Alex. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the most precise relation between Emma and Alex?
explanation: Emma is child of John (brother of Mary) and Linda (sister of Tom). Alex is child of Mary and Tom. Thus Emma and Alex are children of siblings on both paternal and maternal sides, sharing both sets of grandparents. The exact term is “double first cousins.”

question: R’s mother has a brother A. A is married to B. B’s sister C is married to D, who is R’s father’s brother. C and D have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only, in‑law terms limited to spouse), what is E’s precise relation to R?
explanation: D is R’s paternal uncle by blood, so his child E is R’s first cousin regardless of C’s non‑blood status. The maternal‑side aunt‑in‑law B and her sister C do not affect the blood link. Hence the exact term is "first cousin".

question: In a family with monogamy and no adoption, X's mother has exactly one brother, and X's father has exactly one sister. The brother of X's mother has a daughter Y. The sister of X's father has a son Z. What is the precise kinship relation between Y and Z?
explanation: Y is the child of X's maternal uncle, Z is the child of X's paternal aunt. The uncle and aunt are unrelated, so Y and Z share no common ancestor. Thus there is no standard blood kinship term between them—they are unrelated.

question: Brother A and sister B are full siblings. A marries C, whose brother is D. B marries D’s sister E. A and C have a child X; B and E have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: A and B share both parents; C and D share both parents. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents (the parents of A/B and the parents of C/D). They are first cousins through two independent parental lines, i.e., double first cousins. No other term is more precise.

question: L and K are siblings. L has a daughter M. K is married to P, and they have a son Q. M and Q marry each other. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the precise relation between L and P?

question: R’s mother has a brother U, whose daughter is V. R’s father has a sister W, whose son is X. V and X marry and have a child Z. explanation: V is R’s maternal first cousin; X is R’s paternal first cousin. Their child Z is one generation below R’s cousins, making Z a first cousin once removed on both the maternal and paternal sides. The precise term is “first cousin once removed.”

question: Ethan’s father has a sister who has exactly one child, Maya. Maya has exactly one child, Noah. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is Noah’s precise relation to Ethan?
explanation: Ethan’s paternal aunt’s child Maya is Ethan’s first cousin. Maya’s child Noah is one generation below Maya, making Noah Ethan’s first cousin once removed.

question: R's mother has exactly one brother, who has a daughter S. R's father has exactly one sister, who has a son T. S and T marry and have a child U. What is U's relation to R?
explanation: S is R's maternal first cousin; T is R's paternal first cousin. Their child U is one generation below each cousin, so U is R's first cousin once removed on both sides. The precise term is 'first cousin once removed.'

question: John and Mark are brothers. John marries Alice; Mark marries Beth, where Alice and Beth are sisters (no other blood relations exist). John and Alice have a daughter Emma; Mark and Beth have a son Liam. What is the most precise standard kinship term for Emma and Liam?
explanation: Emma and Liam share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. Hence they are double first cousins, a distinct term from ordinary first cousins.

question: Anna’s mother has a brother Mark. Anna’s father has a sister Lily. Mark’s daughter Clara and Lily’s son Daniel marry each other. Their child, Ethan, is born. What is Ethan’s precise kinship term to Anna using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Mark is Anna’s maternal uncle, so Clara is Anna’s first cousin. Lily is Anna’s paternal aunt, so Daniel is also Anna’s first cousin. Ethan is the child of Anna’s first cousin (on either side), making him Anna’s first cousin once removed. No other blood link changes this relation.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M and O have a child X; N and P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father M and Y’s father N are brothers, and X’s mother O and Y’s mother P are sisters. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, giving them the exact term “double first cousins.”

question: T is the child of the only child of H’s brother, and also the child of H’s sister’s only child. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is T’s precise relation to H?
explanation: H’s brother’s only child is H’s niece/nephew; that child’s child is H’s grand‑niece/nephew. question: In a family with monogamy and no adoption, X is the son of the sister of Y’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is X to Y?
explanation: Y’s mother’s sister is Y’s maternal aunt. The son of that aunt is Y’s first cousin. No other blood link is involved, so the precise term is “first cousin.”

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O and N marries P, where O and P are also siblings. M + O have a child X; N + P have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?

question: John’s mother has a brother Mike, whose daughter is Anna. John’s father has a sister Laura, whose son is Ben. Anna and Ben marry and have a child Sam. What is Sam’s relation to John?
explanation: Anna is John’s maternal first cousin, Ben his paternal first cousin. Sam, being the child of a first cousin on each side, is John’s first cousin once removed (the same term from both lines).

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O; N has a son P. O and P marry and have a child Q. What is the precise blood‑relationship term for Q with respect to M’s mother?

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N is married to W and they have a son P. O and P marry each other and have a child Q. question: Tom and Sam are brothers. Lily and Nora are sisters. Tom marries Lily and they have a daughter Alice. Sam marries Nora and they have a son Brian. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Alice and Brian?
explanation: Alice and Brian share both sets of grandparents (Tom and Sam’s parents, and Lily and Nora’s parents). Hence they are first cousins with doubled ancestry, i.e., double first cousins, the exact term required.

question: Man X’s mother is the sister of Woman Y’s father, and X’s father is the brother of Y’s mother. Assuming monogamy, no adoptions, and that all siblings are full siblings, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relationship between X and Y?

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let N be a person. N’s mother has exactly one sibling (an aunt/uncle) and N’s father also has exactly one sibling (an aunt/uncle).
